Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Banihal, Oct 12: Aspirants from Ramban district have urged the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB) and the district administration to establish examination centres within the district for upcoming recruitment tests, citing the financial burden and travel-related hardships caused by allotment of centres in distant locations.
Several recruitment examinations, including those for Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA), Sub-Inspector (SI), Police Constable and other posts, are expected to be held in November–December 2026, prompting aspirants to seek timely intervention from the authorities.
Candidates said they are often allotted centres in Jammu, Udhampur, Samba, Srinagar, Budgam and other districts, forcing them to spend additional money on transportation, accommodation and food.
“We are already spending considerable time and money preparing for competitive examinations. Travelling to distant districts adds to our expenses, particularly for candidates from economically weaker families,” aspirant youth said.
They added that Ramban’s mountainous terrain, difficult road conditions and long travel distances make the journey especially challenging for candidates from remote areas, who may have to travel a day before the examination.
The aspirants have appealed to JKSSB to establish suitable examination centres in Ramban and urged Deputy Commissioner Ramban to take up the matter with the concerned authorities ahead of the forthcoming recruitment tests.
“Our demand is for accessible examination facilities, not any relaxation in recruitment standards. Local centres would reduce unnecessary expenditure and help candidates compete on equal terms, irrespective of their financial background,” the candidates said.
The aspirants expressed hope that the authorities would consider their demand before the November–December examination schedule, ensuring that financial constraints and geographical challenges do not become additional hurdles for the district’s unemployed youth.

- On, Oct. 8, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed reports that the U.S. military was planning to livestream the U.S. Army firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, which is currently set for Dec. 3.
- A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 during a shooting at Fort Hood in Texas.

On Oct. 8, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed (archived) reports that the U.S. military was planning to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, which is currently set for Dec. 3.
A military jury sentenced Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, to death in 2013 after it found him guilty of killing 13 people and injuring 30 more during a shooting rampage at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas in 2009. U.S. President Donald Trump approved (archived) Hasan's death sentence on Oct. 2, clearing the path for his execution.
On Oct. 8, Hegseth shared an X post by CBS News that read:
The U.S. military plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, when he faces a firing squad on Dec. 3, a Pentagon official said.
Hegseth wrote, "Correct."
One day later, on Oct. 9, the Associated Press reported that Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution. "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he reportedly said.
Following Hegseth's confirmation, discussion abounded online about whether executing Hasan in such a public manner was legal (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the legality of the planned livestream.
The military justice system, which is separate from the civilian justice systems in the U.S., carried out Hasan's trial and sentencing in 2013. On Oct. 5, Hegseth's assistant secretary for public affairs Sean Parnell wrote on X (archived) that the Army's firing squad would execute Hasan, meaning his execution would be governed by Army regulations.
At the time of this writing, the U.S. Army did not have regulations explicitly allowing it to livestream an execution. Rather, Army Regulation 190–55, which covers procedures for military executions, included requirements that would likely hinder the Army's ability to provide a public livestream.
Gary Barthel, a former U.S. Marine Corps officer and managing partner at the Military Law Center, told Snopes on Oct. 9 that if the Army wanted to legally livestream Hasan's execution, officials would have to either seek an exemption to regulation 190-55 from the Office of the Provost Marshal General as laid out in the regulation itself or amend the existing regulation to allow livestreaming. 
We contacted the Department of the Defense to ask if it was planning to do either of these things and await a reply.
Because the legality of livestreaming Hasan's execution was potentially subject to change, we leave this claim unrated.
What Army regulation says
Chapter 2-5 of regulation 190-55 lists who may and may not witness a military execution. According to the chapter, no person younger than 18 years old may witness an execution and the Army must approve the list of witnesses beforehand.
Those two stipulations could make it difficult for the Army to provide a public livestream without violating its own regulations because it would have to vet the audience's age. Hosting a truly public livestream would make it impossible to approve a list of "witnesses" ahead of the execution because people might log in to watch on the day without registering beforehand.
Barthel told Snopes via phone on Oct. 9:
The Army is required to follow its regulations. If the Army wants to stream this execution they need to change the regulations to allow it. And, either way, I would anticipate that there is going to be some efforts to stop it.
Barthel said that Hasan's defense team could still ask a civilian court to stop the execution and live stream by filing a habeas corpus petition. Such a petition allows a detainee to challenge their detention in court.
Would public execution be 'cruel and unusual punishment'?
Daniel Maurer, an associate professor at the Claude W. Pettit College of Law at Ohio Northern University, told Snopes that livestreaming Hasan's execution could raise constitutional concerns that would ultimately play out in court.
Hasan's defense could bring up such constitutional concerns as part of a habeas petition. Maurer said via email on Oct. 9 that Hasan's defense could argue that being executed on livestream amounted to "cruel and unusual punishment," which is banned by the U.S. Constitution's 8th Amendment. Maurer wrote (links ours):
The remaining legal issue is maybe more complicated and would need courts to resolve it: does such a practice violate Hasan's 8th Amendment protection from "cruel and unusual punishments?" - this protection is also stated in the UCMJ, article 55, and Army Regulation 190-47 ("The Army Corrections System") so it applies to prisoners already confined, not just defendants at court-martial sentencing.
In order to establish whether livestreaming Hasan's execution amounted to cruel and unusual punishment, the courts might apply the "Evolving Standard" test, according to Maurer. The test allows courts to consider whether a punishment is cruel and unusual under current societal standards, rather than according to standards at the time the Constitution was written.
Cornell Law School's Legal Information Library wrote that "in the context of capital punishment, the Court has generally viewed the Eighth Amendment to prohibit punishments that 'involve the unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain.'"
Though livestreaming may not inflict "unnecessary and wanton" pain, Maurer said there are other factors at play:
Given that federal law prohibits photographic or other visual or audio recording of an execution of any other civilian federal prisoner, this is strong evidence that our own federal government (of which the DoD is of course a part) would consider it to be "cruel and unusual," and thus would be an 8th Amendment violation.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, called the decision to livestream Hasan's execution "sick-making" when speaking to Snopes on Oct. 9. He previously told DRM News that a habeas petition could postpone Hasan's execution past the end of the Trump administration as it progressed through the civilian court system. That means Hasan's execution and any potential livestream could be halted by an administration without "the same penchant for executions," Fidell reportedly told the Associated Press.
It was unclear whether Hasan would file a habeas petition. The Associated Press reported that Hasan had begun his 2013 trial by firing his lawyers and telling jurors that he was the gunman in the 2009 shooting. The outlet reported that this move "convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan's only goal was to get a death sentence." It remained unclear whether Hasan's goal remained the same in 2026.
The nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center wrote that Hasan's execution would be the first military execution in the U.S. since 1961.
The Washington Post, citing the center, reported that the last high-profile public execution of any type in the U.S. took place in 1936. Another public execution took place the year after.
For further reading, Snopes compiled 17 claims about the death penalty that we've investigated over the years.

Arab political parties could hold the key to government formation in Israel’s upcoming elections, with opinion polls suggesting that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition may secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. A poll of polls published by The Jerusalem Post puts the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett level with Netanyahu’s bloc at 54 seats each, while Arab parties are projected to win eight seats. A separate survey by Israel’s Channel 12 also projects 54 seats for the opposition bloc, 49 for Netanyahu’s coalition and eight for Arab parties. Meanwhile, a poll published by Maariv gives both Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition 52 seats each, with Arab parties projected to win 12 seats. Yoaz Hendel’s Reserve Party is forecast to secure another four seats, without committing to either camp. Israel’s Knesset has 120 seats, and a government needs the support of at least 61 lawmakers. If the main blocs remain short of a majority, Arab parties could become crucial to determining who forms the next government. The projections suggest that support from Arab lawmakers could help the Jewish opposition assemble a parliamentary majority and replace Netanyahu. However, the prospect of Arab parties formally joining a government remains politically contentious. Yousef Jabareen of the Joint List has said his party would use all available means to replace Netanyahu, while ruling out formally joining the opposition alliance led by Eisenkot, Lapid and Bennett. “After the election, we'll impose our conditions on any political constellation in Israel. We have full freedom of action, with no limits, to replace the Netanyahu government, and we will use all the tools at our disposal,” Jabareen said, as per The Times of Israel. His remarks indicate that Arab parties may be willing to support an alternative government without necessarily becoming formal members of the governing coalition. However, most leaders of the Jewish opposition parties have rejected cooperation with Arab lawmakers to form an alternative government, complicating the path to a parliamentary majority. The Maariv survey offers a more detailed breakdown of the projected seat distribution. Netanyahu’s bloc is forecast to win 52 seats, including 20 for his Likud party, eight for Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, seven each for United Torah Judaism and Shas, six for Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, and four for Ofer Winter’s Amcha Israel. The Jewish opposition is also projected to win 52 seats. Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is forecast to secure 21 seats, followed by Naftali Bennett’s Together party with 13, and Yair Golan’s Democrats and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu with nine seats each. Arab parties are projected to win 12 seats, with the Joint List led by Jabareen securing seven and Mansour Abbas’s United Arab List winning five. Hendel’s Reserve Party is forecast to take four seats but has not declared which bloc it would support. Israel has previously seen an Arab party play a pivotal role in forming a government. In 2021, Mansour Abbas’s United Arab List joined the coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, helping end Netanyahu’s 12-year stretch as prime minister. The arrangement was significant because an Arab party became a formal participant in an Israeli governing coalition. The coalition, however, was ideologically diverse and faced disagreements over contentious policy issues. It eventually collapsed, paving the way for elections in 2022. Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as the largest party, and he returned to power with the support of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. Despite their potential parliamentary influence, Arab parties face considerable public opposition to formal participation in the next government, according to Anadolu Agency. The Maariv poll found that 59% of respondents opposed an Arab party joining the government after the election, while 36% supported the idea and 5% were undecided. The survey found a different response to the participation of ultra-Orthodox Haredi parties: 53% supported their inclusion in the next government, 41% opposed it and 6% were undecided. The upcoming election is the first since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which triggered the war in Gaza and contributed to a wider regional conflict. The Maariv survey also found that 46% of respondents preferred former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot over Netanyahu as prime minister in a direct contest, compared with 40% who preferred Netanyahu. Fourteen per cent did not give a clear answer. When respondents were asked to choose among several candidates, Netanyahu received 38%, followed by Eisenkot at 24% and Bennett at 14%. Other candidates received less than 10% each. Israelis do not directly elect their prime minister. The position goes to the leader who can form a government backed by a parliamentary majority. Why we remember: One student's journey into memory
SAN JOSE, Calif. — Amit Biligiri, a junior at Evergreen Valley High School in San Jose, Calif., sits on a big, right-angle couch in his living room alongside his mom, Kalyani Urs. They're recounting the story of a fight they've often had — that every teenager has with their parents.
Amit says he's often up late, and his mom, who tends to work late, "would be mad at me and say, 'Hey Amit, why are you going to sleep so late?'"
Urs laughs. Getting Amit to go to sleep, she says, has been "a constant battle."
"I was like, 'I'm not really sleepy,'" Amit remembers telling her. "And I looked into this, and I found out that the sleep cycle for teenagers is actually delayed by a few hours. And that means that teenagers — it's healthier for them to sleep later and then also wake up later."
Still, Urs remembers telling her son: "You need more sleep, you're forgetting things."
"I keep asking you, 'Did you submit this? Did you submit that?' You forget. And so it clearly shows your memory is affected," Urs remembers telling Amit.
But recently, her son surprised her. He said, "I remember when I had fries with Scooter Muttha."
The man known as Scooter Muttha is Amit's great-grandfather — Urs' grandfather — who died many years ago. Urs was raised by her grandparents, and the man remains a beloved figure in their family. Amit's point to his mother that day was, if he is so forgetful, why does he still vividly remember such a small moment: being 6 and sharing fries with Scooter Muttha at a Burger King in Bangalore?
Urs didn't know what to say. Memory is a mysterious thing.
In fact, this debate got Amit thinking: How does memory work? And Urs, an avid NPR listener, encouraged him to explore the question for NPR's annual Student Podcast Challenge.
Good thing she did, and he did. This year, some 1,500 students competed in the eighth year of the annual competition, and Amit's What Happens to Memories won the top prize.
The podcast
"There were entire weeks of my life I barely remember," so begins Amit's winning podcast. "What I ate for lunch last Monday, what assignments I turned in, what someone said to me in the hallway three Tuesdays ago."
As a busy 16-year-old, Amit says in the podcast, he was struck by how much of his daily life simply disappears from his memory. He was also intrigued by the moments that do last.
Like being 6 years old in a bright Burger King in India. "I'm sitting across from Scooter Muttha, as I fondly call my great-grandpa. He's 87. We are both wearing flimsy gold paper crowns and we're sharing a plate of french fries. Just two kings eating fast food."
An old photo captures the two kings, one at the beginning of his life, the other nearing the end of his. But Amit didn't know his father had taken the picture until he began working on his podcast.
This memory has outlasted so many others, Amit says, even though nothing really happens.
"I don't remember what we talked about, but I remember the salt on the fries, the energy of the room and the way his crown sat slightly crooked on his head." Amit says in the podcast that he started wondering, "Why does my brain let go of a math lecture from yesterday but hold onto a paper crown from a decade ago?"
In his seven-minute audio story, Amit offers a few different answers. "It turns out, memory isn't a filing cabinet. It's more like a construction site. And the foreman of that site is the amygdala."
It's during sleep that our brains clean up that construction site, saving some memories and throwing out others. So his mom was right: Without enough sleep, the cleaning crew can't do its job. It also doesn't help, Amit says, that teens often let phones muddy their memory-making.
"When we experience life through a screen, hunting for the right filter, the perfect caption, we experience it halfway: half-online, half-distracted, half-present. And emotion is exactly what gives memories a better chance of sticking."
As an example, Amit says in his podcast, he's spent time volunteering in a senior living community, and many of the people he's met there don't remember or talk about the big events of their lives. Instead they cherish memories of intense feeling. Like Amit's memory of being 6 in a Burger King and feeling loved unconditionally by his great-grandfather.
"Science can explain the neurons and the glymphatic system, but it doesn't fully explain why, years later, seeing an old man on the street makes me feel a sudden pang of warmth and loss. I don't just see a stranger. I see a flicker of a gold paper crown."
Amit says, since he finished the podcast, he's found his mom listening to it, by herself.
Urs tears up and says the podcast "makes me feel closer to my grandpa."
Maybe memories are more than just stored information, Amit says at the end of his podcast.
Maybe they're proof that something — or someone — really mattered.

A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.
An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.
The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.
In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.
After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”
The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.
In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.
The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.
Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.
On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”
On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.
The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.
The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.
Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.
The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.
Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.
It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.
Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.
Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.
The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.
The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”
The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.
The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.
Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.
The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.
Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.
Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

Federal prosecutors have been weighing a perjury and obstruction of justice case against Cassidy Hutchinson, who implicated President Donald Trump in the January 6 Capitol riot in testimony four years ago, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
The efforts mark the Justice Department’s intent to proceed against Hutchinson, a former aide to ex-Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, though prosecutors are not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment at least until after the midterms, the sources say.
Hutchinson testified as a star witness to the committee that investigated the riot, recounting that Trump encouraged his supporters to march to the Capitol even though he knew many were armed. She sat for several interviews in addition to her public testimony, where she recalled hearing that Trump had lunged at one of his Secret Service agents after being told he could not join his supporters at the Capitol.
In recent months, prosecutors at the Justice Department have focused on the fact that the former special counsel, Jack Smith, did not corroborate much of Hutchinson’s account to the committee, and the Secret Service’s denial of any altercation in the presidential limo, the sources say.
By comparing the transcripts of Hutchinson’s interviews with the committee and against her testimony to Smith’s team, prosecutors have been trying to construct a case based on how her testimony has changed, the sources say.
Prosecutors have also taken a special interest in Hutchinson’s claim that she had penned a statement on a notecard for Trump to release during the Capitol riot—a claim disputed by former Trump White House counsel Eric Herschmann, who said he had written the note.
It was not immediately clear whether prosecutors intend to ultimately proceed with both perjury and obstruction charges, which have been under consideration for several months. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Hutchinson and her lawyer did not respond to texts and calls seeking comment. Hutchinson, now 29, has kept a low profile since publishing a memoir of her time in Trump’s first administration in 2023 titled “Enough.”
Punchbowl News first reported the Justice Department’s interest in charging Hutchinson.
The grand jury investigation is the latest example of the Justice Department pursuing criminal cases against Trump’s perceived political enemies. Trump fired former Attorney General Pam Bondi in April partly for moving too slowly to bring such cases, sources familiar with the matter said.
Some Justice officials have been skeptical about whether there is a viable criminal case against Hutchinson, in part due to the high bar for successfully prosecuting perjury charges, the sources say. To prove that Hutchinson lied to Congress, prosecutors would need to show beyond a reasonable doubt that Hutchinson lied, that she did so knowingly, and that it materially impacted the investigation, former US Attorney Joyce Vance tells WIRED.
The investigation into Hutchinson became a priority for the DOJ after a criminal referral by Representative Barry Loudermilk, a Georgia Republican who for years has been deeply critical of the January 6 committee investigation. Loudermilk had separately sought to depose Hutchinson until he was blocked by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who was concerned it could surface damaging texts of a sexual nature between lawmakers and Hutchinson.
In an unorthodox move, the referral ended up getting assigned to the Civil Rights Division at the DOJ, as opposed to the US Attorney for the District of Columbia or the Criminal Division, which would usually handle public corruption cases.
Under Justice Department guidelines, the Civil Rights Division is only supposed to take cases with a nexus to a civil rights violation. The division is led by Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump loyalist who has been a reliable advocate for the Trump administration's prosecutorial agenda.

The Debian Linux project has opened a call for community artwork submissions ahead of the release of the upcoming Forky (Debian 14). If you think you’ve got the artistic chops, your art could appear on the boot screens, login prompts, and desktop wallpapers of millions of users. The submission deadline is November 26.
Continuing Debian’s community-driven ethos, the artwork submission process mirrors that of previous releases. The artwork must feel distinctively “Debian,” integrate cleanly without the need for core software patching, and remain visually appealing for the long term.
Elise Couper’s “Ceratopsian” theme was chosen as the winning default for Debian 13 Trixie. For anyone who might not be up on the latest from the Toy Story franchise, the release names echo character names from the animated films. Trixie was a triceratops introduced in Toy Story 3, hence the “Ceratopsian” wink in the winning submission. It makes sense that the next version of Debian continues this trend with Forky, a character introduced in the franchise’s fourth entry. The Debian team cautions against overly busy designs that may cause user fatigue, but if anyone can successfully incorporate Forky’s googly eyes into the design somehow, know that you’d at least win the contest for my Debian desktop wallpaper.
Debian celebrated its 33rd anniversary in August 2026 and continues to position itself as the “universal operating system,” with support and compatibility stretching across different hardware architectures. Debian’s latest point release, Trixie 13.7, arrived on September 12, 2026. Forky (Debian 14) is now in the later stages of its development cycle, with the artwork selection process marking one of the final boxes to be checked before the release is made available. Interested artists can review the submission requirements on the Debian Wiki.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.

Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
- Published
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.
In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.
“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.
Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.
The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.
Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases
The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.
Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.
With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.

Why Elon Musk is taking on India's richest man over Starlink
- Published
Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.
The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.
India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.
Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment
The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.
The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel.
In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment.
Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers.
"You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".
On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.
"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.
Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries.
"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.
Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.
The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.
Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.
Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.
Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.
SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.
Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.
Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.
Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.
India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.
Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday.
The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.
In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

A former security guard, who allegedly kidnapped and murdered a five-year-old girl before concealing her body in a water sump at a gated residential community in Kowkoor, was arrested by the Malkajgiri police within 24 hours of the crime being reported. The accused had planned to extort ₹20 lakh from the child’s parents but decided to kill her after realising that keeping her captive until the ransom was paid would be difficult, police said.
The accused, Vikram Kumar, a native of Nalanda district in Bihar, had worked as a security guard at Villa Orchids between September 22 and October 6, 2026, the same residential community where the victim, Aurelia, also known as Monu, lived with her family. His employment at the premises had ended just four days before the incident.
The victim was the daughter of Milton Fernandes Moses, 44, a research scientist. The family resided at Villa Orchids, behind Janapriya Apartments in Kowkoor.
According to Malkajgiri Police Commissioner B. Sumathi, Aurelia, who was studying in PP-2, usually went cycling and played in the games zone near the clubhouse around 6 p.m. before returning home by 7 p.m. However, on Saturday (October 10, 2026), she did not return home.
When her father returned from work around 7.45 p.m., he learnt from his father that an unidentified person had called the family, claiming that the child was in his custody. Shortly afterwards, Milton received a call from the same mobile number, with the caller demanding ₹20 lakh as ransom and claiming to be in Secunderabad.
Based on his complaint, the Bolarum police registered a kidnapping case and launched a search operation. Ten special teams comprising personnel from the Malkajgiri Zone, Special Operations Team, Crimes and Special Branch were deployed to trace the child.
Investigators tracked the mobile number, call records, CCTV footage and other technical evidence. When the initial searches yielded no results, the police intensified their search within the residential community, including the clubhouse and adjoining areas.
“During the search, the child’s body was discovered inside a water sump in the clubhouse cellar. Forensic teams examined the scene to establish the circumstances surrounding her death,” said the commissioner.
The investigation subsequently led the police to Vikram Kumar. Police examined his employment records, residential details in Kowkoor, previous employment history and association with his roommates before tracing him.
“He was apprehended around 4.30 p.m. on Sunday (October 11). During interrogation, he admitted to murdering the child as part of a plan to demand ₹20 lakh from her parents,” the officer said.
According to investigators, Vikram entered the gated residential community around 6.40 p.m. on October 10 with the intention of kidnapping the girl and demanding ransom.
The commissioner added that he wanted to become wealthy and was unwilling to continue working as a labourer. He consequently devised a plan to kidnap the child and extract a substantial amount from her family.
However, after taking the girl, he realised that keeping her captive until the family paid the ransom would be difficult. He then decided to kill her and conceal her body in the water sump, believing that the clubhouse cellar was rarely visited by residents.
The police said his formal arrest was effected on Monday (October 12) and that he was being produced before a court. Investigators said they would complete the investigation at the earliest and pursue the case before a fast-track court, seeking capital punishment for the accused.
Residents gather at Commissioner’s office, demand justice
Meanwhile, families residing in Villa Orchids gathered at the Malkajgiri Police Commissioner’s camp office in Begumpet, demanding justice for the child and stringent action against those responsible for such crimes. They demanded strict action and death penalty against the accused.
The residents expressed concern over the safety of children in gated communities, pointing out that many parents leave their children at home while going to work.
They said the murder had raised serious questions about the safety of children even within residential complexes where security personnel are deployed and access to outsiders is regulated.
The families urged the police to take strict action against such offenders, stressing that parents should not have to fear for their children’s safety while they are away at work.
Police call for background checks of security staff
Following the incident, the Malkajgiri police urged residents and residential welfare associations to strengthen background verification of security guards, domestic helpers and watchmen.
The police called upon gated communities to participate in the Mee Suraksha domestic helpers verification initiative and the Nenu Saitham 2.0 CCTV surveillance programme.
According to the police, an awareness meeting had previously been conducted in the same residential community, encouraging residents to register the details of domestic helpers, security personnel and watchmen.
The police stressed that gated communities could not rely solely on access control and security personnel for protection, and that residential safety required thorough background verification, vigilant residents and coordination between residential associations and the police.
The Malkajgiri police also announced that personnel involved in the investigation and apprehension of the accused within 24 hours would be suitably rewarded.
