Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Zelenskyy says Russia violating Trump's 'energy ceasefire' as attacks on Ukraine continue
Zelenskyy says 'ceasefire' can help end war 'if Americans truly step in now'
Russia has violated an energy ceasefire announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, urging Washington to step in to ensure that Moscow abided by the terms of the putative agreement.
"There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump," Zelenskyy told a security conference in Warsaw via video link.
"We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take," added Zelenskyy, who said he had learned about the ceasefire deal from the media.
"This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it."
- Trump announces Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire,' which Zelenskyy says he hasn't seen but supports
- Video Trump claims Ukraine, Russia have agreed to an 'energy ceasefire'
A Monday statement from the Regional Prosecutor's Office of Kharkiv in northeastern Ukraine said Russian forces had attacked an energy facility on the outskirts of the city.
That came after Zelenskyy said Sunday that while he "welcomed" Trump's announcement, Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in the capital Kyiv and in Kharkiv.
Trump's brief social media post on Sunday announcing the purported agreement to mutually cease attacks on energy sites said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"
Trump had also claimed in a social media post on Sept. 14 that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either and nothing came of the purported agreement.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter."
Ukraine, meanwhile, has levelled strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory. That's prompted Trump to blame Zelenskyy for high diesel prices in the U.S. only weeks before the country's midterm elections.
Moscow did not immediately comment on the purported deal.
EU foreign policy chief skeptical
The European Union's top diplomat on Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg. "Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy."
A firefighter puts out a fire following a Russian air attack at a residential building in Kharkiv on Monday. (Andrii Marienko/The Associated Press)
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Trump on Sunday and that he told the U.S. president that Ottawa has "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, the Prime Minister's Office said in a statement on Sunday.
Kallas also emphasized the need for European countries to continue supporting Ukraine's efforts to defend against Moscow's full-scale invasion, even as Trump struck a deal on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin for the U.S. to purchase diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections.
Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort. On Monday, several EU foreign ministers said the diesel deal is unlikely to bring energy prices down, and appears aimed at helping Republicans win the midterms.
In a readout from the PMO on Sunday, Carney also told Zelenskyy that Canada believes the Trump-proposed diesel deal with Russia is "in direct opposition" to the goal of supporting Ukraine and that such a move would enrich the Kremlin and help finance its war effort.
Russian attack kills 3
Meanwhile, a Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office.
Investigators said the attack occurred at approximately 7:25 p.m., striking a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores and sparking a fire.
Ukrainian air defence forces shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones overnight Monday, Ukraine's Air Force said in a Telegram post. The attack involved one Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and 121 drones, including 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, the statement said.
Strikes were recorded at 15 locations in Ukraine, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
Russia also attacked gas production facilities of Ukraine's state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, causing a fire, the company said on Monday.
"The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system," Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said on Telegram.
The Russian Defence Ministry on Monday said its air defences overnight intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions as well as the illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
In a separate statement, the ministry said its forces overnight carried out drone strikes on Ukraine's unspecified port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Ukraine's port city of Odesa with military cargo on board.

Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossover debuted in 2021, one of VW’s first new electric vehicles designed in the wake of dieselgate. A year later, the company began local production in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unit in the process. But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4 earlier this year. And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.
Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.
VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.
Alongside the mainstream name, it has a more mainstream look, though it’s part of VW’s new design language. For those keeping track of the various interesting names car companies give their design languages—it can’t just be me—this one is called Pure Positive. The automaker says it wants the ID. Tiguan to feel like it belongs to the premium rather than mainstream segment, both inside and out.

DNA, vehicle-tracking help investigators recover stolen Renoirs and makes arrests
DNA left on a painting cover has helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover plans for another heist, according to a French prosecutor
NANTERRE, France -- DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday.
Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said.
One painting, “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano,” suffered a tear. The other, “Young Woman at the Well,” had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros ($4.7 million).
The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that “apparently caused the perpetrators to panic,” Bessone said.
"As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve,” he said.
The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said.
Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said.
Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection.
The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003.
Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent.”
The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of “theft committed by an organized gang” and “criminal association,” among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. The have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said.
The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said.
The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of “concealment” of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France.
Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge.
The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice.
The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France.
Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country “is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage” in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries.
French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.

Geneva, Oct 12: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the AP via the phone.
“What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation,” Coissac said. “They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened.”
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, “mainly because it was overcrowded.”
“The local authorities did their best,” Coissac said, “but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore.”
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
“They're all in a state of shock,” Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday, said. “I tried to talk to some of them but it's very difficult.”
Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.
At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
“This is a devastating loss of life,” said Coissac. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.”
In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.
Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project.
“No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.”

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."
- The runner who went viral and sparked a campaign for change for women

- Mashed potato & 19 minutes' sleep - Entrekin's epic race

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

PharmEasy parent API Holdings narrowed its consolidated net loss by 67% to ₹520 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026 (FY26) from ₹1,572 Cr in the previous fiscal, with its operating revenue growing 12.7% YoY to ₹6,618.5 Cr. The company attributed the improvement to its focus on customer experience, higher-value profitable segments, capacity utilisation, increasing wallet share and leveraging digital capabilities. In its FY26 annual report, API Holdings said it improved margins by focusing on higher-margin products, particularly its private label brands, and optimising discounts in its B2R business. Including other income of ₹70.8 Cr, the company’s total revenue stood at ₹6,689.2 Cr for FY26. However, it continued to report a loss before tax of ₹456.1 Cr. In the first quarter of FY27, API Holdings reported a 10% YoY increase in revenue to ₹1,754 Cr while EBITDA rose to ₹39.3 Cr. Gross margin improved to 21.4% from 19.9% in FY26, and EBITDA margin reached 2.2%. Its B2B business grew 8.2% YoY to ₹1,006 Cr revenue and turned EBITDA-positive at ₹70 lakh. The company said that PharmEasy’s B2C business posted ₹348 Cr revenue, with EBITDA losses narrowing to ₹17 Cr. Thyrocare reported 24% YoY revenue growth to ₹240 Cr, processed 5.4 Mn patients and conducted 55.2 Mn tests. Where Did API Holdings Spend In FY26? API Holdings’ consolidated expenses declined marginally by 0.9% to ₹7,146.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹7,208.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Purchases of stock-in-trade remained its largest expense, while lower employee benefit costs contributed to the overall reduction. Purchases Of Stock-In-Trade: The expense rose 10.9% to ₹5,244.8 Cr from ₹4,729.6 Cr, accounting for about 73% of total expenses. The increase came as the company’s operating revenue expanded during the year. Employee Benefit Expense: Employee costs fell 47.5% to ₹476.9 Cr from ₹908.4 Cr in FY25. A substantial part of the decline came from lower employee share-based payment expenses, which dropped to ₹62 Cr from ₹482.2 Cr in FY25. Other Expenses: This category increased 7.5% YoY to ₹656.7 Cr from ₹610.7 Cr. Major components included ₹111.8 Cr of contractual payments to delivery associates, ₹73.4 Cr of sales promotion and marketing, ₹72.6 Cr of manpower charges, and ₹63.4 Cr of legal and professional fees. API Holdings also reported a tax expense of ₹64.2 Cr, comprising ₹68 Cr in current tax, offset by a deferred tax credit of ₹4.2 Cr, and a prior-period charge of ₹0.4 Cr. Products Account For 86% Of Revenue API Holdings generates revenue from the sale of products and services. Product sales contributed ₹5,670 Cr, or 85.7% of revenue, in FY26. These include pharmaceutical, over-the-counter (OTC), surgical, consumable and private label products. The company sources products from manufacturers and wholesalers and supplies them to local chemists, large pharmacies, doctors, clinics, online retailers on the PharmEasy platform and hospitals. A significant part of this business flows through its chemist-focused distribution operations, while Aknamed supplies hospitals. The group also generates product revenue through collection kits sold by Thyrocare. Services contributed ₹941.3 Cr, or 14.2% of revenue, in FY26. This includes diagnostics, teleconsulting, licensing and technology services. Thyrocare’s diagnostic operations account for a substantial part of this stream, serving franchise partners, consumers, hospitals, diagnostic companies and independent phlebotomists. API Holdings also earns service revenue from diagnostic tests sold through the PharmEasy marketplace, fulfilment services and technology platforms, including Retailio, which connects pharmaceutical wholesalers and pharmacies. How API Holdings’ Subsidiaries Contribute Although API Holdings has six direct subsidiaries and 18 step-down subsidiaries, four businesses account for much of its activity across B2B distribution, diagnostics and consumer healthcare. B2B: Ascent Wellness And Pharma Solutions, Aknamed Ascent Wellness and Pharma Solutions supplies pharmaceutical products to chemists and institutions, sourcing directly from pharmaceutical companies and enabling retailers to place orders through a platform. Aknamed supplies hospitals with pharmaceutical products, consumables and surgical products sourced from pharmaceutical companies and distributors. Together, the B2B businesses generated ₹4,082.4 Cr in revenue in FY26, with an EBITDA loss of ₹3.6 Cr. In Q1 FY27, they recorded combined revenue of ₹1,005.6 Cr and EBITDA of ₹70 Lakh. Diagnostics: Thyrocare Technologies Thyrocare, API Holdings’ listed diagnostics arm, is a key contributor to the group’s profitability. In FY26, it operated 41 laboratories, offered 1,275 tests, processed about 21 Cr tests and had more than 10,800 franchisees. Its revenue grew 24% YoY to ₹240 Cr in Q1 FY27. B2C: PharmEasy PharmEasy operates the group’s consumer-facing healthcare marketplace. In FY26, the segment generated ₹1,334.5 Cr in revenue and reported an EBITDA loss of ₹44.1 Cr. In Q1 FY27, it recorded revenue of ₹347.9 Cr, alongside an EBITDA loss of ₹17 Cr.

- Germany won’t be intimidated into dropping its support for Ukraine, chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Sunday as he announced €1bn ($1.1bn) in military aid during a visit to Kyiv. Merz said Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production. Speaking alongside Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Merz also announced €350m for repairs to the energy sector.
- German officials said company executives who travelled with Merz had signed 14 agreements with Ukraine worth about €6.6bn. They included an agreement with Germany’s Diehl Defence for the supply of IRIS-T air defence missiles, as well as a deal for radar equipment with Hensoldt and for jet drone interceptors with Quantum Systems.
- Air raid sirens and explosions rang out repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital during the German chancellor’s visit. A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Later on Sunday, a Russian airstrike hit Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, killing one person and injured another six, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
- In Kyiv, Merz said Germany’s financial help was not only about protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity. “We do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” he said, adding that Russia was carrying out cyber-attacks and disinformation campaigns targeting European democracy. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
- Zelenskyy said on Sunday he believed Russia might have shared jet-drone technology with its ally North Korea. Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy told journalists: “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don’t know about the ballistic and etc but I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles.”
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has again used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine,  foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has become “a hell on earth” under Russian occupation since 2022, according to residents. Sybiha, who has previously accused Russia of starving residents, said the latest delivery contained almost four metric tons of food and medicine. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said last month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate.
- As Zelenskyy on Sunday said the US wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with Ukraine and Russia by the end of October, India said it was seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the war, the foreign minister said. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Sunday that India had been advocating for a peace deal “for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard”. He said India was starting with Black Sea safety of shipping but also including discussions about grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities”.

Quick Answer
OriginOS 7 adds useful upgrades like a customizable Control Center, Pet Pals themes, custom stickers, Liquid Glass controls, and Vivo Office Kit for seamless file sharing, clipboard sync, and screen mirroring across Windows and Mac.
Chinese smartphone makers replicate their software to look like iOS, aiming to appeal to users who want something familiar with an iPhone-like design. Vivo is no different. Their newly announced OriginOS 6 is a slight departure from the older Funtouch OS, which mimics iOS.
Vivo recently unveiled Origin OS 7 based on Android 17. Once again, Vivo gets heavily inspired by iOS and brought some of the biggest changes, many of which are welcome, while some I wish they had never made. You can view the full changelog here.
I have been using Origin OS 7 on my Vivo V80 for the past several days. Here are the 5 best Origin OS 7 features I found genuinely useful.
Table of Contents
5 Best OriginOS 7 Features
Adjust Liquid Glass Design
With iOS 26, Apple introduced a Liquid Glass design that most people hated.
The new glossy design made text harder to read and requires more power to render. Many Android skins have quickly adopted the Liquid Glass design, whether users like it or not, and Vivo is no different.
Vivo OriginOS 7 has incorporated the Liquid Glass design throughout the system. Unlike Apple, which introduced Liquid Glass transparency control a year after launch, OriginOS 7 offers three modes out of the box. You can set it to Realistic, Neutral, and Soft. If you are not a fan of Liquid Glass design, you can set it to Tinted.
One big note: the new Liquid Glass design seems limited to high-end smartphones, and the Vivo V80 lacks the feature entirely. It runs on Snapdragon 7 Gen 4. The biggest reason might be that mid-range chips can’t handle the heavy rendering required by the new glass design. Believing this, Vivo might have restricted this feature on other older and mid-range devices too.
Customizable Control Center
Another feature that Vivo borrowed from iOS is the ability to customize Control Center. For years, Android Control Center has remained the same. But with OriginOS 7, Vivo has taken a similar approach to Apple, letting you fully customize the layout and individual tiles.
The biggest change is that you can no longer be forced to use the default layout. You can rearrange or resize tiles however you want. With this functionality, you can also change the connectivity cards and media player, and remove them completely from the Control Center.
You can also rearrange the volume and brightness sliders, and even the network and media player, similar to what Apple allowed in iOS 26. If you’re not a fan of this new approach, Vivo also lets you choose the older Control Center layout in Settings.
However, by default, it is set to the old controls, and to change the layout, follow the steps below. Plus, you can also resize app icons on the home screen. You can simply long-press and drag them to your preferred size.
Lock Screen Customization and Pet Pals
Customization is the biggest focus on OriginOS 7. Vivo has brought several new theme options. I particularly liked the Pet Pals themes, where cute little pets appear on your home and lock screen and perform different actions based on the time of day, such as while the screen is on, tilting your phone, tapping, while your phone is on low battery, and also while you are doing actions such as listening to music and charging, and much more.
Stickers
In addition to more themes and lock screen customization, Vivo also added the ability to add custom stickers to the Home or lock screens; you can even add them to the always-on display.
Like widgets, you can drag and drop these stickers anywhere on the screen and resize them as you like. But these stickers won’t have any functionality like widgets or let you tap them to open an app. They are purely there for looks. Vivo offers some built-in stickers to get you started. However, you can also create any sticker using AI or photos already on your phone. You can tap it, convert it, and add it to your stickers; once done, you can add it anywhere on supported screens. Vivo also designed dedicated themes for adding stickers.
Vivo Office Kit
Vivo introduced Vivo Office Kit with OriginOS 6, and while it isn’t particularly new in OriginOS 7, it still remains one of the favorite features if you want to create an ecosystem. It lets your Vivo connect to your computer and sync the clipboard, share files, remote control, mirror your screen, sync your notes, and much more, similar to what you can do if you have an iPhone or Mac with the Apple ecosystem.
The best part is that it also works on Mac and other Windows devices. So unlike Apple, you don’t need to own a Mac and iPhone combination to use it. Whether you use Windows or Mac, your Vivo phone can connect to either of them and get all those handy features.
Even if you have never been in the Apple ecosystem, you might find these features very useful. Especially since every company has tried hard to bring an ecosystem between Android and Windows, or Android and macOS, or vice versa, and failed.
But somehow, many Chinese brands have figured out how to break the Apple ecosystem and connect a Vivo phone to an Apple device. And not just Vivo; OnePlus did the same with O+ Connect. Similarly, OPPO devices can connect to any PC or Mac apps.
Final Thoughts
Those are the five best features I truly love about OriginOS 7. To sum it up, OriginOS 7 brought Liquid Glass design to the OS. If you don’t like it, Vivo does offer options to disable it.
Next, it offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to add stickers (which I found unique) and new Pet Pals themes, which are my favorite. Plus, it has plenty of AI features, some of which run locally on your device, that can help with tasks like formatting text, plus AI features in the Photos app to edit and remove unwanted backgrounds.
Finally, the Vivo Office Kit is a great way to connect the Vivo phone to any PC, including Windows or Mac, and it lets you easily sync your clipboard and share files. Finally, Android’s Control Center is also customizable, similar to iOS, where you can set different sizes for each tile and rearrange them to suit your preferences.
Another feature that is missing on my Vivo V80 is a workbench feature. It is designed for power users who multitask a lot. You can place apps side by side and switch between them easily, just like windows on a PC. The best part is that you can rearrange them the way you want with different layouts, which makes proper multitasking possible on a small screen.
Another feature I really like is the ability to connect your Apple Watch or AirPods directly to your Vivo phone. Previously, Apple Watch only worked with an iPhone. With OriginOS 7, you can pair your Apple Watch and sync your data with a Vivo phone; for AirPods, it also shows the battery level and total, just like on iPhones.
Vivo officially announced OriginOS 7 globally, but still hasn’t announced an official global supported device list. However, we keep track of all the latest OriginOS 7 updates in a separate timeline post. You can bookmark the post for the latest OriginOS 7 updates.

Ukraine: ‘I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline’
Andriy Zholob, vocalist/guitarist, Beton: When MTV arrived in Ukraine, I heard Nirvana, the Offspring, Bad Brains, Social Distortion and thrash metal, and realised that all this started from punk rock. Our drummer and I were in a ska-punk band first, but when our vocalist became pregnant we started Beton in 2017 and played lots of festivals.
Everything changed with the invasion. In 2022, I started military service as a surgeon on the frontline. We were attacked many times and on at least four occasions I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline and every evening we’d play just to relax. At one point, my commander gave me eight days off to record a battle song for our brigade and Beton did a cover of the Clash’s London Calling – Kyiv Calling – to raise money for the Ukrainian resistance. I wanted to use punk rock to stand against evil.
I finished my service two years ago, quit medicine and now work with veterans, many of whom come to our gigs. There are guys and girls with prosthetics, slam dancing, singing along and everything. It’s a real moment of punk rock unity. We play two or three shows every month, but I like to spend time in the mountains. Although I play punk rock, sometimes I need silence.
Morocco and Spain: ‘People would tell me: you love Satan’
Nao, vocalist, Taqbir: In the Muslim community of Morocco, where I come from, the punk look is not accepted. For a long time, I had to perform anonymously, with my face covered, in case people recognised me and wanted to hurt me. Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted. Even in Spain, where I live now, I felt isolated as an immigrant and as a woman who did crazy things to my hair. People would tell me: “You love Satan.”
I heard Crass when I was 13. They were the first band I heard where I recognised myself in the lyrics, because I felt oppressed by religion. Then through chatting with friends online, I discovered more. I’d go to shows in Madrid, take off my hijab and wear makeup. It was a double life that meant I finally felt free to be myself, but for a long time punk cost me my relationship with my family.
Being in Taqbir really helped. I was very angry, so fronting the band was like a cure for this rage. People seem to connect with the rawness. We’ve played in north Africa and the UK and my dream is to be able one day to play in Morocco. Punk has helped me see that things don’t have to be black and white: people can be punk and Muslim and gay. Although there’s anger, our message is positive. If you’re feeling oppressed or that you cannot be yourself in this society, Taqbir are for you.
South Africa: ‘Being from Soweto automatically makes you political’
Abdula Skink, vocalist, Twenty One Children: A lot of kids in Johannesburg got into punk because there were no jobs or infrastructure for us. I grew up in a hip-hop house, but found bands such as Suicidal Tendencies and Black Flag through video games and older friends who skated. Punk just flicked all these switches in my head. Our guitarist, Thula, used to play in TCIYF, the first all-black punk band in South Africa. When we started our band in 2023, I was an assistant teacher for 21 autistic kids, so that became our name. I was also 21, so it felt like a lucky number.
Being from Soweto automatically makes you political. All the great revolutionaries – Hugh Masekela, Nobel prize winners, Desmond Tutu and so on – came from here. Our motto is: if something isn’t true, we won’t sing about it. Our song Scab is about a time I was stopped by police because I was skating through a historically Afrikaans/white area. I had green hair and the policeman was like: “You’re on drugs.” He ripped my Suicidal Tendencies T-shirt, dropped my laptop from my bag on the street and tried to take my skateboard. I wasn’t doing anything illegal. They were just fucking with me. Mostly, we try to make a difference in our communities. Thula built the first DIY skate park in Soweto; we’ve done charity shows for orphanages and such. For us, punk is not so much a livelihood but a way of life.
India: ‘We were bombarded with threatening messages’
Aditya Naik, vocalist/guitarist, Punk on Toast: I grew up listening to Bad Religion, NOFX, the Sex Pistols and the Clash and saw a satirical commentary about our times, so I started the band when I was 17 so I could talk about what was happening around us. In India, you see cruelty or injustice on every corner, so we don’t relate to mainstream music, which ignores this.
At the moment, there’s a lot of oppression of artists. After our song Modified talked about what the right wing are trying to do with us, we were bombarded with threatening messages online. People went through all our profiles, trying to find our phone numbers, where we live, our employers. It felt like being molested. Although we’ve had coverage in Rolling Stone India, the punk scene mostly flies under the radar, but that means we’re freer to sing about what we want.
We took part in the recent Cockroach protests in Mumbai, which alerted people to how things are and got everybody out on the street. Before that, India felt like a small elite club where everyone else is the “cockroaches”, so it was like seeing a phoenix: hope. The punk scene is growing, with our friends Pacifist and Emergency Trigger and bands such as the Light Years Explode and the Riot Peddlers. It’s more about documenting our times and standing for what’s right rather than selling lots of records, but punk rock gave me the greatest superpower: question everything.
Brazil: ‘Under a military dictatorship, there were kids brave enough to play with passion and fury’
Henrike Baliu, vocalist, Blind Pigs and Armada: When the original UK punk explosion happened in 1977, my dad was a naval engineer stationed in Southampton. He saw the Boomtown Rats performing Lookin’ After No 1 on Top of the Pops and told the guy in the record shop: “Give me everything you’ve got” – which meant the Sex Pistols, Generation X and so on.
Years later, when I was 12, I played some of my dad’s records to my friends and they told me about the punk scene in Brazil. Bands such as Ratos de Porão, Inocentes and Cólera sang about life under a military dictatorship, which Brazil was in the 80s. People were disappearing or being murdered, so it blows my mind that under a dictatorship with virtually zero news, poverty and police brutality there were kids with spiky hair brave enough to wear fake leather jackets and play with passion and fury. Those bands were pioneers who paved the way for us.
Blind Pigs were probably the biggest punk band in Brazil over the last 30 years, but now I’m focused on Armada. We are bilingual and sing in Portuguese and English. When we recorded our English language album, Tales of Treason, the country was going through another crazy time politically and the right wing were on the rise again. With the music, I wanted to warn people to learn from history: “Dudes, you don’t want that again.”
Latvia: ‘On stage I let out all my anger’
Evisa Petrovka, vocalist, Depustūtes: In high school, I didn’t really like pop, so I got into metal, but I felt it was missing lyrical depth, so punk really resonated. Ramones and the Sex Pistols sang about the same stuff that made me mad or frustrated. The Dead Kennedys’ political commentary really connected and then I discovered riot grrrl. As I got older, I realised there was a punk scene here in Riga and a whole community of people like me.
There’s so much going on in the world – I’ll never run out of topics and writing and singing in the band never gets boring. On stage, I let out all my anger. Whether I’m running or crawling on the floor, it’s just pure emotion. Singing in Latvian makes it easier to sing about local politics. Lately, we’ve been addressing how people who actually benefit society aren’t getting paid as well as those who aren’t, but I sing about societal norms and stereotyping.
Our song Mrs Pieklājība (Mrs Polite) starts, in a mocking way: “I love listening to men and being obedient.” It was inspired by people telling me “you should smile more” or “women don’t dress like that”. There’s always been at least two women in the band, but most people are really supportive. I love inspiring other girls’ lives. A lot of them come up after shows and say: “That was so inspiring. I wish I could speak as freely as you.”
China: ‘Our albums were confiscated and our work was taken offline’
Wu Wei, vocalist, SMZB: Wuhan and Beijing were the first cities in China to have punk music. I founded the first punk band in Wuhan in 1996 after falling in love with tapes that my friends sent me from the US – initially the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Ramones and then bands with other styles, such as US Bombs, Suicide Machine and Rancid. Through punk, I finally found a way to express myself. Although the scene is still quite small, we were one of the first bands to go on national tours, which influenced the development of punk in other cities. We sing about the environment we operate in: political aspects and things I’ve witnessed in daily life under the system in China.
A few years ago, the authorities prohibited us from performing. Some albums were confiscated, our work was taken offline and our record company was forced to terminate our contract. Despite this, our audiences have a wide age span and range from other punks and bands to art workers, students and ordinary wage-earners. Punk has brought me so many things, from running the bar Wuhan Prison to my personal life. I’ve now settled in the UK with my family, but frequently return to Wuhan for rehearsals and recording. SMZB just released a bilingual album, When the Party Is Over, for our 30th anniversary. Punk has given me my life.
Greenland: ‘I’m 38, a father, still have my piercings and still consider myself a punk’
Jenseeraq Olsen, vocalist/guitarist, Uummat: We have a running joke with Iceland that they are green and we are ice, so most people live on the coast. I was in Denmark for a festival recently and realised that there were more people there – 70,000 – than the entire Greenlandic population. Punk is very much a minority interest here, but I was always rebellious when I was young and didn’t like the mainstream pop my friends were into.
After I saw an advert for Blink-182’s Enema of the State album after the movie American Pie, I realised they were the band I’d been searching for. I was teased for having multicoloured hair and ripped clothes, but Blink were a big influence on Uummat, which means “heart”. We were different from other bands in Greenland and people connected with it: we’ve played to 2,000 people.
I’ve never really written political songs, but Trump’s threat to annex Greenland has made a lot of people emotional, stressed and nervous, which I’m sure will come out in the music. I’m 38, a father and manage a youth centre now, but Blink resonate as much as they did when I was 15. I still have my piercings and I still consider myself a punk. Meanwhile, my 11-year-old son listens to the same music and plays guitar like me. He thinks labels like “punk” are for adults, but he likes the word, so he’ll probably follow in my footsteps.

Attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more, Saudi authorities say
CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition.
The attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi-backed government forces there.
The statement, which did not assign blame for the attack, said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport that killed four people — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.
Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis. "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. The rebels at times take days to claim responsibility.
Riyadh airport operations were suspended
Saudi civil aviation authorities earlier said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. Statements later turned to condolences.
Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and a Houthi-launched ballistic missile had been intercepted in Al-Kharj governorate, southeast of Riyadh.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
Earlier Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of "supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions" in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

Indian opposition leaders to march to top court to demand election chief resign
- Published
India's opposition parties are set to march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.
This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital.
Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained.
Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge.
The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons".
He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter.
"Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters.
Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march.
Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march.
Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.
On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.
The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.
But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.
The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest.
They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.
Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists.
"Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.
Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.
BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

On Tuesday (October 6, 2026), Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case after a Kenyan national who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died in Nairobi. According to media reports that quoted Kenya’s Health Minister Aden Duale, he had lived in the DRC for years and had travelled back home by road before taking a flight to Nairobi.
After the DRC declared an Ebola outbreak in May, Uganda also reported cases and deaths from Ebola. However, after Uganda was declared free of the disease by the World Health Organisation (WHO), the cases have occurred only in the DRC. This is the first case in which an Ebola death has occurred in another country, raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities.
What are the details of the case
According to Mr. Duale, the Kenyan national had been living in the DRC for several years and had fallen ill about a month ago. He had been treated in several hospitals in the DRC and died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had travelled by road from DRC to Uganda and then boarded a flight to Nairobi, undergoing public screening with other passengers at the airport, but missed being picked up. He went home and was taken to hospital by a relative when he became sicker. He tested positive for the dangerous Bundibugyo strain, which has neither specialised treatment nor a vaccine until now. (Human trials for a vaccine were started in July, and three other candidates are in the pipeline.)
Eight of the patient’s family members and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined. Screening at all airports. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the flight he took from Uganda are also being traced. The traced individuals will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be allowed to leave if they do not show any symptoms.
Why is this fresh cause for concern?
The virus is highly infectious and spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids. This is the 17th outbreak in the DRC and is said to be its deadliest, having claimed over 4,000 lives since May this year. Over 8,300 cases have been confirmed across the country.
Meanwhile, the WHO has warned that the epidemic will surpass the regional 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed over 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Despite an outbreak in the region, the global health body has not been in favour of imposing travel and trade restrictions on the affected regions. However, not all international travellers are required to fill out a self-declaration form specifying whether they have been in any of the Ebola-affected countries or if they have suffered any symptoms lately.
In Kenya, health authorities explained that the patient who died had managed to pass through the screening without raising any red flags because the medicines he was on probably masked the symptoms as he walked past.
The course ahead
Now that the virus has entered Kenya, the key task for health authorities in the country is firstly to stop the chain of transmission, beginning with the primary contacts already isolated. As per the outbreak protocol, this includes rapid contact tracing, immediate isolation of anyone who develops symptoms, and testing. Strict infection-control measures must be put in place in Kenya, and targeted information on prevention and control disseminated among communities.
Screening and surveillance have been intensified at airports in Kenya. However, at a time when it is impossible to stop global movement, it’s crucial to make sure that all nations maintain vigilance at their entry ports and pick up patients with detectable symptoms. Port authorities should also stress on the seriousness of honestly declaring travel history and symptoms.

Karnataka has urged the Centre to extend price-control measures beyond cancer medicines to other high-cost, life-saving drugs used to treat cardiac and kidney diseases, following the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) in-principle approval to cap trade margins on certain non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines at 30% of their maximum retail price (MRP).
Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Health Minister U.T. Khader said price rationalisation should translate into direct savings for patients, and urged the Union government to extend similar measures to other essential medicines where high treatment costs place a burden on patients.
At its meeting on October 8, the NPPA gave in-principle approval to rationalise trade margins on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines identified under Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. The measure is subject to finalisation of the list of medicines to be covered.
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been asked to constitute an expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services to recommend the anti-cancer medicines to be brought under price control. The committee is expected to submit its report by October 14.
The Centre estimates that the measure could reduce the MRP of several anti-cancer medicines by 20% to 70%, potentially saving patients around ₹2,500 crore. “The financial strain of cancer treatment often pushes families into debt, making it inevitable for them to exhaust their savings and sell assets to meet medical expenses,” Mr. Khader said.
Citing examples, the Minister said a cancer drug/injection costing around ₹3,250 was reportedly priced at ₹23,347. Medicines with a landing cost of about ₹3,000 are being sold at a cost of ₹27,000. Under the 30% trade-margin cap, the maximum price of a medicine would depend on its applicable pricing base and can substantially reduce out-of-pocket expenditure for patients, he explained.
Also Read: Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
Karnataka’s representation to the Centre
In a letter dated September 23 to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, the Karnataka government had sought national-level action after inspections in the State found substantial differences between the procurement costs of medicines and the prices charged to patients. The State identified pricing concerns involving 253 medicines and consumables with mark-ups.
Karnataka had sought the inclusion of advanced chemotherapy, targeted therapy and other expensive cancer medicines under the ambit of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, along with a comprehensive cap on trade margins for high-cost and life-saving medicines.
The State had also called for expanding the NPPA’s price-control oversight and strengthening enforcement against excessive charging and profiteering.
Disclosure of medicine costs in hospital bills
The State has also sought greater transparency in the prices charged to patients. A circular issued on October 1 asked healthcare institutions to disclose both the purchase or landing cost and the MRP of medicines in patient bills. The instructions are advisory in nature and are proposed to take effect from November 1.
Karnataka’s call follows observations by the Supreme Court questioning why the MRP of essential medicines, including cancer drugs, could not be capped at 16% above the price to retailers, as is applicable to scheduled medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.
The State said the proposed 30% trade-margin cap on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines should be followed by wider action to cover other essential, high-cost medicines, including those used in cardiac and kidney treatment, so that the benefits of price rationalisation reach patients directly.

India’s leprosy programme is falling short of several projections set for 2025-26. The country reported 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, 41.2% higher than the projected 65,000. New cases among children were 91.6% above the projection while the rate of Grade 2 Disability (G2D) among new cases was 1.34 per million, against a projected one per million.
India’s national prevalence rate was 0.56 cases per 10,000 population at the end of March 2026, below the elimination target of a prevalence rate below one case per 10,000.
But the burden remains concentrated geographically. Chhattisgarh had the highest prevalence among States/UTs at 1.66 cases per 10,000 population, followed by Jharkhand (1.51), Chandigarh (1.49), Odisha (1.25) and Maharashtra (1.14).
At the district level, 14.8% of districts had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 in 2025-26, down from 18.6% in 2013-14 but 114 districts still remained above the programme’s elimination target. Moreover, only 148 districts have provisionally achieved interruption of transmission, against a projected 300.
G2D was also concentrated in a few States/UTs. Chandigarh, Delhi, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha together accounted for 42.5% of the 1,945 G2D cases reported in 2025-26. Chandigarh recorded the highest rate at 13.54 per million, followed by Delhi (11.53) and Chhattisgarh (7.87).
Single-Dose Rifampicin Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (SDR PEP), a preventive dose given to people who have been in contact with a leprosy patient, was administered to 91.2% of the 16.94 lakh eligible contacts in 2025-26, up from 71.4% of the 6.48 lakh in 2019-20.
Source: National Leprosy Eradication Programme (2025-26) and National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027
