Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.
For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.
“What we really like to think is that we’re building the perfect victims for scammers,” Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us. “A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people being reached out to by that exact same scammer,” he says, referencing the ability for scammers to use automated dialing tools.
Kaafar says Apate’s platform, which is used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots. They not only pick up calls, but also infiltrate scam chat groups online and respond to text messages with similar goals of frustrating scammers while collecting intelligence from them. He says the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters in real-time, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.
The bots have different personalities, language skills, and profiles, Kaafar says, so scammers hopefully don’t detect that they’re conversing with an AI. Like real people, “sometimes [the bots] do have WhatsApp, sometimes they don’t. Sometimes they pick up the phone, sometimes they just actually hang up on the scammer saying, ‘I'll come back to you later,’” he says.
But are they convincing? Kernel Panic tested the tool using a demo version where users play the role of the scammer and talk to one of Apate’s AI “victims.” The personas are designed to express a healthy amount of skepticism but leave enough openings for scammers to continue to try to win them over, a dynamic that we could immediately feel and found intensely frustrating.
Scammers are likely familiar with this type of skeptical interaction, and Kaafar says that Apate calls regularly go on for more than two hours. In our testing, the Apate system was engaged and responsive, and the timing of the conversation felt natural, even with both of us tag-teaming the AI as a friend, “Lucy,” and her financial adviser “Mickey.” We did not succeed at getting the Apate AI system to invest in our cryptocurrency opportunity even after six minutes of diligent effort. (The returns are truly incredible, though, we swear.)
For now, even with Apate’s massive swarm of bots on the case, it’s only a matter of time before you get your next scam call or text. Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year, with the most sophisticated operations running physical, industrial scale scamming sites. And while professional scambaiters and initiatives to infiltrate scam operations have done critical deterrent work for years, law enforcement and research efforts haven’t been able to stop the expansion of digital scamming overall.
But AI could create a new era for anti-scam efforts, not just scammers themselves. Better intelligence sharing between cops, social media companies, banks, and other industries is desperately needed and could potentially be aided by AI-driven monitoring and data analysis. Increasingly, too, innovative efforts have been looking to disrupt cybercriminals by exploiting their “psychological vulnerabilities.” In some cases, these psyops have included directly trolling those behind ransomware attacks. As the focus on disrupting scammers and cybercriminals expands, the use of generative AI as a way to keep them preoccupied, wasting resources, and not launching other attacks appears to be increasingly effective.
Take honeypots, for instance. For years, companies and security researchers have deployed false virtual machines to attract hackers, waste their time, gather information, and understand their secret hacking techniques. Mark Vero, a doctoral researcher at the department of computer science at ETH Zurich, says open source honeypot providers have increasingly been incorporating LLMs into their systems to make them appear more realistic.
In recent research, Vero and colleagues found an LLM-powered honey pot would keep AI agents attacking their system “significantly longer” than a honey pot with more predictable behavior. “The agentic attackers are much more convinced by the LLM simulated honeypots and they also mark them as actual honeypots at a much lower rate,” he says. “If these systems are built well enough, then I think it’s quite advantageous for defenders.”

Time to rise? Ranking European football's sleeping giants
- Published
Deportivo, Parma, Hamburg. Not just a football hipster's holiday hit-list, but a sample of erstwhile headline acts who have returned to their respective top flights in recent years.
You can throw Leeds United, Nottingham Forest, Schalke and Malaga into the mix too.
But with such footballing royalty back in the big time, where can you find Europe's current sleeping giants? Which one-mighty sides are still snoozing?
We first need to establish some criteria - history, heritage, fanbase, stadium. Clubs with huge potential who currently exist outside the top flight.
Calling a big city home helps, but it is not a deal-maker - sorry to fans of Bristol City and second-tier Russian outfit FC Ufa, where the local population tops one million.
Likewise, some clubs with good-sized stadiums have not made the cut. Bari, whose Stadio San Nicola is the third-largest in Italy and was built for Italia '90, stands out, though some of their calcio colleagues outside Serie A also have grounds of more than 30,000 - Hellas Verona, Messina and Palermo among them.
There's a plethora of ex-Premier League teams with top-flight worthy arenas and storied pasts, while Germany is stacked full of historic clubs with huge homes who arguably deserve a spot - Fortuna Dusseldorf, Wolfsburg, Hannover 96 - but we can't include them all.
A sleeping giant must have experienced some element of former glory and Pro Vercelli are the obvious candidate there, winning seven Italian titles by 1922. But, despite being under new ownership, the third-tier side boast neither the ground nor local population to awaken that historic status any time soon.
The other nuance is, that success cannot have come too recently. West Ham, for example, won a European competition three years ago, Wolves are recent top-flight regulars; likewise Stade de Reims, twice European Cup runners-up, and eight-time French champions Nantes.
Leaving out Steaua Bucharest was another big call. European Cup winners 40 years ago and Romania's most dominant club, they now play in Liga II. But, following a deeply divisive split, many of the traditional fanbase follow top-flight FCSB. So who really owns that legacy?
And there was a case for Boavista, title winners in 2001 but whose existence now hangs by a thread. Facing financial ruin, despite fans' best efforts, they have been ejected from Portugal's professional leagues.
Anyway, let's get on with this. Piped through the matrix above, here are my top 10 European sleeping giants - you can have your say in the comments, too.
10. Bursaspor
League titles: One (2009-10). Domestic cups: One (1985-86). Division: 1.Lig, second tier. Stadium: Centennial Ataturk Stadium (43,361)
Historically dominated by Istanbul's elite teams, Bursaspor snapped that long-running streak by becoming only the second club from outside of the capital - and first since Trabzonspor almost three decades earlier - to clinch the Turkish title in 2010.
That meant Champions League nights against Manchester United and Rangers, but in 2024 the Green Crocodiles dropped into the fourth tier for the first time in their history.
Based in a city of about 2.5m people - Bursa sits in the north west, south of Istanbul, near Mount Uludag - and with a unique crocodile-shaped stadium that can house 43,361 fans, Bursaspor have soared up the pyramid since and are looking to return to the Super Lig for the first time since 2019.
9. Dynamo Dresden
League titles: Eight (most recent East German DDR-Oberliga 1989-90). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 89-90). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion (32,085).
Without wanting to turn this into a 2.Bundesliga table, this is the first of four German entries. But Dynamo Dresden, bearing a complex history and situated in the underrepresented east, feel a little different.
Initially enjoying the support of the security forces before their best players were relocated to Berlin, Dynamo became European regulars and lost to Liverpool in the Uefa Cup in 1976 and European Cup two seasons later.
One of East Germany's most dominant clubs, they won eight titles and seven cups and joined the Bundesliga in 1991 following reunification, but they dropped into the third tier four years later amid relegation and mounting debts.
Dynamo, with alumni including Matthias Sammer, have bounced around the regional and lower leagues for many years but now sit in 2.Bundesliga.
Based in a city of more than half a million people, their potential is underpinned by a large, passionate fanbase who averaged over 30,000 for home games in the second tier last term.
8. Kaiserslautern
League titles: Four (most recent 1997-98). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 95-96). Division: 2.Bundesliga. Stadium: Fritz-Walter-Stadion (49,327)
With their 1997-98 success, Kaiserslautern remain the only side to win the Bundesliga immediately after promotion, albeit following a surprise relegation having also been champions in 1991 and enjoyed cup triumphs in 1990 and 1996.
European regulars in the 1990s and early 2000s, it is now almost 15 years since they competed in the Bundesliga, spending four seasons in the third tier before a promotion in 2022.
Despite modest league finishes, the club continue to record average crowds of more than 46,000 and almost pulled off another shock in 2024 when they reached the German Cup final, losing to Xabi Alonso's Leverkusen.
7. Sheffield Wednesday
League titles: Four (most recent 1929-30). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 90-91). Division: League One, third tier. Stadium: Hillsborough (39,732)
Sheffield United fans may argue that they, not city rivals Sheffield Wednesday, should make this list. But the Owls edge it on history and heritage - even if the most recent of their four league titles came almost 100 years ago.
Wednesday were League Cup winners in 1991, and in living memory for many gave us magical moments from the likes of David Hirst, Chris Waddle and Paolo di Canio. Yet they now sit in the third tier after entering administration and enduring relegation last season, before a US consortium bought the club in May.
The Owls, boasting England's 12th biggest club stadium, were relegated from the top flight in 2000, but fans are fuelled with fresh optimism that a reawakening is possible.
6. Hertha BSC
Leagues: Two (most recent 1931). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 2002). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Olympiastadion (74,475).
I'm convinced Hertha have huge potential, if not the history to match some of their counterparts. Their only titles, for example, precede the Bundesliga era.
But the Old Lady once reached a Uefa Cup semi-final and beat Chelsea in the Champions League in 1999.
This season is their fourth consecutive campaign outside the top tier, but Hertha continue to play at Berlin's Olympiastadion and regularly attract more than 50,000 fans. A new ground on the Olympic Park site, housing up to 52,000, is being considered.
Currently top of 2.Bundesliga, Hertha can tap into a deep talent pool on their doorstep - highly rated youngsters Ibrahim Maza and Kennet Eichhorn have joined Leverkusen, goalkeeper Tjark Ernst went to Feyenoord - and look equipped to return to the Bundesliga in fine shape.
5. Bordeaux
Leagues: Six (most recent 2008-09). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 12-13). Division: Regional 1, sixth tier. Stadium: Stade Atlantique (42,115)
Bordeaux's recent troubles have been well documented. Relegated from Ligue 1 in 2022 before administration meant they tumbled into the fourth tier, this summer they were again demoted to the regional sixth tier because of financial issues.
Having seemingly hit the bottom, the 2009 French champions now at least have something to build on after being bought by US investment fund Park Bench for one euro.
Les Girondins are dripping in history. Once home to former greats Jean Tigana and Zinedine Zidane, as well as current France internationals Aurelien Tchouameni and Jules Kounde, their decade-old home hosted a Euro 2016 quarter-final - albeit Bordeaux are not playing there at present as they try to shape their future.
4. FC Nuremberg
League titles: Nine (most recent 1967-68). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 06-07). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Max-Morlock-Stadion (50,000).
Perhaps it's not overly imaginative to be opting for the current top two in Germany's second tier but FC Nuremberg meet all the selection criteria laid out above.
They have the history - nine titles, with the latest of four cup triumphs coming in 2007; a 50,000-seater home; large local fanbase in a one-club city - and the heritage.
They're nicknamed 'Der Club' because of their status in early German football.
Oh, and World Cup winner and Germany's all-time top goalscorer Miroslav Klose is their boss.
3. Real Zaragoza
Domestic cups: Six (most recent 2003-04). European: Cup Winners' Cup (1994-95). Division: Primera Federacion, third tier. Stadium: La Romareda (under reconstruction but projected 43,000).
David Seaman, look away now. Arsenal fans of a certain vintage will remember former Spurs boy Nayim's long, looping winner beating the moustachioed stopper in the final minute of extra time to give Real Zaragoza the Cup Winners' Cup.
There have been two Copa del Rey triumphs, European journeys and star names since - Pablo Aimar, Diego Milito and David Villa among them - but three decades later, Los Manos find themselves in Spain's third tier.
Ander Herrera, aged 37, is back at his boyhood club, who are in the process of developing a new 43,114-capacity stadium for the 2030 World Cup, in an attempt to help the fallen giants return to former glories.
"Real Zaragoza belong to Europe, they belong to compete for trophies, to be fighting with the biggest clubs in Spain and in Europe," said Herrera.
2. Saint-Etienne
League titles: 10 (most recent 1980–81). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 2012–13). Continental: European Cup runners-up (1975–76). Division: Ligue 2, second division. Stadium: Stade Geoffroy-Guichard (41,965)
Saint-Etienne were, until Paris St-Germain overtook them in the past decade, the most-decorated club in France with 10 league titles in 25 seasons from 1956-57 to 1980-81.
Les Verts reached the European Cup final in 1976, losing to a vintage Bayern Munich side, while their last silverware came in the now-defunct Coupe de la Ligue 13 years ago with a team spearheaded by Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang.
They are presently spending their fourth season in five in the second tier, but they continue to produce top prospects. Star defenders William Saliba and Wesley Fofana came off the production line, while 18-year-old attacking talent Djylian N'Guessan will join Liverpool in January.
Then there is their 41,965-capacity Stade Geoffroy-Guichard home, nicknamed the 'cauldron', which was a whisker from seeing Ligue 1 football again this term - Les Verts lost to Nice in the promotion/relegation play-off, meaning the wait to rejoin France's elite continues.
1. Sampdoria
League titles: 1990-91. Domestic cups: Four (most recent 93–94). Continental: Cup Winners' Cup (89–90), European Cup runners-up (91-92). Division: Serie B, second tier. Stadium: Stadio Luigi Ferraris (33,205)
Sampdoria were once continental big-hitters, not merely domestic champions during a golden era of Italian football.
Buoyed by Paolo Mantovani's investment, the Genoa outfit won the Coppa Italia four times between 1985 and 1994, clinched the Scudetto in 1991 and reached three European finals, winning the Cup Winners' Cup in 1990 a year after losing to Barcelona in the final.
In 1992, the team of Gianluca Vialli, Roberto Mancini and Gianluca Pagliuca were again beaten by Barcelona in extra time of the European Cup final at Wembley.
More big names followed in the period between Sven-Goran Eriksson's side winning the club's last major trophy in 1994 and a first relegation five years later - Clarence Seedorf, Juan Sebastian Veron and Ariel Ortega included.
Samp had spells back in Europe before finishing bottom of Serie A in 2023 amid serious financial problems and almost dropped into the third tier.
Under new ownership, though, fans hope the club's future is more stable - and the architecturally iconic Stadio Luigi Ferraris home they share with rivals Genoa is set to undergo an expensive redevelopment before Italy host Euro 2032.

William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.
When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”
Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.
“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.
As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.
Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”
Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”
Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.
Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.
For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

For at least several decades, people have attributed the following quote as something physicist Albert Einstein once said: "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow."
On social media, users' posts pairing the quote with Einstein's name have appeared, for example, on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived).
(@ramblingsloa via X)
However, no evidence supported the claim that Einstein ever said the words. Research into historical records found that other people expressed the exact same thought without Einstein's name as early as the 1970s. Other persons from decades prior shared the same general idea, albeit in different words, about learning from the past (yesterday), that you can only live in the now (today) and have aspirations for the future (tomorrow).
No records from the years during or immediately following Einstein's 1955 death featured the quote with his name. The authoritative compendium "The Ultimate Quotable Einstein" also did not include the quote — or similar thoughts — in its text, not even in its list of misattributions.
If Einstein had truly spoken or penned the thought, credible historical documents, such as books or newspapers, would contain that information. It would not only appear in social media posts and on quote-collecting websites — two types of sources that can lack credibility.
Some posts, for example on Facebook (archived) and Reddit (archived), featured the incorrectly attributed quote with the added line, "The important thing is not to stop questioning." Einstein truly once said that sentence while talking about pursuing curiosity in life. Life magazine printed the "not to stop questioning" quote without the "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow" part in 1955.
Researching the quote
As a small part of beginning our research, we noted that searching Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo failed to locate any credible historical records documenting that Einstein said, "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow."
To perform deeper and more meaningful research, we then looked to archives of literature via Google Books, as well as newspapers on Newspapers.com, where we found several interesting results — though none indicated Einstein ever said the words.
For example, in 1965, a Kentucky newspaper credited a teacher named Donna Jean Roberts as saying, "Learn from yesterday and hope for tomorrow, but live today for today."
A 1971 Indiana newspaper article reported, "HERE'S A slogan which makes sense to Mack McGinnis: 'Live for Today—Dream for Tomorrow — Learn from Yesterday."
In 1972, a newspaper in Illinois printed the earliest record we found of the exact quote that users later wrongly attributed to Einstein. The paper credited the thought as the class motto for Gardner High School in Gardner, Illinois. Some books published in the 1970s also featured the exact quote without any direct attribution.
A 2000 classified advertisement for a California mobile glass company featured possibly the earliest newspaper record of the quote containing the attribution to Einstein. According to Google Books, the 1998 edition of "The Michiganensian," the University of Michigan's annual yearbook, also showed the quote with Einstein's name.
In 2011, an author wrote a book with the quote as the title, saying in the text that he was inspired to publish the work thanks to Einstein supposedly penning the thought.
1930 article about meaning of 'Today'
In all of our searches, one California newspaper article from 1930 featured the Chicago Journal of Commerce opining in a unique way about the meaning of "Today":
We live only today. Yesterday we lived, and through all the multitude of yesterdays, each of which had its influence in making us what we are today. What we do and are today will have its effect on what we shall do and be tomorrow.
We all live in the present—not in the past, which is gone forever, nor in the future which we cannot know until time makes it the present for us. We all have aspirations as to what we shall be and do in the future, but we have only our todays in which to put in action the principles and forces by which we may make our tomorrows what we would have them be.
We may, and must, learn from our yesterdays in order to make today count in our ambitions. Our mistakes in the past are warnings. Our achievements alone can encourage us by promises for the future. We all have our settled purposes as well as our past experiences, to guide us. Thus memories have power to help us to the future we desire. The purpose is a powerful incentive, strengthened by the knowledge if what has been accomplished in the past through definite purpose.
We learn from the past that all good things come slowly, that we must earn every advance we make. That is what makes today so prodigiously important to thinking men. It is the introduction to our tomorrow. When we go to bed after having done our level best, we have the finest assurance that we can do better tomorrow.
For further reading, we previously reported that Einstein truly married his double cousin.

Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph 
  - Published19 January
- Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes 
  - Published24 February
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
- Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe 
  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.
- How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it? 
  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Man City's statement win has feeling of irrelevance with season in limbo
- Published
Manchester City made what they will regard as a powerful statement in the most hostile territory against Liverpool at Anfield - but is it a statement that carries any weight during a Premier League season in limbo?
City's attention turned to on-field matters in their first game since being found guilty of 114 charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.
The fates, and fixture list, decreed it would be at Liverpool, whose fans nurse the most burning sense of injustice after finishing second to City in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22.
Their argument centres on the belief those titles could have been theirs had City not possessed the high finance of their Abu Dhabi-based owners, using it in the manner that led to them being investigated.
With this as the backdrop, City strode into this fevered Anfield atmosphere, with Liverpool fans high on adrenaline and determined to make their contempt for their rivals obvious - then outclassed Andoni Iraola's side in a 3-0 win.
On another day, in other circumstances, the manner of City's victory would have fed the narrative that this was a performance of champions, a winning marker laid down to their rivals as they hold a three-point lead at the top of the table.
Not here. Not in the Premier League's dysfunctional state.
Instead, once the predictable sound and fury had been diluted by City's composure and the swift realisation they were not unnerved by Anfield or the storm raging around the club, this was a surreal experience.
After the feast of excitement delivered when Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp presided over the greatest domestic rivalry of recent years, this was an occasion - remarkable as it seems - that seemed robbed of a sense of jeopardy by the circumstances surrounding it.
Yes, it was a statement display and City celebrated wildly at the final whistle, but will it count for anything given they await potential sanctions suggested including Premier League relegation or a record points deduction?
As Erling Haaland looked close to tears in front of Manchester City's fans, including his father Alf-Inge, and head coach Enzo Maresca pumped his fists in jubilation, Anfield's DJ slipped Fleetwood Mac's 'Little Lies' on to the loudspeakers in a final message of defiance.
Maresca said: "We knew there was going to be noise but we need to make our own noise by winning games. We need to learn to deal with the noise but the message is to win games.
"For me it's quite easy. I try to focus on things I can control. There are things that are not in my hands so I don't stress about them.
"I cannot control things outside football, so why stress? I stress about gameplan, day-by-day training sessions, but the rest it's not in my hands."
Haaland added: "For every single person part of Manchester City, every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time. It was tough. It was hard, but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone.
"It's always tough to come here. If you look at the record it's tough. With the Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp era it was tough for both teams, always has been. It was important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about. The thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That's the only thing we can do."
City have appealed against the verdict, but until the dust settles and final decisions are made, this Premier League season is in a holding pattern.
When City come to Anfield and win, especially as convincingly as they did here, it should be a win without qualification or questions.
This does not apply amid the current uncertainty.
Every victory, every league table, will come with a metaphorical asterisk until clarity and finality comes. No-one knows when this will be.
City's players did their jobs to perfection, victory secured by second-half goals from Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki. It is all they can do.
There can be no escape, however, from the cloud hanging over Manchester City because every win will carry the same rider - producing a state of inertia that is not good for the Premier League.
In the end, a day that promised huge discomfort for City ended in a stroll.
City navigated the hostile reception awaiting them at Anfield by arriving through the staff and contractors' entrance - while an inevitable febrile environment awaited them.
Even the derided half-and-half scarves were doing a roaring trade, until it was noticed the sky blue half read: 'Shamchester City - The Cheats'.
The announcement of City's line-up was drowned out by deafening jeers, while banners around Anfield carried a variety of messages.
They including 'A Generation Of Supporters Cheated', 'And After All You Really Robbed Us All' and - in a nod to the Oasis song Stop Crying Your Heart Out, written by Noel Gallagher who was at Anfield, 'All Of Your Stars Are Fading Away'.
This was all watched by an impassive City chief executive Ferran Soriano, but any notion their fans would turn on the owners was dispelled by a flag reading: 'In Khaldoon We Trust. We've Won It All', a gesture of support for the embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.
City's fans also waved hundreds of inflatable bananas, an old habit when they spent time in the lower leagues in reduced circumstances. There remains the possibility they will get the chance to wave them down the tiers once more in the near future.
The first half did much to pour cold water on what started as a red-hot atmosphere, further diluted by City's second-half domination, although Liverpool's fans rammed home their disgust until the final whistle, chanting "cheat" every time their opponents passed in a lengthy period of possession.
Former Liverpool and England defender Stephen Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live: "This needs rectifying as quickly as possible, but this isn't an easy thing to come to a conclusion. It's never-ending. It's so difficult and it's going to take so long to sort out."
He added: "The hard part is that this is a brilliant Manchester City team, but you have to caveat it and say they have done it illegally and they bought their way. You're caught in what you're thinking about this City team.
"I admire them because they're so good individually and so great, but the way it has been done and put together has not been put together correctly."
While ex-Man Utd striker Wayne Rooney, added: "I know what it is like from managing Derby County when they had a points deduction. The mindset and message to the players was simple – just try to win the next game.
"All the noise around the club, from the media and other fans, will make them even hungrier to succeed."
As City walked off, they were accompanied by the taunt of "You're going down" from the Kop.
City's fans answered with the trademark: "We're not really here."
This, in essence, is what makes this Premier League campaign one that might yet be rendered void. City might win the title - but who knows if they will be here next season?
As Maresca's side move into top gear and threaten to accelerate away from the chasing pack with wins such as this, no-one has a clue what their final destination will be.

Mystery still surrounds the fatal shooting on the set of Alec Baldwin’s Western Rust, an incident that claimed the life of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. Did the actor pull the trigger on a prop gun as he rehearsed a scene (he denies that), or did the weapon malfunction and misfire? How did a live round get into the revolver and who brought the lethal ammunition to the set? Why were prosecutors in Santa Fe, NM so intent on charging Baldwin with a crime for what many impartial observers — though not all — saw as a tragic accident?
The answers to some of those questions are provided in the new documentary The Trial of Alec Baldwin, directed by Rory Kennedy, which opens in Los Angeles on Friday. The film begins by dispelling one false rumor – that Baldwin initiated the project as some sort of attempt to repair his damaged reputation. Text on screen states flatly, “Baldwin was given no editorial control, nor did he provide any financial support or receive any compensation.”
Kennedy underscored that point at the Bend Film Festival in Oregon over the weekend, where the documentary played. At a Q&A that followed the screening, the Oscar-nominated filmmaker told the audience it wasn’t Baldwin who came up with the documentary idea, but the other way around. “I approached him,” she clarified.
Watch on Deadline
They had met many years before the Rust tragedy. “I have known Alec probably for 20 years,” Kennedy said. “I would say we were friends. We wouldn’t go out and have dinner, but I knew him. Alec is actually a great supporter of documentaries and is associated with the Hamptons Film Festival and also does a summer doc series. And so I’ve been lucky enough over the years to have a number of my films be a part of that. I’ve gotten to know him largely through that.”
The documentary project began at a point when it didn’t appear the actor would face criminal allegations.
“When we entered this story,” Kennedy told the festival audience, “it really seemed like the Rust story was going to be resolved pretty early on and that [the documentary] was really going to be much more of a biopic with the Rust story interwoven maybe as a through line, kind of the backbone of it, but would be pretty thin. And then it just kept coming back and continuing. And we were always there when it had sort of dramatic turns.”
Those dramatic turns included Baldwin and Rust armorer Hannah Gutierrez-Reed being charged in January 2023 with involuntary manslaughter. A few months later, the charges against Baldwin were dropped. But then in January 2024 a grand jury indicted Baldwin on felony involuntary manslaughter charges and special prosecutors re-filed their case. The prosecution of Baldwin, the film strongly suggests, had less to do with the evidence than with the special prosecutor’s personal animus toward him as a Hollywood star with a history of volcanic behavior.
“It just seemed pretty clear that people were going after him and he was being taken to task [for the Rust shooting] in a way that seemed not entirely justified or fair,” Kennedy observed. “And then it started raising questions about how in this day and age with the internet and social media, we hold people to justice outside of the judicial system. Then as the film and the story unfolded, you started seeing how that narrative in social media started impacting the justice system.”
Kennedy described the larger concerns raised by the Baldwin prosecution. “You start thinking, okay, how does this kind of [social media] chatter that we’re all doing… how is it affecting our larger institutions? How is it affecting government, for example? …How is it affecting the judicial system? I think it’s an important question that we should be observing and asking ourselves.”
Baldwin, it becomes clear, was being tried twice – in the court of public opinion and in a court of law. The film builds to an astonishing crescendo, resulting in the case being dismissed in the middle of the trial (I won’t give away what happened. Close watchers of the case, including my colleague Dominic Patten who covered it for Deadline and appears as an expert in the documentary, know the ins and outs, but they came as a revelation to me).
There would seem to be plenty for Baldwin to appreciate about Kennedy’s film, given how the court case ended. And yet…
“When they [Baldwin and wife Hilaria] initially saw the film, they did not like the film,” the director reported. The cause of their displeasure has to do with scenes woven throughout that illustrate how Baldwin got his reputation for angry outbursts – confrontations with paparazzi through the years, for instance. Kennedy also explores a serious stain on Baldwin’s reputation from 2007 – the infamous voicemail he left for his then 11-year-old daughter Ireland in which he called her a “rude, thoughtless little pig.” That ugly lambasting came in the context of a bitter custody battle over Ireland between Baldwin and his ex-wife Kim Basinger.
It’s a crucial piece of background because the special prosecutor referred to that incident in private communications in which she expressed loathing for the actor. “Because the prosecutors were, in my opinion, going after his reputation and not after what he did on the set,” Kennedy said, “we had to show what that reputation was, and we had to show it honestly.”
A bit too honestly, perhaps, for Baldwin’s liking. “I think it was just very hard [for him] to see all that… showing his ex-wife in there and then [him wondering], ‘Why are we doing that?’ Well, the only way to really get to the voicemail is to understand that history, to understand what the motivation of the voicemail was. And you can’t get there without having that context.”
Baldwin seems to be warming to the film, after hearing feedback from viewers.
“I think he’s now come around and is much more supportive of it,” Kennedy noted. “I think there are a lot of people who say… this film is important and in many ways redeems him and also really helps people understand him and understand what he went through and understand the injustice of what happened to him.”

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

SSC GD Constable Result 2026: The Staff Selection Commission (SSC) has declared the SSC GD Constable Result 2026 on its official website, ssc.gov.in. Candidates who appeared for the computer-based examination held on April 27 and May 30 can check their qualifying status by downloading the result PDF from the portal.
According to the result data, 21,56,776 candidates appeared for the examination, of whom 1,97,408 have been provisionally shortlisted for the next stage of the recruitment process.
The shortlisted candidates include 15,782 female candidates and 1,81,251 male candidates for forces other than the Secretariat Security Force (SSF). Additionally, 375 male candidates have been shortlisted against all-India SSF vacancies.
SSC GD Constable Result 2026: Steps to check the result
Candidates can follow these steps to check their results:
Step 1: Visit the official SSC website at ssc.gov.in.
Step 2: Click on the Results section on the homepage.
Step. 3: Look for the SSC GD Constable Result 2026 link.
Step 4: Open the relevant result PDF.
Step 5: Search for your roll number or name in the document.
Step 6: Download the PDF and save it for future reference.
Candidates should ensure that they access the result through the official SSC website and retain a copy for subsequent recruitment stages.
What’s next?
Provisionally shortlisted candidates in the online test shall be called for the Physical Efficiency Test (PET) and Physical Standard Test (PST) and thereafter go through the stage of document verification and other stages in the selection process as may be applicable.
The shortlisted candidates shall keep themselves posted about the physical tests through the website of the SSC.
Final selection shall be made subject to recruitment rules and selection process as applicable.
SSC GD Constable Result 2026: Recruitment Details
The SSC GD Constable exam is held to select candidates for the posts of Constables (GD) in CAPFs, the Secretariat Security Force, and Rifleman (General Duty) in Assam Rifles. The recruitment process has declared 25,487 posts in total among the participating forces, out of which the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) has declared the maximum number of vacancies.

A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
It may seem like everyone is getting sick right now, but does an early flu season mean a rougher one?
Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?
Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.
The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.
"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
- Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
- 1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.
Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
Here's what we know.
Is everyone getting sick right now?
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.
Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.
It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.
But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.
In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
How effective is the flu shot this year?
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.
This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.
- Nova Scotia opens COVID-19, flu vaccine bookings ahead of respiratory illness season
- Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
- Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.
It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)
Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.
The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?
Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26.
In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20. It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.
- Updated COVID-19, flu vaccines available in N.B. on Oct. 13
- Alberta now providing free RSV antibodies to newborns after calls from pediatricians to expand access
Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta, with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.
In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.
COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.
Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.
Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.
In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

An Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said.
Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.
“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.
“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.
“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”
The Melbourne man was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker.
His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco.
The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

Women's billion-dollar boom leaves players behind, says Fifpro
- Published
Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress.
That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro., external
Players were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46% of respondents, up from 13% when Fifpro conducted its previous survey in 2017.
Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors.
"Players are now very visible," she said.
"Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive."
While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone.
"Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said.
In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs.
- Most women players earn less than £15,000 - Fifpro 
  - Published18 December 2025
- Legal action against Fifa to include women's schedule 
  - Published8 September
- Women's football could become 'billion pound' industry 
  - Published13 July 2023
The report states that global revenue in the women's game is expected to rise from about $581m (£439m) in 2024 to over $1bn (£756m) in 2027.
It also highlights emerging psychological pressures facing professional women's footballers.
In an increasingly digital world, players are more accessible than ever through social media, bringing them closer to fans but also exposing them to online harassment and abuse.
The Fifpro survey suggested that although salaries, visibility and investment have risen significantly since 2017, much of the professional game still operates in precarious conditions.
For Culvin, the sport's commercial growth is not yet being matched by safeguards for the players driving it.
"The economic case for women's football has been made," she said.
"I think the institutional regulatory and policy case needs to catch up quickly to protect and enhance our women's players and enable them to perform maximally."
Players don't see themselves as 'professional'
One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status.
Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing.
In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur.
All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club.
However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football.
"Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said.
The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (£1,250).
Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (£363) in Africa.
While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage.
Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels.
Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries.
Short-term contracts and late payments
Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income.
"Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin.
"There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year."
She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities.
Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere.
Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis".
The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension.
'Wake-up call' is needed, says Culvin
Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality.
"I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said.
However, not all trends were negative.
One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood.
In 2017, nearly half of respondents said wanting a family could drive them out of football.
That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago.
"What we've concluded, which I think is incredibly important, is that targeted regulatory intervention works - maternity regulations were introduced in 2021," said Culvin.
The report highlights a widening divide within the women's game. The sport's elite clubs and players have benefited from investment and visibility, yet much of the global workforce remains vulnerable.
"You've got an industry that's very focused on the top 5% of players," Culvin said.
"But then what you've got is the rest, which is 95% of the industry who are not paid on time, who have short contracts. They don't get paid for 12 months - they are in incredibly vulnerable and precarious environments."
Despite that, Fifpro insists the solution is not to slow down growth but to ensure that commercial success and player welfare develop together.
"There doesn't need to be a choice for those between commercial growth and player protection," said Culvin.
"Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem."
Her conclusion is clear.
"What we're saying is enough is enough and the industry needs to react to the players' needs and centralise the players' voice, ensure that players have a seat at the table when decisions that affect them are being made about them."

Leh, Oct 12: Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Ladakh Rahul Sharma today chaired a meeting with representatives of recognised political parties at his office chamber in Karzoo, Old Raj Niwas, Leh, to familiarise them with the ongoing revision of municipal electoral rolls for the Municipal Committees of Leh and Kargil and apprise them of the relevant eligibility criteria, enrolment procedures and timelines for submission of claims and objections. The CEO highlighted the importance of public awareness in ensuring the enrolment of all eligible electors. He encouraged representatives of recognised political parties to disseminate information about the revision exercise among the public and sensitise eligible residents, particularly those whose names may be missing from the draft rolls, about the prescribed procedures and the deadline for submission of claims and objections.

The CEO urged them to facilitate awareness among eligible residents and encourage them to verify their electoral details and take the necessary steps within the stipulated timeframe.
