'Please understand': Delhi high court refuses Monday hearing of plea against Jantar Mantar closure
The court agreed to hear the plea on Tuesday, with a petition filed by NSUI, seeking a probe into the alleged assault on the public by anti-social elements.
The Delhi High Court on Monday agreed to hear a petition on Tuesday challenging the closure of Jantar Mantar as a protest site and the government’s failure to designate an alternative venue for demonstrations,
However, a bench comprising Acting Chief Justice Nitin Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma denied the request to schedule the hearing for Monday. This comes amid protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The court also agreed to hear a petition filed by the National Students’ Union of India (NSUI), seeking a probe into the alleged assault on members of the public by anti-social elements during a protest demanding Kumar’s resignation on October 10.
The petitions were mentioned before the court by counsel representing the respective parties.
Deep Dive
Same-day hearing denied
The lawyer appearing in the Jantar Mantar matter urged the court to take up the plea on Monday, arguing that no designated site was available for peaceful protests and that Jantar Mantar had also been closed for demonstrations.
Meanwhile, counsel for the NSUI also mentioned the organisation’s plea seeking an investigation into the alleged assault by anti-social elements, saying that some on the protest carried out on October 10, some outsiders entered the protest site and harassed people with lathis.
However, the court said both matters would be heard on Tuesday.
Concerning the petition concerning the closure of Jantar Mantar, the bench observed that the Supreme Court was already seized of the issue.
“Please try to understand. The Supreme Court is seized of the matter. The Supreme Court has called upon the Union to file affidavits. Once the Supreme Court is looking into it, to what extent can we look into it? Thus, let’s hear it tomorrow,” the bench observed.
In its petition, the NSUI submitted that the victims were ordinary members of the public who were unarmed, posed no threat to anyone, and were on their way to participate in a peaceful protest. The plea alleged that the assailants were groups of anti-social elements dressed in civilian clothes, who held no official position and had no legal authority to act in such a manner.
“A public protest demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India has been underway at and around Jantar Mantar since 02.10.2026, and a further gathering was called for 10.10.2026. On that day, at about 2:00 PM, groups of men in civil dress collected at Connaught Place. They surrounded, manhandled and beat persons who had come for the protest, as well as passers-by. The incidents were recorded by persons present and by reporters of news outlets,” the petition stated.
It thus sought a time-bound probe into the alleged assaults on members of the public at Connaught Place and areas adjoining Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on October 10, to identify those involved, including the individuals, and initiate appropriate legal action against them.
It also seeks constituiton of Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by an officer not below the rank of Deputy Commissioner of Police, drawn from outside the New Delhi district, to conduct the probe under the supervision of an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner of Police, preservation and handover to the investigating team of CCTV footage recorded on October 10, 2026, between noon and 6 pm, from cameras installed from Inner and Outer Circles of Connaught Place, Indira Chowk, the stretch outside Khadi Gramodyog Bhavan, Sansad Marg, Janpath, Jantar Mantar Road and Rajiv Chowk and Janpath Metro stations.

A heroic, 7-day bike ride made this teen a global star. Where is she now?
Fame is a strange beast. It brings applause, attention and promises of a better life. But when the spotlight moves on, those promises are often forgotten. No one knows this better than 22-year-old Jyoti Kumari.
When she was 15 years old, during the peak of India's COVID shutdown, she shot to international fame for cycling over 700 miles, from northern India to her village in the eastern state of Bihar, with her injured father riding on the back of the hot pink bike she'd bought for $20.
Her dad, Mohan Paswan, drove an autorickshaw for 20 years in Gurugram, a city near Delhi, sending money to his wife and five children in the village of Sirhulli. After he suffered a debilitating road accident in January 2020, Kumari and her mom took the train to Gurugram to care for him.
Five months later, he still hadn't made a full recovery and his family was running out of money for food and rent. The family decided they would all be better off at home. But at the time, authorities had shut down public transportation for the pandemic lockdown. No one knew how Mohan Paswan could make the journey. That's when Kumari insisted she would bring him back home, riding on a pad attached to the main seat of her bicycle.
She cycled for seven consecutive days on a relatively empty stomach at the height of the lockdown to get him to safety. Even though it was a test of sheer endurance, Kumari discovered that she loved cycling — it came naturally to her.
लॉकडाउन था, सो अपने पिता को साइकिल पर बैठाकर गुरुग्राम से दरभंगा ले गई बेटी...
वीडियो: मोहन भारद्वाज और सीटू तिवारी pic.twitter.com/Mc7hkmyB4O
— BBC News Hindi (@BBCHindi) May 19, 2020
Her epic ride grabbed headlines around the world. NPR's previous reporting noted promises of cash rewards, training for a career as a cyclist, even a movie deal.
Six years later
That was in 2020. "Now — life is hard," Kumari told NPR in a phone call from her home in Bihar.
What happened to all the promises made — for financial support, especially to support cycling as a competitive sport?
Many promises were not kept, she says.
"The politicians who made promises, saying they would give money for my sports or education — nobody actually gave anything," she says. "Whatever reward money we collected back then [from individuals who extended help and a government award that came with a cash prize], we put it all into our house, rebuilding it. We had a brick house before, but it only had bare walls. Now we have completed it, added a toilet, a bathroom, and a running water connection. By doing all that, the house has finally become livable," she says.
This is no small achievement. An estimated 300,000 people are homeless in the state of Bihar in spite of government programs. For a family living in poverty, having a home can make a huge difference in the fight for survival.
For Kumari's family, making their house livable meant securing something that burst of fame had failed to deliver on — a more stable place from which to build their lives.
But they are doing so without her dad.
Mohan Paswan passed away of a heart attack in May 2021, just months after his daughter brought him home. Kumari says she felt heartbroken. After his passing, financial security has been precarious for the family.
At the moment, her mother works as a cook. Her meager income supports Kumari and her three siblings at home (an older sister has married and moved out).
"There are days when we go to sleep hungry," she says. "Our brother-in-law used to help us earlier, but now he also has a child, a wife and his father to take care of. He works a small job in the city — how much can he really do? So now he isn't able to help us much."
Still she holds out hope for a better future.
"Once my education is fully complete, only then will I be able to do something else. Only then can I prepare for things and look for a job," Kumari says.
But she has yet to pass the final exam required to complete Class 12, her final year of secondary school. That's an important credential to apply to university or qualify for certain jobs. It's a stepping stone to a better life, especially for disadvantaged students.
A typical day
Finding time for her studies has been a challenge. Kumari's day begins at 7 a.m. She cooks and cares for her younger siblings after her mother rushes off to work. "I give my brothers breakfast for school and get things ready for my sister. Then, I clean the house, mop the floors, do the dishes, wash clothes by hand, take a bath," she says.
By the time she can turn her attention to her studies, she says it feels as if she has already done a gazillion chores. "There are days when I sleep because of the sheer exhaustion of it all."
What she hopes for
Whatever the future holds, she is determined to stay in their native village rather than seeking employment in the big city, as her father did. His experience showed her how precarious day labor can be — he had no savings and no medical support after his injury.
Kumari is firm about living in their native village. "Whatever I do, I want to do from here," she says.
She says she still loves cycling as much as ever. She loves the wind in her hair, the feeling of going somewhere, of feeling free. That's what the bike represents to her. But she doesn't have the time to do it as much these days as she's bogged down by household chores and small but persistent everyday worries. She can't just cycle for the joy of it or train as a competitive sport. She only cycles to do errands for the family.
With her own progress on hold, the family has quietly set their hopes on her younger sister who will take her 12th grade exams in mid-2027. If she manages to pass and get into a good college, their prospects will improve once she graduates and starts working.
But Kumari hasn't given up. "When you're poor, fame doesn't help. Only education can help you out of your difficulties. Otherwise, life becomes a never-ending obstacle course," Kumari says.

On 10 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised a major protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which protesters claim led to arbitrary voter deletions. In response to the demonstrations, authorities imposed a security crackdown, shutting down dozens of metro stations, cancelling trains, and enforcing prohibitory orders across the capital. Police have detained thousands of individuals, including political figures like Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Mamata Banerjee, as well as CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who were later released.
In this context, a video (here & here) showing large groups of people rallying on the road is being shared with claims that it depicts protesters marching toward Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing protesters marching towards Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest on 10 October 2026.
Fact: The video is unrelated to the October 10 CJP protests. The visuals date to January 2021 and depict the farmers’ protests. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to an Instagram post (archive) from January 2021 linking the footage to the farmers’ protest in Delhi. The same video has since been misattributed to several other events (here, here & here).
Further research revealed that visuals identical to those seen in the viral video were published by media outlets like the Associated Press and Firstpost, as well as on stock image websites like Alamy, in January 2021. According to these sources, the visuals are from the 2021 farmers’ protest. This proves that the viral video predates the October 10 CJP protest and is entirely unrelated to it
To sum it up, an old video from the 2021 farmers’ protest is being falsely linked to the October 10 Jantar Mantar CJP protest.

A skin problem can begin with something familiar. An itch that persists. A rash that returns. A patch that looks different from the rest of the skin. What happens next often depends on where a person lives and whether appropriate care is within reach.
The Global Access to Skin Health Observatory is a landmark global study led by Esther Freeman in collaboration with the International League of Dermatological Societies (ILDS) and L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. Published in JAMA Dermatology, it brings together data from 158 countries representing 97% of the world’s population.
For India, the findings raise questions about where specialists practise, how patients reach them and what happens when treatment is delayed.
What the numbers miss
The study proposes a benchmark of 5.63 per lakh, derived from countries reporting adequate access to dermatological care. This, however, is a reference point, rather than a universal staffing prescription. Dr. Freeman, who is associate professor of dermatology at Harvard Medical School and director of global health dermatology at Massachusetts General Hospital, places India’s dermatologist density well below the benchmark at around 0.5 to 1 per lakh people.
Ramesh Bhat, the Indian co-author of the study and professor at Father Muller Medical College and head of research at Father Muller Research Centre, Mangalore, cautions against directly comparing India with Europe or the Americas, because their health systems differ. What surprises Prof Bhat is that shortages persist despite the number of postgraduate dermatology training seats. He points to the urban-rural divide, with a concentration of specialists in urban areas, and in many cities in southern India, while rural communities face a different reality, where access even to a doctor may be limited.
The study reports that, globally, 79% of dermatologists practise in urban areas. National averages can therefore conceal substantial local gaps. “Dermatologist density gives us an important starting point, but it does not tell us whether a patient can actually receive care,” Dr. Freeman says.
When care is delayed
For Prof Bhat, the consequences are visible in clinical practice. He identifies “delay in diagnosis, wrong treatment, steroid abuse” among the problems arising when appropriate care is unavailable. He singles out leprosy as a condition where delayed diagnosis has implications beyond the individual patient. His concern brings the discussion back to what happens before someone reaches a specialist and whether the treatment they receive along the way is appropriate.
Dr Freeman emphasises the breadth of skin disease, from common infections to chronic inflammatory conditions and neglected tropical diseases. She argues that skin health must be recognised as an essential part of healthcare, with investment directed towards services that already reach communities.
The question is, how to make those services capable of recognising and managing skin disease safely.
Bringing expertise closer
“We need more dermatologists, but we cannot train our way out of this problem with specialists alone,” Dr Freeman says. Primary-care physicians and health officers already manage substantial amounts of skin disease. She advocates practical training, essential medicines and clear referral pathways, allowing common conditions to be treated locally while complex disease and uncertain diagnoses reach specialists.
Prof Bhat also proposes that medical colleges adopt villages, strengthening their links with surrounding communities. He also sees a role for the district residency programme, which takes residents into district settings, and for health camps in reaching rural and tribal populations.
These approaches sit alongside his call for rural specialist clinics and teledermatology. His emphasis is on extending the reach of existing teaching institutions and services, while giving residents the training needed to work effectively beyond major urban centres.
Making remote advice useful
“Teledermatology can be implemented,” Prof Bhat says. But he cautions that training healthcare workers must not result in unqualified practice or drug misuse. Expanding access requires clarity about who can manage a condition and when specialist assessment is necessary.
Dr. Freeman makes a related point. Teledermatology and Artificial Intelligence use need trained frontline providers, available treatment, and reliable referral arrangements. A patient requiring a biopsy, urgent assessment or specialist therapy must still be able to obtain it. “The goal is not to replace dermatologists, but to make their expertise reach much further,” she says.
A remote consultation needs to connect with treatment and follow-up. Advice alone cannot resolve the practical difficulties of obtaining medicines or reaching a referral centre.
What progress should look like
In 2025, the World Health Assembly recognised skin diseases as a global public-health priority. The next step is translating that recognition into national funding and delivery plans.
Prof Bhat’s priorities include an adequate health budget and insurance coverage for dermatological medicines such as biologics and for procedures. He also calls for better training of dermatology residents and dermatology nursing as a separate speciality within nursing education. These proposals bring together workforce development, treatment affordability and rural services, addressing several barriers to appropriate dermatological care.
Measuring progress will require listening more closely to patients. Dr. Freeman acknowledges that the Observatory relied on national leaders and health-system informants, rather than patients directly. Future work should examine waiting times, travel, affordability and diagnostic delays, alongside outcomes and quality of life.
Her planned next phase will examine selected countries more closely to understand where clinicians choose to train and practise, what retains them in underserved areas and which models improve access in different settings. “Five years from now, success should not simply mean there are more dermatologists,” she says. “It should mean that where someone lives is less predictive of whether they can get appropriate care for their skin disease.”
For India, that would mean earlier recognition, appropriate treatment and dependable referral, with fewer patients left to navigate the gaps themselves.
(Dr. Monisha Madhumita is assistant professor, department of dermatology, Saveetha Medical College and Hospitals, Chennai. mail.monisha.m@gmail.com)

NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.
The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.
In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.
Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.
For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.
For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.
Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.
The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

The Trump administration announced Thursday that it is investigating nine universities for alleged fraud related to visas commonly used by postdoctoral researchers, a core part of the nation’s biomedical workforce.
Vice President JD Vance announced during a press briefing that Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Pittsburgh, and UC Davis are under investigation by the Department of Labor. During the briefing, Vance asserted that these schools are improperly using J-1 visas, the main class of visa used by international postdocs, to bring in cheap labor rather than relying on domestic researchers.
“They’re using these visas way too much,” he said. “They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”
Vance asserted that these schools employ researchers on J-1 visas for work connected to federal grants at a rate of 61% compared to a national average of 38%. STAT contacted the White House and the Vice President’s office for clarification on where these figures came from but did not receive immediate replies. National Science Foundation data show that nearly 60% of postdocs in science, engineering, and health are temporary visa holders; most of these researchers would be on J-1 visas.
The labor department’s inspector general, Anthony D’Esposito, said during the briefing that his office has already issued subpoenas to the schools under scrutiny. He added that he will investigate whether “foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research.”
“If an American university is breaking the law to save a dollar while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal,” he said. “I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is. Break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square.”
Kimberly Allen, an MIT spokesperson, confirmed in an email to STAT that the university received a “very broad subpoena” on Thursday morning that it is now reviewing. She did not elaborate on the details of the subpoena or what kinds of information had been requested.
“Each J-1 visa holder at MIT has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government, and we take seriously our obligations to follow U.S. law,” Allen wrote.
Spokespersons for Stanford, Yale, and Harvard did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
It’s unclear how much evidence the administration has to support its visa fraud concerns, and D’Esposito’s office didn’t immediately respond to questions about the investigation’s scope or expected timeline. But Thursday’s announcement fits into a series of moves by the Trump administration to more tightly restrict the entry of international students and scholars into the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security has attempted to place a four-year cap on how long foreign graduate students and postdocs can stay in the country, alleging that the current system allows these scholars to remain indefinitely and incentivizes fraud. On Wednesday, the Trump administration announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program used by international students seeking professional experience. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as engineering and biotech.
These proposed restrictions have yet to take effect and have in some cases been temporarily blocked by lawsuits. But Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney in Boston, warned that these efforts send a clear sign to international scientists that their contributions are no longer valued, a message she worries could compromise U.S. scientific leadership.
“This is an incredible series of self-owns,” she said. “The government also knows that none of this will stand up in court. They just want to send a message: Don’t come here. But we will lose [out] on so much. It’s going to take decades for us to repair the damage when this is over.”

The federal government has released new quality ratings for Medicare Advantage insurers for 2027, with Humana emerging as the biggest winner.
But deep uncertainty remains around Medicare Advantage quality measures, which come with tens of billions of dollars in extra revenue for the highest-performing plans. One health insurance company, Alignment Healthcare, has already threatened to sue the government after its star ratings were downgraded — a now-common occurrence for almost any insurer that is unhappy with its grades.
Nearly 71% of Medicare Advantage enrollees are currently in a plan that will have at least four out of five stars for quality, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Getting at least four stars triggers bonuses, which total $13 billion across the industry annually. Ratings for 2027 lead to bonus payouts in 2028.

DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season
- Published
The DP World Tour will not allow any player who signs up to LIV Golf next season to be a member of its circuit in 2027.
The European tour says players must "make a choice" regarding where they play and has taken a significantly tougher stance than it has done in recent seasons.
Players must be members of the DP World Tour to be able to play for Europe in the Ryder Cup.
Deadlines for both tours are in the next five weeks, although there remains uncertainty surrounding LIV Golf's future, despite it securing a possible $300m in funding as it attempts to restructure.
"Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, CEO of the DP World Tour, told BBC Sport.
"We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by.
"Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."
In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV.
Next year, however, players will be asked to disclose which tours they intend to play on, and their answer will be taken into account when deciding on their membership.

Around 15 LIV players, including Rahm, Hatton, Victor Perez and Tom McKibbin, have "status" with the DP World Tour, meaning they have eligibility under one of the membership categories.
Other LIV players, like Joaquin Niemann and Thomas Pieters, do not have such status so would either need to go through qualifying school or sign agreements with the DP World Tour whereby they would receive invitations to a set number of tournaments.
However, those agreements would only be available to players who were not part of LIV in the future.
BBC Sport has been told that the DP World Tour will not accept membership from anyone intending to play on what is being called LIV 2.0.
If players do not disclose their intentions to play LIV and go on to do so, that will be considered grounds on which to have their membership terminated.
LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September as it attempted to restructure, following the withdrawal of its multi-billion dollar funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.
Last week, it announced it had secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.
LIV equity offer changes DP World Tour's approach
While the DP World Tour agreed to grant conditional releases with nine players this season, it is understood the change for 2027 is predominantly down to LIV offering players equity in future and a feeling this is incompatible with the European tour being a members organisation.
However, it also comes at a time when the DP World Tour's strategic alliance with the PGA Tour is being negotiated, so the move likely reflects a desire to put itself in the best position possible in those discussions.
Players will have until 16 November to sign up to the DP World Tour for next year.
Under the terms of its court-supervised restructuring process, LIV Golf needs to sign players up by 25 October.
Ted Goldthorpe, head of BC Partners Credit, told BBC Sport last week he was "confident" LIV would have a "critical mass" of players.
But since then two-time major winner Rahm has said he will not continue playing on the LIV tour.
Lawyers representing a number of other players, including fellow major winners Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith, sought clarification from the court that rejection of contracts would equate to "termination", enabling players to hold discussions with third parties about their futures.
Richard Bland is currently the only player to have stated publicly a desire to play on LIV 2.0.
However, Perez indicated last month he hoped there would be a future for the league.

Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department plans to set up next spring a section dedicated to the investigation and prevention of accidents involving autonomous driving, the force has said.
High-level knowledge and skills are necessary to investigate the causes of such accidents and the Tokyo police hope to accumulate expertise and share it with police departments in other prefectures amid the spread of autonomous driving trials held across the country.
The new section, to be created within the police department’s traffic bureau, will be in charge of handling applications for Level 4 services — under which a system handles all driving operations under specified conditions — as well as investigating accidents and advocating accident prevention.
Taxi-hailing app operator Go, U.S. self-driving technology firm Waymo and taxi operator Nihon Kotsu announced in September that they will jointly launch driverless taxi services in Tokyo in 2027, marking Japan’s first such commercial service.
The service would use Level 4 autonomous driving and the companies plan to expand the fleet to about 100 vehicles gradually.
The government aims to increase the number of buses, taxis and trucks operating with autonomous driving services to 10,000 vehicles in fiscal 2030.

Supreme Court stresses due process as detentions continue; Opposition and CJP vow to press on with protests
Monday will also see the Opposition return to the streets with a march to the Supreme Court.
A phalanx of 40,000 security personnel detained roughly 700 people on Sunday as sporadic protests against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar continued to bubble up across the Capital for a second consecutive day as the Supreme Court underlined that detentions must be lawful and traffic movement eased with the metro running and fewer road barriers.
The leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) –– a satirical movement that forced the education minister’s resignation three months ago –– were released after signing a bond promising “to maintain peace and good behaviour” for one year. But a day after their dramatic detention from a flight, the CJP leaders said they’ll press on with the protests and seek permission on Monday for a new stir.
“The CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated…we will hit the streets again,” CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said on X before heading back to Maharashtra to deal with a bereavement. Dipke also said he had not signed a bond barring him and other CJP leaders from staging further protests.
Deep Dive

CJP leaders vow to resume protests after release
Monday will also see the Opposition return to the streets with a march to the Supreme Court. Leaders of the INDIA bloc said they had an appointment to meet Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Monday afternoon but court officials denied the claim.
The developments came a day after security personnel turned the Capital into a fortress to thwart the planned protest, launching an unprecedented clampdown that saw the detention of 7,000 people, internet services suspended near Jantar Mantar, cancellation of many long-distance trains to Delhi and the controversial closure of 45 Metro stations.
In addition, right-wing groups thrashed many protesters in front of the police, laid spike strips on arterial roads, erected thousands of yellow barricades that choked traffic, and put up loudspeakers that blared prerecorded police warnings against unlawful gatherings.
Also Read | No illegal detention of protesters in Delhi; metro, internet to run normally: Supreme Court
Delhi sees partial return to normalcy after security crackdown
Sunday was relatively calmer, with the Metro open, trains back on track and some roads opened. But central Delhi was shrouded in a security blanket even as some protesters made it past barricades for short-lived agitations that melted away as police bundled them away into buses, triggering allegations of brutality. Many journalists and bystanders were also picked up, sparking a controversy.
Sanjay Kumar, who was visiting Delhi from Bihar, said, “I had come for an excursion to the India Gate on Sunday but police said I would not be able to sit on the lawns, or even walk to monument. They asked us to take a photo and leave.”
The drama on Sunday began around 3am when YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was released from detention. He alleged he was abducted. Around 9.30am, CJP leaders Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were produced before the executive magistrate and released on a surety and a bond of ₹50,000.
Roughly two hours later, in a special hearing, the Supreme Court ordered that peaceful, unarmed protester cannot be detained except in accordance with the “procedure established by law”, while further directing that metro and railway services in Delhi operate normally, internet connectivity remain undisturbed and free movement of people be restored.
The court also ordered authorities to remove a notice imposing prohibitory restrictions around the Supreme Court and other court complexes to ensure unhindered “access to justice”.
A special bench of justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the directions after an urgent hearing on petitions alleging mass detentions, restrictions on movement, suspension of internet services and non-compliance with the court’s October 9 order on transport curbs.
The bench directed that metro and rail facilities run normally unless restrictions are required to address a public order situation within the framework of Article 19(2) of the Constitution. It further ordered that people’s free movement in the city be permitted subject to law, internet services remain undisturbed in accordance with law, and no person be detained except in accordance with the procedure established by law, particularly in the case of peaceful, unarmed assemblies beyond the area covered by a prohibitory order under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
“We would like to ponder on how far the police acts fall in sync with the requirement of expression under Article 19,” the court said after many petitioners challenged the preventive detention of Opposition leaders, and questioned the legality of the restrictions and sought accountability for alleged police excesses.
By then, hundreds of protesters had reached Connaught Place to shout slogans against Kumar, only for them to be picked up ––triggering allegations that the police were breaching the apex court’s orders.
“Manhandled, dragged, assaulted and misbehaved inside a police vehicle and dumped by the roadside - for the crime of speaking to the media. This is not merely an assault on an MP. It is an assault on democratic freedoms and the rule of law. More chillingly, it happened within hours of the Supreme Court issuing directions to safeguard peaceful protest and constitutional rights,” said MP John Brittas, one of the detainees.
The Delhi Police public relations officer did not respond to requests seeking comment.
Detentions continued in central Delhi, RK Puram, Nigambodh Ghat, and RK Ashram, especially after Left student leader Neha Bora marched in protest around 2.30pm. Police picked up at least 12 journalists –– many of them from prominent media houses –– and detained many people walking on the road, standing or passing by.
Rapid Action Force, Central Reserve Police Force personnel and anti-riot vehicles were deployed in Connaught Place, and 30 traffic diversion points set up across the city. Police personnel were seen stopping people and checking their identity documents on roads leading towards central Delhi. HT saw officers questioning people about their source and destination.
Detentions continued till around 8pm –– including that of a man sitting inside a fast food joint in Connaught Place. Police said the detainees were released “before 10pm”.

SIR row adds to pressure on chief election commissioner
The unrest is part of a longer string of events that have mounted pressure on Kumar over the controversial special intensive revision –– which has already deleted 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls –– and other allegations. The developments come after an Indian Express investigation said election commissioners SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded written dissents and objections at least 14 times between November 2025 and August 2026 and even written to the cabinet secretary. It also alleged that election officials found their access to the ECI software curtailed by the central IT team. ECI said differing views and observations were a normal part of deliberation and that all its digital platforms operated under strict data security protocols.
Delhi BJP spokesperson Praveen Shankar Kapoor said the CJP and AAP were misleading young people.
“These leaders are pushing young people into a movement that could ruin their careers,” he said.
Despite the mass detentions, there appeared to be no hold-up in the unrest.

The State informed the Kerala High Court that in-principle approval had not been granted to Keralam for establishing an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar enquired into the reason why Keralam was not prioritised for building an AIIMS, even though the matter had been pending for almost 10 years. The Bench was considering a petition seeking establishment of an AIIMS under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY).
The court observed that the matter was presently at the stage of inter-ministerial consultation and any decision for setting up an AIIMS could be taken only after the continuation of the PMSSY scheme for the next five financial years, FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, was approved.
In a previous order, the court noted that the idea of having an AIIMS in Keralam was raised in June 2016 and four locations were identified for this purpose. The court opined that Keralam should be considered on a priority basis considering the density of population, and asked the Union government to take a conscious decision concerning the proposal for the institute.
Prioritising other States
The Deputy Solicitor General of India, O.M. Shalina, informed the court that since Keralam had better health-care conditions than other States, the Union government was prioritising those States with a weaker health sector. At this point the court enquired whether the Union government’s stand was that Keralam did not require an AIIMS. The court orally asked whether the hospitals in the State were a disqualification or a ‘handicap’ to consider the establishment of the institute. The court orally remarked that Keralam had the highest density of population in the country, and that the existing hospitals would not be sufficient to provide medical facilities to the needy and poor.
The Union government responded that while considering all other States and Union Territories, Keralam’s status was much better, and that was the reason for the delay in approval. The court then enquired why there was an AIIMS in Delhi and two or three institutes in some other States, if the criteria was availability of medical facilities.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.

As what was left of Hurricane Isaias moved north on Sunday, bringing moderate to heavy rainfall across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region, nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power.
Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the south-eastern US, especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and south-eastern Atlantic coasts.
According to the National Weather Service, parts of the Carolinas and Virginia, including Raleigh, Richmond and Washington DC were under threat of tornadoes on Sunday.
At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell on to homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.
Isaias came ashore as a category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. This has been the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024.
Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
In Florida’s Escambia county, sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home – and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from four to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds.
One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, the city’s fire chief, Cory Moon, said. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour county, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.
Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.
Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after the president did the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid.
The US Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve to address disruptions in supply because of the storm.
The NWS said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened to 155mph (250kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a category 5 storm, as it approached Mexico’s coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall beginning on Sunday to parts of south-western Mexico with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Forecasters say that conditions brought by Simon are spreading northward along a stretch of coastline that includes Puerto Vallarta. Rain could average 8-16in over sectors of south-western Mexico, with as much as 30in possible in places across Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco through Monday.
A woman, a man and their dog in Burke county, North Carolina, were rescued on the Catawba River after their camping trip was overflown by the rising water brought by remnants of Simon that caught them off guard.
Tropical storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and southern California. The National Weather Service has issued a flash flood warning in parts of San Diego, Riverside and Imperial counties. Officials issued mandatory evacuation orders for some residents in the Long Beach peninsula through Tuesday.
Eight buildings have been red-tagged, or deemed unsafe to enter, and one has been yellow-tagged amid conditions from Rachel. Long Beach officials have provided about 11,000 sandbags for the storm to protect homes from the rising tide.

Burnham to release details of Man City meetings
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.
An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.
Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.
"I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast.
"I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester.
"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."
The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".
However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.
Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.
City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.
Burnham defends comments on Man City
Burnham was mayor of Manchester from 2017 until earlier this year and his tenure took place during a sustained period of success for City.
As mayor, he championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.
"I don't think I misspoke," said Burnham of his past comments on Man City's owners.
"What I would say is my mind hadn't been on all of the issues. My mind had been on Labour Party conference and I was doing interviews in relation to it.
"And also, I didn't link those two things. You know, the questions linked those two things. What I would say is they're very separate.
"The football issues are different from the investment issues. People will try and conflate those two things, but they shouldn't, in my view.
"The football issues, the findings of the independent commission are serious, as I said in the interview."
The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.
An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.
The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".
A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

In a tent camp in Ceuta, migrants weigh justice, safety and returning home
Migrants in Ceuta face a humanitarian crisis, with some alleging abuse by Spanish soldiers
CEUTA, Spain -- Many of the migrants in a sprawling tent village in Ceuta came searching for better economic opportunities. Others fled war and violence, or sought refuge in Spain because of their gender or sexuality.
With a humanitarian crisis unfolding, some have come forward with allegations of abuse.
Interviews at the now-demolished camp revealed migrants' motivations for seeking protection.
A Moroccan migrant recalled pressing his shirt against his head in the early morning. The blood kept flowing.
A group of Spanish soldiers had tied his head to a tree that September morning, he said, and struck him in the head, on the back and on his arms. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear for his safety.
The soldiers had approached him and another migrant and told them to follow, saying that their superior would register them, according to a police report he filed, which The Associated Press has reviewed.
“They stuffed us into the trunk of a car, locked us in and drove us to the forest,” he said in an interview on Oct. 1. His mouth was covered with gray electrical tape, he said.
“When they were beating me, I saw death, only death," he said. “Imagine your face being tied to a tree while they strike your head, taking hit after hit, right to the front of your face.”
He received staples in his head for his injuries, he said, and showed the AP his healing wounds. He said he wants to hold the soldiers to account.
Spanish prosecutors are investigating reports of torture and mistreatment of migrants in Ceuta, including minors. Amnesty International published a report in September detailing allegations of inhumane treatment by Spanish soldiers.
“I never thought anything like this could happen,” the artisan said. “We truly believed the people here are good and that the government is decent."
“Sometimes I ask myself why I even came here, but other times I tell myself that God will help me.”
A transgender teen swam to Ceuta in July from the Moroccan city of Fnideq. Soon, he thought, he would be in a shelter. Instead, he spent nearly two months at the beachside camp.
He left home because of the challenges of being transgender, he said. He spoke on the condition of anonymity due to fears of reprisals for his gender identity.
“People in Morocco don’t have any mercy," he said in an interview on Sept. 29. “They look at the outside of you, not the inside.”
In Ceuta, he said he briefly lived with extended family, but they kicked him out after learning about his identity. “They didn't accept my situation,” he said.
Spain's asylum law recognizes gender identity and sexual orientation as valid grounds for seeking protection. Cases are assessed individually.
In early October, he returned to Morocco after police cleared the camp.
A soft-spoken 34-year-old man left Tetouan, in northern Morocco, after his brother found pictures of him and his boyfriend on his phone and threatened to report them to the police.
The brothers were already in a bitter dispute over the sale of a family home. In a previous argument, he said his brother had burned him with hot oil.
He spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals from his family, community and the Moroccan government.
Consensual sexual activity with members of the same sex is illegal in Morocco, and can be publishable by fines and up to three years imprisonment. Hundreds of men and women are prosecuted annually under such laws, according to the U.S. State Department.
Homosexuality is regularly cited as an asylum claim for Moroccans attempting to flee.
“I left Morocco because being gay is so hard," he said.
A 28-year-old Moroccan asylum seeker said he received death threats for posting content online that is critical of Islam.
In 2025, he hosted TikTok livestreams focused on the religion. He began receiving death threats, and says he was kidnapped in Marrakech by a follower.
“That was the tipping point,” he said.
The AP was not able to independently verify his claims, but viewed a copy of his asylum paperwork in which he detailed them to Spanish authorities.
He spoke on condition of anonymity due to fear of reprisals. Publicly criticizing Islam in Morocco can lead to criminal prosecution, carrying prison sentences and fines.
He crossed into Ceuta in July, joining tens of thousands more.
“The first week was pure survival” he said. “It felt like running from zombies; some people wanted to attack you, others wanted to rob you.”
He fears for his safety if he is sent back to Morocco.

Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
- Published
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.
"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."
It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".
In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.
That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.
"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."
Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."
Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.
"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.
The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.
"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.
"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."
In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.
"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.
"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.
"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.
"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is among the most widespread of human viruses. More than 90% of adults are estimated to have been infected during their lifetime. Most people acquire the infection during childhood without developing symptoms. In some, particularly those infected during adolescence or adulthood, it can cause infectious mononucleosis. The virus then remains in the body for life.
A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates that about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. The analysis incorporates recent evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer and places EBV among the infectious agents responsible for a substantial cancer burden worldwide.
What is Epstein-Barr virus?
EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, belongs to the herpesvirus family. It spreads mainly through saliva, including through kissing or sharing drinks, food, eating utensils and toothbrushes.
According to WHO, many people infected with EBV have no symptoms. When illness occurs, symptoms can include fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and marked fatigue. Infectious mononucleosis generally improves within a few weeks, although fatigue can last longer.
After the initial infection, EBV remains in the body in a dormant state. In most healthy people, the immune system keeps the infection under control.
EBV is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen. It has established causal links with several cancers, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma. The latest IARC analysis also incorporates evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer.
Who is at risk?
Most people infected with EBV do not develop cancer. The infection is therefore not, by itself, an indication that a person will develop cancer.
People with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of serious EBV-related disease. This includes some people who have undergone organ or stem-cell transplantation and those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.
The cancers associated with EBV also vary geographically. Nasopharyngeal cancer, for instance, is particularly prevalent in parts of eastern and southeastern Asia. The development of EBV-associated cancer is thought to involve factors beyond the infection itself.
How is it diagnosed?
A person does not normally need to be tested simply because EBV is common.
When infectious mononucleosis is suspected, doctors may make a diagnosis based on the symptoms and clinical examination. Blood tests can provide supporting evidence. These include tests for heterophile antibodies and EBV-specific antibodies, which can help determine whether an infection is recent or occurred in the past.
In suspected EBV-related cancers or serious disease in people with compromised immunity, more specialised tests may be needed. These can include testing for EBV genetic material in blood or other samples and examination of tumour tissue for the presence of the virus.
A positive EBV antibody test does not mean that a person has cancer. Since infection is so common, evidence of past infection is expected in most adults.
What are the treatment options?
There is no treatment that removes latent EBV from the body and there is currently no vaccine against the virus.
According to WHO, treatment for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis is mainly supportive. Rest, adequate fluids and medicines to control fever and pain may be advised. Antibiotics do not treat EBV because it is a virus.
People with mononucleosis may also be advised to avoid strenuous activity and contact sports for a period, particularly if the spleen is enlarged, because of the risk of splenic injury.
When EBV is associated with cancer, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted treatment or a combination of these.
Can EBV be prevented?
There is currently no vaccine against EBV. Preventing transmission can also be difficult because infected people may spread the virus without knowing that they have it.
WHO advises avoiding the sharing of drinks, utensils, toothbrushes and other items that come into contact with saliva.
The development of an EBV vaccine is an important area of research. The latest IARC analysis adds to the evidence on the virus’s contribution to cancer and highlights the need for continued research into prevention.

Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option. The new Fitbit Edge slots right in between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air, featuring a compact screen and more health sensors than the Air. You won’t get all the apps and features of the Pixel Watch 5, but the Edge is only about half as expensive.
The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic. Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge. It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection. Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6. It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck.
The Edge works with Android or iPhones via the Google Health app, and it can run for about seven days on a charge. If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data). However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode. If you turn it on, battery life drops to about two days, barely longer than the Pixel Watch 5.
The Fitbit Edge plays it right down the middle in Google’s wearable lineup, and not just in price and size—button count also splits the difference. The Pixel Watch has two buttons, the Air has none, and the Edge sports a single tactile side button. You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts. Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though.

Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks.

South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.
The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.
The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.
On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.
