‘Cannot be at the cost of public trust’: Prominent citizens seek independent probe into police entry at Bangla Sahib during anti-EC stir in Delhi
The letter, addressed to the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi and the Delhi Police Commissioner, was issued by Citizens for Fraternity - Bharat (CFF-Bharat).
Seventeen former officials and public figures, including ex-Delhi lieutenant governor Najeeb Jung and former chief election commissioner S Y Quraishi, have expressed “serious concern” over the entry of police into Gurudwara Bangla Sahib during the October 10 protests, and sought an independent, time-bound inquiry, in a letter dated October 11.
The letter, addressed to the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi and the Delhi Police Commissioner, was issued by Citizens for Fraternity - Bharat (CFF-Bharat), with copies to the Prime Minister, the Union Home Minister and the chairperson of the National Commission for Minorities.
“Places of worship must not become extensions of police operations during public demonstrations,” the letter, also signed by former Chief Justice of the Patna high court Iqbal Ahmed Ansari, said.
Deep Dive
CFF-Bharat is an informal group of citizens working to promote fraternity, dialogue and social harmony, and Jung is its chairman. Its letterhead describes its aim as promoting harmony, dialogue, constitutional values and fraternity.
The row stems from the October 10 demonstrations called by the Cockroach Janta Party against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The protests were linked to demands for his resignation, and security was tightened across the capital.
Bangla Sahib, near Connaught Place, is among the most visited Sikh shrines in the capital. The letter says its “longstanding tradition of offering refuge and assistance to all” must not be compromised by the pressures of political confrontation.
Visitors remove their footwear before entering a Sikh place of worship, and entering with shoes on is considered disrespectful. That is why the footage of police personnel at the shrine drew sharp reactions, and why the letter says the sanctity and autonomy of such places deserve “the highest degree of respect”.
The row explained
Videos on social media alleged that Delhi police personnel entered the shrine premises wearing shoes during preventive security operations. The clips spread quickly and made the question of police presence at a religious site part of the debate around the protests.
Police said the footage showed personnel walking along a common passage that leads to the area where visitors remove their shoes. It called the claims misleading and said they were circulated with “malicious intent”.
The cops later registered an FIR on the basis of a complaint by the Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee, naming AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal and other party leaders over the protest and the videos.
Not everyone reads the row the same way. One analysis argued that footage of personnel in the common passage was quickly turned into a political charge that police had entered a gurudwara. The FIR also adds a legal track to the demand for an inquiry.
Two questions are now running together. One is factual, whether personnel crossed the footwear point, which police deny and say their own video shows. The other is about judgment, whether police presence in or near the shrine complex was needed at all. The letter speaks to the second.
What the letter says
The letter takes note of the police clarification, but says it does not resolve the “fundamental question” of whether entry into a revered religious institution was necessary, justified and carried out with appropriate restraint.
It calls for an “independent, transparent and time-bound inquiry” into the circumstances of police entry and the extent of the intervention. The inquiry should also examine any objections raised by the Gurudwara authorities and whether established religious protocols were followed, it adds.
The signatories accept that the State has an “unquestionable duty” to maintain public order. But, they say, its powers must be exercised within constitutional limits, “with sensitivity to religious practices and respect for human dignity”.
They also urged Delhi Police to issue clear operational guidelines, in consultation with religious management bodies. The aim, the letter says, is to prevent “unnecessary police intrusion into places of worship”.
“Public order cannot be maintained at the cost of public trust, religious dignity or constitutional freedoms,” the letter says.
The signatories expect the authorities to address their concerns promptly and to make the findings and corrective measures public.

Leaves are a problem of addition by subtraction: Just a couple of mature trees can drop enough debris that you need to remove, and in the process, consume hours of your weekends. Mowing leaves into mulch is a compelling option, but you’ll still need to wrangle them off driveways, walkways, flower beds, and patios. Gas blowers have long been the standard, but rising noise bans, finicky engines that are hard to start, and battery advances are cutting into their appeal.
If you’re on the fence about a leaf blower, know that owning one of any kind will reduce the amount of raking you do, but rarely eliminate it. For small yards, or if you (or your neighbor) have just one medium-sized deciduous tree, a rake and a tarp may be all you need. On the other hand, if you live in an arboretum, the long runtime of a gas backpack blower may be worth the maintenance headaches—unless you’re willing to invest heavily in multiple batteries.
I’ve tested the newest crop of battery-powered blowers on everything from heavy fabric leaves to gravel, mulch, and even knocking over a concrete paver. Today’s models deliver serious clearing power without the gas-can hassle, though runtime is always the primary trade-off. Here’s everything you need to know about battery-powered blowers.
Featured

Best Overall
When factoring in overall performance along with the quality and diversity of Ego’s outdoor tool ecosystem, this blower is the best option for most users. In testing, it delivered gaslike power, easily knocking over a 5-pound brick paver on high speed where lesser machines required turbo mode, and it cleared the test patch of leaves without issue, without relying on turbo. Even with all that power, it was the second-quietest machine on turbo, registering about 89.7 decibels at an arm’s-length distance of 30 inches—though Ego still suggests hearing protection.
A bright, 1.75-inch LCD serves as the tool’s dashboard and is easy to read even in direct sunlight, though some details, like confirmation that a battery is installed, add clutter without much information. The electronic cruise control is intuitive: squeeze the variable-speed trigger to your desired speed, press the speed lock button, then release the trigger. The blower maintains that pace until you press the speed lock button again.
Ergonomically, the blower’s relatively narrow frame keeps the tool comfortable and tight to your body during operation, and the unit naturally pitches the nozzle towards the floor. A plastic grid covering the air intake and battery location helps prevent stray leaves from clogging the vents. The included fan nozzle widens the airflow for clearing hardscapes, though on a lawn, it can scatter leaves rather than help corral them. The tool sits securely on a wide base so it doesn’t tip very easily, and has a stubby, 4.5-inch-long nozzle beneath the blower tube that works for drying a car or a grill.
Ego's was nearly the most expensive blower we tested, and its 56-volt battery powers a capable range of outdoor power equipment, from lawn mowers to string trimmers and chainsaws, making it a good choice for outfitting your garage or shed. The manufacturer has also branched into lifestyle gear, including portable power stations that run on its tool batteries, fans, wet-dry vacuums, and even a fun-looking mini bike. The downside of this leaf blower is runtime, which Ego attempts to offset by packaging the kit with two 4 amp-hour batteries. It had the shortest runtime of the tested models, a direct trade-off for its high performance. The thinking is that you can charge one battery while using the other, which may work for most users since few people blow continuously for 11 minutes.

FAQs
What to Look for (and What to Skip) in a Leaf Blower
Here’s what I’d focus on when buying a blower for leaf cleanup:
Volts: In the cordless power-tool arms race, leaf blower batteries range from 18 to 80 volts. Some of that difference is marketing trickery: an advertised 20-volt max battery or tool delivers essentially the same power as an 18-volt model, and the same goes for 36- and 40-volt options. But, unless you’re a minimalist who wants one battery to power everything from a drill/driver to lawn and garden gear, you’ll probably be happier with a leaf blower that uses at least a 36-volt battery. A few capable 18-volt blowers use two batteries—either simultaneously to mimic the power of a 36-volt tool or in succession to increase the runtime—but they tend to cost more and only make sense if you already own the batteries. For smaller jobs, though, a standard, single-battery 18- or 20-volt blower may be all you need to clear a patio, clean out the garage or shed, or dry a car.
Amps: Volts get most of the marketing attention on the box, but a battery’s amp-hour rating tells you more about how long a blower runs. Think of voltage as the car’s engine and amp-hours as the size of the gas tank—you want to know both. Batteries with higher amp-hour ratings cost more than otherwise-similar battery voltages, and they tend to be heavier. For leaf blowers, manufacturers typically pair kits with batteries rated from 4 to 8 amp-hours. You can buy higher-capacity batteries separately, and it pays to know the range of options a manufacturer has. A battery with a higher amp-hour typically takes longer to charge.
Systems: Underestimating the range of tools a battery can power in pursuit of “the best” is, in my opinion, a mistake. Often, the difference between two top-performing tools is negligible, and with cordless power tools, that difference often comes down to runtime, which you can address with a higher-capacity battery. If your garage is already stocked with one brand’s outdoor power equipment (OPE), it makes sense to stay within that platform and buy the blower as a bare tool, leveraging the batteries you already have. Switching brands just to buy “the best” probably isn’t worth it to introduce a whole new battery and charger.
If you’re new to OPE—and a leaf blower is a common first purchase—the breadth of tools that share the battery matters. Some manufacturers stick to the lawn and garden basics, so one battery can power a blower, mower, string trimmer, and hedge trimmer, while others offer a much wider range of tools, from log splitters to snow blowers, and even some handy lifestyle products like portable power stations. Before buying, consider what else you can power with the battery that comes with your leaf blower because, chances are, lording over leaves won’t be your only lawn and garden chore.
Traditional 18-volt power tool manufacturers—the ones who make drill/drivers and circular saws—all offer leaf blowers and the simplicity of a one-battery platform, but they’re not powerful enough to replace a gas unit. Ryobi, for example, uses 18-volt batteries across its traditional power tools, and some outdoor equipment, but its most capable gas alternative options run on 40-volt batteries.
Detent clasp: Blowers have two or more connection points: where the tube meets the housing and where the nozzle attaches to the tube. Look for models with a detent at those junctions—a small, often brightly colored spring-loaded clip that snaps into place with a satisfying click when the parts connect. I find these connections hold more securely and last longer than simple friction-fit attachments.
Stubby nozzle: Recently, blowers aimed at car detailers, with short tubes and sometimes a pistol grip, have become popular. Manufacturers responded by adding a stubby, 3- to 6-inch tube that the main blower attachment slides over. When you remove the longer tube, this short one works to direct the volume of air with an overall shorter tool length that’s easier to use around cars or in tight spots (the blower’s nozzle doesn’t fit on this stubby tube, though, so you lose some velocity).
What I’d Worry Less About:
Weight: Across the board, regardless of voltage, a good battery-powered blower will weigh about 10.5 pounds with the battery attached. If you need a lighter option, look for an 18-volt powered blower. Some have better balance than others, meaning that when you hold them without squeezing the trigger, as you would while walking around, the tool stays mostly level or the nozzle end tips down a bit. These models will cause less fatigue than one that forces you to rotate the nozzle upward. With the former, you only need to make a slight horizontal twisting motion to spread the stream of air. Most modern leaf blowers also draw air in a straight line through the rear of the tool, unlike gas-powered models with intakes mounted to the left or right of the engine. Those offset intakes can create a twisting motion that increases hand fatigue and may even suck in your pant leg.
CFM, MPH, and Newton: This sounds counterintuitive, considering how much marketing goes into boasting about a leaf blower’s cubic feet per minute (CFM) and MPH, but these figures are a guide, not necessarily the only reason to buy a specific model. A blower needs both to be useful: CFM tells you how much air it moves, while MPH tells you how fast that air is moving. But there’s no universally adopted testing method for these specifications when it comes to battery-powered blowers (ANSI/OPEI B175.2, the standard test on the books, applies only to internal combustion engines). That means brands can test their units differently — for example, measuring MPH where the motor meets the tube rather than at the end of the blower tube, which gives you a better sense of the airspeed you’ll actually get in use. Some CFM numbers are also measured with the unit running in its max, boost, or turbo setting, rather than on high speed.
Newtons, a unit of force, is a rating that’s appearing more frequently on the spec sheets of higher-voltage, battery-powered leaf blowers and is the best apples-to-apples comparison of blowing power. However, because there’s no testing code for battery-powered leaf blowers, reporting newtons is optional and, like CFM and MPH, consumers have no way of knowing whether the test is standardized. Generally speaking, a good midrange blower will produce around 20 newtons, while models that produce more are typically higher-performing units. Treat newtons as a guide rather than a definitive specification while buying.
Wide nozzles: Some blowers come with a wide-tip nozzle, which can be useful for clearing paved surfaces like patios and driveways or blowing water off flat surfaces. But in practice, it’s not enough of a game changer to be a deciding factor. The narrower nozzle is typically what you’ll use, and you can twist your hand back and forth to create a wider pattern when needed.
How Noisy Are Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers?
When tested from 30 inches away to approximate the noise you’d hear at arm’s length, the blowers ranged from 78.6 decibels on high to 95.2 decibels on turbo. Most user manuals recommend wearing hearing protection when using these tools, particularly for extended periods. By comparison, a handheld gas blower might produce 100 to 110 decibels. That might not sound like a lot more noise, but generally, a 10-decibel increase is perceived by the ear as roughly twice as loud.
Much of the noise reduction comes from eliminating the idling gas engine. Your neighbors will thank you for going battery-powered, too: In open air, sound typically drops by about 6 decibels each time you double your distance from the source. That means your neighbor across the street might hear your battery-powered blower at roughly the same volume as standing next to a washing machine.
What Else Are Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers Good For?
Besides clearing leaves and grass clippings, these fume-free tools are handy for all sorts of jobs. Use one to dry wet surfaces after rain or washing, including your car, patio furniture, or deck. In winter, a blower can remove a light dusting of snow from your car, making it easier to clear areas like the roof. With a cautious trigger finger, you can also clear dry leaves from gutters—just avoid wet, matted debris, which will only turn into a mess below. When grilling or firing up a pizza oven or outdoor fire pit, a gentle stream of air from a safe distance can help get the flames going. Indoors, a blower can clear dust from baseboard heating assemblies or remove lint from your dryer vent.
How I Tested Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers
I put each blower through a series of tests to gauge power, runtime, noise, and ease of use. I spread about 8,800 3x3-inch polyester crafting leaves—nearly 4 pounds’ worth—over a measured 6-by-6-foot area and used each blower to clear the section, noting which models could do the job on high and which required a boost or turbo mode. To test blowing power, I placed a 5-pound concrete paver a fixed distance from the nozzle and recorded which machines could knock it over on high and which needed turbo.
For runtime, I fully charged each battery, ran the blower at its highest standard speed, excluding any turbo or max settings, and timed how long it lasted. I measured noise with a smartphone decibel-meter app held 30 inches from the air intake while each blower ran on high and at any available turbo or max setting. I also performed practical tests to see how well each model moved gravel and wood chips and cleared water from surfaces such as a grill and patio furniture.

There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts.
On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said.
A childhood marked by loss
The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years.
The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said.
In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations.
A legal battle to pursue her dream
Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates.
With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar.
Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals.
From apprehension to acceptance
Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said.
A doctor with a larger purpose
Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said.

How did Spain's housing crisis get so bad it forced the PM to call a snap election?
Pedro Sánchez, a socialist, has made housing centre of campaign but polls point to right-wing victory
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election on Oct. 5 amid unprecedented nationwide demonstrations over housing affordability.
The election, scheduled for Nov. 29, will bring Sánchez's parliamentary term to an end six months early, marking a bold political gamble by a prime minister known for taking risks.
The announcement followed the government's failure to secure parliamentary support for two proposed measures designed to address Spain's housing crisis. But a day after calling the election, the government approved the two decrees with some modifications. They include capping rents, a temporary ban on evictions and restricting companies from buying homes.
"It is only now, with protests and unrest spreading across Spain, that they have started paying attention to social housing and to the question of where people in this country can afford to live," said Sofía Olivares, 25, a student and spokesperson for housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo (Right to Housing).
While polls point to a right-wing victory, Sánchez is betting that the housing crisis will give him the political momentum needed to secure a parliamentary majority. Since becoming prime minister in 2018, he has had to rely on support from other parties to govern, as his socialist party has never held a majority in parliament.
- Spanish PM calls snap election amid mounting housing crisis
- Spanish pensioner Maricarmen, symbol of country's housing crisis, dead at 87
By making housing affordability the centrepiece of his campaign, Sánchez hopes to unite progressive voters while deflecting attention from other pressing political vulnerabilities. Chief among these are corruption investigations targeting his inner circle and the ongoing crisis in Ceuta.
This past summer, an influx of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco reached the Spanish enclave. While most have since returned, thousands remain on the streets or in makeshift camps, overwhelming local infrastructure and fuelling calls from the right for stricter migration controls.
Protests follow eviction, death of senior
The housing demonstrations erupted following the forced eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, who became a national symbol of the crisis before her death on Oct. 7.
In Madrid, protesters camped outside in scenes reminiscent of the Indignados, or 15-M, movement in 2011, an uprising that reshaped Spanish politics by breaking up the two-party monopoly and giving rise to smaller political parties.
María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, 87, waits for police to arrive before being evicted from her home in Madrid on Sept. 23. She died on Oct. 7. (Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press/The Associated Press)
In Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, part of the Spanish archipelago off the west coast of Africa and one of Spain's most popular tourist destinations, residents have also taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest over housing.
Olivares, of Derecho al Techo, blames the regional government for placing tourism above housing. "It constantly holds back housing policies to prioritize tourism," she said, arguing that limited land and a lack of rent controls have further worsened the crisis.
Over the past year, families across the Canary Islands — one of Spain's poorest regions, where almost 30 per cent of people are at risk of poverty — have faced dozens of evictions. This week alone, the housing group has supported more than nine families facing eviction.
Sofía Olivares, right, of the housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo is shown at a protest to stop the eviction of eight families, in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain, on Oct. 7. (Sonia Håkansson Rivero)
"Property funds buy the buildings they live in, refuse to renew their contracts and throw them out onto the street,” Olivares said, adding that promises to rehouse tenants are often broken.
The lack of public housing is another major concern. "We've also been about 10 years without any type of social housing being built in the Canary Islands," she said, adding that more than 30,000 people in the islands alone are on waiting lists for public housing.
Social housing accounts for about 1.7 per cent of Spain's housing stock, well below the level in most European Union countries. The Bank of Spain estimates that the country currently lacks about 750,000 homes, a deficit expected to exceed one million by 2028.
Demonstrators calling for a change in the tourism model in the Canary Islands gather in front of beachfront tourist accommodations in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria on May 18, 2025. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)
Right-wing parties expected to win: polls
Right-wing parties have argued that Sánchez's relatively open approach to migration is placing pressure on Spain’s housing market.
Unlike many European leaders, Sánchez has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. Earlier this year, his government also launched a sweeping regularization program aimed at integrating hundreds of thousands of undocumented workers into the formal economy.
Polling points to a conservative coalition led by the People’s Party, alongside the anti-immigration party Vox, as the most likely outcome of next month's election. Such a result would bring the far right into Spain's national government for the first time since the country's transition to democracy in 1975, following Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
- 'Absolute chaos' as thousands of Moroccan migrants breach Spain's Ceuta border
- Why Spain is aiming to regularize half a million undocumented migrants
The People's Party warns that the rent caps proposed by Sánchez will backfire by driving homes off the market. The government's measures also largely failed to win the support of the real estate industry, which says they don't address the root cause of the problem: Spain’s structural housing shortage.
"We are trying to address a supply crisis without sufficiently increasing supply," said María Matos, head of research and a spokesperson at Fotocasa, one of Spain's leading real estate platforms.
"By focusing on regulating properties, rental contracts and landlords, we risk making it even harder to bring homes on to the market."
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is shown at the Moncloa Palace in Madrid on Oct. 6. He has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. (Bernat Armangue/The Associated Press)
Fotocasa's latest data suggests landlords may already be responding to new housing measures. "In just eight days, long-term rental supply fell by 4.2 per cent,” Matos said. She warns that "measures designed to protect tenants can end up creating barriers for those still trying to find a home."
She also called for greater investment in public housing. "Since 2013, the development of new social housing has practically come to a standstill, forcing more households to compete in the private market."
Matos said she wants more land to be made available for development, alongside faster planning approvals. "We need to unlock public and private land, and speed up building permits to prevent projects from being delayed for years."
A man sleeps on a street near a protest calling for political action to address Spain's housing crisis, in Barcelona on Oct. 6. (Nacho Doce/Reuters)
Garazi González, 36, who now lives with her partner and their baby in an apartment building belonging to his family, said she has experienced the affordability crisis first-hand and supports the protests "100 per cent."
Four years ago, after renting an apartment in central Madrid for eight years, she saw her monthly rent rise from 800 to 950 euros (about $1,275 to $1,500 Cdn). Her landlady then proposed raising it to 1,500 euros ($2,400 Cdn).
"She said prices in the area had gone up and she couldn't keep charging me so little. She gave me just one month to leave," González said.
"I know people whose rents were raised to push them out, or who live in fear of being evicted from homes they've lived in for years. Others live in gentrified areas where vulture funds buy entire buildings and kick everyone out."
Despite her disappointment with the current government, González said preventing the far right from returning to power is now her biggest priority.
"I'm not entirely happy with the left because they haven't done enough on housing or other issues,” she said. "But I want to prevent fascism from coming back. I care about protecting social rights.... As a woman and a mother to a daughter, I worry deeply about her future."

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on the scene of a shooting in upper Manhattan on Thursday has repeatedly been accused in federal court of unlawful arrests and using force during arrests in New York and Minneapolis, a WIRED investigation finds.
On Thursday afternoon, ICE agents shot a man, identified by city authorities as Oscar Belgal, in Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood, near the Bronx. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said agents surrounded the man’s car, in which a 5-year-old child was sitting, before firing multiple rounds—as many as seven, witnesses told local media. Belgal, the New York Police Department said, was hospitalized after reportedly being shot in the neck. The child appeared unharmed.
Footage from the scene shows a man in a high-visibility yellow construction vest brandishing a modified AR-15-style rifle with a pistol grip, sling, and holographic sights. That man, according to court documents, social media posts, and publicly available personal information reviewed by WIRED, is Brenden Cuni—an ICE supervisor with the agency’s National Fugitive Operations team who has been involved in several arrests in the New York City region and Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge last winter.
Cuni identified himself as an ICE agent to NYPD officers, a law enforcement source tells WIRED, and was the only federal agent captured on video brandishing a weapon on scene. In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security claims that ICE agents were attempting to apprehend an undocumented immigrant from the Dominican Republic with a prior conviction for grand larceny.
A WIRED review of federal court cases, social media, and other public records suggests that Cuni has repeatedly been at the center of illegal ICE street arrests in New York and beyond. Court filings accuse him of using a Taser on a handcuffed man, while activists have alleged he is one of the agents seen forcing a pregnant woman to the ground during a Minneapolis operation. In recent months, federal judges have repeatedly found arrests involving Cuni unlawful. One judge called an arrest warrant he signed “fraudulent,” while another said that video evidence contradicts his sworn account of an arrest; in a third case, the government withdrew his sworn statements as inaccurate.
Cuni has been a DHS agent for nearly a decade. According to court declarations he signed, Cuni began his federal law enforcement career with Customs and Border Protection as a Border Patrol agent in San Diego in 2018 before becoming a deportation officer in 2020. In December 2024, he was promoted to a supervisory detention and deportation officer, and in May 2025, he joined the National Fugitive Operations team.
Cuni’s work history before his time with DHS remains unclear. Felician University, a private Catholic university in New Jersey, listed him as a member of its 2018 baseball roster. On that site, Cuni lists his hometown as New Rochelle—a suburb just north of the Bronx.
Cuni has been named in multiple lawsuits alleging violent arrests, both first reported last spring by The City and Documented as part of an investigation into hundreds of ICE street arrests in the New York area. Lawyers for a 21-year-old Bronx man claim that during his arrest in October last year, Cuni tripped him hard enough to break a tooth, then shocked him with a Taser about six times while he was handcuffed on the ground, and later called him a “maldito Mexicano”—damned Mexican. A medical record, obtained by THE CITY and Documented, noted injuries “from taser by ICE agents.”
The following month, another man alleged that ICE agents tackled and shocked him with a Taser three times during an arrest in Queens. According to the man’s petition, ICE’s arrest report lists Cuni among the arresting officers and acknowledges agents used a Taser. The filings do not say who fired it.
Court records also place Cuni in Minneapolis last December, leading a three-person ICE team at a scene where 60 to 70 people had gathered. Agents were trying to arrest a woman who had spray-painted an ICE vehicle; she escaped. Federal prosecutors charged a protester at the scene with assaulting Cuni, alleging that the man had helped tackle him after Cuni pepper-sprayed him. A judge later dismissed that charge with prejudice, writing that the evidence was “weak” and that none of the federal officers who reviewed videos of the encounter “saw a ‘tackle’ or other kind of assault.” Activists later alleged that Cuni was one of the agents seen in video of the encounter forcing to the ground a woman they say was pregnant. WIRED could not independently confirm that identification.
In at least three federal cases this year, judges or the government have found problems with Cuni’s statements or arrest paperwork. In one case, Judge Gary Brown of the Eastern District of New York found that Cuni searched five databases for a Bronx man and found nothing, then signed a warrant saying the searches had confirmed he was undocumented. ICE later added the man to those databases and searched again, creating the record Cuni had said already existed. Brown ruled the arrest and detention illegal, saying that Cuni had tried to “reconcile these falsehoods” after the fact.
In August, US District Judge Brian Cogan, also of New York’s Eastern District, said doorbell footage “largely contradicts” Cuni’s account of Fernando Fabian Chaglla’s arrest. Video reviewed by WIRED shows Chaglla being handcuffed less than three minutes into the encounter. Cuni later said he had typed Chaglla’s name and birth date into Mobile Fortify, an ICE face-recognition app; the search showed no record of lawful entry, but it did show a federal work permit. Cuni said he took the lack of records documenting his entry into the US as evidence that Chaglla was undocumented and acknowledged that he handcuffed him before filling out the warrant by hand. Cogan ruled that the arrest was unlawful.
A little over a week later, Cuni testified that he didn’t recall himself or the agents under his command ever making a warrantless arrest. “In all of the cases that I am aware of, I issued an I-200 prior to the arrest,” he assured the attorneys deposing him. “Now, if you’re questioning my credibility, I don’t know, but again, I’m—can only tell you what I’m aware of.”
In a third case, in June, government lawyers withdrew what a federal judge described as “inaccurate, sworn representations” by Cuni and other officials, including a claim that a detained man had skipped his ICE check-ins.
Cuni did not immediately respond to WIRED’s multiple requests for comment.
An Instagram account apparently associated with Cuni, previously using the handle “shooter.cuni”—now “shooter.914,” seemingly reflecting the Westchester County, New York, area code—contains scores of photographs and videos of Cuni with firearms at shooting ranges across the Northeast. Among the items depicted on the account are a mug that appears to be from ICE’s New York City Fugitive Operations team, a silver and black Rolex watch that closely matches one Cuni appears to be wearing in videos from the Marble Hill shooting, and an AR-15–style rifle with a pistol grip, short barrel, holoscopic sights, and olive-colored sling that appears to match the one he wielded at the shooting scene.
Another photo on the Cuni-linked Instagram account, posted on September 4, depicts a GA Precision Templar VII bolt-action rifle with a telescopic sight mounted on a bipod stand at a gun range. “Cuni” is emblazoned on a suede cushion on the rifle’s stock, and a blue “shooter Cuni” lanyard is visible on a separate cloth ammunition sling. The post’s caption reads, “the finest form of relaxation.”

Medicine and surgery are not the answer for overweight children, the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
Releasing its first guidelines addressing the sharp rise in obesity among children and adolescents, the WHO instead strongly recommended structured diets, physical activity and behaviour changes.
"WHO does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery (surgery that changes the stomach or digestive tract) or weight-loss devices for children aged 0-9 years," it said.
"For adolescents aged 10-19 years, treatment with approved medicines may be considered only when a supervised multimodal lifestyle programme has not achieved the desired results.
"Bariatric surgery may be considered under strict conditions for adolescents with severe obesity."
The recommendations for those aged 19 and under contrast with the UN health agency's guidelines for adult obesity issued in December 2025, following the surge in popularity of a new generation of appetite-suppressing drugs called GLP-1 agonists -- which includes blockbuster brands Ozempic and Mounjaro.
The WHO said the range of weight-loss and diabetes drugs could be used for tackling obesity -- in adults.
170 million affected
In 2024, some 70 million children aged five to nine were obese, as were 100 million adolescents aged 10 to 19 worldwide, according to the WHO.
Among 5- to 19-year-olds, the prevalence of obesity has surged globally, rising from two percent in 1990 to eight percent in 2024.
"The rise of obesity is observed everywhere in all regions," said Luz Maria De Regil, director of the WHO's nutrition and food safety department.
"It's growing in low- and middle-income countries," while some high-income countries are starting to stop the rise of obesity, without yet making reductions.
"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change," she said.
The recommendations also stressed the importance of addressing mental health alongside obesity.
Anxiety, depression and low self-esteem can contribute to unhealthy eating, physical inactivity and social withdrawal, the WHO said.
Children and adolescents living with obesity may experience stigma and bullying, the UN health agency added.
Maria Nieves Garcia Casal, a scientist in the WHO's nutrition and food safety department, told reporters that bariatric surgery may be considered during adolescence for cases of severe obesity accompanied by complications such as type 2 diabetes or hypertension -- if diet and lifestyle changes have failed.

The WPC Energy Congress opened in Riyadh on Sunday as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the gathering despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
Several top energy executives have now been dropped from the event's schedule.
The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected to attend.
But none of them appeared on the agenda released by conference organisers early on Monday.
“To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you,” said Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who opened Monday's session of the gathering for energy policy and industry that takes place once every three years.
“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart…Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”
The strikes are a blow to Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's multi-billion-dollar programme to diversify the economy away from oil, modernise society and position the kingdom as an investment and tourism hub.
Hosting international events is a priority of the programme, which was already facing delays and recalibrations.
Prince Abdulaziz said the kingdom must remain focused on the decades ahead and Vision 2030 must continue.
Prince Abdulaziz said the events of recent weeks were serious and that the kingdom's response must be “equally serious".
A BP spokesperson said the company had "made every effort to participate" in the conference. "Unfortunately, due to travel disruption we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our long-standing partnerships across the region."
Shell declined to comment.
TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil and Chevron did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.
The congress is being held this week at a conference centre some 10 kilometres (6 miles) from Riyadh's international airport.
That airport has been attacked four times in the last week.
One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on the airport on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities reported.
The attack came a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
That was the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.

Boyfriend of murdered backpacker Simone Strobel sues NSW Police over arrest
In short:
Tobias Moran has filed civil proceedings in the NSW District Court against the NSW Police for malicious prosecution.
Mr Moran was charged in 2022 over the 2005 death of his girlfriend Simone Strobel in Lismore, but charges were withdrawn a year later.
What's next?
The civil case will be heard in the NSW District Court in January.
The boyfriend of a German backpacker murdered in northern New South Wales 20 years ago is suing the NSW Police Force.
Tobias Moran, formerly known as Tobias Suckfuell, has alleged police maliciously targeted him rather than searching for the truth about how the woman died.
He was charged in 2022 over the death of 25-year-old Simone Strobel, whose naked body was found near the Lismore caravan park they were staying at in February 2005.
Mr Moran spent 10 days in custody and 10 months adhering to bail conditions before the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions withdrew the charges.
The court ordered the state of New South Wales to pay Mr Moran's legal costs of $190,000.
Mr Moran has now filed civil proceedings in the NSW District Court against the NSW Police for malicious prosecution.
In a statement, Mr Moran challenged the police motive for the arrest.
"This is an important step towards clearing my name and holding the relevant NSW police officers to account for what I believe was a prosecution driven by improper motives rather than a pursuit of the truth," he said.
Death in Lismore
Simone Strobel disappeared from the Lismore Tourist Caravan Park near the city's CBD on Friday, February 11, 2005.
She had been staying their her then-boyfriend, Tobias Moran, his sister, Katrin Suckfuell, and their friend, Jens Martin.
They reported her missing when she failed to return from a walk after a disagreement.
Six days later, Ms Strobel's body was discovered under palm fronds at a bocce court, less than 100 metres from their campsite.
In late 2025, State Coroner Teresa O'Sullivan overturned the findings of a previous inquest.
She found that while Mr Moran could not be completely ruled out as a suspect, it was unlikely he could have killed Ms Strobel without help.
"It is unlikely that Mr [Jens] Martin and Ms [Katrin] Suckfuell were involved in Simone's death; and secondly, it is unlikely that Mr Moran could have acted alone in killing Simone and disposing of her body," Ms O'Sullivan said in handing down her findings.
"I do not, however, accept that the evidence goes so far as to support a finding by me that it is very unlikely Mr Moran was involved in Simone's death".
Mr Moran spoke to the ABC about the unsolved murder earlier this year for the Unravel: Lies in Lismore podcast.
He told ABC journalist Richard Baker he was innocent and that police developed "tunnel vision" about him at the expense of finding Ms Strobel's killer.
"Crucial evidence has not been considered," Mr Moran said in the podcast.
"They've been on the wrong track for 20 f***ing years … I think the Australian public has a right to know that this is a full Muppet show."
Stewart O'Connell SC is representing Mr Moran in the civil action.
He said in a statement that Mr Moran had "consistently maintained his innocence of this horrific crime".
"There has never been any convincing evidence of his involvement," Mr O'Connell said.
"He has had to endure both the shock and pain of Simone's death and the devastation and distress of being blamed, arrested and detained for it.
"These proceedings will examine the investigation and prosecution of Mr Moran and, if found to be improperly motivated, will ensure that Mr Moran receives some justice."
Mr O'Connell said compensation was being sought for Mr Moran, but had not put a figure on the amount being sought.
Mr Moran said he hoped the court action would bring renewed focus on the investigation into Ms Strobel's death.
"She was a very special person who deserved better, and her family deserves better," he said in a statement.
"Everyone impacted by Simone's death and the aftermath deserves some answers and closure."
In a statement, NSW Police said it was aware of the court action, but declined to comment.
The civil case has been listed in the NSW District Court for January 27, 2027.

For years, Swiggy and Zomato have ruled the Indian foodtech sector with an iron fist, building vast restaurant networks and loyal customer bases that have made it difficult for new players to compete. But the duopoly is now facing fresh competition from three directions: Rapido’s Ownly, food delivery startup Swish’s new marketplace, Swish Go, and ecommerce giant Flipkart. Ownly is already handling around 50,000 orders a day in Bengaluru and entered Hyderabad just two weeks ago. Swish, which started with quick food delivery, is expanding into restaurant aggregation with its new marketplace, Swish Go. Ecommerce giant Flipkart, too, is testing its food delivery service, Eat In, in Bengaluru. All three are entering a market where consumers are already comfortable ordering food online. At the same time, restaurants are looking for alternatives to the high commissions charged by Swiggy and Zomato. But onboarding restaurants is only half the battle. What the emerging players need is to convince customers to order from their platforms regularly. Hence, it is only natural for us to ask if these new players can challenge the dominance Swiggy and Zomato have built over the years and what gives the duopoly enough steam to keep the burgeoning rivals at bay. Restaurants Are Hungry For An Alternative Restaurant owners have long complained about the commissions and other charges they pay to Swiggy and Zomato. While online orders have become a major source of sales, delivery platforms can eat into margins, especially as restaurants become more dependent on them. In July, National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI) president and Wow! Momo cofounder Sagar Daryani told Inc42 that food delivery had grown from 10% of a restaurant’s business before Covid-19 to around 50% for some restaurants. This is where the new entrants see an opportunity. Rapido’s Ownly is trying to capitalise on the discontent by offering zero commission to restaurant partners. It has also integrated Ownly into the Rapido app, giving it access to an existing base of mobility users. The company can also draw on its delivery network for food orders, potentially reducing the cost of building a separate operation from scratch. Ownly is already processing over 50,000 orders a day in Bengaluru. After entering Hyderabad last month, it has onboarded 10,000 restaurants in the city, with plans to expand that network to 30,000. The expansion gives Ownly a route to compete beyond Bengaluru. Swish Go is taking a different approach. According to people familiar with the platform, its commission rates vary by order value, with one rate for orders below ₹100 and another for orders above that amount. Restaurant partners find this arrangement favourable, Inc42 has learnt. However, these attractive terms may not last forever. An observer in the restaurant business believes Ownly could introduce commissions as it grows, with Swish Go potentially following the same path. The current offers are a way to attract restaurants that are unhappy with Swiggy and Zomato. However, the person also questioned whether Swish ever intended to focus only on 10-minute food delivery. Established players such as Swiggy, Zepto and Rebel Foods have faced challenges with the format, making it difficult to sustain at scale. Swish Go’s pricing also puts it in competition with Swiggy’s Toing. By waiving packaging and platform fees, Swish Go appears to be betting on a lower-cost ordering experience to attract customers. The Real Battle Is Over The Users Getting restaurants to join a new platform is one challenge, and convincing them to order from it regularly is another. Food delivery is already an established market, and new players must now give customers a reason to try their platforms and keep coming back. An analyst cautioned that making money from these new services could prove difficult because their business models have not been tested at scale. This is pushing platforms towards restaurant aggregation, which allows them to offer a wider choice of food without running every kitchen themselves. Swiggy and Zomato have also experimented with new food delivery formats, but those bets have not lasted. Swiggy shut down Snacc, its standalone app for 10-15 minute food delivery, in February 2026. Eternal, Zomato’s parent company, discontinued Zomato Quick, its 15-minute delivery service, and Zomato Everyday, which offered home-style meals, in May 2025. Earlier this year, Rebel Foods also shut down Quickies. These show that even established platforms with large customer bases have struggled to make certain food delivery formats, primarily quick food delivery, work at scale. A new proposition may attract customers, but sustaining the business without compromising service or profitability will be crucial. Meanwhile, a sectoral expert said that Swiggy and Zomato’s biggest moat is their large user base. But that advantage does not make their position immune to defeat. Rapido already has a consumer base and delivery fleet it can draw on, while Swish is adding restaurants on top of its existing cloud kitchens and a loyal user base. Flipkart is also preparing to enter food delivery. With a user base of 500 Mn and the financial backing to fund expansion, Flipkart could also take a share of Swiggy and Zomato’s food delivery market. The company is likely to roll out the service before the end of 2026. The likes of Swish and Flipkart are making moves at a time when Swiggy and Zomato remain much larger businesses. Eternal reported adjusted food delivery revenue of ₹3,537 Cr in Q1 FY27, up 33% year-on-year (YoY) from ₹2,657 Cr in Q1 FY26. This was up from around ₹3,135 Cr in Q4 FY26. Swiggy’s food delivery revenue reached ₹2,208 Cr in Q1 FY27, growing 23% from ₹1,799 Cr a year earlier and ₹2,075 Cr in the previous quarter. Their restaurant networks are equally extensive. Zomato averaged around 3.28 lakh monthly active restaurant partners in Q1 FY27, while Swiggy reported over 2.7 lakh restaurant partners across more than 720 cities. These numbers show the scale of the duopoly that Ownly and Swish Go must compete against. Beyond attracting restaurants with better commercial terms, the new entrants will need to build a large, active customer base and generate enough repeat orders to sustain their businesses. They do not need to match Swiggy and Zomato across India immediately, but they must prove they can grow in select markets without relying indefinitely on low commissions and other attractive offers. Quick Commerce: The Duopoly’s Strongest Moat According to Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research, Swiggy and Zomato’s biggest advantages are their established customer habits, wide restaurant selection and delivery networks built over years. Ownly’s expansion into Bengaluru and Hyderabad, along with Swish Go’s Bengaluru pilot, puts these advantages to the test in local markets. Since customers and restaurants can use multiple platforms, the incumbents will need to keep their prices competitive and service reliable. Restaurants will also expect a steady flow of orders as new players offer better commercial terms. However, Jain sees a higher entry barrier in quick commerce, which requires local inventory, supplier relationships, replenishment systems and substantial capital. These investments become defensible only when individual locations attract repeat demand and generate profits. Quick commerce may therefore offer Swiggy and Zomato a stronger defence than food delivery alone. For Swiggy and Zomato, food delivery remains an important source of business as they continue to invest in quick commerce. In due time, both businesses will turn self-sustaining at which point the new rivals may not have room to maneuver. Their scale means there is a lot more that rivals have to do to compete in terms of bringing in users, but it does not prevent these new platforms from targeting restaurants with different commercial terms and undercut the two largest players. For Flipkart, Rapido Ownly and Swish Go, the real test, for now, is whether early traction can turn into repeat orders. Only then can they loosen the duopoly’s hold. The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Thai Queen makes first solo flight in fighter jet
Thailand's Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household.
The Queen was shown boarding a Gripen on 8 October at an airfield in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, while King Maha Vajiralongkorn watched from the ground.
The Royal Household has said she is an experienced pilot, having logged about 1,188 hours across several types of aircraft since she began flying in 2010.
She also co-piloted aircraft carrying the King on official visits to other countries, the Royal Household said.

Generic drugmaker Granules India has filed a Paragraph IV certification with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA) in connection with its abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) for Ruxolitinib Extended-Release Tablets.
Based on the timing and status of its ANDA and Paragraph IV certification, and subject to the U.S. FDA’s review and determination, Granules said it believes it is eligible for first-to-file status for Ruxolitinib Extended-Release Tablets.
If confirmed by the FDA and subject to all applicable statutory and regulatory requirements, first-to-file status could make Granules eligible for 180 days of generic drug exclusivity under U.S. law, the company said on Wednesday (September 7, 2026).
The Paragraph IV certification sought is with respect to applicable patents listed in the U.S. FDA’s Orange Book. Granules said it has also issued the requisite notice to the relevant parties in accordance with U.S. regulatory requirements.
“First-to-file opportunities are an important part of our strategy to build a more differentiated and higher-value product portfolio in the U.S. This filing reflects our focus on identifying technically and commercially attractive opportunities where our development and manufacturing capabilities can create sustainable value,” Granules CMD Krishna Prasad Chigurupati said.
Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, was approved by the U.S. FDA in 2011 and is used to treat certain cancers and related conditions. In the U.S., the drug is developed and marketed by Incyte Corporation under the brand name Jakafi. Jakafi and Jakafi XR are trademarks of Incyte.
In May, Nasdaq-listed Incyte announced that the U.S. FDA had approved Jakafi XR, the extended-release formulation of ruxolitinib.
The drug is marketed by Incyte in the U.S. and by Novartis outside the country under the brand name Jakavi.

On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called for a mass protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the voter rolls. The CJP is also demanding an immediate halt to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and the restoration of all names removed since 25 June 2025. Left-wing student organisations have also issued a joint statement announcing that they will join the demonstration in large numbers.
In this context, several videos (here, here, here, here & here) are circulating on social media claiming that members of Hindu organisations, such as the Bajrang Dal, have begun moving towards Jantar Mantar to oppose the protest. Let’s verify the authenticity of these claims.
Claim: Viral videos show Hindu groups, including Bajrang Dal, mobilising activists to oppose the CJP protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026.
Fact: All these videos predate the protest announcement and depict unrelated events, including a Ram Navami bike rally in West Bengal, BJP victory celebrations, and Chhatrapati Shivaji’s coronation anniversary celebrations. Bajrang Dal has also denied plans to mobilise volunteers at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claims made in these posts are False.
Video 1:
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video revealed that the same video (archived) has been available since at least November 2022. Although the exact context of the original video remains unclear, we found that the clip has been repeatedly repurposed for various issues over the years. This confirms that the viral video has no connection to the Jantar Mantar protest on 10 October 2026.
Video 2:
Our investigation revealed that this video, depicting a bike rally, has been available (archived) since at least 28 March 2026. It shows a bike rally from Chandrakona Road to Garhbeta in West Bengal to mark the occasion of Ram Navami. This confirms that the footage even predates the formation of the CJP movement.
Video 3:
We analysed another video of the bike rally and found that it has been available (archived) since 04 May 2026. It depicts celebrations following the BJP’s historic victory in West Bengal, featuring a procession of people waving saffron flags and raising religious slogans.
Video 4:
This video, showing people rallying on the road with saffron flags, has been available (archived) online since at least 09 September 2026. Although the exact context of the clip remains unknown, the footage was uploaded more than three weeks before the announcement of the Jantar Mantar protest.
Video 5:
This video, which features large crowds, has been available (archived) online since at least June 2026. It depicts the crowd at the coronation anniversary celebrations of Chhatrapati Shivaji at Raigad Fort, held on 6 June 2026.
Similarly, some unverified clips are being shared, claiming to show the arrival of Bajrang Dal activists at Jantar Mantar to oppose the protest. However, the Bajrang Dal has rejected these claims. In a clarification (archived) on X, the organisation stated it has no plans to mobilise volunteers or assemble at Jantar Mantar on October 10, adding that some individuals are spreading misleading propaganda.
To sum it up, old, unrelated videos are being circulated with the false claim that they show Hindu activists mobilising at Jantar Mantar to oppose the CJP protest

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission for the demonstration and detained thousands of people, including CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were detained after arriving at Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International AIRPORT. With Jantar Mantar barricaded, some demonstrators protested at other locations. The three leaders were released on 11 October while the Supreme Court directed authorities to uphold the rights of peaceful protesters. The agitation continued on 12 October, with opposition leaders planning further demonstrations against the SIR exercise (here, here, and here).
Amid this, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows protests in Delhi on 10 October 2026 demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows protests in Delhi on 10 October 2026 demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video does not show protests in Delhi on 10 October 2026 demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. It was recorded in Iligan City, Philippines, although the exact date and context of the recording remain unknown. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed a hoarding on a foot overbridge bearing the words “Diyandi Festival”. A search revealed that the Diyandi Festival is celebrated annually in September in Iligan City, Philippines, and culminates on 29 September in honour of the city’s patron saint, St Michael the Archangel.
We also noticed signboards bearing the name “Shann Gadget” in the video. A search on Google Maps revealed that the shop is located opposite Gaisano Citi Super Mall on Roxas Avenue in Iligan City, Philippines. On Google Street View, we identified several similarities between the location shown in the viral video and the Street View imagery, confirming that the video was recorded in Iligan City. The comparison can be seen below.
However, we could not determine exactly when the video was recorded or the context in which it was filmed. Based on the available evidence, it is clear that the video was shot in Iligan City, Philippines, and is unrelated to the protests in Delhi.
To sum up, an unrelated video from the Philippines is being shared as showing CJP protests in Delhi demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.

DOJ investigating five TV networks over White House pool coverage
‘Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act’ a DOJ spokesperson claimed

The Department of Justice is investigating five major TV networks over their White House pool coverage, according to a report.
Coverage of the White House has become a point of controversy in recent weeks, after President Trump tried to ban CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO. That led to ABC, CBS, Fox News, NBC and CNN temporarily suspending their pooled coverage of the White House.
Now, a DOJ spokesperson has told The Washington Post that the Justice Department is launching an investigation into that boycott.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” spokesperson Emily Covington told The Post on Saturday. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
The Sherman Antitrust Act was signed into law all the way back in 1890 and is designed to counter anticompetitive business practices. The law prohibits any action that attempts to monopolize a certain market.
The withdrawal of press coverage meant that the remaining outlets covering the White House sometimes failed to pick up what Trump was saying, leading to awkward moments where he was drowned out by surrounding noises.
At the time, Trump ally Laura Loomer suggested that the DOJ should investigate the boycott.
“This coordinated withdrawal of news coverage is exactly the kind of concerted action a serious antitrust division at the DOJ would examine: whether competing news organizations agreed among themselves to withhold a product the public expects to see,” she wrote on X.
However, on Sunday, Jose Zamora, the regional Americas director at the Committee to Protect Journalists, slammed the DOJ’s announcement.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora wrote on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”
Trump banned CNN, POLITICO and MS NOW from the White House back in September, claiming that they lied about him in their coverage.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social.
The three outlets, whose journalists had their White House press passes revoked, eventually sued Trump and three major White House officials, leading a judge to temporarily reinstate their access.
The three outlets’ lawsuit argued that the press ban had violated the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause as well as the First Amendment.
The TV pool, which involves major outlets taking turns to cover events in order to lower costs, boycotted coverage of the White House in response to the ban and resumed their coverage after the judge’s ruling.
The Independent has contacted the DOJ for comment.
