Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

Nobel memorial prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford
Economists' work has helped manage economic shocks, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences says
American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the two were being honoured for work that has helped policymakers deal with economic fluctuations.
"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy said in a statement.
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: "It's a tremendous honour, it's a surprise."
The Nobel memorial prize in economics is announced in Stockholm on Monday. Hall and Woodford won the prize in for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks. (Anders Wiklund/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume."
'New foundation for stabilization policy'
For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest themselves and help growth get restarted.
"This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn't," said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee.

Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple tradeoffs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell.
But the "stagflation" of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic.
Hall and Woodford set about coming up with an improved model that took into account how consumers and businesses actually made decisions about whether to invest and spend.
"In separate contributions, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford helped build this new foundation for stabilization policy," Hassler said.
Last year, three researchers who study business innovation — including Canadian economist Peter Howitt — won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.
The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.
Nobel honours were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.7 million Cdn), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

On his first day back in office in January 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order “restoring freedom of speech and ending federal censorship.” More than a year and a half later, his administration is instead busy using government power to go after speech it dislikes.
The “grim” state of free speech in the US
Explained by a First Amendment lawyer.
Last year, Federal Communications Commission chair Brendan Carr urged broadcasters to take action against Jimmy Kimmel over his comments following Charlie Kirk’s killing, and in September, Kimmel said the FCC again intervened to stop Kimmel’s late-night show from airing an interview with James Talarico, Democratic Senate candidate for Texas.
Also last month, Trump barred three news outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House over their coverage. That ban was quickly blocked by a federal judge, but both CNN and Politico have since been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips.
Outside of the White House, the fight over free speech is also raging on college campuses. In states like Texas, Republican lawmakers have restricted when students can protest and given governor-appointed university boards more say over what gets taught. In 2025, 15 states passed laws that restrict what can be taught or weaken protections for free expression on college campuses.
To break down what all of this means for the state of free speech in the US — and the future of our First Amendment rights — Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Greg Lukianoff, president and CEO of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE).
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
How would you describe the kind of status of free speech on campus these days?
The status of free speech is in great peril, both on and off campus. I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and it’s about as bad as I’ve ever seen it.
When it comes to the Charlie Kirk backlash cases, we saw about 90 of them. It’s a remarkably high number. We saw an ex-cop go to jail for 37 days just for forwarding a Trump meme in response to a request to go to a candlelight vigil for Charlie Kirk. It’s not good.
If you look at the last two years, we’ve done so many episodes about free speech concerns. There was Jimmy Kimmel; there’s CNN being banned from the White House.
There’s student protesters who are protesting what’s going on in Gaza.
It really does seem like we’re at a moment where so many different types of people claim that their speech is being restricted in so many different types of ways. What is happening in the country?
My worry is I’m very much a small-L liberal. I come from an old ACLU background. That’s where I interned in law school. I went to law school to do First Amendment law. I hyper-specialize in it. This is my passion.
For most of my 25-year career, you could rely on a civil libertarian aspect of the left and a libertarian aspect of the right that would often agree on almost nothing except for things like freedom of speech. And right now, I think we’ve become all culture war all the time, and we have more of a progressive left and more of a populist right.
The only way that you show you believe in freedom of speech is by saying, “I hate that guy, but I think you should have freedom of speech.” If you’re saying, “I think my side should have freedom of speech,” that’s just self-interest. That doesn’t even count.
All the worst people in history wanted free speech for their side. So I’m afraid we’re losing — or maybe even, I hate to say this dramatically, but maybe even have lost it as a shared value as a society.
Well, that’s quite grim.
Yeah. I’m feeling a little grim.
The Trump administration came into office with a promise. And I remember it sounding something like this: “The woke left went too far. They canceled people. They restricted speech. They got out of control. President Trump is going to come back in, and we are going to restore sanity to the country. And as part of sanity, that will include your right to freely express yourself.”
How do you square the promise versus what we’ve seen?
I think Trump is constantly frustrating everyone around him by being Trump. I think there probably were people in the administration who were like, “Yeah, we’re going to be pro-free speech.” And then Trump decides to declare — I mean, I think the recent White House press pool case is hysterical in a lot of ways because he had to get his team to give a sort of constitutional justification for why he was kicking out the press pool. But on Truth Social, he’s like, “It’s because of their viewpoint,” which is, by the way, something you can’t do under the Constitution.
“I’m hopeful for the long-term future of free speech, but in the short term, I’m worried.”
His instincts are very authoritarian. They’re very top-down. So maybe there were people in the administration who, in their heart of hearts, are good on free speech, but Trump isn’t. And it’s the reason why when it came to the new administration, there were a lot of people on the right, but also people on the sort of heterodox left who were like, “Oh, this is going to be good for free speech.”
I was like, “Don’t kid yourself, guys. This is going to be bad.” Although I will say, it’s even worse than I was expecting.
President Trump at some point will be out of office. And what happens then? What do you think? Is there an optimistic scenario where we’re like, “Okay, we’re kind of tired of this crap. Let’s just go back to the way it was in the ’90s”?
It has been cyclical, to a degree. American society gets out of whack, and usually one of the things that does bring us together is that we were lucky enough to have…I’ll just say it, we have a brilliant Constitution. It is unusually clever about human nature, and the Constitution itself — you can have whatever opinion you want about the founders, but it is something to be proud of. And a lot of times those values kind of bring us back together.
That’s my hope. But another thing I will say about Trump: He has played havoc with my ability to predict anything. So what it’s going to look like over the event horizon of 2028, I hope it will be better, and we will fight like hell to make sure it’s better here at FIRE, but will it be better? I’m not sure, and it definitely won’t be better if we think of free speech as something that belongs to my side, not yours.
One of the reasons why I do have hope for free speech in the long term is that free speech works really well. It’s how you know what your fellow citizens think. It’s how you get ideas out there. It’s how you actually be your authentic self.
Societies that actually have freedom of speech are always going to have advantages, real and serious advantages, over ones that don’t. So I’m hopeful for the long-term future of free speech, but in the short term, I’m worried.

An Indian national, who allegedly entered a Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix event area without a valid ticket, has been charged with two counts of criminal trespass, according to a media report on Monday.
Citing court documents, The Straits Times said Daver Arish Adil, 39, was at Gate 2 in Temasek Avenue when he purportedly gained access to a ticketed area at around 1.45 pm on October 9. He was charged on October 10.
He is accused of trespassing again at around 2 pm that day (October 9), when he allegedly entered an area known as “the wharf” in Raffles Boulevard, which was accessible only to Singapore Grand Prix staff.
His case will be mentioned again in court on Friday.
For each count of criminal trespass, an offender can be jailed for up to three months, fined up to SGD 1,500, or both.
The Singapore Grand Prix was held over the weekend, with the final on Sunday, won by Max Verstappen of the Red Bull.

Have you ever felt a chill as you walk down your street, or drive along a dark highway in your home state?
You might want to check this list to see if your state's creepiest urban legend unfolded near you.
Every country, state, and town has its own urban legends known to residents and fans of the paranormal. Some are attempts to explain mysterious phenomena or tragedies, while others are passed down due to our fascination with the dark and macabre.
Some areas have capitalized on local urban legends to attract tourists and boost local economies. In the West Virginia city of Point Pleasant, for example, the legend of Mothman is integral to the community. The Mothman Festival is held every September and includes guest speakers, a street fair, bus tours, live music, food trucks, and more. There's even a Mothman museum.
It's not for nothing. The Main Street Point Pleasant organization told The River Cities Tribune & Register in 2024 that it estimates the festival brings about $2 million to the city's economy every year.
But not every urban legend is that well known. We chose the creepiest urban legend we could find in every state, from the little-known to the mainstays like Bigfoot and the Jersey Devil.
ALABAMA: Hell's Gate Bridge
The generally accepted story of Hell's Gate Bridge starts in the 1950s, according to the Oxford Paranormal Society; a young couple driving over the bridge somehow drove their car off the bridge one night, and they both drowned.
There are two legends associated with Hell's Gate Bridge: one is that if you drive your car out to the middle of the bridge and turn off the lights, the couple will magically appear in your car and leave a wet spot on the seat.
The other, which is how the bridge got its name, is the belief that if you drive over the bridge and look over your shoulder halfway through, the scenery behind you turns into a portal to hell engulfed in flames.
Potentially to curb ghost hunters and bored teenagers, Hell's Gate Bridge is closed to cars, according to The Anniston Star, and it is in such disrepair that walking across is strongly discouraged.
ALASKA: The Kushtaka of the Alaskan Triangle
Everyone knows the story of the Bermuda Triangle, but you might not know about the Alaskan Triangle.
On average, five out of every 1,000 people go missing in Alaska, the Los Angeles Times reported in 2005, so even if there's nothing supernatural going on, it's easy to get lost in the Alaskan wilderness.
The Tlingit tribe, who lives in Juneau, has their own explanation for the high number of missing people: evil spirits called the Kushtaka.
According to books such as "In Search of the Kushtaka: Alaska's Other Bigfoot," the Kushtaka are shape-shifters (half-man, half-otter) who lure women and children to the water with fake cries in order to steal their human spirits and drown them.
ARIZONA: The ghosts of Slaughterhouse Canyon
The story of Slaughterhouse Canyon (not pictured), also called the less-frightening Luana's Canyon, takes place during the Gold Rush, according to The Miner.
During the 1800s, there was a family who lived in the canyon. They were very poor, so the father would venture out for food for his family.
One day, the father did not return, so his family slowly starved and descended into madness. The mother, unable to bear listening to her children's cries anymore, put on her wedding dress, murdered her children, and then threw them into a nearby river. The next day, she succumbed to starvation herself.
The legend states that if you go down to Slaughterhouse Canyon at night, even now, you will hear the loud, anguished cries of the mother who lost her mind.
ARKANSAS: The Boggy Creek Monster
According to Atlas Obscura, the Boggy Creek Monster of Fouke is Arkansas' version of Sasquatch. He's commonly accepted to be around 7 or 8 feet tall and covered in hair. Legend says that he roams the creeks of rural Arkansas.
He was first spotted in 1834 when people reported seeing a "wild man."
These days, after people claim to spot the Boggy Creek Monster, the sightings are documented on the official Boggy Creek Monster's website.
He has been the subject of at least five feature-length films, including 1972's "The Legend of Boggy Creek."
CALIFORNIA: The Char-Man
The Char-Man's origin story, told in the journal "Western Folklore," is gruesome: A father and son were both caught in a house fire and horribly burned in 1948.
After the fire, the son became so mentally unstable that he killed his father. When the police found the son, he was so unrecognizably burned that they didn't realize he was alive, so he ran away before they were able to arrest him for the murder of his father.
The story goes that, ever since then, the Char-Man can be spotted wandering the woods surrounding Ojai, occasionally approaching tents of innocent campers or pretending to be a hitchhiker and attempting to attack them.
COLORADO: The many legends of Riverdale Road
Riverdale Road is the site of not one, but eight creepy stories. Ranging from a "Hell Gate" to ghosts of slaves hanging from the trees, the stretch of road is decidedly spooky, as reported by local news affiliate Fox31.
The creepiest story, though, is that of the phantom jogger.
One day, there was a driver who hit a jogger and left him for dead. Now, it's said that if you park at the site of the crash, you'll hear disembodied footsteps getting closer and closer to your car. People have reported handprints on their windows and banging noises as if someone was kicking the outside.
CONNECTICUT: Hannah Cranna
Known as the "Wicked Witch of Monroe," per CT Insider, Hannah Cranna gained a reputation as a witch in the 19th century when her husband died by mysteriously falling off a cliff — and locals reportedly believed that she had bewitched him. People also believed that she would cast spells on people she didn't like.
Hannah lived to the age of 77, but right before she died, she asked to be carried down to the cemetery in her coffin on foot, not by wagon. After her death, the people of Monroe tried to wheel her coffin down the hill but were unable — the coffin kept falling off — so they were forced to carry it.
When the townspeople returned to her home, it was found to be engulfed in flames, sealing Hannah's reputation for practicing witchcraft.
Now, you can visit her real grave in Trumbull.
DELAWARE: The ghost of Mr. Chew
While not a particularly mean-spirited ghost, Samuel Chew's story, as told in "Haunted Delaware," is still disconcerting.
Chew was the chief justice of the Delaware Supreme Court in 1741. As the story goes, while he was alive, he didn't always get the respect he deserved — people frequently made fun of his name by mimicking sneezes while he walked by.
After his death, people reported seeing his ghost sitting under a poplar tree, wandering the courthouse, and generally creeping out the residents of Dover. Chew would also pull on men's coattails and give women a cold, icy feeling.
FLORIDA: The gravity-defying Spook Hill
Cars that are parked in neutral at Spook Hill will appear to roll uphill, according to Atlas Obscura.
Legends say the hill is either the site of a Native American burial ground or an epic battle of a Native American chief against a crocodile.
But the truth is, it's actually just an illusion created by the hill's surroundings. While cars appear to be rolling uphill, they are still just rolling downhill.
GEORGIA: The ghost town of Lake Lanier
At the bottom of Lake Lanier lie (almost) fully intact towns, ferries, a racetrack, and multiple cemeteries.
In 1946, the Georgia government received congressional approval to create Lake Lanier, and it bought up entire towns to clear the space for the lake. However, it decided to let the water cover the towns rather than demolish them.
Now, Lake Lanier has a decidedly eerie feel about it. There have been an unusual number of freak accidents and deaths on the lake. From 1994 to 2020, there were 203 drownings, CNN reported.
Many of the bodies of people who drowned have never been recovered. People have reported feeling arms and legs in the water, wrote CNN, but have not been able to find them right after, leading people to believe that spirits still roam the lake.
HAWAII: Night Marchers
Night Marchers, according to Honolulu Magazine, are not evil spirits, but they do demand respect. They are spirits of ancient Hawaiian warriors who marched around the islands to protect sacred areas.
Legend says that if you look directly at a night marcher, you will be marked for death. And, if by some chance, you find yourself in the middle of a procession, you are supposed to lie down in the middle of the road.
IDAHO: The water babies of Massacre Rocks
Water babies are a Native American legend found in several places in America, most famously in Pocatello at Massacre Rocks State Park.
The Shoshone tribe was first recorded in 1805, according to the Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, and was roaming the Great Plains as early as the 1500s, so it's not clear when exactly this legend originated.
But the story goes that the Shoshone experienced an extreme famine, and mothers were forced to drown their babies in the river rather than watch their children starve.
Today, some people claim that if you sit quietly at the river by Massacre Rocks, you'll hear the sound of babies crying.
Other stories say that these babies grew gills and fins and survived, and now they seek revenge on their mothers by luring unsuspecting victims to their deaths in the river.
ILLINOIS: Homey the Clown
Throughout the suburbs of Chicago in the '90s, there was a rumor going around elementary schools: There was a creepy man dressed as Homey the Clown (yes, from "In Living Color"), driving around in a white van trying to lure kids into it with candy and money, as reported by the Chicago Reader and The Chicago Tribune.
In some variations, he was a kidnapper; in others, he was a rapist. But in all variations, Homey left a mark on young Chicago kids in the '90s.
INDIANA: The 100 Steps Cemetery
The 100 Steps Cemetery is located in Brazil. While it's unclear when the stories about the cemetery being haunted began, some gravestones date back to the 1860s.
The legend states that if someone finds themselves in the cemetery at midnight, they must climb the steps and count to 100. At this point, a ghost of an undertaker will appear and show the person a vision of their death.
On the way back down, the visitor is supposed to count the steps again — if they count the same number of steps, the vision is false.
People who have visited the cemetery in the past have tried to outsmart the supernatural forces in 100 Steps by avoiding the steps altogether. According to Indiana Ghost Detectives, they've reported being knocked or shoved to the ground by an unseen force.
IOWA: The Black Angel
The Black Angel stands over 8 feet tall in Oakland Cemetery in Iowa City, and she is black due to oxidation. According to Atlas Obscura, multiple legends have cropped up around her, most likely because of her dark appearance.
One legend says that a pregnant woman should never walk under her, or she'll lose the child. Others say that if you touch or kiss the statue, you'll be dead within six months.
Whether haunted, cursed, or completely harmless, the statue is definitely a somber sight to see.
KANSAS: The Devil's Chair
The legend of the Devil's Chair goes like this: An old farmer in Alma refused to sell his land to the city in order to build a new cemetery. Someone got a little too tired of waiting for him to sell, so he was pushed into his own well.
Eventually, someone said that there was a terrible smell coming from the well, so the city sent someone to investigate. The well was ruled empty, and it was boarded up.
Now, if you make your way to Alma, you can actually sit on the boarded-up well, but legend says that people who have sat on the well have been known to mysteriously disappear.
KENTUCKY: The Goat Man of Pope Lick
There's no clear consensus on how the Goat Man came to be. Some say he was a circus performer; others say he was a farmer who tortured his goats for Satan and, in return, was transformed into a hideous goat monster.
However, everyone does agree on his appearance: dark fur, pale skin, goat legs, and horns, reported Wave3, a local news outlet.
The monster is said to hide under the bridge at Pope Lick Creek in Louisville to lure people onto the train tracks, only to see them be hit by oncoming trains.
Sadly, interest in this urban legend has had some dangerous consequences. In 2016, an Ohio woman fell to her death from the bridge while looking for the Goat Man, reported The Washington Post.
LOUISIANA: The Grunch
Grunch Road is an old dirt road that leads deep into the woods and eventually to a dead end.
It was a favorite place for teenagers to go and do whatever teenagers do until they learned about the Grunch.
The Grunch are rumored to be a group of deformed, half-human, half-monsters that resulted from years of isolation in the Louisiana Bayous.
In the present day, it's said that if you find yourself on Grunch Road, don't get out of your car if you see a goat that looks injured. The stories say that the Grunch uses goats to lure people out of their cars so they can eat them and drain their blood.
MAINE: The mysterious stain on Colonel Jonathan Buck's tomb
The tomb of Colonel Jonathan Buck in Bucksport bears a mysterious leg-shaped stain.
The story goes that Buck sentenced a woman to burn for witchcraft, and while she was burning, her leg rolled out of the fire. It's also been said that the witch cursed Buck's tomb to always bear a stain for this injustice, the Bangor Daily News reported.
It is said that people have tried to get rid of this stain twice, but the stain keeps reappearing.
MARYLAND: Chessie the Chesapeake Bay monster
Chessie sightings have been around since the 1930s but really started to pick up steam in the '80s when photographic evidence became more readily available, WBAL-TV reported.
Chessie is said to resemble a snake, measures around 30 feet long, and is the approximate thickness of a telephone pole.
There haven't been any recorded attacks from Chessie, but a 30-foot-long snake does not sound like something most people would want to run into.
MASSACHUSETTS: The spirits of Hoosac Tunnel
In the 24-year-long construction of the Hoosac Tunnel in western Massachusetts, about 200 men died. Death was so associated with the tunnel that it was actually nicknamed "The Bloody Pit," according to Atlas Obscura.
After a particularly gruesome explosion in either 1867 or 1868, 13 miners were trapped inside the tunnel. The other workers assumed that the miners had died, but eventually, it was discovered that the miners had lived, built a raft to combat flooding, and eventually died due to poisonous gas inhalation.
It's said that these 13 miners haunted the tunnel for years, moaning and briefly appearing as ghosts.
MICHIGAN: The little girl on Knock Knock Road
The legend of Knock Knock Road, as reported by 99.1 WMFK, says that there was a little girl who was murdered on Knock Knock Road in the Detroit area, and now she appears to drivers at their car window, knocking, trying to find the person who killed her.
MINNESOTA: The Kensington runestone
In 1898, a Swedish-American farmer found a gigantic slab of rock on his farm with symbols that appeared to be Norse. Since then, no one has figured out where it came from.
While most historians have debunked the rock — now known as the Kensington Rune, according to Atlas Obscura — as a hoax, due to dating and inconsistencies with the Norse language of the time, the myth has persisted.
But if it wasn't the Vikings, who did leave this mysterious rock? And what does it say?
MISSISSIPPI: Deer Island's haunted treasure
The Ghost of Deer Island, reported by the Sun-Herald, originates from an old pirate story.
The story says that back in the 1920s, two men were fishing on Deer Island when they heard rustling in the bushes, a noise they assumed was caused by wild hogs. Eventually, they decided to check it out and encountered a headless skeleton. They ran back to their boat, and the skeleton followed them all the way there.
According to the pirates' story, there was a ship that sailed into Biloxi Bay and buried its treasure on Deer Island. The crew decided to behead one of their own and left his body behind to guard their treasure.
MISSOURI: Momo the Missouri Monster
Momo is Missouri's version of Bigfoot/Sasquatch. He's been said to have terrible body odor, a pumpkin-shaped head, and an appetite for dogs. In 1968, Momo tried to abduct a 4-year-old boy, though no evidence was ever found, a local radio station reported.
MONTANA: The story of Sacrifice Cliff
As reported by the Billings Gazette, the story of Sacrifice Cliff comes from an old Native American legend.
Two members of the Crow Tribe arrived in their village from a trip to find that almost everyone there had been infected with smallpox and had died. So heartbroken about the loss of their loved ones, the two decided to blindfold their horses and ride off the cliff to join the tribe on the other side.
Sacrifice Cliff is visible from almost anywhere in Billings, so it's sad (and a bit spooky) to think about this story while the cliff looms over the entire city.
NEBRASKA: The poisoned girl at Centennial Hall
When Business Insider chose the most haunted place in each state, Centennial Hall was a no-brainer. People claim that multiple ghosts roam the halls.
But the creepiest story of Centennial Hall originates in the 1940s, when it was a high school.
The story says that a student was playing her clarinet, suffered a heart attack, and died — because her reed was poisoned. Now, people claim to feel cold spots, hear disembodied music, and to have witnessed an empty rocking chair start to rock, according to the blog Theresa's Haunted History of the Tri-State.
NEVADA: The truth about Area 51
There is perhaps no urban legend, myth, or conspiracy theory more famous than Nevada's Area 51, a mysterious government facility that is rumored to be associated with aliens. The US government officially states that Area 51 is classified due to national security, which only fuels the fire.
The secrecy surrounding Area 51 is what makes it inherently creepy, and with the government admitting to a program investigating UFOs, the theories about what's actually going on inside continue to seem more plausible.
NEW HAMPSHIRE: The witch of Hampton, Goody Cole
Eunice "Goody" Cole was the only woman in New Hampshire history to be tried for witchcraft multiple times. Her first charge was in 1656, and she was charged again in 1671, according to the Hampton Historical Society.
When she died and her body was recovered, the townspeople were rumored to have staked her through the heart to prevent her from haunting their town, according to Atlas Obscura.
People continue to blame Goody Cole for the misfortunes of Hampton citizens for the past 300 years. For example, a boat full of Hampton residents overturned, and everyone on board drowned, even though they were within swimming distance of shore. People blamed Goody Cole for the crash and for cursing the passengers by having them forget how to swim.
NEW JERSEY: The Jersey Devil
The story of the Jersey Devil has been around since the 1700s, Weird NJ reported. The legend states that a woman named Mother Leeds became pregnant with her 13th child and said, "Let this one be [a/the] devil." Once the child was born, it grew hooves, wings, horns, and a tail.
The monster has been spotted periodically throughout history in the Pine Barrens region of New Jersey. The state has embraced the legend so much that it named its hockey team after it.
NEW MEXICO: La Mala Hora
La Mala Hora, which translates to The Evil Hour, is an entity you don't want to run into on a dark road. Legend says it first appears as a ball of black energy, constantly moving and changing its size and shape. If you look at it, it will drive you insane and will slowly kill you.
At other times, it appears as a scary-looking woman. It's said that if you see her at a crossroads, you or someone in your family will die.
NEW YORK: Cropsey
The story of Cropsey has many iterations, The Lineup reported, but it generally tells the story of a man who stalked a sleep-away camp/psychiatric facility/children's hospital, had a hook for a hand, and killed children who were wandering alone at night. Almost anyone who went to camp in upstate New York has heard about Cropsey.
Things took a more sinister turn when a documentary posited that Cropsey was actually real: a convicted child kidnapper named Andre Rand, wrote The New York Times.
NORTH CAROLINA: The beast of Bladenboro
In the 1950s, multiple dogs were found dead and drained of blood in the North Carolina town of Bladenboro, according to North Carolina Ghosts. People believed a vampiric beast was in the woods, and they tried to hunt the animal.
Today, the town of Bladenboro has embraced its history, and residents actually hold a Beast Fest every year. While some people are convinced the beast was probably a particularly large bobcat, it's never been confirmed exactly what was stalking their town.
NORTH DAKOTA: White Lady Lane
The story of White Lady Lane is a tragic one, according to Only In Your State.
The legend states that a young woman became pregnant out of wedlock, and her religious parents forced her to marry the baby's father. The baby ended up dying after their wedding. The girl, so upset about her baby and her forced marriage, hanged herself from a bridge in her wedding dress. Locals claim to still see her ghost hanging from the bridge.
OHIO: The werewolf of Defiance.
During the summer of 1972, the people of Defiance said they were being terrorized by a werewolf, per Mysterious Universe.
The sightings always happened at night, generally by the train tracks. A couple of women said it would try to get into their houses by rattling the doorknobs. The animal was said to be huge, hairy, and dressed in rags.
But after summer ended, the beast disappeared, never to be heard from again. But the story lingers.
OKLAHOMA: The mysterious Shaman's portal
The mysterious occurrences in Beaver Dunes Park have been attributed to the fact that it was built upon ancient Native American burial grounds, which is why it's called the Shaman's portal, according to Only In Your State.
It's also known as the Oklahoma Bermuda Triangle.
Mysterious things have happened in the park, starting with the Spanish conquistadors who went missing while searching for gold in the 1500s. Since then, paranormal activity seekers have flocked to the dunes. Some people claim that a UFO crashed there, and a group in the '90s who tested the soil said it was "abnormal."
OREGON: The Bandage Man of Cannon Beach
The Bandage Man is the American version of a mummy, wrote the Cannon Beach History Center and Museum.
He is rumored to be the ghost of a logger who died in a sawmill accident and now terrorizes teenagers who hang out at a deserted area of a highway near Cannon Beach. Stories say that he knocks on car windows to try to get in and smells really, really bad.
PENNSYLVANIA: The bus to nowhere
In Philadelphia, there's rumored to be a bus that doesn't have an end destination, according to Only In Your State. The story says that the bus only picks up passengers who are at their lowest moments and need to get away from their problems. Once the passenger is ready to face the world, they can get off the bus.
But the passenger has no idea how long they've been on the bus for — it could have been hours, days, or even years.
RHODE ISLAND: The Devil's footprints
There is a rock on Devil's Foot Road that appears to show a normal human footprint and a cloven hoof, according to a Medium blog about New England folklore.
The story goes that a Native American woman murdered a white man and fled the scene of the crime.
While running, she was stopped by another man. She cried out for the Devil to save her, but the man admitted that he himself was the Devil and stomped his feet on the ground to prove that he had a cloven hoof, which the rock still shows to this day. You can see it on Waymarking.
SOUTH CAROLINA: The death of Julia Legare
In the 1800s, the Legares were a well-to-do South Carolinian family that had homes on the mainland and on Edisto Island. The daughter, Julia, got sick, was pronounced dead, and was buried inside their family mausoleum, according to Edisto's website.
Years later, another member of the Legare family died, and when their tomb was opened up, the remains of Julia were found outside her coffin. The story says that Julia had been in a coma, and had woken up to try to escape her tomb, but sadly died.
After the first reopening of the Legare mausoleum, the door couldn't seem to stay shut. The Legares tried multiple different doors, and every single time, the door was found open. People believe that Julia's ghost didn't want to be locked in that tomb any longer.
SOUTH DAKOTA: Walking Sam and the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation
Purportedly over 7 feet tall and very slim, Walking Sam is said to appear on the streets of the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation at night, and he tries to convince teenagers to take their own lives, per Hot 104.7.
Whether Walking Sam is real, something tragic is going on at the reservation. From December 2014 to May 2015, there were 103 attempts by people to end their lives at Pine Ridge, reported The Daily Dot.
TENNESSEE: The boy in the bathroom at Pine Haven School
The Pine Haven School, located in Jamestown, is old and abandoned, and according to Urban Legends Online, it's said to be haunted.
A tragic story supposedly took place there, where a boy was cornered by a group of bullies in the bathroom and shoved into a mirror, which shattered and killed him.
To avoid getting caught committing murder, the bullies decided to bury the body underneath the floorboards. Today, people say that if you go inside the school, you can see the reflection of the boy if you look in the mirror.
TEXAS: The Candy Lady
According to Urban Legends Online, in the early 1900s, children in an unnamed rural town in Texas started to disappear, and the residents blamed the Candy Lady.
The story says that she would go around leaving candy on children's windows, eventually luring the kids out with notes attached, promising more candy.
The story picked up steam when a farmer reportedly found rotten teeth on his farm and later found the body of a boy with his pockets stuffed with candy.
UTAH: The curse of the Escalante Petrified Forest
While it is illegal to take anything from Escalante Petrified Forest State Park, a legend says that anyone who takes pieces of petrified wood from the park will be cursed with bad luck, sickness, and accidents, KSL reported.
Park manager Kendall Farnsworth told KSL in 2014 that he gets about a dozen packages every year containing a piece of wood from the park and an apologetic letter detailing the sender's misfortunes.
VERMONT: The frozen people
First appearing in a diary that was published in the late 1800s, the legend of the hibernating older people recounts the tale of a poor family outside Montpelier who couldn't afford to feed and clothe the oldest members of their family, so they froze the people and buried them, wrote Vermonter.
Legend has it that when spring rolled around, the elders thawed out and were just fine.
VIRGINIA: The Bunnyman
The Bunnyman's legend starts with what every good urban legend begins with: An insane asylum.
As reported by WAMU 88.5, the people of Clifton were so up in arms about the asylum that they were able to get all of the patients transferred. The patients were being moved on a bus that crashed, and the police were able to catch all the patients except one — the Bunnyman.
According to the tale, the Bunnyman lived in the woods and sustained himself on woodland creatures (like bunnies), but eventually, he attacked humans.
Some people reported being attacked by a man with a hatchet. Other tales say that groups of teens would see a bright light and then would wind up dead and strung up over a bridge, the Washingtonian reported.
WASHINGTON: Bigfoot
Bigfoot is an internationally recognizable name, and has been spotted all over the country. But, Bigfoot has been spotted the most in Washington state, according to an online database compiling all Bigfoot sightings.
Bigfoot is essentially a gigantic ape-like creature who is either a ferocious beast that attacks loggers and hikers, or a gentle giant who wants to be left alone.
Either way, there's something creepy about an undiscovered species of animal wandering around the Pacific Northwest, evading capture.
WEST VIRGINIA: Mothman
In 1966, stories say that West Virginia was visited by an insectoid flying creature with bright red eyes who resembled both a moth and a man, according to Atlas Obscura. He was spotted flying around the town of Point Pleasant, along with shining lights and the equally conspiratorial Men in Black
Mothman's origins have been said to be supernatural, alien, or a government experiment gone wrong.
But Point Pleasant has embraced the monster, erecting a statue, creating a museum, and even dedicating a festival to him. In 2002, a film starring Richard Gere, "The Mothman Prophecies," was released.
WISCONSIN: Boy Scout Lane
The story of what exactly happened at Boy Scout Lane varies, but they all end with the same conclusion: a group of Boy Scouts dead on the road.
In some stories, McDowell News wrote, there was a bus crash with no survivors, or they were murdered by their bus driver, or they just mysteriously vanished into the woods one by one.
Visitors have reported seeing a swinging body in the trees, feeling like they are being watched, and finding child-size handprints.
WYOMING: Devils Tower
There's no scientific consensus on why Devils Tower looks the way it does, but multiple Native American creation stories attribute the landmark's shape to a tragedy.
According to the various stories, two boys were attacked and chased by a large bear, so they ran up the rock formation. The bear tried to follow, but couldn't make the climb and left scratches all the way down the rock as it slid down, according to Rapid City's tourism website.

Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires
- Published
Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.
Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.
Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.
The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.
While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El Niño ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.
Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.
Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.
Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.
Mama Lifa and her child Lifa were found in a patch of acacia trees entirely surrounded by oil palm plantations.
The degradation of their habitat by wildfires as well as a lack of food sources prompted their rescue in mid-September.
Mama Man and her baby, Man, had been monitored by animal rescuers since June, when they were found living in a plantation area adjacent to a small patch of forest.
Fires that spread near to the site restricted their roaming area further, leaving them without a safe route to other forestry. The threat of exposure to the blazes led to them being evacuated in early September, Yiara said.
The reserve these orangutans were released into was chosen because it there is food and water available and it is connected to other forested areas.
Yiari's Argitoe Ranting said: "We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat."
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned that wildfires were burning in habitats containing 52% of Borneo's orangutan population.
It says a large portion of the ape's habitat will become inhospitable to them if climate change continues at its current pace.
This year's El Niño has become the strongest on record and is expected to have a knock-on effect on the climate into next year.
Experts have also pointed to land-clearing practices used to make room for plantations as another factor facilitating the spread of wildfires in Indonesia, with naturally fire-resistant forests replaced by less dense and shaded vegetation.
That the orangutan's original habitats had been burned and fragmented to the point they could no longer sustain the primates was the main driving factor behind relocating them, Yiara said.

Zydus Lifesciences has launched in the U.S. market Riociguat tablets, in multiple strengths, developed and manufactured by MSN Laboratories.
The two companies are the first to launch the product, which is a generic version of Bayer’s Adempas. Approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as a generic equivalent of Adempas tablets, in all five strengths, Riociguat tablets are indicated for treatment of persistent or recurrent chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after surgical treatment, or inoperable CTEPH; and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
“Being first to market with generic riociguat is a milestone for our U.S. business and for patients with pulmonary hypertension. It reflects the strength of our complex-generics pipeline, our ability to execute day-one launches in specialty categories and the strength of our partnerships that complement our commercial reach in the U.S.” Zydus Lifesciences Managing Director Sharvil Patel said in a release on Monday.
MSN Laboratories founder and CMD MSN Reddy said “Riociguat is a technically demanding molecule and bringing the first generic to the U.S. demonstrates the depth of MSN’s integrated API and formulation R&D and the scale of our manufacturing. Together with Zydus’ established U.S. commercial platform, we are confident of delivering consistent, high-quality supply of this important therapy.”
Thus far, Riociguat was available in the U.S. only as the branded product. Sales of drug are not reported by IQVIA. According to Bayer’s annual report 2025, the global sales of Adempas were around Euro 745 million (approximately $850 million) in 2025, Zydus said.

In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.
The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.
The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.
The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.
Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”
He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.
The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)
All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.
Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.
But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.
Adding to the excitement was Steve Jobs’ willingness to redesign the iPod every year. Apple could have maintained its original iPod for a long spell, but almost immediately the company began a series of significant reinventions. Every cycle yielded an iPod with a different size and shape. With each iteration, the iPod seemed to grow smaller and cooler. First came the mini, then came multiple variations of nanos and shuffles in crazy colors and configurations. iPhone updates have kept people buying, but without the fun of a total reshaping of the product.
Is there an alternate universe where Apple continued making the iPod as a dedicated digital music player? I called Tony Fadell to discuss. Fadell is often referred to as the father of the iPod; he headed its hardware team and delivered the product in an amazing sprint of less than a year. He later was deeply involved in developing the iPhone, and his post-Apple career includes cofounding Nest, becoming a successful tech investor, and writing a well-received book.
Fadell resigned from Apple in 2008 and consulted for two years after that, when Apple was still supporting the iPod. But he recalls Jobs and other execs agreeing that the device was on a course to oblivion, despite being a great product with an enthusiastic user base. With the iPhone proving to be a monster success that also helped boost the Macintosh, and Apple pursuing potentially mass-market innovations like the iPad, iPod sales were becoming less relevant to the company’s bottom line. Jobs was a relentless prioritizer, and his successor Tim Cook felt the same way.
Fadell says that there was very little hand-wringing about the iPod’s fate. “The discussion was about Apple [not] doing lower-value things,” he says. Yet he agrees with me that the iPod’s disappearance created a hole that hasn’t been filled.
In retrospect, he says, what made the iPod invaluable is what it didn’t do—connect with the internet. “Because the iPod wasn't connected, you didn’t have all these other things going on to distract you. Today, you get all the annoyance of being connected without being able to get the same listening experience. You can always be distracted and go somewhere else.”
“This thing should still exist,” he says.
A lot of people seem to agree. There are multiple active communities on Facebook and Reddit of refuseniks who go to great lengths to mod old iPods—putting in large flash drives, installing Bluetooth. There’s even an app that makes your iPhone look and play like an iPod Classic. It works great, but you’re still one swipe away from your feeds, your mail, and everything else in your life that isn’t as fun as music.
I ask Fadell how he regards the iPod’s legacy. Tellingly, his answer speaks to Apple’s history more than exhilaration for the product itself. “The iPhone never would have existed without it,” he says. “That means that the Apple we know of would never have existed without the iPod.” It helped turn a computer company with a limited user base into a consumer electronics giant.
“And the crazy thing is that it was exactly 25 years ago—which is half the years that Apple has existed. There was the Apple II, and then the Mac, and then, boom,” he adds.
I prefer to remember the iPod for what it was, not what it led to. Not long ago, I exhumed my iPod Classic. I have an old boombox with a cradle designed for the iPod, with the old 30-pin connector. I put it in shuffle mode and blissed out.
I suspect a lot of others might like to return to iPod Nation. New CEO John Ternus has no incentive to revive the product, of course. I do find it sad, however, that a generation exists that doesn’t know what it’s like to have a dedicated music device that will never interrupt a tune with calls, texts, and notifications. They don’t know what they’re missing.

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”
Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”
Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.
An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.
Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.
“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.
The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.
In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.
Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.
The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.
“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.
Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.
Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.
The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.
Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.
This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”
When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.
Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

At the United Nations High Level Meeting (UN HLM), in New York in September 2026, India made official remarks on the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention Preparedness and Response (PPPR). The Declaration is part of the emerging global legal regime on pandemics led by the WHO-Pandemic agreement (PA).
Shaping the framework
The PA was adopted by 124 member-states in 2025, including India. No country voted against it, while 11 abstained, reflecting alignment across high-, middle- and low-income countries (HICs/LICs/LMICs). The negotiations hinged on how to balance national sovereignty with international cooperation and solidarity, exposing the fault lines between the Global North and the Global South. Key issues included whether a global treaty can set binding targets for measures such as ‘One Health’ without securing funding for countries with fragile health systems. Or whether national pandemic regulations can be harmonised through global frameworks. And whether private manufacturers can be required to share vaccines in real time at affordable prices.
The PA is not yet open for ratification because negotiations are still ongoing for an annex concerning the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system. PABS could help ensure that, during a pandemic, LICs and LMICs receive a fair share of vaccines, medicines and other therapeutics.
Even without ratification, the PA has created a first-of-its-kind global legal regime for the PPPR. Operationalisation requires countries such as India to balance interests of the HICs, LICs and LMICs. This will determine whether the PA will further entrench the inequities of the COVID-19 pandemic or make global health governance truly inclusive.
Editorial | Landmark agreement: On the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement
At the UN HLM, India succeeded in enshrining the multilateral components of the PA within the principle of national sovereignty. India reiterated its commitment to strengthen global pandemic preparedness but stressed that effective pandemic management requires that international coordination is demonstrated. The first is equitable access to drugs, vaccines and therapeutics and the creation of global public goods, such as digital infrastructure (which admittedly align with its own national priorities).
The second is a respect for national sovereignty and the primacy of member-states in shaping global policy interventions according to national circumstance. As a contrast, the United States rejected the Declaration, calling the PABS and WHO’s role in declaring pandemics as a challenge to its national interests.
India’s line
In its remarks, India has acknowledged the concerns of the Global North and the South. Both sides have upheld national sovereignty as paramount in several provisions. The African countries did not give consent to commitments to monitor the human-animal-environment interface, a key source of pandemic outbreaks, without significant funding, which was not guaranteed by the Global North. Similarly, countries in the Global North did not want binding targets with regard to technology transfer (and other similar provisions).
But as India said at the UN HLM, ‘Global Solidarity must be demonstrated through action’; India must be an active player in the finalisation of the global PPPR regime. India is already actively engaged in the PABS negotiations and must lead the Global South in the post-PABS context. India can consider three options. First, developing partnerships on technical areas of the PA (One Health, surveillance, health workforce strengthening) to build trust with other countries in the Global South, and a ‘store’ of operational solutions to tricky national sovereignty problems.
Second, leveraging its leadership role within existing global political groupings. For example, the H20 summit (a health and development G-7 and G-20 partnership) will take place under the United Kingdom’s G-20 leadership at the end of 2027; pandemic preparedness is one of the core health agendas. During India’s G-20 presidency in 2023, India launched the Global Initiative for Digital Health and holds considerable influence within the platform’s health initiatives. Another is ‘Partners for Multilateralism’, which was launched in 2026 by the European Union (co-sponsors are Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya).
Third, strengthening and aligning domestic policy and regulatory architecture around its own priorities for the PA. Global leadership always rests on domestic strengths. India must ensure that its national policies on PPPR such as regulation of access to biological material and distribution of the benefits uphold the highest standards of equity which India can then demand at the global level.
A South-South health role
An equitable global regime on PPPR is in India’s interests as much as a responsibility towards the Global South. India is the pharmacy of the world, manufacturing one of the largest shares of vaccines in the world in terms of volume. Yet, it needs an equitable global vaccine distribution regime. The patents for the vaccines that India manufactures are held by global pharmaceuticals. India is also import-dependent for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs).
India needs access to the latest technology from the Global North to strengthen the manufacturing of high-grade personal protective equipment and medical devices. At the same time, India needs to lead South-South Cooperation and share its technological strength with other countries in the Global South.
India’s health system has a continental scale, and as India’s Health Secretary stated at the UN HLM, its interventions in digital health infrastructure, laboratories networks and One Health are valuable as global public goods. An effective PA needs an engaged India, and a strong PA will strengthen India’s own pandemic management.
Priyadarshini Singh is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). This article is based on a forthcoming CSEP working paper on the Pandemic Agreement.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

SpaceX has a deal to purchase nationwide low-band spectrum licenses for a planned terrestrial mobile network that would complement the space-based Starlink cellular service.
SpaceX will buy up to 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band from investment firm Grain Management, which bought the spectrum rights from T-Mobile earlier this year. T-Mobile had obtained the spectrum when it bought Sprint in 2020 and was required to sell the licenses under a merger condition imposed by the US government.
“This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US,” SpaceX said yesterday. SpaceX this week also received US approval to launch 15,000 satellites for an upgraded version of its mobile service that it says will be far more powerful than the current offering.
The 800 MHz spectrum licenses cover “approximately 100 percent of the US population,” the Federal Communications Commission said in a July 2026 order approving Grain’s purchase of the T-Mobile licenses. While the licenses are nationwide, it’s not a huge amount of spectrum. It ranges from 4.85 megahertz to 14 megahertz depending on the county. The FCC said the 800 MHz spectrum can be used for terrestrial service, satellite-to-mobile service, or both.
SpaceX’s low-band purchase is in addition to 65 MHz of nationwide mid-band spectrum licenses it is buying from EchoStar. The FCC approved that $17 billion purchase in May 2026.
“While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings. Critically, most existing mobile devices already support this underused band,” SpaceX said.
SpaceX’s big mobile plans
SpaceX’s spectrum deal is likely to be approved by the FCC, but it could face opposition from small carriers. The Rural Wireless Association opposed EchoStar’s spectrum sales to AT&T and SpaceX, saying the deals “continue the troubling pattern of spectrum aggregation that disadvantages rural wireless providers.” Across all carriers in the US, there is about 1.1 GHz of licensed spectrum allocated to mobile operators, with the big three holding dominant spectrum portfolios.

Cheetahs to play European games in Swansea

South African side Cheetahs will play their European Challenge Cup home matches this season at St Helen's in Swansea, the home of Welsh side Ospreys.
Cheetahs host Dragons on Sunday, 13 December and Perpignan on Sunday, 17 January with both games a day after Ospreys' home matches in the same competition.
