Hincapie and Zubimendi injured in post-match training session
- Published
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says it is "far from ideal" that Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi were injured in a post-match training session after the Gunners' 2-1 Premier League win against Leeds.
A training session was held after Saturday's match at Emirates Stadium for players who either did not feature in or did not play the full 90 minutes against Leeds.
Ecuador defender Hincapie was carried off by goalkeeper Illan Meslier during the session, and Arteta later confirmed Spain midfielder Zubimendi was also hurt.
Hincapie, 24, came on after 82 minutes as Arsenal saw out victory against Leeds, while Zubimendi, 27, was an unused substitute.
"We had a training session planned after the match for everyone that didn't get enough minutes, and in two unfortunate actions we lost two players," Arteta said in a news conference before Tuesday's Champions League match against Lille.
"They'll have further scans to see where they are and we'll have that time frame for how long they are going to be out for."
When asked by the media what could have been done to prevent the injuries, Arteta joked the pair should not have trained.
"Never train and they don't get injured. The consequence of that is when you ask them to play they have no rhythm and no impact in the game," the Spaniard added.
"It's never happened in seven years I've been here. It could happen in the training session the next day.
"It's happened now and hopefully it doesn't happen again, but what can you do?
"If I had a crystal ball I would just say 'guys, get in the jacuzzi and I will see you tomorrow'."
Hincapie has made three Premier League appearances off the bench this season but started Arsenal's Champions League win over Napoli last month.
Zubimendi has also largely featured as a substitute, making five Premier League appearances from the bench.
How did the injuries happen?
Arsenal had planned for the players who did not play a full game or had not had minutes in the 2-1 win to train at the Emirates Stadium so that all of the squad could have a recovery day on Sunday and then train on Monday.
Arteta regularly arranges for the players who have not played a full match to take part in a small-sided game on the pitch, and this is how Hincapie and Zubimendi picked up the injuries.
The manager does this so that all of the players have a similar output when they are navigating their busy fixture schedule.
Arteta, who says it was done to get "everybody in the best rhythm", said Hincapie's ankle injury was more serious than Zubimendi's.
Substitute goalkeeper Meslier was seen carrying Hincapie off the pitch on his back, even though there were staff members present.
And this is something that Arteta does not seem to be happy about, saying: "that's something else, not to discuss here".

The tropical Pacific has seen heat build for months as a “super” El Niño takes shape.
A climate phenomenon that forms every few years, this year’s iteration of El Niño has been on a tear of daily records and is forecast to reach unprecedented strength this winter. While it’s characterized by hotter-than-normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific, El Niño is a global problem.
It’s fair to wonder how another global problem is interacting with El Niño: climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels. While a hotter climate begetting a hotter El Niño might seem like a done deal, “I have more questions than I have reactions” to what’s happening, says Christopher Callahan, a climate researcher at Indiana University. In other words, the relationship is still an area of active research—and this year’s event could provide vital insights.
El Niño’s added ocean heat affects the atmosphere, causing weather patterns around the world to shift. Consider it kind of like a domino run, where one tile starts a chain reaction. Such a major slug of heat in the Pacific will act more like a shove then a light flick on the atmosphere, and the resulting shifts in weather are expected to be generationally intense.
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting 100 percent odds of an extremely strong El Niño through December and above 80 percent odds it stays that way through February. Data shows this El Niño has already set multiple all-time daily heat records including a recent peak of 3.4 degrees Celsius.
NOAA issues its El Niño forecast as a three-month rolling average, and the agency predicts heat could peak at 2.7 degrees Celsius above normal for the period from October to December. (It’s not out of the question that heat could surpass 3 degrees Celsius, though.) If the forecast holds true, it would smash the previous record of 2.4 degrees Celsius, which was set during the 1982-1983 event.
How Is Climate Change Impacting El Niño?
There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is likely playing at least some role in influencing El Niño. The magnitude and frequency of the phenomenon has increased over the past 60 years, says Francisco Estrada, coordinator of the Climate Change Research Program at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, and so has the variability and how the effects are distributed around the world. He says there shouldn’t be a debate framed as a choice between a “natural El Niño” and an “El Niño caused by climate change” but rather as an interaction between the two processes.
“You can’t separate El Niño from global warming—they’re inextricably linked,” he explains.
Modeling also indicates that El Niño is likely to strengthen as the planet warms, though Callahan notes that many models struggle to accurately represent long-term temperature trends in the eastern tropical Pacific. That can give researchers some pause, but there’s also other evidence that climate change is juicing El Niño.
“The majority of climate models say that El Nino amplitude shall go up in a warming climate, and all of our paleoclimate records say that we're currently in a more active period of El Niño than the last several 1,000 years,” Callahan says.
Research published in August uses data collected from ancient coral, and provides that 1,000-year glimpse Callahan mentions. (He wasn’t involved with the study.) The scientists found an uptick in El Niño amplitude that neatly mirrors when humans started pumping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, though they didn’t attempt to attribute the shift to climate change.
This year’s El Niño will provide another data point to help researchers suss things out.
How Is El Niño Impacting Climate Change?
But as Callahan notes, there’s also an important question about how El Niño is layering on top of climate change.
“Even if climate change has not made the event itself stronger, even if the [sea surface temperature] anomalies are totally natural, the presence of those SSTs in a climate that has been changed by global warming might produce unprecedented impacts,” he says.
El Niño’s impacts on weather—known as teleconnections—are well known, from increasing the odds of drought in the Amazon and Indonesia to juicing precipitation in the Southwest US and lowering the odds of Atlantic hurricanes.
Such an extreme event layered on top of climate change doesn’t mean teleconnections get thrown out the window, though. In fact, some of them may be even more intense.
“We can no longer place as much confidence in the knowledge we’ve gathered from data regarding how El Niño manifests in terms of weather and climate in different parts of the planet,” says Estrada.
What El Niño Means for Climate Risk
From a risk perspective, Estrada believes it’s important to understand how the two phenomena interact and how that combination will affect societies.
He and Callahan’s main concern is not merely whether this El Niño will be the most intense on record but rather the combination of an exceptional event with a climate that has warmed significantly.
“Surprises are the last thing you want when you’re trying to manage risk,” Estrada says.
Callahan’s work shows that the impacts of El Niño on society are extreme, with the most severe events knocking off trillions of dollars from the global GDP. Ecosystems also suffer greatly, particularly coral reefs, which are facing a mass bleaching event.
Given this scenario, the United Nations and other international organizations have called for urgent adaptation measures to safeguard the well-being of the at-risk populations and ecosystems. Some places are already doing that: California preemptively declared a state of emergency last month.
“El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world. Impacts will hit even harder, travel even farther, and cross borders with devastating speed,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said last month.

We got our first look at Prime Video’s new sci-fi series Blade Runner 2099 in July at San Diego Comic-Con. With the show’s premiere roughly six weeks away, the streamer unveiled the full trailer this weekend at New York Comic-Con. Co-stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) joined showrunner Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) onstage for the big reveal.
As Luisa described the show during the NYCC panel Saturday night:
We are 50 years after [Blade Runner] 2049 and, bad news, the worst has happened. The replicant uprising that has been bubbling up in the films has taken place and the humans have lost. So the creations have surpassed their creators. And the series, the big question it asks is, ‘What happens when our time as a species ends?’ 2099 is taking place at a junction point when one species is ending and a new one is rising. The first film, something I loved about it, was that it was looking at mortality on a micro level. Roy Batty and the other replicants were fighting for more life. This show asks that same question but on a macro level. Mankind—what happens when we realize our time is running out? And are we going to accept that loss? Can we hold on to our humanity during it?
Yeoh stars as Olwen, the dying Replicant, while Schafer plays Cora. The cast also includes Hugo Hamlet as Buster Friendly, as well as Dmitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Matthew Needham, Tom Burke, and Maurizio Lombardi—all in as-yet-undisclosed roles.
Prime Video will drop all eight episodes of Blade Runner 2099 on November 25, 2026.

India’s cleantech startups attracted substantially more capital in Q3 2026, with large electric mobility rounds driving funding growth alongside an increase in deal activity. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, cleantech startups raised $433 Mn across 23 deals, compared with $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter. The report tracks funding announced up to September 24. The increase stood out against a subdued funding environment. Overall startup funding rose just 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn, while funding for fintech and ecommerce startups declined 11% and 31%, respectively. However, the cleantech funding surge was heavily concentrated in electric mobility. River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette attracted $85 Mn. Together, the three startups accounted for $298 Mn, or nearly 69% of the sector’s funding. Adding to this, Simple Energy raised a mega $180 Mn round at the end of the month of September, further adding to this trend. The numbers raise two questions: what is drawing investors towards these businesses and how far does the momentum extend beyond a handful of large EV rounds? Commercial Viability Shapes Investor Bets For investors, the appeal is increasingly tied to whether technology can solve a tangible problem and support a commercially viable business. “What's different this cycle is that capital is backing businesses and not just the energy transition,” Elev8 Venture Partners managing partner Navin Honagudi told Inc42. The VC firm led River’s $120 Mn Series C in August. The round alone accounted for nearly 28% of the quarter’s cleantech funding. Shubham Jhuria, CFO and partner at Aeravti Ventures, also pointed to a shift in how investors assess the sector. “The biggest change we are seeing is that the cleantech conversation is moving beyond the climate-impact narrative towards businesses solving very specific economic and infrastructure problems,” he told Inc42. Funding activity extended beyond the three largest EV rounds, with Omega Seiki Mobility, Electric.AI, Simple Energy, and Yuma also raising capital during the quarter. Cleantech deal count increased about 44%, while the average cheque size rose to approximately $19 Mn from $7 Mn in the year-ago quarter. EVs accounted for 57% of deals, according to the report. This suggests that the increase was not solely the result of larger cheques, although electric mobility remained central to both funding value and deal activity. EV Adoption Supports The Investment Case Rising EV adoption is giving investors a more tangible basis to assess demand and business models. JMK Research estimates that 15.41 Lakh EVs were registered in H1 2026, up 43% YoY. According to Vahan, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in September. E2W registrations increased 12.2% to 2.07 Lakh units from 1.84 Lakh in August. Honagudi said electric mobility has matured into a demand-led market. He pointed to River’s position among India’s top seven electric two-wheeler brands by registrations, despite having far fewer retail outlets than established players, as evidence of product-led demand. Over the next 3-5 years, Elev8 expects deeper localisation of motors and electronics to improve margins and supply-chain resilience. Honagudi cited last year’s rare earth magnet shortage as an example of the vulnerabilities that localisation could address. He also expects consolidation to leave “a handful of scaled independents” alongside established incumbents. Can The Momentum Broaden? Stronger adoption does not automatically translate into attractive investor returns. Jhuria cautioned that investment appetite could moderate if businesses struggle to convert technological capabilities into scalable solutions or continue to require substantial capital without improving their unit economics. The quarter’s numbers reflect both wider deal activity and substantial concentration. More cleantech startups attracted funding than a year earlier, but three EV businesses still captured more than two-thirds of the capital. For the momentum to broaden, investor conviction will need to extend beyond large electric mobility bets. Within EVs, the test will be whether rising demand and deeper localisation translate into stronger margins and businesses that can scale without repeatedly requiring outsized capital infusions.

‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

‘Pause SIR, independent audit of voter deletion’: INDIA bloc petition to Supreme Court lists 10 requests
The petition raises concerns over the “unilateral and arbitrary exercise” of the election body's collective powers by CEC during the ongoing SIR.
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, along with 10 INDIA bloc leaders, filed a petition in the Supreme Court on Monday against the Election Commission of India (ECI) on issues linked to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and alleged poll irregularities.
As Gandhi could not reach the Supreme Court to file the petition in person, his advocate, S Prasanna, filed it, naming the ECI, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, and the two other election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, as respondents.
What the INDIA bloc petition says
The petition raises concerns over the “unilateral and arbitrary exercise” of the election body's collective powers by CEC Gyanesh Kumar during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the integrity of the electoral process, and the alleged infringement of eligible citizens’ constitutional right to register as voters and exercise their right to vote. Here are the key points:
Suspend ongoing SIR until the issues raised are considered
Deep Dive
It directs the ECI to suspend the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls across the States of the Union until the issues raised in the petition are considered and decided, to protect the rights of eligible voters and preserve the integrity of the electoral process.
Petition seeks SIR decision records, ECINET and ERONET access logs
The petition seeks a directive to the Election Commission of India (ECI) to place on record the complete files, agendas, minutes, notings and objections relating to each disputed decision concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
It also seeks the relevant ECINET and ERONET access logs and the complete file recording the decision dated June 24, 2025, to commence the SIR across the country, in furtherance of the rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 21, read with Article 324 of the Constitution of India.
Review SIR decisions under Article 324 and relevant law
The petition seeks a review of whether the disputed SIR decisions comply with Article 324 of the Constitution, Section 18 of the 2023 Act governing the Election Commissioners, and the Supreme Court’s ruling in T.N. Seshan v. Union of India. It also seeks to have any decisions found to be unlawful quashed or set aside.
Action against those responsible
The petition also seeks against those responsible for violating the constitutional or statutory provisions governing the preparation and revision of electoral rolls, including Section 32 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
ECI decisions on SIR to be recorded
The petition also seeks a direction to the Election Commission to ensure that every decision of the Election Commission relating to the Special Intensive Revision is taken and duly minuted in accordance with Section 18 of the 2023 Act.
Ensure compliance of Form 6 with prescribed rules
The petition directs the commission to ensure that the online Form 6 conforms to the form prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, unless and until the said Rules are lawfully amended in accordance with the applicable procedure.
Constitute independent committee
The petition also seeks the constitution of an independent committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge, with technical experts and other eminent citizens, to audit voter deletions and modifications during the SIR, as well as access to and changes made to electoral-roll databases, including ECINET and ERONET.
It further seeks a review of decisions, policies, procedures and technical systems relating to Electronic Voting Machines, in line with global best practices to ensure free and fair elections.
Directive to issue booth-wise list of deleted voters, reasons for deletion and restoration
The petition also seeks the election commission to publish booth-wise lists of all voters deleted during the SIR, along with the reasons for each deletion and a gender- and age-wise breakdown, and to provide an effective mechanism for restoring the names of eligible voters to the electoral rolls.
Notice before voter deletions, inclusion deadline for eligible voters in poll-bound states
The petition further seeks a direction that no voter’s name be deleted from the electoral rolls without prior notice and a reasonable opportunity of hearing in accordance with law. It also seeks to ensure that eligible persons in Punjab and other poll-bound states are permitted to apply for inclusion in the electoral rolls until the last date allowed by law.
Petition seeks any other relief to protect electoral integrity and voting rights
Lastly, it is prayed that this court may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present case, in order to protect the integrity of the electoral process and the right of every eligible citizen to vote.

- The claim that Matthew Ingalls, one of seven Cornell University students accused of rape in a September lawsuit, fled to Dubai is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an article in the Daily Mail, a British tabloid, which cited an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle, who said they believed the accused man is in Dubai.
- Using old yearbook photographs and searches of public records, Snopes was able to determine Matthew Ingalls also was known as Umar Matthew Ingalls, an alumnus of Dubai International Academy. While we know Ingalls lived in Dubai at some point, we cannot confirm his current whereabouts.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Ingalls, the Dubai International Academy, Ingalls' former school in Washington state and the person tabloids identify as Ingalls' father in Dubai and are waiting for responses.
In October, several weeks after a lawsuit was filed accusing seven male students at Cornell University of drugging and raping a female student in 2024, a rumor spread about the whereabouts of one of the accused men. According to the claim, Matthew Ingalls — who reportedly initiated the encounter with the accuser, named in court documents only as Jane Doe — fled to Dubai, where he previously lived.
Posts on Facebook (archived) and Instagram claimed Ingalls, who the posts said also goes by Umar Matthew Ingalls, was in Dubai with his family:
Umar Matthew Ingalls, one of the "Cornell 7" accused in the alleged 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi house, is now reportedly in Dubai, where he grew up. Neighbors of his relatives in Connecticut told the Daily Mail they believe he's back in the Middle East with his dad. How convenient.
Quick refresher on Mr. Ingalls. He's the one Jane Doe says invited her to the house that night. He's also the one who, according to messages filed in her lawsuit, shared a photo of her in the frat's Snapchat group chat and wrote "Like you can walk in and whip it out." The New York Post reports he added "Boys come whip it out." Truly the words of a gentleman.
(Facebook user Feminist News)
The rumor originated from a report in the Daily Mail, a British tabliod, that relied on anonymous sources. Snopes is unable to verify Ingalls' whereabouts as of this writing, so we have left this claim unrated. We have, however, found records of an Umar Ingalls who studied at the Dubai International Academy in Emirates Hills, Dubai, whose appearance matches that of Matthew Ingalls.
We have reached out to Ingalls — whom The New York Times reported had been expelled from Cornell — via his old college email address, to a person believed to be his father, to the Dubai International Academy and also to the Annie Wright School in Tacoma, Washington, where Ingalls reportedly studied as a child. We will update this story as we learn more.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls as Umar Matthew Ingalls and spoke to an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle in Connecticut, where Ingalls' address was listed in court records. That neighbor reportedly told the tabloid Ingalls hadn't been seen at the home in some time and that they thought he was in Dubai.
Our public records search for Umar Matthew Ingalls found his name appeared connected to an address in South Dartmouth, Massachusetts, that also was linked to the name Matthew B. Ingalls.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls' father as a Yale-educated professor at the American University in Dubai. We found a Matthew B. Ingalls listed as an associate professor of Middle Eastern studies at the American University in Dubai. Snopes reached out to him to verify his identity and relationship to Ingalls and will update this story as we get more information.
Several purported photographs of Matthew Ingalls have circulated, including one showing him wearing a Cornell rugby T-shirt and another from what appears to be his now-deleted LinkedIn account. According to the university's student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, the school's rugby club confirmed Ingalls was previously a part of its roster.
We found that Ingalls' image from his deleted LinkedIn account had SynthID markers — which are inserted into images created with some generative artificial intelligence platforms — and was thus likely edited with AI. However, the photograph of Ingalls in his rugby shirt did not. We then compared that photograph to other images we found of him and found several matches.
Dubai International Academy's 2022-23 yearbook identifies Umar Ingalls as a member of the class of 2023 and part of the athletics team. The person in the yearbook photo appears to be the same person wearing the Cornell rugby shirt.
(Dubai International Academy)
Umar Ingalls also was mentioned in a 2022 story in the Khaleej Times, a Dubai newspaper. The article reported on a group of students who created their own version of a lunar rover. The accompanying photograph is blurry, but the student in the back right has a strong resemblance to Ingalls.
A 2020 blog post on the website for Annie Wright Schools, an elite private school in Tacoma, Washington, identified Umar Ingalls as half-American. He appeared to have studied at the Lower School until 2016 and lived in Dubai at the time the article was written. He commented on how Americans were perceived in Dubai after the election victory of U.S. President Donald Trump.

South Africa hope to host first African Olympics
- Published
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.
Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.
The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.
Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.
After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.
The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.
Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.
Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.
The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.
Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.
Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.
Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.
The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.
Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.
Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.
The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.
The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.
The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

Last month we covered the winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu’s use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).
According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug (Cyerce kikutarobabai) on the move.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed extending restrictions on advertisements of prescription medicines to drug retailers, wholesalers and distributors, seeking to close a regulatory gap in the Drugs Rules, 1945.
A draft amendment notified through Gazette notification G.S.R. 861(E) on September 28 proposes inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 to prohibit holders of licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute drugs listed under Schedules H, H1 and X from advertising these medicines without prior sanction of the Central government.
Under the existing framework, pharmaceutical manufacturers are prohibited from advertising drugs covered under these schedules without prior government approval. However, the corresponding restriction does not explicitly cover entities involved in the retail and wholesale sale and distribution of medicines.
The proposed amendment seeks to extend the requirement across the drug supply chain, strengthening oversight of the promotion of prescription medicines and reducing the risk of inappropriate self-medication.
Misuse of prescription drugs
The medicines covered by these schedules include drugs that require medical supervision, including certain antibiotics and psychotropic medicines. Unauthorised promotion of such medicines can encourage their use without appropriate medical advice, raising concerns over patient safety and the misuse of prescription drugs.
The proposal follows recommendations made at the 93rd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) on February 16, 2026, which examined the need for provisions regulating advertisements by holders of drug sale and distribution licences.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days of the date on which copies of the Gazette notification containing the draft rules are made available to the public.
The submissions received within the prescribed period will be considered by the Central government before the amendment is finalised.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has announced a protest march to Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 10 October 2026, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The party’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced the protest after demonstrations in Mumbai on 02 October and in Delhi in the days that followed. CJP leaders have said they will continue the protest even if the police stop them from reaching Jantar Mantar. As of 09 October 2026, Delhi Police had not granted permission for the proposed gathering and had tightened security ahead of the demonstration. CJP has also alleged that authorities were detaining its members and volunteers across the country to prevent them from participating in the protest, with party leaders vowing to continue the agitation (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows women police personnel assaulting students during the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026.
Fact: The video predates the October 2026 Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest and shows a confrontation between the family of a man found dead under suspicious circumstances and the police in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, in July 2026. Although clashes between protesters and police were reported in Delhi during the first week of October amid demonstrations demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, the viral video is unrelated to those protests. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts (here, here, and here) dated 01 August 2026 featuring the same video, confirming that it predates the October 2026 CJP protest. According to these posts, the video shows an incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, where a young man named Ganesh was found dead in a rented apartment. Following the incident, his family staged a protest by blocking the road and making serious allegations against the landlord. The posts also describe a clash between women and police personnel during the protest.
We also found news reports (here, here) published around the same time covering the incident. According to these reports, tensions erupted in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, after the body of a 30-year-old man named Ganesh was found under suspicious circumstances at his rented house on 31 July 2026. His family accused the landlord of murder and staged a roadblock, during which they alleged that the police assaulted them. The reports also state that a woman dressed in black, identified as the deceased’s aunt, alleged that a police officer had snatched her mangalsutra and pulled her hair. These findings confirm that the viral video shows a confrontation between the family and police in July 2026, unrelated to the CJP protest in October 2026.
Meanwhile, during the first week of October 2026, clashes broke out between protesters and police in Delhi during demonstrations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Police detained several protesters and stopped groups from reaching protest sites, while some demonstrators alleged that police personnel pushed, dragged, and assaulted them (here, here, and here). However, the viral video predates these demonstrations and shows an unrelated incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, in July 2026.
To sum up, an unrelated video is shared as showing women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi.

More than 100 foreign trekkers stranded in flood-hit region of Nepal, official says
Authorities rescued 321 people, including 12 foreigners, after a landslide blocked the Budhi Gandaki River.
KATHMANDU: More than 100 foreign trekkers are stranded at different locations after the flooding of a river in central Nepal at the weekend swept away hiking trails and bridges, an official said on Monday (Oct 12).
Authorities rescued 321 people, including 12 foreigners, on Monday after a pre-dawn landslide at the weekend in Gorkha district, about 100 km (62 miles) west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, leading to downstream flooding. The army said the rescue operation would continue on Tuesday, even as the water level in the river had receded.
The river is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.
There were no reports of fatalities in the flood, but five villagers were out of contact after black muddy sludge and debris washed away homes and damaged infrastructure, including three hydroelectric plants, national disaster authorities said.
Bhuwan Raj Ojha, an official of the Manaslu Conservation Area Project that includes a popular trekking route, said there were more than 100 foreign trekkers stranded in different areas who could not return because part of the trail had been swept away.
"Those hikers who want to return because of the flood need to be rescued. Those who want to continue their trekking can do so from locations that are safe," Ojha told Reuters from Gorkha.
"There are restaurants and tea houses along the route. They are safe."
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said the latest flood may have been triggered by the failure of a temporary river blockage created by a landslide, according to preliminary accounts from Nepal's authorities reviewed by ICIMOD.
"This event is another reminder of how exposed mountain communities and river corridors remain to sudden, cascading hazards," Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said.
"While response efforts must remain the immediate priority, understanding what triggered this flood will be critical for reducing future risks and strengthening resilience."

Student protesters have alleged high-handedness and brute force by security personnel during a demonstration in Delhi. Sharing their accounts, students Sneha, Manish, and Lucy detailed how they were detained near Connaught Place and RK Ashram. Sneha stated that protesters were dragged along roads, placed behind barricades, and had mobile phones confiscated to stop recording, adding that female detainees were put into buses lacking female personnel before being held until nighttime. Manish claimed personnel pulled his hair, pushed him, and forced him to sit on the road without identifying nameplates before being freed around 9:15 PM. Lucy recounted being detained before raising slogans and warned against recording, witnessing male demonstrators being beaten. The bulletin highlighted that following the incidents, the top court issued a contempt notice to the Home Secretary and Delhi Police Commissioner.
A large-scale protest in Delhi brought together political leaders, students, and citizens demonstrating in defence of democratic rights. Senior Congress leaders, including Shashi Tharoor and Digvijaya Singh, spoke about public participation on the streets, describing the gathering as spontaneous and heartening. Shashi Tharoor noted that the action would move to the Supreme Court. Citizens, activists, and students from various states shared their motivations for joining the demonstrations, highlighting concerns over democratic freedoms, voting rights, and alleged crackdowns on student protests. Protesters expressed solidarity with the movement despite police deployment, barricades, and water cannons.
In an exclusive interaction, CPI(M) Member of Parliament John Brittas detailed his alleged assault and detention by the Delhi Police and CRPF in Connaught Circus. Speaking about the incident, Brittas stated that he was speaking to media persons regarding civil liberties and public transport closures when personnel forcefully took him away despite knowing his status as an MP. He described being thrown into a police vehicle, saying, 'They just threw me into the van and they pinned down me on the seat.' Brittas noted that he was released only after a senior police officer intervened over phone. He also highlighted his earlier eight-hour detention alongside the former Chief Minister of Kerala at Mandir Marg Police Station, asserting that political suppression will not deter the Opposition.
In an interview, Bharatiya Janata Party Rajya Sabha MP Sujeet Kumar addressed the opposition protests in the national capital, arguing that political parties ought to learn the ethics of protest from the BJP. Criticising the INDIA bloc's actions, Kumar stated, "First of all, parties should learn how to protest from BJP," highlighting that dissent should occur in a dignified manner without damaging public property or disrupting citizens' daily routines. He questioned the opposition's march to the Supreme Court while issues remain sub judice, describing the demonstrations as theatrics and chaos. Responding to concerns regarding police detentions and clampdowns, Kumar maintained that authorities are mandated to protect public property and restore order, claiming the demonstrations were hijacked by elements with violent intent. Furthermore, addressing allegations of foreign interference, he noted that the participation of foreign nationals, criminal elements, and questionable financial trails warrants a thorough investigation by intelligence agencies.
Leaders of the INDIA alliance and Congress took to the streets of New Delhi, marching towards the Supreme Court of India to file a petition against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise. The judicial route follows CJI Suryakant's refusal to meet Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, citing principles of separation of powers and judicial propriety regarding sub judice matters. During the demonstrations, the opposition urged the CEC to step down, while leaders highlighted the backing of youth and civil society groups. The BJP firmly rejected the allegations, questioning the opposition's political motivations in the unfolding multi-front confrontation across parliament, streets, and courts.

South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
- Published
South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.
A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.
The charges relate to allegations that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking.
Sibiya has denied all the charges. He says he did have sex with the 18 year-old but says it was consensual.
He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago after his bail application was denied.
Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external.
The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals.
The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began in September 2025 and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
He denied the allegation.

A student hated reading for years. Her podcast explores finding the right diagnosis
LONG ISLAND, N.Y. — Cora Walsh walks home from middle school every day. It's only a few tree-lined blocks in Rockville Centre on Long Island, but the movement helps clear her head of the school day. She probably thinks about how the brain works more than most seventh-graders.
"I want to be a doctor," she says. "And I want to go to Princeton and major in neuroscience."
Her fascination started a few years ago when she was struggling to figure out what was happening in her own head.
"It's kind of confusing what it is like in my brain," she says. All she knew back then was that reading was hard. Even when she spent more time working on it than her friends, she could never reach their level.
Like millions of Americans, Cora has dyslexia, but it took her almost five years to get the correct diagnosis.
Her podcast about the journey to understanding her own mind is the grand prize winner for middle school in this year's NPR Student Podcast Challenge. "Dyslexia and MEE" was chosen from nearly 1,500 submissions from 42 states and the District of Columbia.
"I feel really excited," Cora says about her victory. Her parents, who spent the whole journey right by her side, are thrilled too.
"This is a kid that works so hard and has such a good attitude," says her mom, Emily Johnson. "I'm so proud of her."
Finding the right learning style
Cora has come a long way. She has received tutoring for her dyslexia for two years now.
Her podcast takes the listener along to one of her lessons. She sounds out words over Zoom, and her tutor gives her feedback and tips. They don't move too fast, making sure Cora really understands something before moving on.
It can be tedious, but her hard work outside the classroom is starting to pay off.
"I think I'm a better reader now, and I enjoy it a lot more," she says. "I feel more comfortable reading bigger books, but not too big!"
Her mom says that this summer marked a turning point: She saw her daughter reading the first book in the Hunger Games series.
"She would pick it up for fun, and she would go read to [her pet] rabbit. Or we were traveling this summer, and she read on the train," Johnson says. "I mean, it's the first time that's ever happened."
It was a winding road to get to this point, but Cora and her parents are excited to see where it goes. Winning NPR's national competition is another bright spot.
"I'm kind of just proud of myself that I overcame this hard, annoying thing," she says. "And proud of myself that I created something really cool and interesting that everyone can listen to."
Cora hopes that her podcast might help dyslexia feel a little less scary for listeners and maybe even reach younger students who are still trying to figure out their own learning styles.
"I would say: Always try your hardest, and don't sell yourself short," she says. "I think trying is … the best thing you can do."
Cora Walsh is still trying: She just checked out that second Hunger Games book from the library.

Before the 2017 ODI World Cup, journalist-turned-broadcaster Gaurav Kalra led a media training session for the women’s cricket team in Mumbai. In an ecosystem rife with clichés like ‘trust the process’ and ‘control the controllables’, Kalra was tasked with helping the women get comfortable with media engagements, pushing them to be honest about their stories and journeys so their own lives inspire at least one other.
Kalra remembers Harmanpreet eagerly raising her hand to say, “ Sir, aap bol to rahe ho ki apni story bataon, par koi sunna hi nahin chahta” (Sir, you’re asking us to tell our stories, but no one wants to listen).
Life for the ecosystem nine years on looks starkly different. India has become a force to reckon with, taking its place among the game’s competitive (and not just monetary) elite. It enters tournaments among the favourites. Its players are household names now, not just in India, but also in pockets abroad where some feature regularly on the franchise circuit.
The roots of this new era of the women’s game can be traced back to this eager 28-year-old (relatively) newly appointed full-time T20I captain. She forced people to stop and listen, eventually becoming the protagonist of the vertical’s most cherished chapter (so far).
Taking space
“Sardaran hai. Ladne ki thaakat toh uski khoon mein hai” (She’s a sardarni, that fighting spirit is in her blood) - this is former chief selector of the Indian national team Neetu David’s first adjective for Harmanpreet. Fighting is a three-act phenomenon in the life of this maverick from Moga, Punjab.
First, there was the fight to play.
Young Harmanpreet was a sports buff, playing anything and everything she could. She even tried hockey, where the stick and ball ultimately became part of a game of cricket, much to her school teacher’s chagrin. “ Bohot mushkil se bacchon ko cricket se hockey tak le aaye hai hum. Aap yeh na karein (It’s taken a lot to get kids to pivot from cricket to hockey. Don’t do this now),” she once cheekily recalled.
“ Pehle hi dekha ki jo log six marte hain, unki bohot value hai (It was evident to me very early on that those who hit sixes, their value is a lot higher),” Harmanpreet said of her formative days in the sport. Her coach Kamaldeesh Pal Singh Sodhi spotted heroics of the sort watching her smack the ball while playing with a group of boys. He didn’t know if she was a boy or a girl, given her long locks were tied up in the trademark sikh high bun.
Young Harman only knew the bat and ball in her hands. She knew not of any pathways of progress, or what would come of her life should she stick with cricket and nothing else. The 80s and 90s had no women’s cricket on television, so there were no ambitions for her to soak off a screen.
But Sodhi did and he saw what Harmanpreet would mean for the sport if she could extrapolate the raw spunk he saw into enduring legend. So did her father Harmandar Singh Bhullar. Given his own sporting success at state level, he wanted his daughter to go past him and clinch the honour of donning an India jersey some day. All when his daughter did not even know of the existence of the women’s side.
Sodhi built a women’s team around Harmanpreet and she repaid the faith by eventually building a new culture of excellence which ultimately led her and her pack to the sport’s biggest podium.
Simple pleasures
Former India international Soniya Dabir’s earliest memory of Harmanpreet is one from the manual - a six she hit in the U-19 inter-zonal match in Pune. She was the local manager then.
“That was the first time I saw a player at that level hit such a long six. She could smack sixes at will and the difference was immediately apparent in the stance, the backlift… She decides ki abhi aane wala hai and we prepare,” Soniya says.
In a domestic Challenger series, the pair were teammates and eventually even became roommates during the 2010 T20 World Cup in the West Indies.
That Harmanpreet was naive, untouched by the burdens of spotlight and just grateful to make cricket her life’s fulcrum. She would happily eat the same food regularly, diligently follow workout regimes on repeat and also, unfortunately for Soniya, play the same song on loop for days on end.
“I would keep a lot of songs loaded on my phone, but hers had just one song called Tere Liye. For almost 12-16 hours, she would play it. I had enough eventually. There were no Hindi channels in the Windies at the time.”
“She had a routine she followed strictly. She prayed everyday, she did her things a certain way. It stopped for nothing, no one and no result. She used to be able to switch off really well. Kuch carry forward nahi hota tha pichle match ka (Nothing carried forward from one match to another) . That was a good thing, to take each day for what it is.” Fifteen years later, that very trait would help Harmanpreet bhangra her way towards the ODI World Cup trophy before a manic crowd at the D.Y. Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai on a dewy November night.
Legendary Indian legspinner Neetu David, who was the chair of selectors when India reached the One-Day zenith, fondly remembers the Punjaban who took on Railways in the domestic circuit.
“Back then, the Indian Railways was as good as the Indian national side,” Neetu says. “The way she fearlessly tackled our bowlers and as good as led the batting effort made us feel like this girl would go places and maybe even captain India someday.”
After getting employed by the Western Railways, Harmanpreet – who now can’t venture out into any street in India without being mobbed – would sprint through streets to catch the Mumbai local, shuttling between work and training at Bandra Kurla Complex. She unabashedly admits to sitting on Diana Edulji’s head to get exemptions sanctioned so her stomach wouldn’t kill her heart’s desires.
Diana’s condition was clear: help Railways win the domestic tournament first. The rest eventually fell into place.
Unending hunger
From here, Harmanpreet realised just how much ‘change’ would come to define her chapter in Indian cricket. She moved from the Railways to Punjab Police to be able to be closer to home. The Women’s Big Bash League came calling in 2016 when she became the first Indian to feature in an overseas league, having signed with Sydney Thunder.
It reinforced a love affair with the systems Down Under that began in the late 2000s when she and M.D. Thirushkamini were sent for an exposure trip there.
Former India captain Purnima Rau, who had selected her for that tour in 2007, took charge as head coach in 2014, two years after Harmanpreet had stepped up in the absence of an injured Mithali Raj and Jhulan Goswami to lead India to the first of what would eventually be four Asia Cup triumphs.
“She was a very raw, energetic kid who was very hungry for knowledge. That ambition was evident in her eyes,” she says.

Bring up Harman and her thoughts go back to an earnest 26-year-old who stayed back for advice after the dressing room had cleared post a series win against New Zealand.
“I am usually the last one to get out of the dressing room or the team bus so I can check if players have left anything behind. One such day, I found Harman standing there. She held my hand and said, “Ma’am, I want to do much better than what I’ve done. What should I do?”” Purnima remembers being asked.
She recalls copious notes on technique, on how she urged Harman to be audacious on the front foot and tweak her elbow placement to extend her field of strokemaking.
In Purnima, the evangelist Harmanpreet would eventually become for Indian cricket found her first believer. Both agreed on one fundamental element - India was talented enough and gutsy enough to win not one ICC title, but three. This was without the Women’s Premier League, little to no media attention and a system that made it a point to tell the girls they were good, but just not good enough.
A disappointing home T20 World Cup campaign, where India sank in the group stage, meant India found itself increasingly jaded by Mithali’s steady, risk-free brand of leadership. Harmanpreet’s aggressive, unbending style of batting was already turning heads. It wasn’t long before Mithali made way for her deputy in the shortest format.
But all of that would be eclipsed by a superhuman effort in Derby in the 2017 ODI World Cup, a monstrous knock that would lay the foundations of ‘Harmonster’ as she would come to be called, and a particular penchant for treating the world’s most decorated and dangerous side - Australia - like a puppy slinging around a rope toy.
Harman vs the odds
That unbeaten 171, which both made and, many times, broke Harmanpreet has to be among the most documented knocks in the history of the game. Like a raging Spanish bull, a red-faced and hungry Harmanpreet hacked Australia down.
For Purnima, however, it was Harman’s effort 149 days prior to that knock that has her respect.
“Everytime I’ve coached a side, I gave my captains a book when they won a series. Mithali got seven books from me. Harman got one, for the ICC qualifier before the 2017 World Cup. One by Shiv Khera,” she remembers.
Chasing 245 for victory against South Africa in the final, India needed eight runs off the last two balls. Harmanpreet, the stand-in skipper, smacked the ball over the midwicket ropes and then ran two to send her dugout into a tizzy at the P. Sara Oval in the heart of Colombo.
“She fought with the last wicket (Rajeshwari Gayakwad). That six she hit sums up everything about her. Forget her captaincy. She did well, that’s a given. But for me, as a player, tagda thi wahan pe (She was tough),” Purnima declares.
2017’s big high and equally ravenous low came and went, but what remained was the adulation and then fascination of the general public, all waiting for the next big news from this bunch.
Unfortunately, the squad served rotten meat to vultures waiting to feast and from singlehandedly sculpting a memorable pièce de résistance, Harman suddenly became the face of one of the biggest controversies to rock the system. A bitter tussle for power which involved leaks and snide comments and much in between saw Harmanpreet and Mithali on two sides of what looked like an irreparably torn national side.
The 2018 T20 World Cup became the battleground.
Facing England in the semifinal, skipper Harman made a temerarious decision to drop Mithali for the knockout fixture. Mithali had batted in just two games in that campaign, scoring 50s on both occasions. She picked up a knee injury and didn’t feature in India’s 48-run group stage win against Australia. Harman defended her decision saying she wanted to stick to a winning combination.
Things, however, didn’t go as planned, with India folding for 112 in 19.2 overs, its last eight wickets falling for just 23 runs. England didn’t blink as it sealed an eight-wicket win.
“Whatever we decided, we decided for the team. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, no regrets. I’m proud of the way my girls played through the tournament,” she said defiantly then. But the apple cart had been blown to smithereens.
The fallout of this incident added to an already tumultuous time for the side, with two coaches – Purnima and Tushar Arothe – finding themselves out of the scheme of things rather unceremoniously, documented to be at the behest of the players. Ramesh Powar, earlier an ally to Harmanpreet, was also shown the door, not once but twice. W.V. Raman, too, was not retained, and with no explanation.
Team first
Raman unenviably walked into a broken dressing room masquerading as a team.
“Harmanpreet was obviously hurt, and she felt she was blamed for no fault of hers about a lot of things that happened before. It’s very easy for us to live in the past. I sat them both down and said I didn’t intend to go back there. Let’s try and start with a clean slate.”
He pushed Harman to be large-hearted and focus on the time she has to leave her imprint behind as captain and player.
“I told her that she needed to try and make an identity for herself. Of course, she had been doing that as a player but for her to make an impact as captain, she couldn’t afford to be distracted by the past or by how people outside were trying to box her in. At some point, I even read an interview where she said she contemplated leaving the game. Fortunately, she carried on,” he says.
Harman was not one for diplomacy and Raman cites that as one of her attributes he values the most.
“A lot of things have been said about her for the simple reason she just spoke her mind. She did not have the finesse like some of her predecessors to try and convey things in such a manner. No matter what the implications were, no matter what people might think about her decisions, she came across as somebody who did things the way she felt she needed to do. Perhaps, that’s not something people always look at kindly. But that is Harman for you. It’s always good for people to be different, or the world would be a very boring place,” he shrugs.
The musical chairs in leadership positions is an Indian cricket staple, particularly in the women’s game. Purnima remembers how friends quickly became foes as selectors rolled in and rolled out ‘one series captains’ in their blind quest for results, which is why she underlines that permanence as the enduring legacy of both these players.
“Stability is important for any captain,” Mithali says. “But a long tenure also has to come with accountability. You have to keep assessing whether the team is progressing and whether the captain is still the right person for the next phase.”
“Harman had that time, and there were different phases to her tenure, good and difficult. But that continuity allowed her to shape the team in her own way. That is ultimately the value of giving a captain a long rope,” she adds.
Breeding belief
In the eight years that passed, Harmanpreet first defined her (in capital letters) side as one that could enter tournaments as favourites, that could give Australia and England a run for their money.
India’s march to the final in the 2020 T20 World Cup was imperious. The campaign was propped on the captain’s unflinching faith in the prodigious abilities of a 16-year-old Shafali Verma. However, like it had many times before, India’s ambitious castles were watered down by the mighty Aussies, with nearly 90,000 people watching at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.
ALSO READ: Mandhana, India’s new captain, has earned her job
“It would have been the perfect gift if we were to win on that day because it was played on her birthday. That was not to be, unfortunately. It would have kept the side going through the COVID-19 pandemic which followed for a year and a half right after. That was a challenging phase,” Raman reminisces.
“Maybe it was the early stages of her captaincy or the fact that India was so near yet so far all the time… That victory could have perhaps proved to the world that they’re capable of winning a World Cup, that she is capable of winning a World Cup. And that’s something that she wanted for the team to do because India was always looked upon as an entity that didn’t have the wherewithal to win the World Cup. She wanted to change that. A lot of things were riding on that particular final. So it was a bit frustrating.”
This was around the time calls for a women’s Indian Premier League were growing increasingly louder. Losses saw even board officials lament about not having sufficient talent to stage a league. Harman credits former BCCI secretary Jay Shah for breaking that cycle, breaking the unending chase the women’s team was set on to first achieve before having the guts to ask for foundational sporting architecture.
Another opportunity presented itself in 2023. Once again, Australia stood in India’s way and would eventually push India back like a bully cordoning off privileged territory. An unfortunate run out involving Harmanpreet and some stinging yet nonchalant criticism from new captain Alyssa Healy triggered the makings of a memorable rivalry to spice up a vertical bedrotting in the lull of Meg Lanning – its most decorated commander – shockingly calling time on her international career.
The group stage exit in the 2024 T20 World Cup, by their own admission, hurt the side the most. Systems were changing. The Women’s Premier League had turned two. Harmanpreet and Smriti Mandhana, her eventual successor, had won the first two editions. With new coach Amol Muzumdar, experiments and fresh perspectives were the Women in Blue’s oxygen. But the side returned from the arid Emirati deserts with their tails tucked between their legs.
A desolate Harmanpreet, spacing out at the post-match presentation after yet another gutsy fight against Australia, became the image of that dismal campaign. That perhaps explains why the tears were so unaesthetically raw in 2025, when India overcame the mighty Aussies before a raucous home crowd in the semifinal in Navi Mumbai.
When Jemimah Rodrigues and Amanjot Kaur brought India home, Harmanpreet sat with trenches for creaselines on her forehead in the dugout, Smriti hugging her as they saw victory inch closer. As Smriti led the entourage out to embrace a tired and emotionally broken Jemimah, Harmanpreet roared away into the dugout, with Deepti Sharma and Muzumdar enveloping her from either side.
“I would actually say the World Cup victory. For me, that will define her captaincy more than anything else. Indian women’s cricket had waited a long time for that ODI World Cup, and Harman was the captain when it finally happened. There were different phases to her tenure, but that achievement will naturally stand out. That is a significant part of what she leaves behind as captain.”Mithali Raj
She might have enjoyed one single song on loop for days on end all those years ago in the West Indies, but she was tired of the same old taunts, disbelief and the “go back to the kitchen” jibes.
History repeated itself.
Once, Harman validated the aspirations her father and coach saw for her. On October 30, 2025, Harman’s team realised hers. The coronation a few days later, the unquestionable cementing of her legacy, may have taken some doing, but was a mere formality.
India’s own angry, young woman
Amitabh Bachchan popularised the trope of the angry, young man in Indian cinema, allegorical of the mood of the nation then. Harman became that symbol for the women’s game. Remember how she rained down on poor 19-year-old Deepti when she almost ran Harman, then on 98, out. Evidently, Harman was not hunting the ton, but the win. The pair hugged and made up soon after and India clinched that epochal win.
That same Deepti she reduced to tears in Derby had Harman’s complete backing at Lord’s in 2022, when she ran out Charlie Dean at the non-striker’s end which helped India seal 3-0 ODI series sweep.
When asked, Harman snapped back at why the other nine wickets weren’t as interesting to talk about before unequivocally stating, “I will back my player. She’s not done something which isn’t in the rules. It shows our awareness.”
Little under a year later, Bangladesh faced Harmanpreet’s wrath enough for her to become a yardstick for bad behaviour for the system there. Stumps were smashed, nasty things were said, umpires were accused of favouring the home side and a prompt two-match ban was slapped on the Indian skipper too.
Harman, consistency personified, quietly served the ban without an ounce of regret. “I don’t think I said anything wrong to any player or any person. I just said what happened on the field. I don’t regret anything,” she said later.
That unbridled anger is something Raman remembers from his early days with the mercurial (now) former Indian skipper.
“In the run-up to the 2020 World Cup, there was a murmur in the side. The girls were a little scared, a bit peeved by Harman giving everyone a piece of her mind. One of our warm-up games was rained out, so I sat her down and began talking about a couple of other captains. Harman knows me to be direct and was a little puzzled by why I was beating around the bush and asked me in so many words.
“I then told her that different captains have different methodologies but this cannot be a system of top-down management all the time. It might not always work. She needed to do what was possible to get the best out of her teammates.
“Apart from the World Cup title, she’s won so many Test matches for India as captain. That’s an equally good record. India, for the longest time, didn’t play Tests. It’s not easy to win these against England and Australia when you’re leading a side in all three formats. Winning that Test match at Lord’s after exiting the T20 World Cup, where they had to sit and watch other teams get through the end and push for a win in the Lord’s Test, was incredible. Credit to her for that record too!”Soniya Dabir
“I suggested that if she wanted to let loose, we could nominate a player for every game to be her punching bag (not literally, of course) and we’ll get on with it. She slept over it and came back back and said there was merit in what I said. Things then suddenly changed. She hardly said anything on the field.”
“Players came raising issues with that too and all I said was, ‘You can’t complain about everything.’ Harman controlled was better than her letting loose,” he quips.
Legacy and a wheel that refuses to break
A year is a long time. India soaked in the hysteria of a World title far too many thought would never arrive. Soon, it was time for another World Cup, but a disastrous campaign in 2026 and another group stage exit followed.
Harmanpreet Kaur’s captaincy record: 211 games across formats
A now 37-year-old Harman, with diminishing returns with the bat, could not fight the pendulum swinging towards Smriti, long understood to be India’s captain-in-waiting and in the form of her life. The 30-year-old growing increasingly vocal of her ability and willingness to lead the nation only fanned a flame that needed no help spreading.
That image from 2025, the camaraderie from the ones before that, all seemingly made way for subtle distances that rabid fanbases of both players frothed at the mouth to blow up online.
In early October, images emerged on an Assamese news portal of Harman and Smriti in Guwahati with BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia. A day later, Harmanpreet announced her decision to step down from Indian captaincy.
This is a woman who jumped up for the World Cup-sealing catch in the final with an injury in her left knee. The same woman who played that 171 knock with a dislocated finger had to be held back by the team doctor from venturing out for the second innings despite severe dehydration. Somehow, though, the words of her resignation felt loaded with far more pain.
ALSO READ: India wins first gold medal of Asian Games 2026 after women’s cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final
There is an interview with Harmanpreet where she describes how the balance and make of the bat don’t matter, but the grip does. If it doesn’t feel like she has full control, it ruins the full experience. Now, the grip has been yanked away.
For a Punjabi girl growing up on a sporting diet, the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics was the perfect carrot to push her ageing and hurting body through a few more sporting summers for that one coveted gold medal. She comes from a hockey and athletics hotbed and a State that values Olympic golds like divinity. She still has a shot at it, but not as the bird leading the migration.
She won the fight to play and the fight for collective belief. But she couldn’t prolong the fight to lead.
Paisa and pyaar
Harmanpreet’s journey cannot be detached from the financial whirlwind that has embraced the women’s ecosystem. Noopur Kashyap, her manager, has seen Harman’s “value’ grow into a bankable commercial face for big brands.
“In 2017, women’s cricket was still emerging. Viewership was still quite limited. We began with digital campaigns so she could at least be seen,” Noopur explains.
Harman got a lot of webinars around the lockdowns and that gave her team the confidence that people want to hear what she has to say. That translated to on-ground events and activations and eventually to big brand deals, the arc hitting its peak right after the 2025 ODI World Cup. When Navi Mumbai woke up to continue ringing in India’s triumph barely five hours after the final, Harman had already been named brand ambassador for real estate firm Omaxe Ltd. And that was just the start of more to come.
Harman loves a photoshoot but the larger world of brand engagements was alien territory for her for quite a while.
“For her to be at a shoot for eight hours would be draining, with the lights, arrangement and people. But send her to a cricket field for as long and she’d be totally fine. That shift came about with the WPL. It taught players to balance training and matches with shoots thanks to how advertising and appearances are coded into franchise operations,” she explains.
Noopur stepped in for Harman at a time when the math involved in being a ‘brand’ in sports left her utterly confused. The fear of being misled or cheated was there too and since then, Noopur has been Harman’s firewall. Over the years, a girl who was once mistaken for a boy now loved seeing herself on posters, cover shoots and ad films.
Noopur sees this next phase of her career as an opportunity for Harman to finally make her life’s favourite thing – cricket – about herself.
“Harman’s never been one to have a big circle. You won’t see her doing dinners, outings etc very often. She has missed out on all this and wants to experience it all. She’s drawn her legacy. She also wants to be more socially available. Captaincy and its responsibilities came with several personal restrictions. Even going home was a challenge. She lives away from her parents to be close to an airport so she can report for duty anytime. Those are things she will be able to address now,” she says.
In the 2025 final, after a job well done, Harmanpreet running to her father and Bhullar lifting her up like she was five again was among the unforgettable frames of that triumph. It was anything but just the adrenaline from the night, Noopur suggests.
“Harman comes from a very simple, non-city background. She wants time with her family. Her parents are getting older. She watched her sister’s wedding on video call. Both her siblings stay abroad. She doesn’t talk about all this but it really matters. It’s why that hug with her dad after the final means so much. That’s what she misses.”
Epilogue
This exercise of documenting Harman the captain might seem like an end-of-career tribute piece. It’s perhaps inevitable considering how much of Harman’s life in this sport has gone into taking the lead in some form.
“Captaincy suited her. She wanted things to happen all the time and wanted the team to win. It suited her personality and her mindset. She’s been a captain all along. She now has a chance to show what kind of a leader she can be. It’s time to create an ever bigger legacy,” Raman says.
“Captaincy does add pressure, because you are thinking about the team even when you are batting. But I wouldn’t put Harman’s batting inconsistency entirely down to captaincy. She has always had periods of outstanding batting and periods when she hasn’t been as consistent, even before she became the all-format captain,” Mithali explains.
“What captaincy does is add another layer to that. When you are not scoring, you are answering questions about both your batting and your leadership. Now she doesn’t have that additional responsibility. So she has the opportunity to concentrate on her batting and let her performances speak for her,” she adds.
Harman has been the genesis of the rule of fitness and form in this ecosystem and now stands consumed by the very frameworks she cemented in place.
She was part of a side that is infamously reported to have pushed for a male coach – which led to Purnima’s sacking. But she is now also part of a franchise setup — Mumbai Indians — that has always championed women in the coaching staff, from Charlotte Edwards and Lisa Keightley to India’s own Jhulan Goswami and Devika Palshikar.
It’s been a long vigil for an unapologetic servant of the game, who now finally has the space and reason to fire up this next chapter just for herself.
As one of her early coaches told Harman (as documented in Sidhanta Patnaik and Karunya Keshav’s “ The Fire Burns Blue”), “No bowler can get you out unless you want to get out. Everything is in the mind.”
Chardi Kala, Harmanpreet.

Yemeni attack on Riyadh airport kills 12 and injures over 300 as Houthi-Saudi war escalates
It was the third strike on the capital’s airport this week
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
