Join today
Already a member? Log in
At least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured following a strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday – the third attack this week – as Yemen’s Houthi forces stepped up their campaign against the kingdom.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the casualties, saying four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and a person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan, and Egypt were killed.
At the latest count, officials said 309 people were injured.
Hospitals were overwhelmed with casualties brought in by ambulance and helicopter, according to people briefed on the situation. Some of the injured were reported to be in critical condition.
The attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in almost a decade, struck without warning, as no alert was issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. Two earlier attacks this week targeting King Khalid international airport left four people dead and severely damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac.
The fatal strikes highlight vulnerabilities in the country’s defence capabilities while it conducts an air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen. A Saudi-led military coalition promised to retaliate.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni forces backed by it claim to have launched hundreds of strikes against targets in Houthi areas in recent weeks. The Houthis say the air raids have killed civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said operations at the Riyadh airport were temporarily suspended on Saturday and all flights were diverted. The airport serves a city of about eight million.
Following the strike, the head of the Houthi media office posted on X that the movement had "shut down Riyadh international airport".
The Houthis warned commercial airliners to avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a military operations zone after the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched an offensive on Monday.
In the US, president Donald Trump was asked by reporters if Washington intended to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio condemned the raids, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life”.
An eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then several casualties lying injured on the ground inside the facility. More than a dozen ambulances were seen heading towards the building, with video verified by Reuters showing emergency vehicles at the scene.
An injured passenger told Reuters they saw an object flying through the sky outside the terminal before part of the ceiling collapsed near a departure gate.
Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015, leading an Arab coalition to attempt to drive the Houthis from the capital Sanaa after the rebels had seized the city the previous year.
The war resulted in a devastating stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and starvation.
Saudi Arabia subsequently signed a 2022 agreement with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.
That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a rapid Houthi advance that seized the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el Mandeb from Saudi-backed forces. The Saudi-supported forces launched a new offensive this week to reclaim that territory, making slow progress even as Houthi forces placed Taiz, the country's third-largest city, under siege.
Flight-tracking service flightradar24 showed that all incoming flights to Riyadh were redirected or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one stage.
Houthi strikes earlier in the week had already driven several airlines to suspend or cancel flights to the Saudi capital, shortly before it was scheduled to host major energy and investment conferences.
Organisers of those events stated prior to Saturday's attack that they would proceed as planned.

The visuals in the footage have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer.
On Oct. 4, a social media user posted a video purportedly depicting a man leading a group of Arkansas farmers in prayer, asking "baby Jesus" for "more Mexicans" to replace the "Mexicans we had deported" to save their farms.
The user posted the footage to Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). The audio seemingly shows the man leading the prayer saying:
Dear Baby Jesus, please help us. We're losing our farms. We know we sent all the Mexicans away. Dear Lord, please send us some more Mexicans to replace the Mexicans we had deported. We're going to lose our farms; please, Baby Jesus and all things holy. Amen.
The clip spread amid numerous reports of rising prices and trade wars impacting U.S. farmers.
In short, the visuals in the video have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer. Therefore, we rate the audio as fake.
The authentic footage originates from a broadcast by KATV 7, a TV news station in Little Rock, Arkansas. The channel posted the segment to YouTube on Sept. 2, 2025 (archived), more than a year earlier than when the edited clip was circulating. It shows hundreds of Arkansas farmers in a school gymnasium seeking the federal government's help regarding their financial struggles.
At about 2:24, the video cuts to a man leading the farmers in prayer. He can be heard saying:
Farmers, in my opinion, dear Lord, and it's only my opinion, are closer to you than anyone else on this Earth because we deal with your Earth every day. Dear Lord, we're hurting, dear Lord. We can't help what's happened to us.
According to KATV 7's article about the event, also published on Sept. 2, 2025, the farmer then said, "We need help, dear Lord."
Another piece of evidence that the "more Mexicans" iteration of the clip is edited is the quality of its audio. The prayer in the edited version is sharp, clear and lacking an echo. Inside a school gymnasium, the audio of the farmers praying should, in reality, feature an echo, like the man's voice does in the original footage.
Both Facebook and Instagram identified the audio as original to Aaron Beltrán, the person who appeared to first post the edited clip on both platforms.
Snopes reached out to Beltrán to ask whether he originally edited and posted the manipulated video, if the voice is his own and if the content was meant to be satirical. We will update this story if we receive a reply.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status
Measles is the most contagious disease known. It can rip through a population without immunity like wildfire. Just look at what's happening in Pennsylvania, says Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a public health effort led by the National Infectious Diseases Foundation.
"In January in Pennsylvania, they had 12 cases. Now we're seeing 100 plus cases per week and over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania," she says. "If Pennsylvania can see it spread that fast, that can happen in any state that has low immunization rates."
As vaccination rates have fallen across the country, many communities have become vulnerable. Nationwide, more than 4,000 measles cases have been reported this year alone — the highest number in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported five deaths. New York state declared a measles emergency.
Stinchfield says the recent measles surge has got many people wondering if they're at risk.
"It's a very common question for people to ask, 'am I immune? Am I OK? What do I need to do?' And that is exactly the right question everyone should be asking themselves right now," Stinchfield says.
The best defense is vaccination. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective — meaning 97% of people will have an immune response.
"The measles vaccine is safe. It's highly effective, and it confers lifelong immunity," says Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of Booster Shots, a history of measles.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
But what if you don't know your immunization history, or you only got one dose of the measles shot? Should you get another dose? Infectious disease experts say that depends on several factors.
If you were born before 1957
People born before 1957 are presumed to be immune because back then, measles was so common, just about everyone got it in childhood, says Dr. Larry Kociolek, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
"It was thought that pretty much everyone in the U.S. was infected with measles as sort of a rite of passage in childhood," Kocielek says. He says anyone who's ever had measles can be confident they're protected.
That is of course, if you survived. Before vaccines, measles used to kill 400 to 500 people each year in the U.S.
If you were vaccinated before 1968
People who were born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 may need an additional dose. That's because a small group of people who were immunized during that time received an early, less effective version of the vaccine that used inactivated or killed virus.
If you're not sure which vaccine you got, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends talking to your doctor about getting one or two doses of the MMR vaccine.
If you only got one dose of the MMR vaccine
At first, children in the U.S. received just one dose of the MMR vaccine. But that changed in 1989, after public health officials determined that a single dose wasn't enough to prevent outbreaks. That year, the official recommendation switched to two doses of MMR vaccine for children, which is still in effect today.
Kids need the higher protection "because they tend to be at higher risk of exposure, since they're oftentimes in group settings like schools and daycares," Kociolek says.
If you're in a higher-risk group
One dose of MMR vaccine is 93% effective, and traditionally, Kociolek says, that was considered enough protection for most adults, unless they were at higher risk of being exposed to measles. Health care workers, people in a college setting and those travelling abroad are all in this group. If you live with or are in close contact with someone who is immunocompromised, you also need two doses of vaccine to protect them.
But given the recent, dramatic rise of measles across the country these days, "if you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose," Kociolek says.
Ratner says it's definitely worth asking your doctor if you should get a second dose.
While measles is often considered to be a childhood disease, a large proportion of people sickened this year have been unvaccinated adults — and people over 20 who lack immunity are at higher risk of serious complications.
No matter your age, "measles is a serious disease," Stinchfield says.
She notes that getting two doses of the vaccine can also help others at higher risk who can't get the MMR shot, including people who are pregnant, severely immunocompromised and infants under 6 months of age.
If you really don't know your immunization history
If you're just not sure if you're protected against measles and you can't find records of immunization, you could get a test to check your blood antibody levels. But those tests aren't perfect, says Dr. William Moss, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
"It's possible that a person could actually be protected and test negative on one of those," Moss says.
Depending on your circumstances, your insurance might not cover the blood test. But most private insurance plans and Medicaid must cover another MMR vaccine at no cost.
Moss says if you can't confirm how many doses of MMR vaccine you've had, "I would say it is easier and less expensive to just get another MMR vaccine, and there is no harm in getting a second MMR vaccine or even a third, additional MMR dose."
After all, it's much better to be protected than infected.

2026 అక్టోబర్ 2న, ఓటర్ల జాబితాలో అక్రమాలు జరిగాయనే ఆరోపణలపై ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేశ్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ, అక్టోబర్ 10న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద భారీ నిరసన చేపట్టనున్నట్లు కాక్రొచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ప్రకటించింది. ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ (SIR) ప్రక్రియను వెంటనే నిలిపివేయాలని, 2025 జూన్ 25 నుంచి ఓటర్ల జాబితా నుంచి తొలగించిన పేర్లన్నింటినీ తిరిగి చేర్చాలని కూడా CJP డిమాండ్ చేస్తోంది. లెఫ్ట్ వింగ్ విద్యార్థి సంఘాలు కూడా ఈ నిరసనలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో పాల్గొంటామని ప్రకటన విడుదల చేశాయి.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, బజరంగ్ దళ్ వంటి హిందూ సంస్థలకు చెందిన కార్యకర్తలు నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు జంతర్ మంతర్ వైపు వస్తున్నారంటూ పలు వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ వాదనల్లో నిజమెంతో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరిగే CJP నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు బజరంగ్ దళ్తో సహా హిందూ సంస్థల కార్యకర్తలు సిద్ధమవుతున్నట్లు వైరల్ పోస్టులు పేర్కొంటున్నాయి.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోలన్నీ నిరసన ప్రకటనకు ముందే ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో పశ్చిమ బెంగాల్లో జరిగిన రామనవమి బైక్ ర్యాలీ, UGCకి సంబంధించిన ర్యాలీ, ఛత్రపతి శివాజీ పట్టాభిషేక వార్షికోత్సవ వేడుకలు వంటి వేర్వేరు సంఘటనలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు ఉన్నాయి. జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద తమ కార్యకర్తలను సమీకరించే ప్రణాళిక లేదని బజరంగ్ దళ్ కూడా స్పష్టం చేసింది. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టుల్లో చేసిన వాదనలు తప్పు.
వీడియో 1:
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఈ వీడియో నవంబర్ 2022 నుంచి ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం (ఆర్కైవ్). అయితే, ఈ వీడియో మొదట ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో స్పష్టంగా తెలియలేదు. కానీ, గత కొన్ని సంవత్సరాలుగా ఇదే వీడియోను వివిధ అంశాలకు సంబంధించి పలుమార్లు ఉపయోగించినట్లు గుర్తించాం (ఇక్కడ). దీంతో, 2026 అక్టోబర్ 10న జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరిగిన నిరసనకు ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదని స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
వీడియో 2:
కాషాయ జెండాలు పట్టుకుని రోడ్డుపై ప్రజలు ర్యాలీ ఈ వీడియో 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచే ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉంది (ఆర్కైవ్). అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను మొదట ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో దృవీకరించలేకపోయినప్పటికీ, జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద నిరసన గురించి ప్రకటించడానికి మూడు వారాల కంటే ముందే ఈ వీడియోను ఆన్లైన్లో అప్లోడ్ చేశారు.
వీడియో 3:
భారీ సంఖ్యలో ప్రజలు కనిపిస్తున్న ఈ వీడియో 2026 జూన్ నుంచే ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉంది. (ఆర్కైవ్). 6 జూన్ 2026న రాయగఢ్ కోటలో ఛత్రపతి శివాజీ పట్టాభిషేక వార్షికోత్సవం సందర్భంగా జరిగిన వేడుక దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తోంది.
వీడియో 4: 
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఈ వీడియోను షేర్ చేసిన ఒక ఎక్స్ (X) పోస్ట్ (ఆర్కైవ్) కనిపించింది. ఆ పోస్ట్లో “బజరంగ్ దళ్, ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ ఇప్పుడు వీధుల్లోకి వస్తే ఎలా ఉంటుందో ఊహించండి” అనే క్యాప్షన్తో ఈ వీడియోను షేర్ చేశారు. అయితే, ఆ వీడియోకు సంబంధించి ఎలాంటి అదనపు వివరాలను అందులో పేర్కొనలేదు. కానీ ఇది 22 జూలై 2026 నుండే, అంటే జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద నిరసన గురించి ప్రకటించడానికి ముందే సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చయ్యబడుతోంది.
వీడియో 5:
ఈ వీడియో గురించి ఫ్యాక్ట్లీ ఇంతకముందే ప్రచురించింది. UGC 2026 ఈక్విటీ నిబంధనలను ఉపసంహరించుకోవాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ, కర్ణి సేన జైపూర్లో చేసిన ధర్నాను ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తుంది.
వీడియో 6:
ఈ వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగిస్తూ రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చైయగా ఈ వీడియో 2026 జూలైలో జరిగిన ఒక ర్యాలీకి సంబంధించినదని మేము గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోకు 2026 అక్టోబర్ 10న జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరిగిన నిరసనకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు.
అదేవిధంగా, జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరుగుతున్న నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు బజరంగ్ దళ్ కార్యకర్తలు అక్కడికి వస్తున్నారంటూ కొన్ని ధృవీకరించని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. అయితే, బజరంగ్ దళ్ ఈ వార్తలను ఖండించింది. అక్టోబర్ 10న జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద తమ కార్యకర్తలు సమావేశమయ్యే లేదా అక్కడికి వచ్చే ప్రణాళిక ఏదీ లేదని, కొందరు వ్యక్తులు తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని X ద్వారా తెలిపింది (ఆర్కైవ్).
చివరిగా, CJP నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు హిందూ కార్యకర్తలు జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్దకు వస్తున్నారంటూ సంబంధం లేని పాత వీడియోలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Bangkok, Oct 12: Asian shares were mixed and oil prices fell about USD 1.50 a barrel Monday as US President Donald Trump's plan to purchase diesel from Russia drew criticism from some lawmakers.
US stock futures gained more than 0.3 per cent after Wall Street finished its record-setting week with gains. This week will bring updates on inflation and retail sales in the US. The biggest US banks will report earnings from the most recent quarter.
In Asian trading, South Korea's Kospi lost 3.1 per cent to 6,416.17. Markets in Tokyo were closed for a holiday.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged 0.2 per cent higher to 24,253.70 and the Shanghai Composite index slipped 0.1 per cent to 3,809.08.
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 surged 0.9 per cent to 8,790.70.
Taiwan's Taiex gave up 0.2 per cent and the Sensex in India inched up 0.1 per cent.
On Friday, the S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.8 per cent. The Nasdaq composite rose 0.6 per cent.
Oil prices have continued to yo-yo because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal to buy Russian diesel with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call, aiming to tamp down a spike in fuel prices ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections.
The president said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The plan runs counter to US efforts to cut the flow of money Russia gets from oil and gas sales that can be used to pay for its war against Ukraine.
Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
A bipartisan group of six senators called Sunday for the administration to “immediately reverse course" on the plan.
The price of Brent crude, the international standard, was down 1.4 per cent at USD 103.31 per barrel early Monday. US benchmark crude oil fell 1.7 per cent to USD 90.31 per barrel.
Share prices have surged upward, supported by expectations of strong corporate profits, even as Americans say they're feeling more squeezed by high inflation.
A preliminary report from the University of Michigan said Friday that US consumers are raising their own forecasts for how bad inflation will be over the coming year.
They're expecting inflation of 4.7 per cent, up from their forecast of 4.6 per cent a month ago and just 3.4 per cent in February before the war with Iran began.
Sentiment among consumers is falling sharply for Americans with lower incomes and smaller investments in stocks, who can least afford the fast increases in the cost of living.
The pressure is on companies to deliver strong growth in profits after their stock prices ran toward records despite the downward push from high bond yields. This week will bring high-profile profit reports from big banks, including Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo all on Tuesday.
In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 158.27 Japanese yen from 158.23 yen. The euro climbed to USD 1.1211 from USD 1.1191.

Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
- Published
A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.
Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.
Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities.
The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.
Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault
Catching My Teacher
Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia
Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external.
The student detectives
Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.
They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.
By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.
Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.
Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.
Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.
In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.
"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.
Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.
In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.
Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.
Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".
The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.
More students come forward
The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.
One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.
"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."
Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students.
"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."
Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.
"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.
Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.
"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.
Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.
The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.
NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.
In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.

MacBooks have taken most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.
But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.
Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.
The Best for Everyone: Mac Mini
Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.
The Mac Mini isn't the ultra-cheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.
The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.
I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.
Shipping times on the M6 Mac Mini have improved to the point where you can buy one and pick it up today from an Apple Store. The M5 Pro models, however, may take up to four weeks to ship.
Only for Pros: Mac Studio
Like with the Mac Mini, there are really two distinct versions of the Mac Studio. The base configuration comes with an M5 Max (the same chip in the MacBook Pro), sporting some really impressive GPU performance in particular. And that's the main thing to consider when deciding between the M5 Pro Mac Mini and the M5 Max Mac Studio. Like choosing between those two chips in a MacBook Pro, the main upgrade is in graphics performance. Going with the M5 Max also lets you configure it with up to 128 GB of unified memory, which matters if you plan to run heavy local AI models. On the other hand, this puts you over the $5,000 price point rather quickly.
And then, there's the M5 Ultra. This massive chip is literally two M5 Max dies stitched together, and to my surprise while testing, it sometimes resulted in double the performance, such as in GPU performance. But look, don't even bother considering this unless you know exactly what you intend to use it for. Just so you know what you're getting into, the model I tested had 256 GB of memory and cost over $11,000. You read that right. It's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk.
But I downloaded and started running on the M5 Ultra some of the largest and most powerful AI models I could find, and soon enough I had a foundation-tier LLM running completely on-device—no cloud needed. That means direct access to your computer for a powerful agentic AI to run wild with, all without the privacy and security concerns. Some simple agentic tests I ran on the M5 Ultra took minutes, whereas it took five times as long on my M5 Max MacBook Pro.
And while this thing is clearly not intended for gaming, I was pretty blown away by how fast games like Cyberpunk 2077 ran. I've definitely never seen games play this smoothly on a Mac before.
Unfortunately, shipping times on the Mac Studio are still dicey. If you want anything with 128 GB or more of memory, you'll be waiting up to a month and a half for the M5 Max models. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, will take up to four months to ship at this point.
Don't Buy the iMac Right Now
The iMac has been downplayed in recent years. The once-iconic all-in-one computer, which comes with the display, stand, and accessories, used to be an affordable go-to choice for students, families, businesses, and even content creators. But as Apple has shifted focus, the iMac seems less and less of a focus, with sporadic updates over the years. It hasn't been updated since 2024 and still uses the M4 chip.
It's not a bad computer, though. The screen is brilliant, and the performance is solid, even by today's standards. Its age, however, isn't reflected in the price you'd pay right now: $1,499 gets you 16 GB of RAM, 256 GB of storage, the M4 chip with an eight-core GPU, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a 4.5K IPS display. A second M4 model with a 10-core GPU and four Thunderbolt 4 ports starts at $1,699. (Like nearly all Apple products, the iMac got a price increase.)
The main issue for me is that there's currently only a 23.5-inch model, which is smaller than what most people will probably want. Until Apple releases a 27-inch model (as it has in the past), perhaps with an option for a “Pro” M-series chip, I can't see the iMac as a good choice for most people. The simplicity will be a draw, especially if researching and buying a separate monitor and peripherals sounds daunting.
Interestingly, it is also the only desktop-size Mac monitor that isn't at least 5K (it's 4.5K). So, while it's cheaper than buying a Studio Display paired with a new Mac Mini, the iMac also locks you into a one-time purchase you can't upgrade later. And as the focus on local AI only grows, I can't imagine the iMac regaining the relevance or attention it once had. On the plus side, it's the only Mac desktop available in seven colors.
At the very least, I hope it gets a refresh to the M6 in the next couple of months. It'll have been long overdue! Either way, now's not a good time to buy an iMac.
Why Is Everyone Buying a Mac Mini?
Before the launch of the M6 model, Mac Minis had been sold out for most of this year. Orders for Mac Studios were similarly backlogged for months before you could get one. The reason? Well, according to Apple on an earnings call, both computers are “amazing platforms for AI and agentic tools,” and that “customer adoption of that is happening faster than we expected.” In other words, they were caught off guard. AI frameworks released in 2026, such as OpenClaw, run best on a dedicated machine that never turns off and has lots of available RAM—such as a Mac Mini.
What Happened to the Mac Pro?
The last incarnation of the Mac Pro was one of Apple's most short-lived Macs. The most recent design was relaunched in 2019, alongside the Pro Display XDR. When it was unveiled, it was an exciting re-entrance for the Mac, focusing not only on Pro-level performance but also on upgradability. Unlike the current Mac Studio, the Mac Pro had modular components you could swap in and out—or upgrade. The design was much more akin to a traditional tower PC. For a company that had been moving in the opposite direction for so long, it was a breath of fresh air.
But it wasn't meant to last, and it survived only a few upgrade cycles. With the advent of Apple silicon and the rapid scaling of these system-on-a-chip (SoC) designs, the Mac Pro's focus on modularity made less and less sense. Apple didn't officially discontinue the Mac Pro until March 2026, but by then it had been almost three years since the Mac Pro was last updated. The Mac Studio with the “Ultra” chips has since fully replaced the Mac Pro.
M6, M5 Pro, M5 Max, or M5 Ultra?
Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio have two configurations to choose from, which gives a clean delineation between the two in terms of performance. When you move from the base chip to the Pro and Max chips, the main differences are GPU cores and, in some cases, the maximum amount of RAM you can upgrade to. Certain applications and tasks benefit greatly from stronger GPU performance, speeding up things like video rendering, 3D modeling, gaming, and AI inferencing. These are the same chips that are available in the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.
The jump between the Max and Ultra chips, however, is much more significant. This is where you enter performance territory not possible on a MacBook. It has twice the CPU and GPU cores of the standard Max chips, delivers far stronger performance, and lets you configure it with up to 512 GB of unified memory.
The iMac is still holding onto the M4. For most people, the chip is more than capable, but considering the age and the price of the iMac today, it's outdated for a new machine.

Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he would have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung.
Leo said the nodule was found at a "very early stage" with doctors recommending surgery.
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," Leo said during his weekly Sunday noon blessing in St. Peter's Square.
The surgery is due to occur at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which is the primary location for popes to receive medical attention.
Leo has had no known previous health problems.
"I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers," Leo said to the crowds on Sunday.
According to the American Cancer Society, a lung nodule is a small abnormal area, less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. These tests are often conducted as routine screenings for "trauma, heart disease, non-cancer related lung disease, or lung infection."
Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said in a statement that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."
Leo's next major international trip is scheduled for early November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear if the surgery would affect his travels.
During his papacy, Leo has been outspoken about peace throughout the world. He spent part of his Sunday address renewing calls for peace in Ukraine.
"I make a heartfelt appeal to the parties to the conflict to allow the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea," Leo said. "The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war."
On Saturday, the Pope also called for the death penalty to be abolished, saying on X that it is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."
"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo said.

Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code. But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code, meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.
A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”
Cut once, measure twice
To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish, which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.
To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.
In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.
But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.
Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.
Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.
Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.
But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.
On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.
In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.
Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.
Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”
The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.
Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.
Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31.”
Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.
Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”
“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”
Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%.
But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.
Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels.
Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.
Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.
Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.
Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout.
“This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”

Poland's police warn of a possible plot to attack Prime Minister Donald Tusk
Polish authorities have arrested a man suspected of threatening and planning to attack Prime Minister Donald Tusk
WARSAW, Poland -- A man suspected of threatening and planning to attack Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was arrested, the country's interior minister said Sunday.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack planned.
Poland has been on high alert following a series of school stabbings this week, as well as fears of a possible Russian hybrid attack to weaken Western support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
“The man who threatened an attack was detained,” Tusk wrote on X. “Thanks to the police for fast and decisive action.”
Poland's police had said earlier on Sunday they received information about a possible plot to attack Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
“We take this matter extremely seriously,” said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister overseeing Poland's intelligence services. He said authorities considered there was a “high probability” the threats would be carried out.
Dobrzyński was speaking after an emergency meeting of security services, police and representatives of the Interior Ministry on Sunday. He said information about the threat first reached the state protection service, which then passed it to the police.
He gave no other information about the reported plot, but said the intelligence services were receiving an increasing number of various threats with every month.
Government spokesperson Adam Szłapka told Polish media Tusk learned about the threat first thing on Sunday morning. He said that, even if officials do occasionally get threats, this one was “exceptionally concerning.”
Three attacks at schools in Mazovia province in central Poland took place within four days this week, leaving one dead and many wounded, including children.
In September, Tusk warned about likely intensified hybrid attacks by Russia on NATO’s eastern flank. He said Russia was planning strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland, with the goal of weakening Western support for Kyiv's fight against the Russian invasion. Moscow has denied any such plans.

Renshaw delivers again as Australia close on win
- Published
First Test, Durban (day four of five)
Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56
South Africa 284 & 102-4: Bedingham 46, Markram 45*; Hazlewood 2-20
South Africa need 319 runs to win
Australia are primed to earn a statement victory and end South Africa's unbeaten run under captain Temba Bavuma after Matt Renshaw's remarkable Test continued on day four of their series opener in Durban.
Renshaw, in his second game back after a three-year absence, followed his 190 in the first innings with 89 to allow Australia to declare on 314-6. The 30-year-old then dismissed Bavuma with his part-time off-spin late in the day for his first Test wicket.
Captain Pat Cummins followed with a perfect set-up of Tristan Stubbs - pushing him back with shorter balls before nicking him off with a full delivery - to leave South Africa 102-4 at the close.
Set a world record 421 to win, they need to bat out the final day for a draw with six wickets remaining.
South Africa have won 11 and drawn one of their Tests under Bavuma's captaincy, including their run to the 2025 World Test Championship final where they beat Australia at Lord's.
This is the first Test in a South African summer that includes two more against the Australians, two against Bangladesh and three against England over Christmas.
Even bad light, which cut short the first three days, did not come to South Africa's aid on the fourth evening.
Why Markram holds the key
The Proteas' hopes rest largely on the shoulders of opener Aiden Markram who battled to 45 not out from 115 balls.
The right-hander scored a sensational 136 against Australia in the fourth innings of their Test Championship final win and only one active player - Sri Lanka's Kusal Mendis - can better his average of 45.56 in the fourth innings of Tests.
Dragging South Africa out of this position will require immense skill, however. Only twice has a team survived 140 overs to save a Test in the past 13 years.
While Markram shared a stand of 66 in 19.4 overs with David Bedingham the pitch appeared becalmed, but by the close even Renshaw was finding extravagant turn.
One thing in Markram's favour is he has now faced 313 balls from Australia's premier spinner Nathan Lyon in Tests and is yet to be dismissed.
Australia may also be without the fielding excellence of Steve Smith. The former captain spent time off the field on day four having been hit on the helmet by a Anrich Nortje bouncer in making 27.

Pope Leo said on Sunday (October 12, 2026) that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.
Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
“Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained.”
“The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for the next few days.”
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.
Leo, elected pope by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.
The Vatican press office said Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope’s health.
Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.
Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake.”

Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
- Published
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said.
Officials say they have rescued 95 people, including nine foreigners, along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing.
A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex.
Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.
Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar.
More than 200 homes were damaged and more than 650 people were impacted by the flood, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
Some settlements have been completely cut off and are now only accessible by air, a local official told The Kathmandu Post.
Nepal's army said it had mobilised four helicopters for search and rescue operations.
Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies.
Ganesh Karki, a resident of Jagatbagar, told The Kathmandu Post that he and others took shelter about 500m (0.3 miles) uphill in a nearby forest after receiving a warning call about the flood early in the morning.
"We never imagined a flood of this size," he said. "The water surged for about 15 minutes and then stopped repeatedly throughout the morning. We are afraid to return home at night."
The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the disaster management authority said.
Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said.
Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location."
However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August.
What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche.
Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood.
"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said.
"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet."
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.
Nepal is prone to disasters, from earthquakes to landslides and floods, as a result of the unpredictable natural environment in the Himalayas. Hundreds of people were killed in August after floods tore through villages along the Nepal-Tibet border. That disaster was caused by an avalanche of rock and ice near the peak of Lantang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.
Experts say climate change, which is making glaciers melt faster, is likely raising the risk of such disasters, leaving local communities increasingly vulnerable.

Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
- Published
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.
But Zaw Min has no choice.
"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.
"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."
Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.
According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.
Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.
Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.
The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.
Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.
"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.
The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.
They said they had no comment on the matter.
With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.
The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.
International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.
In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.
Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.
"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.
Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.
"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."
Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.
"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."
Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.
The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.
In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.
U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.
When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.
But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.
"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.
"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.
"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."
In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.
The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.
She does not know where her husband is now.
Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.
Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.
"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."
In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.
The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.
BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.
"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.
"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."
While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.
So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.
Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".
But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.
It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.
The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".
In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.
Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.
As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

Have you ever taken months off training – maybe due to an injury, a new baby or crushing work deadlines – and come back convinced you were starting from zero?
Research from our team has some good news: At the cellular level, you probably weren’t.
We found that muscle and liver cells store memories fromevery training session in ways that may help improve endurance, control blood sugar levels and even slow weight regain after inactivity.
Use it or lose it? Maybe not
For most of the past century, long before fad diets and fancy workout trends took off, exercise was considered one of the most effective lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, several cancers and early death for people of all ages. But people typically understood exercise as something whose beneficial effects fade away over time: You use it or lose it.
When you stop training, your maximum oxygen uptake, muscle gains and insulin sensitivity drift back to where they started, often within weeks. Physical activity guidelines are built on this fact, which is why they emphasise consistency above all else.
Consistency, however, is a luxury that roughly 3 in 4 American adults aren’t able to enjoy. People can experience injuries, illness, pregnancy or jobs that limit their time for or ability to exercise. If adaptation really resets, every time you step into the gym would be as if you’ve never been there before. But that scenario doesn’t match what coaches and returning athletes typically describe: In practice, people who have trained before can get fit again faster than those who haven’t undergone similar training.
In recent years, however, scientists have started challenging the concept of “use it or lose it.” New research hints that your cells might keep a record of your training history so all of your gains are not completely lost.
More than muscle
We areexercise physiologists who study how cells remember exercise. Our lab and others have shown that the body is able to store a form of exercise memory across different organs.
To study how this exercise memory works, our team of researchers use an ON-OFF-ON exercise training protocol in mice, which involves an initial four- to eight-week training period, followed by detraining – a period of no exercise – and a second training bout. This method allows us to examine how cells form a memory of exercise, maintain a record of exercise through detraining, and recall memories of prior training when exposed again to exercise.
Using this strategy, our team found that skeletal muscle memory accelerates muscle growth. Compared to mice with no training history, mice who retrained grew bigger muscles, and the individual muscle fibers inside those muscles grew too. Larger muscle fibers meant that the working cells were themselves getting bigger, rather than the surrounding tissue.
Looking more closely at these muscle cells, we found that retrained muscle is better at matching energy production to demand – meaning, the muscles were better at drawing from energy stores when it’s needed most – and this ability persists without further exercise. This memory held even when the mice ate a high-fat diet, suggesting that prior training can still offer benefits even when diet is working against those gains.
Muscle isn’t the only body part that learns from exercise. Working muscle needs fuel, and the liver supplies it during and after training sessions.
My colleagues and I found that liver cells also store exercise memory and uses it to feed muscle more efficiently. In both mice and people who trained, stopped, then trained again, their livers released higher levels of a family of enzymes called carboxylesterases. These enzymes chop up lipids circulating in the blood, delivering fat in a form that muscle can take up and burn as it grows.
A record that outlives you
Recorded cellular memories of exercise may even be passed down to future generations.
In mice, we found that three to four weeks of maternal and paternal endurance exercise can have a lasting effect on their offspring. Compared to offspring born to sedentary parents, parental exercise granted protection against poor blood sugar levels and excess weight gain for an entire year after birth.
Researchers have hypothesized numerous ways that prenatal exercise may affect offspring. For example, maternal exercise might allow offspring to spend more time developing in the womb or lead parents to producer higher quality milk.
But there remains much to be discovered on how parents influence the health of their children and whether their lifestyle could provide a fitness advantage across generations.
Every cell remembers
Biology has traditionally granted memory to a short list of cells. Neurons store memory in the connections between them. Immune cells store memory so they can recognize pathogens faster and more strongly the next time they encounter them.
Researchers previously considered all other cells to be memoryless; a cell responds to a signal, then returns to baseline without keeping a record of that interaction. But that assumption is now coming apart.
Skin stem cells can keep a record of inflammation, allowing them to heal a new wound faster months later. Human fat cells keep a record of obesity that persists even after substantial weight loss, which may account for why you gain weight faster when switching back to a high-calorie diet – the so-called yo-yo effect.
We propose that every cell in the body remembers exercise, regardless of how little or how much someone trains. The question is how long these records are stored and whether researchers could prolong or expand each cell’s storage capacity. Better understanding of how cells learn and remember exercise, where they store memories and how those memories are preserved could help improve exercise guidelines for those who cannot exercise for prolonged or consistent periods of time.
To be clear, none of these findings are evidence for skipping the gym; nothing in our data suggests the effects of past training can substitute for present training. But there is hope that the work you put into getting in shape isn’t completely lost over time.
Somewhere, deep in your cells, there is a record waiting to be replayed the next time you lace up your running shoes, pick up a pair of dumbbells or want to fulfill a New Year’s resolution.
Diego Hernandez-Saavedra, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Yi-Heng (Hank) Huang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
