- In October, a claim recirculated online that McDonald's lost a lawsuit against TV chef Jamie Oliver, who — according to posts — proved that the fast food chain's food is "unfit for human consumption" because it is "highly toxic." The claim is unproven.
- Snopes previously investigated a variation of this claim in 2018 and September 2026. On each occasion, we found that Oliver said in a 2011 TV program that beef trimmings used for a product he called "pink slime" were "not fit for human consumption." We found no evidence that he specifically called McDonald's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic," as numerous posts have repeatedly suggested.
- The American Meat Institute, a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry, said in 2012 that beef trimmings used to make "pink slime," which it calls Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, are edible.
- However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode where Oliver discussed "pink slime" to see if he specifically mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether Oliver has ever called the fast food chain's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" or whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver and are waiting for responses.
A persistent claim recirculated online at the start of October that fast food chain McDonald's lost a lawsuit against Jamie Oliver after the TV chef proved the restaurant's food is "unfit for human consumption" because it is "highly toxic."
For example, one Facebook user has written, in part (archived):
McDonald's loses lawsuit against chef Jamie Oliver, who proved that the food they sell is unfit for human consumption because it is highly toxic.
Chef Jamie Oliver won a lawsuit against the world's largest fast-food chain.
Oliver demonstrates how hamburgers are made.
According to Oliver, fatty cuts of meat are "washed" with ammonium hydroxide and then used to fill the hamburger patties. Even before this process, the TV presenter says, this meat was unfit for human consumption.
Snopes readers contacted us about the claim throughout the start of fall 2026. We previously reported on the claim in September 2026 and January 2018.
The claim contains three parts: that McDonald's sued Oliver, that Oliver made the comments about "pink slime" and that Oliver's alleged comments were specifically about McDonald's.
We found no evidence in online searches (archived, archived, archived) that McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver. AFP Fact Check reported in December 2021 that Oliver had never taken legal action against McDonald's.
According to an excerpt of a 2011 episode of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," Oliver said that the meat used to produce a specific type of beef product that the celebrity chef called "pink slime" is "not fit for human consumption."
McDonalds reportedly ceased using "pink slime," which is also known as Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, in their food in 2011, as we noted in 2018 when we fact-checked a previous version of this claim. Oliver did not mention McDonald's specifically in excerpts of the 2011 episode of "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" that Snopes reviewed.
However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question to see if it mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
Snopes contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether the fast food chain ever lost a lawsuit involving the TV chef, whether Oliver had ever proved McDonald's food was "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic," and to ask whether the restaurant used Select Lean Beef Trimmings in 2026. We await replies to our queries.
Oliver's allegations
In the first episode of the second season of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," in which Oliver attempted to reform school lunches and fight obesity in the U.S., the celebrity chef held a demonstration where he showed children and adults where on a cow different cuts of meat come from.
According to a segment of the episode (archived) that an internet user uploaded to YouTube in 2016, after spray-painting prices on a live cow to show where various cuts are found, Oliver then addressed what happens to the remainder of the animal.
He said (time code 00:01), "The public loved seeing that, that, equalling a steak. They never for a minute thought I would clear all the meat and cuts away and introduce them to a new world of food. It's called pink slime."
Oliver added (time code 00:12), "When you've broken down a whole beast, you're left with trimmings. You know, in my industry, we call those trimmings [BLEEP]."
Speaking to a crowd of people, Oliver described the trimmings used for "pink slime" as (time code 00:36) "not fit for human consumption."
Oliver went on to say that processing plants took trimmings that were "not fit for human consumption," separated the meat from the fat, killed harmful bacteria using ammonium hydroxide and sold the end product, which he called "pink slime," as human-grade food. Ammonium hydroxide is a watery solution that can be used to regulate acidity in food or in hair dye or cosmetics.
In an excerpt from the program included in a 2012 CBS report, Oliver said (time code 00:32), "We're taking a product that would be sold at the cheapest form for dogs, and after this process we can give it to humans."
(Snopes could not locate a complete video of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question. The clips we have found online appeared genuine and do not indicate any signs of possible manipulation.)
FDA says ammonium hydroxide 'generally safe'
Around 11 months after Oliver's episode discussing "pink slime" aired, the American Meat Institute President J. Patrick Boyle issued a statement to say that Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings is "a safe, wholesome and nutritious form of beef" that helps prevent food waste by utilizing trimmings that would otherwise go to waste.
The institute is a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry.
Boyle's statement says, similarly to Oliver's demonstration, that processing Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings involves first separating the meat from the fat and using "food grade ammonium hydroxide gas" to destroy bacteria before blending the product into foods like ground beef.
However, he denied claims that the trimmings used to create Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings are not edible. The statement says:
Some recent media reports created a troubling and inaccurate picture, particularly in their use of the colloquial term 'pink slime.' The fact is, BLBT is beef. The beef trimmings that are used to make BLBT are absolutely edible. In fact, no process can somehow make an inedible meat edible; it's impossible. In reality, the BLBT production process simply removes fat and makes the remaining beef more lean and suited to a variety of beef products that satisfy consumers' desire for leaner foods.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which regulates ammonium hydroxide use in food, says the ingredient is "generally recognized as safe." This was also the case when we last reported on these claims in 2018.
In sum ...
While Oliver did call the cuts of meat used for Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings "not fit for human consumption" and claimed (time code 00:59) the product was "admitted to being in at least 70% of ground beef products" in a 2011 program, the episode excerpts Snopes reviewed do not show him specifically accusing McDonald's of using the product or calling the fast food chain's products toxic.
McDonald's said in a 2013 statement it had not used Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings in its products since 2011.
We found no evidence McDonald's had lost a lawsuit involving Oliver since then. Given the prominence of McDonald's and Oliver, such a lawsuit would have been widely reported by reputable news media sources. That has not been the case.
While the FDA generally recognizes ammonium hydroxide, which is used to process Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, as safe, reporting by food safety publication Food Safety News claimed that fast food giants like McDonalds, Taco Bell and Burger King had all stopped using the product by January 2012.
Both ABC, which broadcast Oliver's program, and the chef himself have faced lawsuits over their coverage of the product.
ABC settled out of court in 2017 in a $1.9 billion defamation lawsuit brought by Beef Products Inc., a producer of Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, over Oliver's program and other stories the network had reported about the product in March and April 2012.
A man who Beef Products Inc. laid off after negative press heavily affected the company's sales sued Oliver, ABC and other defendants in 2012. He dropped the case in 2013.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

A claim that retired professional U.S. soccer star Megan Rapinoe called for Super Bowl champion and ESPN analyst Jason Kelce's firing began circulating online this week.
Snopes readers searched for references to Rapinoe and Kelce on this website, which led us to consult search engines DuckDuckGo and Google for basic details about why the two names were making the rounds together. We located a popular Facebook post (archived) that appeared on the Empire Sports Facebook page on Oct. 5, reading in part:
MEGAN RAPINOE: Calls for Jason Kelce to be FIRED..
Megan Rapinoe criticized Jason Kelce after he used Washington's former team name during a live broadcast.
"I know Jason Kelce said that racist name on purpose to create division. He should be fired immediately."
— Megan Rapinoe
The comments under Empire Sports' post indicated some people believed Rapinoe truly called for Kelce's firing.
Other users shared the rumor on Facebook (archived) and Threads (archived), though the original Empire Sports Facebook post earned far more likes, comments and shares than other examples.
In sum, while it's true Kelce mentioned the old Washington Redskins' team name during a TV broadcast, Rapinoe did not call for his firing.
The Empire Sports page displays a disclaimer acknowledging it publishes fabricated content of a parodical and satirical nature, reading, "Delivering the Finest of Sports Parodies / Satire / Updates / Insider News & much MORE." In other words, Empire Sports does not publish authentic news reports.
The aforementioned searches of DuckDuckGo and Google located no news media outlets credibly reporting Rapinoe said any such things about Kelce. Rapinoe's active Instagram page also did not feature any content about him.
Snopes emailed representatives for Rapinoe and Kelce to ask if either wished to address the popular made-up story. The Empire Sports page didn't display a Messenger button or any other contact methods.
Purveyors of misinformation and fabricated stories — whether labeled as parody and satire or not — have long wielded Rapinoe's name and image as politically-fueled engagement bait, whether for social media posts or website traffic, sometimes thinly disguised as satire. Part of the reason for the firestorm of controversy in this instance stems from U.S. President Donald Trump's comments about Rapinoe, and vice versa.
What Kelce said
On Oct. 4, Kelce served as an analyst during the ESPN-owned NFL Network TV broadcast of the Indianapolis Colts' 30-13 victory over the Washington Commanders, which took place in London.
A video from that broadcast shows Kelce apologizing to the Washington Commanders after he used the team's former name. In the clip, Kelce breaks down the Commanders' defensive coverage, saying, "The Redskins right now are doing a great job of not only staying tight but making the play when the ball is in the receiver's hand and keeping it short of the sticks."
Announcer Dave Pasch laughs, telling Kelce he accidentally said Redskins, to which Kelce responds, "Oh my gosh! I almost made it out." Pasch then says he, Kelce and former Super Bowl MVP Kurt Warner, also working as an analyst, all had a "gentleman's bet" regarding who would slip up first. Kelce replies, "Well, sorry Washington."
Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before, including past satire-labeled rumors suggesting Rapinoe was leaving the U.S. due to a "massive red wave," going bankrupt and was banned from the Olympic sports.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration says its ongoing safety review of the nation’s main abortion pill will continue into next year, a timeline that was quickly condemned by abortion opponents hoping to see the drug’s use curtailed.
The FDA gave a court-ordered update on its progress in a legal filing late Wednesday, providing the first substantive information about the controversial reevaluation ordered by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Mifepristone was first approved by the FDA in 2000. The agency has repeatedly reaffirmed the pill’s safety and effectiveness over the years, in addition to easing a number of restrictions on the drug, including dropping a requirement that it be dispensed in person.
But since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, anti-abortion groups and their allies in Congress have pushed the administration to revisit the pill, in the hopes of restricting its use.
The FDA said in its filing that it expects to complete a safety study of the pill by mid-December this year. A report on the findings is expected “no later than March 2027,” after which the agency will decide whether to impose new restrictions or other changes on the drug’s use.
Gavin Oxley of Americans United for Life, an anti-abortion group, criticized the move as a lack of “true leadership” by Trump administration officials.
“The administration continues to find itself on the wrong side of women’s health, clearly uninterested in mitigating the ongoing harms caused by the abortion pill,” Oxley said.
The two-drug regimen of mifepristone, combined with a second drug misoprostol, is the most common form of abortion in the U.S.
The FDA was directed to provide the latest update by a federal judge in a case brought by the state of Louisiana alleging that mail-delivery of mifepristone undermines the state’s abortion ban. It’s one of several state lawsuits related to mifepristone winding their way through the courts.
Last month a three-judge panel for the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals questioned the merits of Louisiana’s case, including whether the state had the legal standing to challenge FDA’s oversight of mifepristone.
Any ruling from the 5th Circuit on the Louisiana case would not immediately change the landscape because the Supreme Court has blocked changes to the drug until it sees the case again.
The FDA said Wednesday it is using a “statistical data mining method” to discover “unknown safety concerns,” that may exist with the drug. The data comes from an electronic database that collects reports of medical injuries and drug side effects from major health networks and insurers.
In addition to the safety study, the agency said it is considering a number of petitions proposing changes to how mifepristone is prescribed and distributed.
Abortion opponents have focused most of their efforts on a 2021 decision allowing doctors to prescribe the drug online and send it through the mail during COVID-19. That decision, made permanent under President Joe Biden in 2023, had the effect of undermining a number of state abortion bans, since women can receive the drug through the mail.
— Matthew Perrone

Central government-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund has approved 19 second-level fund managers (SLFMs) with a total commitment of ₹7,131 Cr. The Ministry of Science and Technology’s Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS) approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) for this purpose earlier this month, the ministry announced. The selected entities will channel capital from the RDI Fund to eligible technology enterprises undertaking research, development and innovation activities at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 and above. The fund managers are also expected to mobilise private capital equivalent to the RDI Fund’s contribution, potentially expanding the pool of financing available to research-driven businesses. Alongside approving the first cohort of fund managers, the EGoS approved five additional technologies for coverage under the RDI Fund. The government did not specify these technologies in its announcement. The government said it would continue inviting applications and onboarding additional cohorts of fund managers, expanding the reach of the scheme and encouraging public-private investment in India's research and innovation ecosystem. Launched in November 2025, the RDI Scheme has an overall outlay of ₹1 Lakh Cr and aims to address the funding gap faced by companies developing high-risk, high-impact technologies. It is managed by an independent business unit housed within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST). The fund is designed to spur private investment in research-intensive businesses. However, its impact on investor sentiment, however, remains unclear. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms linked to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries. The report raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest. Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate, but said visibility into the process remained limited. Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure that required independent oversight, while 14% said potential conflicts could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said the issue was not a concern, arguing that the focus should be on selecting the right companies. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startup funding in the September quarter zoomed 176% YoY to $290 Mn raised across 28 deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The sector outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn.

Winning a Nobel Prize is a matter of great prestige. Winning a Nobel Prize also means the award going to a small number of people while a large number are left out, even if they really deserved to win.
This is partly because of the prizes’ rules. Alfred Nobel’s will said nothing about the number of people that can be awarded at one time but the Nobel Foundation’s statutes limit each prize to at most three people at a time, and no one that has died by the time a prize is announced. Also, scientists need to have been nominated by nominators who have their own eligibility criteria.
A big-picture view of the science Nobel Prizes through history brings another pattern into view: a preference for singular breakthroughs rather than lifetime achievements.
Boyden, Bamberg, and beyond
Start with the Nobel Prize this year for physiology/medicine, to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel, for their work on optogenetics. In 2002, Austrian scientist Gero Miessenböck & co. had first sensitised to light some neurons that were not naturally light-sensitive. Miessenböck is now at the University of Oxford, where his profile page describes him as an ‘inventor’ of optogenetics.
Hegemann and Nagel have been feted for identifying and characterising the protein channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2). The next step was to show that it could control neurons. The first author of the paper that did was Edward Boyden, who helped pioneer the application of ChR2 to neuroscience. Boyden is now a professor of neurotechnology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the Broad Institute.
Another author of this paper, Ernst Bamberg, had supervised Nagel’s PhD and was part of the team that established the importance of ChR2. A page on the website of the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics, Germany, where Bamberg is now an emeritus professor, says he was instrumental in translating the ChR2 finding into practical applications.
Yet another author, Feng Zhang, is also at MIT now, and in 2007, he was a member of one of two teams that adapted another protein, called halorhodopsin, to silence neurons with light instead of activating them. The other team, consisting of Xue Han and Boyden, had demonstrated the same capability.
These contributions together — rather than only those that the laureates led — turned the ability to control neurons with light into a tool of neuroscience with real-world applications, including in medicine.
No lone wolf
Next, the physics prize — which this year demonstrated the brokenness of the Nobel Prizes on a whole other level. Francis Halzen won the prize all by himself “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. But IceCube is an international collaboration involving around 450 experts from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Crucially, the prize-giving committee was not constrained to give the prize to one person here. The Nobel Foundation statutes allow the committee to decide whether its prizes can be awarded to associations or organisations. But the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry, and economics prizes, does not seem to have adopted this option. If it had, the physics prize could have recognised the IceCube collaboration as a whole.
But even if this rule did not exist, it is hard to say why the committee picked Halzen alone. In 1988, Halzen and (today) University of Hawai’i physics and astronomy professor John G. Learned reported the idea of using Antarctica’s ice mass as the target in which neutrinos from outer space could interact with atoms together. Learned then focused on an underwater neutrino experiment called DUMAND while Halzen pursued a project that eventually became IceCube.
Also, in 2012, while searching IceCube data for neutrinos coming from outer space with very high energies, scientists found two candidate events. The data quickly snowballed into evidence proving that neutrinos could be energised significantly by natural phenomena in space — and the prize citation credits this feat to Halzen alone.
But in real-life (as opposed to Nobel-life), the IceCube collaboration had credited Japanese physicist Aya Ishihara with finding those two candidate events, and for which she received an International Union of Pure and Applied Physics award in 2013. This particular oversight is oddly reminiscent of the infamous Jocelyn Bell Burnell story. Ishihara is currently a professor at Chiba University, where she continues to study high-energy neutrinos and develop the next generation of neutrino detectors.
Furthermore, the 2013 Science paper that reported the high-energy neutrinos also named three scientists named Claudio Kopper, Naoko Kurahashi, and Nathan Whitehorn as its corresponding authors.
The physics prize for Halzen is not misplaced. Halzen was very good — but the point is so were very many others. Aside from the scientists named here, it also required engineers and technicians who could build it in one of the most hostile locations on our planet. And all these people had to work together to make the project and its subsequent achievements possible. Halzen alone could never have done it.
Drawing difficult lines
Finally, the chemistry Nobel Prize this year illustrates the problem with the rule that it cannot be given to people who have died by the time the prize is announced. In 1953, the British physicist Frederick Charles Frank came up with a mathematical way to explain how a small chemical imbalance in a specific kind of reaction could force the reaction to make that imbalance the norm. This way required the reaction to have three properties, called autocatalysis, enantioselective catalysis, and mutual inhibition.
Between 1986 and 1995, Henri Kagan in France and Kenso Soai in Japan had reported evidence of all the conditions of Frank’s model, providing experimental evidence that it could work in the real world. However, Frank died in 1998, aged 87.
That said, the 1995 paper by Soai et al. included Takanori Shibata, who made essential contributions to this branch of chemistry (and was second author on the paper). And whereas Kagan and Soai had demonstrated different aspects of Frank’s model, Shibata was the first author of a 1999 paper that extended the work of Soai et al. to demonstrate the reaction Frank had tried to model. Shibata is currently at Waseda University. And again, it is not easy to rationalise the prize-giving committee’s decision to not include him among this year’s chemistry laureates.
On the other hand, the committee’s decision to exclude U.S. chemical engineer Donna Blackmond throws light on one possible line of reasoning. A technical statement accompanying the chemistry prize credited her with extending Kagan’s attempts to use mathematics to understand non-linear effects in chemical reactions. Blackmond and her team later also took big strides in making sense of the mechanism of the so-called Soai reaction.
And yet, the committee elected to reward the discovery of the validity of Frank’s model rather than work that explained and further extended it.
The S.N. Bose example
In the final analysis, the citations for the Nobel Prizes should not be mistaken for the history of science. Scientists build on the work of others and science advances in these slow but steady increments. When Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the Nobel Prize for physics in 2013 for predicting the Higgs boson, there was some clamour in India for not recognising the work of Satyendra Nath Bose. The objection was fair to the extent that you can’t have a fruit without the whole tree and yet petty because it is not reasonable to expect one prize to laud the entire history of a field.
This is why each Nobel Prize award can be a chance to reflect on its limitations, and remember that it is not an ultimate recognition. No prize is.
In that vein, we should also not confuse the number of winners every year with the number of people it takes to do excellent science — from grad students who perform simple experiments to senior colleagues to discuss complicated ideas with. In fact, depending on where in the world you are and your socio-economic standing, your ability to be a good scientist may turn on something as deceptively simple as having someone to help with household chores.
Perhaps most of all, while the Nobel Prizes recognise good science, not all good science wins Nobel Prizes.

The Union Health Ministry is engaging with youth volunteers to find people with tuberculosis (TB) who may be missing from the health system. JOSH teams of the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and MY Bharat volunteers are deploying for household-level outreach in 55 districts across 11 States and Union Territories.
Health Minister J.P. Nadda launched the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) teams under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan on Thursday. The teams will work at block and ward levels to identify people with symptoms, encourage testing, and support patients so they can complete treatment.
Each team will comprise five NCC cadets and five MY Bharat volunteers and will function under a designated Class-I officer. The initiative is being implemented jointly by the Ministries of Health and Family Welfare, Youth Affairs and Sports and Defence.
The government’s emphasis is on active case finding, with the Health Minister stating that people could be living with TB without recognising their symptoms and therefore remain outside the formal healthcare system. “Awareness is important, screening is important, but our responsibility does not end there,” he said, stressing the need to ensure diagnosis and completion of treatment.
The Centre also felicitated 67,933 Panchayats across 697 districts that were declared TB Mukt in 2026. The JOSH initiative is expected to be expanded to other districts after orientation and mobilisation of volunteers.

What happens to Google and Apple accounts when the owner dies?
Your accounts won't forever haunt the internet after you die.
The death of a loved one typically comes not only with the immense emotional weight of grief, but also an onslaught of administrative tasks — a home to sell, a cell phone bill to cancel and belongings to offload. As we increasingly live our lives online, our deaths have become more digital as well. So when preparing for the inevitable, what should you do about your Google and Apple accounts — and what should you do if a loved one dies?
Much of how accounts are dealt with after a death has to do with whether the account holder made any preparations while living. Many platforms have programs to help you handle your digital legacy, but these require conscious decisions before death to transfer access to a trusted representative. Without this, the fate of accounts depends largely on the policies of the platforms in question, which vary across Apple and Google. Whether getting your own affairs in order or a loved one has recently passed and you're trying to decide what to do, here's what you should know.
What happens to a Google account when someone dies?
The short answer is that nothing will happen to your Google account after death if you haven't planned for it, but the company is making it easier to manage legacy options. In 2013, Google launched an Inactive Account Manager tool, which allows users to specify what should be done with their account in the event that it becomes inactive for an extended period of time.
Through this program, users can request to have data deleted after three, six, or 12 months of inactivity. They can also elect to have their data (including messages, contacts, YouTube channels and more) forwarded to up to 10 trusted contacts. "We hope that this new feature will enable you to plan your digital afterlife in a way that protects your privacy and security," Google product manager Andreas Tuerk wrote in the blog post announcing the new tool.
If you do not set up an Inactive Account Manager, Google may simply delete your inactive account, which its system prompts after a minimum of two years without activity. Google detects activity through sign-ins, usage of the Gmail app and other actions using any Google products. In circumstances in which a user did not set up Inactive Account Manager, family members can reach out directly to Google to request that their deceased relative's account be deactivated before the standard two years of inactivity, though they will not be provided with any data from the account.
What happens to an Apple account when someone dies?
Like Google, Apple has a system in place to manage a user's accounts and digital life after their death, but using this feature similarly requires a bit of foresight. Apple allows users to designate up to five people as "Legacy Contacts" — people who have the legal right to access the user's iCloud data and devices in the event of their passing. Legacy contacts can be designated through Apple Account settings, which will generate an access key for the contact to use in the case of a user's death. After a user dies, the designated legacy contact can access personal data like photos, messages, notes, files, and device backups by sharing the access key generated when they were selected as a legacy contact. They will also be required to share a death certificate with Apple to access this information.
Once a legacy contact presents a death certificate and the access key, they have three years to download Apple's data before the account is deleted permanently. Notably, the legacy contact will not have access to purchased content like music, movies, or books. Unlike a DVD or book collection, digital media cannot be passed on to would-be heirs. If you don't set up a legacy contact, Apple's time limit for deleting inactive accounts is shorter than Google's: After just one year of inactivity on iCloud, the user will receive a warning email, and the account will be deleted 30 days later.

India opener Abhishek Sharma said he had to find ways to counter the West Indies’ plans against him after smashing a 30-ball 69 to power India to a 14-run win in the third T20I here on Sunday.
India took a 2-1 lead in the five-match series with Abhishek’s quickfire knock, his 108-run stand for the second wicket with Ishan Kishan (37), and Arshdeep Singh’s 3/44 setting up the victory.
Abhishek said the West Indies opening with off-spinner Roston Chase and field placement on the off side prompted him to explore more scoring options.
“I wouldn’t say it was deliberate, but it was there in my mind that they had a plan against me,” Abhishek told reporters after the match when asked about his off-side strokes.
Also read | Sai Sudharsan hobbles off field during Tamil Nadu’s Ranji Trophy match against Rajasthan
“(With the) off-spinner bowling against me, it was just a battle between him and me. I gave him respect in the first over because he is bowling really well in this series, so it is just the plan that went pretty well for me as well.”
“…because in the powerplay, I was trying to just get a few runs and they had a plan for me, and I had to play better than that,” said Abhishek, who smacked six fours and five sixes in his innings.
He added, “I don’t think and play deliberately. It just happens when I see the field placement, whenever they have a field placement which allows me to just give myself room and play those shots.”
India restricted the West Indies to 209 for seven after being bowled out for 223. Abhishek said India wanted to be ruthless against the Caribbean side.
“West Indies is such a team that you can never say that the match is now on our side.This was on our mind because we saw in the last match that whichever batsman comes in, (with) the conditions that we have here, it is very easy for them to take the match to their side.”
“So that was in our mind even when we were losing wickets, we were saying that we would be ruthless thereon and we will not give them a single chance to come back,” he said.
“The way (Shamar) Springer batted, I was really surprised by the way he played those shots; those weren’t easy shots. You have to be ready all the time, (even) if they are at 50/5 as well, I think they have that capability to turn things around for themselves. In that case we were very much prepared this time.”
Also read | From Ludhiana to Puducherry via Hobart: Nikhil Chaudhary’s life-come-full-circle moment
Abhishek backed his Punjab teammate Naman Dhir, who claimed 2/39, to do well for India in the coming years.
“I’ve seen him from Under-14 days so I know how well he can bowl. You have to just tell him the plan; probably a bowler doesn’t think too much at that moment when he has got hit for two sixes back-to-back.”
“We wanted to delay him a bit and wanted him to just bowl the best ball, that is his off spin. But I think the way he is bowling, he is going to do really well for India in the next few years as well.”
Abhishek said he would like to see Kishan more relaxed when he comes out to bat.
“… he doesn’t laugh that easily while batting so I have to (first) make him laugh and relax him a little because he likes to be in that zone when he comes to bat,” Abhishek said.
“But I feel there is a bonding between the two of us, we have had so many partnerships even in IPL. We understand each other pretty well and whenever Ishan comes in when one wicket is down, (initially) that little (amount of) pressure is there.”

Delhi SIR: CEO says 20 lakh voter discrepancies resolved, assures ‘no eligible voter will be excluded’
CEO Delhi has said that around 20 lakh voter list entries flagged under Logical Discrepancy or unmapped categories have been resolved so far.
The Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Delhi, on Monday said that around 20 lakh out of the 33 lakh voter list entries flagged under Logical Discrepancy or Unmapped categories have been resolved so far.
In a post on X, the CEO further said that a proactive campaign was launched to resolve the discrepancies, adding that “no eligible voter will be excluded from the voter list”.
Verification of electors served notices intensified
The verification of electors who received notices as part of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll has been stepped up in Delhi, with 14,947 Booth Level Officers (BLOs) directed to verify at least 10 daily for speedy disposal of cases ahead of the publication of the final list on December 4.

The daily target translates into verification of nearly 150,000 electors. BLOs are required to visit electors at their residences and assist them in furnishing the required documents and information.
Officials in the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO)’s office said the move was necessitated by the initially low pace of verification. They added it has helped significantly increase the number of electors being cleared. Over 1.3 million of the nearly 3.3 million electors issued notices under the SIR exercise have now been verified.

Notices, claims, objections to be disposed by Nov 30

Officials said the daily verification target was introduced to ensure that the process progresses at a steady pace and that the large number of pending cases are addressed within the stipulated timeline.
“Targets have also been given to Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs). We have set a target of November 25 for completing the process of verifying electors,” said an official aware of the matter.

For patients with advanced cancer and other life-limiting illnesses, palliative care often needs to extend beyond hospital wards to their homes, where families grapple with pain, emotional distress, and the demands of long-term caregiving.
At the State-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology (KMIO), the Department of Palliative Medicine has made home-based care a key part of its services, reporting more than 750 home-care visits, over 12,000 km travelled and more than 3,000 beneficiaries, including patients and caregivers.
These services were highlighted while observing World Hospice and Palliative Care Day on October 10, which this year carried the theme ‘Pain management: An essential part of palliative care’.
“With the help of volunteers and NGOs, we also extend financial support for children’s education. We provide waterbed and airbed, ration kits, and nebuliser machines for use at home. It is not just about treating the patient,” M.K. Yadhuraj Gowda, Head of the Department of Palliative Medicine at KMIO, told The Hindu.
The home-care service is intended for patients who find it difficult to travel to the hospital because of advanced illness, reduced mobility, or other challenges. Multidisciplinary teams provide medical assessment, symptom management, nursing care, and support in familiar surroundings, helping reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.
The department’s approach also recognises that serious illness affects entire families. Caregivers may need help managing the practical demands of looking after a patient, as well as support in coping with emotional and financial pressures, Dr. Gowda said.
Beyond death
Palliative care also includes bereavement support for families after the death of a loved one. KMIO’s department provides guidance to help family members cope with grief, manage emotional distress and access support during the grieving process.
The service reflects the broader role of palliative care, which addresses not only physical pain and other symptoms but also the psychological, emotional, social and spiritual needs of patients and their families. Volunteer services add another layer of support for families navigating serious illness and loss.
Pain relief and care for children
Institute director R. Krishnappa said the department provides inpatient palliative care for patients who require specialised management of pain and other distressing symptoms, with capacity for more than 30 patients. Its services include medication and interventional procedures such as nerve blocks and neurolysis for selected patients with severe cancer-related pain that remains inadequately controlled with conventional treatment.
It also provides paediatric palliative care, with age-appropriate pain and symptom management, emotional support and guidance for families caring for children with cancer and other serious illnesses, he said.
Music and sound therapy sessions are conducted for inpatients on Wednesdays, while yoga therapy sessions are held on Thursdays to promote relaxation and emotional well-being alongside medical treatment.
Teleconsultations extend specialist support
The department has relaunched its ‘Call for Care - Neravina Kare’ service to connect patients living outside Bengaluru and in distant locations with specialist palliative care. Through telephone and video consultations, a team comprising a palliative care physician, nurse and clinical psycho-oncologist offers guidance on symptom management and emotional support. Patients and caregivers can contact the service on 9008441708.

In a bid to make cancer treatment more affordable and reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure, the Union government has decided to cap trade margins at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP) for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
Also read | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The measure will cover branded and generic drugs, domestically manufactured and imported medicines, and patented and non-patented products. An expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) will finalise the list of medicines to be brought under the measure.
Current mark-ups up to 700%
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), which analysed market data, found that the average trade mark-up on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was around 170%, with mark-ups reaching up to 700% in some cases. It also found substantial differences between prices charged through retail, hospital, and online pharmacies.
The government said the decision was prompted by the high financial burden of cancer treatment. Around 75% of cancer treatment expenditure is estimated to be borne out of pocket.
The anti-cancer medicines market comprises around 225 drugs and 500 formulations, with an annual turnover of approximately ₹12,500 crore. Scheduled cancer medicines account for about ₹2,250 crore.
Massive savings
A senior official said that the government is drawing on the experience of a similar intervention in 2019, when the NPPA capped trade margins on 42 selected non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs by invoking its extraordinary powers under Paragraph 19 of the Drug Price Control Order, 2013. The exercise had reportedly resulted in price reductions of up to 91%, with annual savings of ₹984 crore across 526 brands.
The latest intervention is expected to result in price reductions of up to 70% of MRP and annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore, the government said.
‘Production must be maintained’
Under the new framework, the trade margin will be capped at 30% of MRP, equivalent to 42.86% of the price to stockist.
“To ensure availability, manufacturers will be required to maintain their existing production level,” said the official.
The government said the measure would regulate trade margins rather than manufacturers’ selling prices or revenue, with the intervention aimed at reducing the margins retained across the distribution chain.

How the ICE surge in Minnesota could impact the midterms
Minneapolis neighbours organize to protect the midterms with tactics learned during ICE operation
Chairs scrape across the floor of a small St. Paul, Minn., community centre as neighbours start to file in for "democracy defender" training offered by one of several grassroots organizations in the state.
The attendees are preparing for potential scenarios of disruption at the polls for the Nov. 3 midterms.
They learn how to form groups in their neighbourhood, divide into zones and create communication networks so they can make sure they are in contact with everyone on their street.
At several points they break into groups to discuss: What if the administration starts pushing falsehoods about voting rules? What should they do if federal officers attempt to enter the polling places?
Community groups are holding 'democracy defender' training sessions like this one in St. Paul, Minn., to train citizens how to protect the polls if there is federal interference with voting on Nov. 3 and beyond. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)
Helen Kouba says she signed up because she felt she owed it to her seven-year-old after Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration’s sprawling immigration crackdown earlier this year.
“My trust in some of the systems that I was brought up to believe in and not question has faltered and it has been really disappointing and disheartening,” she said.
It’s been roughly nine months since 3,000 federal immigration officers flooded Minnesota, arresting some 4,000 people and clashing with residents trying to slow them down.
In January, two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by federal officers just weeks apart, eventually leading to the ouster of two prominent Trump immigration officials: Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem and Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino.
The memorial to Renee Good, who was fatally shot by an ICE agent in Minneapolis in January, still draws visitors who come to pay their respects. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)
Many in Minneapolis, where the operation was centred, organized themselves into groups to respond to and observe ICE raids often by recording interactions with their phones, blowing whistles to alert others, blocking traffic to slow down Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, and by creating encrypted group chats to communicate.
Now many of those same people have signed up for training to protect the polls in a Senate race that could be pivotal.
Fears of federal overreach
The Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to assert control over aspects of voting even though elections are administered by the states.
It tried to put limits on mail-in voting, which was subsequently quashed by the Supreme Court. It has continued to sow seeds of doubt about election integrity and the statistically rare cases of non-citizens illegally casting votes. U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to rule out sending federal officers to the polls, including the FBI and ICE.
In a Minneapolis neighbourhood where ICE made several raids over the winter, Shae Alcamo drops handwritten notes to her neighbours. She stops people on the street to make sure they are registered to vote and to see if they are interested in signing up to join the grassroots effort to protect the polls.
Shae Alcamo goes door to door in her Minneapolis neighbourhood to make sure everyone is registered to vote and to enlist help to keep the vote secure on election day. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)
“Ever since Metro Surge happened, I've really been focused on how we defend ourselves from the next threat,” she said.
“It's a really hard conversation about what is possible for us when we've already seen state violence take away two members of our community.”
- Renee Good's family sues U.S. government, ICE officer and others over Minneapolis killing
- Anti-ICE protests continue in NYC after agents shoot man in car with child
Concerns about federal interference run well beyond the neighbourhoods of the Twin Cities, all the way to the office of Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon.
“I've had this job for a while, and never ever before have I had to seriously think about the prospect that our own federal government will be an instigator of something that could interfere with the freedom to vote,” said Simon, a Democrat.
“You have a very short runway, so to speak, if say the weekend before the election something happens, a new executive order or a new proclamation or declaration of some kind or deployment of federal law enforcement.”
Minnesota’s Secretary of State Steve Simon says he has never had to prepare for a scenario in which the federal government might interfere with the vote in his decade in the job. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)
Simon has been meeting with his counterparts in other states to plan for different scenarios as a precaution.
“Operation Metro Surge is still a fresh wound,” he said.
Simon said that one of the lessons Minnesota learned from Metro Surge was how effective non-violent pushback can be on what he called undue or unlawful interference in the community.
“We are ready now in a way that we might not have imagined we would have to be before Operation Metro Surge.”
Minnesota could be ‘decider’
In a midterm election where the balance of power in Congress is at stake, University of Minnesota political scientist Larry Jacobs said “Minnesota could be the decider.”
For Democrats to take control of the Senate, they’d need to win at least 17 of the 35 seats up for election this time — including several close races without incumbents, like Minnesota.
“It had been assumed that Minnesota would be safely Democratic in terms of a new senator being elected. But now we're seeing polls, and it's a toss-up,” said Jacobs.
“That's gonna be perhaps a deciding factor in whether the Democrats or Donald Trump maintain control of the U.S. Senate.”
Political scientist Larry Jacobs says Metro Surge could tip the race for Minnesota's open Senate seat toward the Democrats. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)
Former NFL sideline reporter and Republican candidate Michele Tafoya is neck-and-neck in the polls with the state’s Lieutenant Governor and Democrat Peggy Flanagan. The race has tightened, in part, Jacobs said, because of a number of damaging headlines about fraud and wasteful spending which have marred the state’s Democratic leadership.
Jacobs said many other issues have captured voters' attention in the months since Operation Metro Surge including affordability, the price of gas, and the Iran war.
But the very populations targeted by the immigration crackdown could determine the outcome of the Senate race.
“We may have a very, very close Senate race ... and the impact of Donald Trump's Metro Surge and the immigration policy in general could be just what's needed to tip the race away from the Republicans and towards the Democrats,” he said.
The Somali community in particular — targeted during Operation Metro Surge and frequently insulted by the U.S. president — typically turns out in high numbers to vote in a state which regularly has the highest voter turnout. Minnesota has the largest Somali community in the U.S.
On Thursday, Trump again resurfaced his attacks on Somali Minnesotans in a social media post saying they had taken over the state and there was “Violence Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State.” He also offered to send the federal government to the rescue.
Anti-immigrant rhetoric posted by Trump on Truth Social on Thursday. (realDonaldTrump/Truth Social)
“There's always been a number of Somalis, perhaps a third or a quarter, who had voted for the Republican Party,” Jacobs said. “But with the Metro Surge, there's been some erosion of that support for the Republicans within the Somali community and among other immigrants.”
Immigrant communities pivotal
In 2024 Salman Fiqy stood behind Trump at a rally in St. Cloud, Minn., and worked on his campaign. For nearly a decade he said he felt a natural affinity with the GOP ticket.
“Somalis are a very religious, very conservative community and that conservatism drew me to the Republican Party,” he said.
Salman Fiqy split from the Republican party when U.S. President Donald Trump called the Somali community 'garbage.' He says he is now politically homeless. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)
But all that changed in December 2025 when Operation Metro Surge began. Fiqy remembers the exact moment he broke with the party he had long supported.
“It was when Trump was sitting in his office and he called the Somali community ‘garbage’, that was the thing that broke the camel's back,” Fiqy said. “But also I'm still a conservative, but I'm disavowing my connection with the Republicans as it is right now.”
Fiqy said if the Republicans want to do better in Minnesota, a traditionally blue state, they need to make inroads with immigrant communities. He accuses the Republican party of being spineless in its reaction to Trump's comments about Somalis.
Metro Surge disrupted the work he and other conservatives had done, Fiqy said.
“It actually struck fear in our community to the point where it disrupts the daily activities of the Somali community, who are — the majority of them — are citizens,” he said.
Fiqy believes Somali Minnesotans are going to show up at the polls in full force for Flanagan in the Senate race.
"Because Somalis are typically very politically engaged and especially if they feel a threat, then they respond in the election," he said.

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Antonelli moves to brink of title
- Published
Lewis Hamilton apologised to his Ferrari team after overriding the pit wall and choosing his own strategy during the Singapore Grand Prix.
Ferrari were on course to finish second and third with Charles Leclerc and Hamilton, but instead the seven-time champion fell back to sixth in the closing laps as he fought a losing battle to hold off three cars while on fading tyres.
Hamilton apologised to the team over the radio on the slowing-down lap after the race, saying: "Sorry, boys. I let you down today with that strategy. My call, and I lost us valuable points. I'll try and make up for it in the next one."
Team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "Clearly we asked them to pit. Charles pitted. Lewis didn't want to pit because he... I don't know why. And then he realised it was the wrong call. It's why he apologised to the team.
"Now it's not a drama for me that he made the wrong call. I'm making mistakes, he's making mistakes, we're all making mistakes sometimes. Now we have to look ahead and make mistakes positively."
- Verstappen dominates for first Singapore Grand Prix win 
  - Published9 hours ago
- Verstappen perfect and Antonelli hugely mature - driver ratings 
  - Published6 hours ago
Hamilton did not speak to the media after the race after saying he felt unwell and being given permission to miss the interview zone, known as the media pen.
In a statement released by Ferrari, he said: "Under the virtual safety car, the team called me in but I missed the entry. After that, I decided to stay out and try to hold track position to the end but in the closing laps, I was struggling massively with tyre degradation and lost three places, finishing P6, which doesn't reflect the pace we had in the car.
"A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made. Not every call will work out, and I can accept getting it wrong but I'm sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend, and I wanted to deliver more for them. I'll continue to put the work in and come back fighting at the next race."
Ferrari called both cars in to the pits during a virtual safety car that was called mid-race. Stopping under the VSC saves about 10 seconds versus stopping under racing conditions.
Hamilton said in the statement that his decision was based on his improved pace on the soft-compound tyre after he had been forced to make an earlier pit stop than planned because the medium tyre on which he started the race was not performing.
"At a track [where it's] difficult to overtake, you need to try something different and I chose to start on a new medium tyre, to go long and try to make a one-stop work," he said.
"Unfortunately the medium didn't perform as well as the soft. I had a good second stint and the pace was back, but I couldn't make the progress I needed."
His first stop was six laps before Leclerc's and when the Monegasque emerged on to the track, Hamilton was right behind him and initially faster.
At one stage, he pointed out to the team that he had "lost two seconds on that lap", but the team decided not to invert the cars. Hamilton followed Leclerc within two seconds for a further 10 laps before slowly starting to lose ground a couple of laps before the VSC.
Vasseur said the team decided to leave Leclerc in front because he had pitted later than Hamilton.
"The tyre advantage was for Charles, that he pitted six laps later," Vasseur said. "I think it was the right call."
However, that argument appears to be somewhat undermined by the fact that the medium tyre emerged as the worst option for the race - as Hamilton had found out in the first stint and other drivers later discovered.
Leclerc was put back on the soft when he stopped under the VSC.
Antonelli knows title is 'very close'
Hamilton's error means Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli is in a position to clinch his first world title at the next race, the US Grand Prix in Austin, after finishing third behind race winner Max Verstappen and Leclerc.
Antonelli's lead over team-mate George Russell, who finished ninth after starting from the back of the grid, has extended to 102 points and 111 over Hamilton.
The Italian needs to leave Austin with an advantage of at least 125 points to clinch the title, with five races at most remaining after that.
He will do so if he wins the race with Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower at the Circuit of the Americas on 25 October.
If he becomes champion this year, the 20-year-old will be the youngest in Formula 1 history.
Asked if he would be daring to dream about the title on the flight home, he said: "For sure, but at the same time, I know it's very close, I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can.
"The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can.
"This weekend I haven't particularly driven that well. I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that a week to reset and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin.
"But at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that."
There is some doubt about the mathematics of the championship because it is not completely clear how many races are remaining.
F1 is pushing ahead with the original schedule, which ends with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, despite the war in the Middle East, having been reassured the countries are safe.
But if the war intensifies before mid-November, those races will have to be cancelled. In that event, the season would end at Imola in Italy, on the same 6 December date as Abu Dhabi, after a two-week break following the Las Vegas race on 22 November.
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "I haven't looked at it from that perspective, because the moment I have the thought of 'how many points is it actually, and when could he win it,' I remind myself that this is motor racing and crazy things have happened.
"The aim must be to score points, not to lose too many on the others, like today, gaining on Lewis, which was unexpected, and then it's going to come towards him, whether that's in Mexico or Brazil [immediately after Austin] or further down the line."
Mercedes 'need to go back to winning ways'
Mercedes split their cars between two different specifications in Singapore in an attempt to understand why a major upgrade introduced at the previous race in Malaysia did not work.
Antonelli drove the new spec and Russell the old, and by the end of the weekend the team said they had made some progress in understanding the new aerodynamic package.
Antonelli said: "We're just trying to understand how to extract more potential out of it because we do see the gains, we do see what it could bring.
"It's just that the window is very small at the moment where the car operates and is very sensitive to the way you drive it, the way you take a corner, the way you brake. So it reacts very differently.
"So hopefully now in Austin, we have three free practices, so we can be very open-minded with set-up and hopefully we can find a way and we can use the full potential of the package and finally see the gains."
Russell was asked how he viewed the rest of the season now the championship was almost over. He replied: "The goal is to improve the car. We were dominant for so long and since the break we have seen Red Bull be exceptionally fast on many different types of circuits and we need to go back to winning ways."
Verstappen may need 'new spine' after Austin bumps
Verstappen's victory was his first grand prix win in Singapore. It was also his second in succession, emphasising Red Bull's return to the front after a difficult start to the season.
"Very different tracks that we have gone well at now. That's of course always nice to see," said the 29-year-old.
"Our car has taken a really nice step forward. It's just been more driveable and more predictable. That's what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front. And I hope that we can carry that momentum forward.
"We don't really have anything to win in the championship, right? Kimi is miles ahead. I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth. It doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun until the end, you know, try to go for a day's success."
But the four-time champion was cautious about the prospect of being competitive at every race before the end of the season.
"It's very difficult to say and I don't want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin," he said.
"Yeah, the last few weekends have been great. But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we'll see how it will go there. But it's again a very different track.
"From what I saw in WEC (the World Endurance Championship), the track is incredibly bumpy. Oh my God, yeah, I'll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. Yeah, I'll become like Robocop. Yeah, crazy. That's again a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps.
"And then we just go from there. We have to go to Mexico, high altitude, everything will run super hot, and we need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it's very different.

“ReelShort’s the next iteration of how the younger generation in our country consume content,” said Ben Houser, head of scripted and unscripted & development for WWE. “They have really perfected the experience of a long-term narrative story and being able to consume that in bite-sized chunks. Popular on Variety
“Agent of Shadows” features established microdrama stars like Chase Mattson, Marc Herrmann, and Katherine Gibson. They are joined by WWE talent including Drew McIntyre, Jacob Fatu, Joe Hendry, Nikkita Lyons, Michael Hayes, and Booker T among others.
McIntyre in particular takes on a central role in the show, playing Roscoe, the right-hand man and tech expert to secret agent Adam Hawke (Mattson). This is the latest major acting role for McIntire, who has starred in a number of films in recent years.
In addition to his role in the 2024 action film “The Killer’s Game,” McIntyre has filmed roles in the upcoming “Highlander” reboot with Henry Cavill as well as “The Last Druid” starring Russell Crowe.
“I was actually in Barcelona filming ‘The Last Druid’ when I got the call from Ben Houser,” McIntyre said. “I’ve known him for years through the WWE. When he comes with an idea, I know it’s something good…Right from the first conversation, I was like, ‘This is something I want to be involved in.'”
And while McIntyre says he still has “many years” left in his WWE career, taking on acting roles outside the company has given him the chance to stretch himself in new ways.
“The movies that I’ve been lucky to be involved with, I’ve never wanted to be big bad guy number three,” he said. “I want something that challenges me, my ability to show my range, and this is exactly that.”
But despite the fact that he regularly performs in front of arenas full of people on live television every week, McIntyre was still nervous when he made his first movie.
“I was so nervous until I spoke to Dave Batista, who I’ve known for years, and he was like, ‘Wait till the red light goes on, and you’ll know exactly what to do,'” he said. “And sure enough, when the red light goes on, I relax, and it’s so exciting.”
Mattson, whose past microdrama credits include “Married to the Don” and “My Poor Husband Is a Billionaire,” was impressed with McIntyre from the moment he stepped on set.
“I was told ‘He’s tall and he’s big,’ and I’m like, ‘Okay, I’m tall and big.’ Then he walked on set and I thought, ‘This dude is like The Iron Giant,'” Mattson said with a laugh. “He was a really nice guy, and I think I told him, ‘You need to keep pursuing acting because you really have the the knack for it. You’ve got the natural chops.'”
Having been in the microdrama space for years now, Mattson said that watching the evolution of the genre has been an incredible experience.
“I started back when we were using iPhones, and now we’re using ARRIs and REDs,” he said. “This is a full production, like a cinema microdrama, and it’s really cool…We’re shooting 12-14 hours a day, and we’re shooting maybe 20 scenes, so we’re moving pretty quick. So everybody is very professional, and they know exactly what they’re doing.”
ReelShort’s head of talent and business development Sammie Hao said that the company saw the “shared DNA” between themselves and WWE right away. “Both types of storytelling are aery dramatic, a lot of larger than life characters, and moments that make people want to figure out what’s next,” Hao said.
Hao feels that the WWE partnership represents a milestone for ReelShort, and portends well for the future of working with other major brands.
“Like with Crocs, the first show we did for Crocs is aiming for Valentine’s Day this coming year,” she said. “So not only can we use the content to tell branded stories, we can definitely help them aim a specific campaign or season or a new product launch…And in terms of brands, I do see that it will become an alternative marketing campaign or campaign options for other brands.”
“Agent of Shadows” premieres Oct. 23.

Raphinha's brilliant Barcelona start interrupted by injury concerns
- Published
Raphinha has made a phenomenal start to the season for Barcelona, cementing his status as one of Europe's most formidable attackers.
The 29-year-old has scored 14 times and provided three assists as the Spanish champions have racked up eight successive wins in all competitions.
His performances have been so impressive that his omission from the 30-man Ballon d'Or shortlist prompted debate, with some arguing his form warranted greater recognition among the game's elite.
Yet, just as Raphinha appeared ready to take his game to another level, injury concerns have interrupted his momentum and he looks set to miss Barcelona's next two fixtures.
Facing a demanding run of fixtures, including meetings with Paris St-Germain and Real Madrid this month in the Champions League and La Liga, keeping the Brazilian fit could prove just as important as making the most of his remarkable goalscoring form.
'Was it necessary for him to play in Australia?'
Raphinha withdrew from international duty with a right thigh injury after he was substituted at half-time in Brazil's match against Australia.
"The tests show something," Barcelona boss Hansi Flick told the media.
"It's not a serious injury, but we have to be careful because he had three injuries last year, and we have to take care of him."
Flick defended Raphinha's decision to want to play for Brazil.
"It's the national team and everyone wants to play for their national team," he said. "That's Raphinha's mentality. Always give 100%."
Although the setback does not appear to be major, the timing has not been ideal.
"We must reflect on whether it was necessary for him to play in Australia, travelling so many thousands of kilometres," added Flick. "It's incredible. They have to choose friendly matches and in Europe it is not possible because of the Nations League."
With tough tests to come, Flick will want all his leading attackers available and hope even a short spell on the sidelines won't disrupt Raphinha's rhythm.
The situation has also presented Flick with a familiar dilemma. At the start of the season, there were concerns Barcelona had no established number nine after veteran Poland striker Robert Lewandowski left the club.
Raphinha has mainly been playing as a false nine this season, rather than his usual role on the wing and the team have looked unstoppable.
They sit top of La Liga, five points clear of Atletico Madrid and Real Betis, with Real Madrid a point further back in fourth place, and thrashed Feyenoord 5-1 in their Champions League opener. With 36 goals scored and eight conceded, they've been dominant at both ends of the pitch.
For now, fellow Brazilian Gabriel Jesus - a deadline-day arrival from Arsenal in September - is likely to cover Raphinha's absence for the next two matches against Getafe on Saturday and then the European trip to Galatasaray.
Flick, though, has huge depth in his Barcelona squad, and Anthony Gordon, Dani Olmo and Karim Adeyemi could all play as a false nine if necessary.
Huge impact as Barca close in on record
Raphinha's numbers tell an impressive story, but his contribution to Barcelona extends beyond the stats.
He is the team captain and has become a central figure in their aggressive, high-intensity approach, combining direct attacking play with relentless pressing and a willingness to work for the team.
His finishing has become a defining feature of his game. Rather than relying on creating chances for others, Raphinha has developed into a consistent source of goals himself and Barcelona's performances so far have reflected that influence.
The former Leeds United player has been a key factor in why Flick's side have looked so threatening in the final third and could equal the 2013-14 record for the best start to a La Liga season if they beat Getafe for an eighth straight league win.
Avoiding repeats of last season
Raphinha, though, will be determined to avoid a repeat of last season, which demonstrated how quickly fitness problems can complicate the club's plans and ambition.
He was restricted to 33 appearances, with recurring fitness issues and a hamstring injury contributing to his absences.
Raphinha played seven times in the Champions League but, crucially, was missing as his side went out in the quarter-finals with defeat by Atletico Madrid.
His tally of 21 goals helped deliver the league title and he scored twice in a standout performance in the Spanish Super Cup final against Real Madrid.
Given his importance, the temptation for Flick to rush Raphinha back will be understandable and Barca will hope this is a brief interruption rather than the beginning of another frustrating injury cycle.
