Since at least February, people have shared a meme alleging that 163 Democratic Party votes for former U.S. President Joe Biden's 2020 election victory all came from the same Oklahoma address.
The rumor touched on President Donald Trump's long-standing false claims that fraud plagued the 2020 election in battleground states. In 2021, The Associated Press investigated all of Trump's claims in six key states and found nowhere near the amount of fraud needed for Trump to have won.
In an email, a Snopes reader shared the meme, which featured an image of a modest single-level home in a rural-looking setting with a one-car garage and what appears to be a twin-size mattress leaning against the wall on the front porch.
The meme read, "Why do we need voter ID? Because in the 2020 election, 163 Democrats used this one address to cast a vote for Joe Biden." The reader asked, "Any truth to this?"
A reverse-image search found other people sharing the same meme both in Facebook posts (archived) and comments (archived), as well as on LinkedIn (archived), Reddit (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
(@250_Revolution via X)
As of this writing, we have not yet located enough evidence to conclusively debunk (or confirm) what appears to be a false rumor. We also have not yet determined who created the meme, which we found showed a house in rural Oklahoma. As such, we have not added a fact-check rating to this story.
Researching the meme and finding the house
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo found no news media outlets or political blogs reporting about 163 votes being cast for Biden using the address of the home pictured in the meme. That complete lack of reporting included conservative blogs, which would widely report on such a purported Democratic Party election fraud attempt — had it actually happened. Our searches also failed to locate evidence of users promoting the rumor prior to this year, more than five years after the 2020 election concluded.
A reverse-image search for the home pictured in the meme found real estate listings displaying a similar photo of the same house, for example on Realtor.com. The listings featured the address 401 N. Sycamore Ave. in the town of Stratford, Oklahoma, in Garvin County. The home appeared in Google Maps Street View on the east side of Sycamore.
Snopes emailed the Oklahoma State Election Board, a Garvin County elections official and the Garvin County Sheriff's Office. We presented the claim and asked whether officials were aware of any such election-related crimes occurring in relation to the home address.
We will update this article if we locate or receive any further credible information.
Trump secured more votes than Biden in every county in Oklahoma in the 2020 election, defeating Biden by a margin of more than 2-to-1. Trump also earned more than 81% of the vote in Garvin County.
For further reading, we previously reported about a rumor that Trump thanked tech billionaire Elon Musk for making every Republican vote count three times.

NAMSCON 2026, the 66th annual conference and convocation of the National Academy of Medical Sciences (India), will bring together medical professionals, researchers and academicians from across the country in Chennai from October 8 to 11.
Hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, the conference will focus on the theme ‘Synergy of Science and Technology in Healthcare for a Healthier Tomorrow’.
Tamil Nadu Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar will inaugurate the conference as the chief guest.
The four-day programme will include pre-conference workshops, symposia, keynote addresses, National CME sessions, and oral and poster presentations.
The scientific sessions will cover antimicrobial resistance, CAR-T cell therapy, biosimilars and biologics, senolytic therapies, rare genetic disorders, emerging infections, pandemic preparedness and the Indian diabetes phenotype. Discussions will also focus on medical education, robotics in surgery, organ donation and transplantation, and evolving approaches to tuberculosis management.
Eight workshops on October 8 will cover trauma care, neonatal resuscitation, AI in clinical research, spine surgery, endoscopic gastroenterology, palliative care, diagnostic reasoning, and physician entrepreneurship.
Among the speakers are Shekar C. Mande, president, Indian National Science Academy; Abhijat Sheth, Chairman, National Medical Commission; Mohan V., Chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai; Mohan Kameswaran, Managing Director and Senior Consultant, Madras ENT Research Foundation; Vivekanand Jha, Executive Director, The George Institute of Global Health, India; and Gobardhan Das, Member, NITI Aayog.
M. Srinivas, member (Health), NITI Aayog, will deliver a plenary lecture on ‘Good Governance for Transforming Medical Institutions in India and Quality Research during Residency’. He will also interact with undergraduate and postgraduate students on research during residency.
Founded in 1961, NAMS is a non-statutory body that advises the Government of India on health policy and planning. NAMSCON 2026 will be the first annual conference of NAMS to be hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre.
The conference is being organised under the leadership of R. Jayanthi, Organising Chairperson and Dean, SRM MCH&RC, and Melvin George, Organising Secretary and Head, Centre for Clinical Pharmacology and Clinical Trials Research, with Rajarajan Swaminathan as State Convenor.

UK prime minister says it's 'clear' Russia interfered in Brexit referendum
Countries across Europe are facing the same threat, Burnham says.
LONDON -- U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham says it is clear that Russia interfered with Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, adding it was important to put Moscow’s tampering on the record because countries across Europe are facing the same threat.
In excerpts from “The Rest is Politics’’ podcast released Sunday, Burnham said that when he became prime minister in July he asked his advisers whether Russia had interfered with the 2016 referendum. The full podcast is scheduled to drop on Monday.
“I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,’’ Burnham said. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Russia has long said it does not meddle in other countries’ elections or referendums.
Burnham’s comments come as U.K. intelligence agencies warn about the increasing threat of Russian interference in Britain’s democratic institutions. The intervention is believed to be the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the Brexit vote.
Burnham said he spoke to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin.
“You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe,” Burnham said. “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” he added.
Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government failed to fully assess the impact Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts could have had on the EU referendum.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?

A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.

The American Hospital Association is once again suing the Trump administration over its plan to test revamping a federal drug discount program into one that provides after-the-fact rebates instead of upfront discounts for certain drugs.
It’s the second time the powerful hospital lobbying group has sued over such a plan. The first time, in 2025, a judge agreed to temporarily halt a more limited version from taking effect, and the Health and Human Services Department voluntarily withdrew the plan after losing on appeal. In February, the agency announced an expanded version, set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, that would target 25 of the costliest, most widely used drugs covered under Medicare. The original plan included 10 drugs.
The AHA’s argument is largely the same as in the first case: the government failed to accurately account for the costs hospitals would incur by having to pay market prices for drugs and then apply for rebates. The lawsuit says that the Health Resources and Services Administration, the HHS division that administers 340B, received more than 2,400 comments on the rebate model’s second iteration, including hospitals describing in “granular detail the catastrophic impact” it would have.

AdBlock360 is a system-wide ad blocker for Windows 10 and 11 that blocks ads in browsers, YouTube, Spotify, and other apps. It also blocks trackers and supports custom filters and whitelisting. A free version is available, but app-level blocking requires premium. It does not support ARM-based Windows devices.
Ads are very common across apps and websites. Most apps and websites use a freemium business model, which has ads in the free version. This model is proven and benefits both the creator and the consumer. But a few apps cross the line and make the whole experience cluttered by aggressively pushing ads.
This is where an ad blocker can come in handy. It blocks intrusive ads on any web page or app, making the whole experience a lot cleaner and clutter-free.
Ad blockers come in many forms. The most popular ones are ad-block extensions used in browsers, but because of the changes in Google Chrome Manifest Version 3, which restrict access to some browser features for ad-blocker extensions.
Another common way of blocking ads is using an ad-blocker DNS. I personally use it on my mobile devices.
Finally, if you want to get rid of ads throughout the system, the easiest way is by installing an app.
If you use Windows, AdBlock360 for Windows can come in handy. It offers a complete solution to block all types of ads on your Windows device, whether they are in a browser or system-level apps, even ads on YouTube and Spotify, without requiring premium subscriptions. AdBlock360 blocks most ads on your Windows device. I have been using AdBlock360 for the past few days, and here are the five features that stood out during my usage.

One of the biggest advantages of using AdBlock360 is that it runs natively on Windows and blocks ads at the system level. It eliminates the need to install ad blockers for your browser separately. It uses a kernel-mode Windows Filtering Platform driver for system-wide network filtering. Because of this, it won’t have any restrictions, unlike the ones recently raised due to Chromium changes. So it works even if your browser is updated to the latest Manifest V3.
You also don’t need to install separate ad-block extensions for your browser. One ad blocker is enough for blocking all system-level ads on your Windows laptop, including ads from browsers and even on YouTube, Spotify, or any third-party or native apps that consist of ads.
Block YouTube and Spotify Ads Using AdBlock360
Not just the browser, AdBlock360 also blocks ads on YouTube, including the watch page and pre-roll ads that appear before the video. If you upgrade to the AdBlock360 premium version, it also skips the sponsor segments in a video. Not just that, this ad blocker also works for other popular platforms, including Spotify, where ads in the free version can be annoying. AdBlock360 works natively on Windows, so it can work on any app that’s installed on your Windows device.
Protect Your Privacy From Trackers and Fingerprinting
Some websites and apps aggressively track your background to serve you relevant ads. This is why, when you search on any e-commerce platform, you immediately see ads related to the product you searched for.
AdBlock360 says it blocks ad trackers at the network level; ad providers inside browsers or platforms won’t be able to fetch your ad profile data from advertising and other analytics or tracking servers to serve you ads.
This way, not only the ads but also the tracking and the data collected by these trackers will be blocked.
Choose What to Block With Custom Filters
While AdBlock360 is a convenient way to block ads across Windows, sometimes it may not block certain ads that use a different architecture or newer techniques to bypass Ad blockers, or ads on your own websites or the sites you want to support and whitelist.
AdBlock360 also offers you the option to set custom filters, so you will have complete control over which types of ads to block. We can also whitelist certain apps and websites to show you ads.
Works on Low-End PCs and Offers a Free Version
Apps like ad blocker applications generally don’t require advanced PC configurations, so it is the same for AdBlock360.
It works on both Windows 10 and Windows 11. It requires just 2 GB of RAM (although 4 GB is recommended) and only 200 MB of free space.
Low-spec Windows devices are most affected because of the ads. Sometimes they can make constant requests to the backend, which can bring a laggy experience if you have installed any apps that display ads on your Windows PC. AdBlock360 works in the background and requires a minimum amount of processing power, which can be an advantage if you want to block ads completely on your low-end Windows devices.
Not everything about AdBlock360 is bells and whistles; there are a few notable limitations to the app. First, the app is limited to Windows. If you bought a premium version, you can only use it on Windows. If you use other devices like a mobile phone, you won’t benefit from the premium subscription you bought for your Windows device.
Moreover, the AdBlock360 app is not available for ARM-based Windows laptops.
I tried to install the app on my Snapdragon X2 Elite-powered ASUS ProArt PZ14, but it showed an error stating “ARM64 devices are not compatible,” which you can see in the image below.
So, although the app is exclusive to Windows, it still requires an x86-compatible device to run this ad blocker on your Windows device.
The HTTPS filtering requires installing a root certificate. Although the process is easy, it can be limited if you have advanced security settings enabled on your Windows device.
You also require a premium version to block ads inside apps and to skip sponsored content on YouTube.
Finally, the app can also be overkill if you just want to block ads on your web browser.
A Simple Way to Block Ads Across Windows
Running ad blockers natively is extremely important today, especially at a time when popular browsers are limiting ad-blocking extensions and websites, and apps are aggressively putting more ads on their sites.
AdBlock360 is a nice solution to block different types of ads. It blocks ads in your browsers, as well as ads from native apps in the premium version, including YouTube ads and ads on third-party apps like Spotify.
With just one subscription, you get a clutter-free experience. AdBlock360 also comes with a free version, so you can try AdBlock360 out right now on your Windows device and check if it works for you.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

Sweating the details: Sauna's potential health benefits draw scientists' interest
For more on the science of healthy living, try NPR's Health newsletter.
Scientists have long marveled at how the human body tolerates extreme heat — and what that means for our health.
In the late 1700s, British scientists ran bold experiments on thermoregulation, subjecting themselves (and a dog) to a piping hot room and observing that — unlike the steak and eggs accompanying them — their own bodies did not cook.
The acute physiological response to heat is now well understood.
Faced with extreme temperatures, our blood vessels dilate, heart rate speeds up and blood is pushed to the skin where it's cooled down as we sweat. Our body releases hormones and activates heat shock proteins that protect our cells.
This understanding of our physiology has shaped medical care, for example, with heat-related illness. However, the other side of the equation — the potential therapeutic benefits of heat exposure — have received considerably less attention from modern medical science.
Meanwhile, age-old practices, such as sauna, built around stressing the body with heat are enjoying newfound popularity.
From social sauna meetups to the broader wellness and optimization movement, the level of public interest has surprised even long-time devotees like Dr. Hans Hägglund, a hematologist and stem-cell researcher at the Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm.
"It's really booming," says Hägglund, dubbed the "sauna doctor" in his home country thanks to a popular book he authored on the subject. "Unfortunately, there is still not very much evidence out there."
At least, not the caliber of studies that Hägglund and other scientists can point to if they want medical societies and government agencies to view sauna and other forms of heat therapy as a bonafide intervention — a lifestyle approach that can be recommended for preventing and treating chronic health conditions.
But Hägglund and a small group of international scientists are pushing to make this happen — and organize what's been a niche and disparate area of research.
Bringing science to the sauna
In late September, about 15 of them convened for the first time at the International Heat Therapy Research Symposium to hash out how to rigorously study heat therapy — a bucket that includes Finnish sauna, infrared, hot water immersion and more — and to form an organizing scientific body that will help steer the field forward.
The two-day gathering was held at a trendy resort outside Oslo, Norway, called The Well, where nude bathing is the norm and essential-oil-infused rituals, based on traditions like the German Aufguss, are held throughout the day. It took place on the eve of the International Sauna Congress, an event that attracts hundreds of sauna lovers and experts every four years.
Some of the symposium's organizers, like Ashley Mason, a clinical psychologist at the University of California, San Francisco, acknowledge their goal is partly to dispel the whiff of wellness hype.
"We want to introduce this as an actual field of research, not something fringy, or woo-woo," says Mason, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral science who is currently running trials on heat therapy for depression, sleep and other aspects of mental health.
While sauna has been studied on and off for decades, very little of that research comes from well-controlled human trials. And it's often hard to draw firm conclusions from what evidence does exist; the studies are small, the methods vary significantly and key measurements are sometimes missing.
"We're all over the place," Mason says. "If we want to be taken seriously, we need to have consistent terms, so that people understand how to refer to and talk about our work."
The nuances of measuring environmental humidity and body temperature, or how to best define heat therapy, may be afterthoughts to the average sauna-goer, but all of this matters enormously when pulling together data from different countries and institutions.
Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montreal Heart Institute who's spearheading the initiative, says scientists first need to agree on standards. That's a painstaking process involving dozens of other experts that will ultimately set the stage for the kind of larger, multisite trials that can get at some fundamental questions for scientists and the public.
What are the actual benefits? How often do you need to go? What are the risks? Just how hot does it need to be?
"People want information. I know 'listen to your body' doesn't cut it,'" says Lee, "but I really can't give you recommendations, and that's the honest truth of it."
Early evidence suggests benefits from sauna exposure
There are certainly reasons to believe heat – delivered as a strong stimulus in a time-limited manner — holds promise for health.
"Passive heat therapy," as it's known in the scientific literature, works the cardiovascular system in ways that are similar to light physical activity and delivers some of the same benefits, such as improvements in blood pressure, arterial stiffness and vascular health.
Some experiments also indicate improvement in markers of inflammation, though, here, as with many areas, the findings are not conclusive, says Lee.
There's particular interest in how heat can help people with cardiovascular and metabolic conditions, as well as the elderly, says Ant Shepherd, a professor of clinical environmental physiology at the University of Portsmouth in the U.K.
For example, his lab has shown spending time in a hot tub improved resting metabolic rate and some measures of insulin sensitivity for people with Type 2 diabetes.
"Exercise is king, exercise is medicine, but for those who can't do that easily, can we get some of the same effects?" he asks. "It looks like we can."
In one of the only randomized controlled trials on sauna bathing, Lee has found that adding it to an exercise regime conferred added benefits for people at risk of cardiovascular disease. He's now running a trial on patients undergoing cardiac rehabilitation.
Separately, several research groups are exploring whether heat can help treat depression, building on a landmark study that showed meaningful decreases in symptoms after one session in a special infrared machine.
"We've got lots and lots of lovely little studies," says Shepherd, "The governments aren't going to listen until we put the hardcore, randomized-control trials in front of them."
Sauna research gathers steam
The uptick in recent scientific interest largely stems from a series of observational studies done in Finland.
The first — published just over a decade ago — showed using the sauna four to seven times per week was associated with a 40% to 60% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and death, compared to those who only went once a week.
"It was a strong signal and the impetus for a lot of labs to stand up and say, 'Hey, there might be something here,'" says Lee, who earned his Ph.D. working with the research leader of the group at the University of Eastern Finland, Dr. Jari Laukkanen.
Subsequent studies suggested other benefits, like lower rates of Alzheimer's, respiratory disease and lower markers of chronic inflammation. Long-running studies from Japan have also linked regular hot tub use with lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
While promising, experts stress you can only extrapolate so much from this kind of observational data because it relies on self-reports and the results can be skewed by other factors.
"The effects are quite large, so we're fairly optimistic, but that's about as far we can go as scientists," says Shepherd.
In countries where heat practices are deeply interwoven into society — such as Finland and Japan — public funding has supported some of this research. In the U.S., the National Institutes of Health is funding Mason's work related to mental health.
The Montreal Heart Institute's Lee says this newly formed research group hopes to secure funding from public agencies in Europe, but the kind of expensive, large-scale trials that scientists dream of doing may largely rely on foundations and private funders, too.
The Oslo symposium was funded by the Norwegian Sauna Society, the wellness resort where it took place and the Sauna Research Foundation, a nonprofit backed by a Minnesota-based longevity entrepreneur and several other private funders.
While not at the gathering, Laukkanen, who has led much of the influential research on sauna in Finland, said he welcomes the effort to organize the field and look for ways to replicate their findings in other parts of the world.
The challenge with conducting the necessary studies, he notes, are the same as with other lifestyle habits like exercise or diet.
"They are really demanding," said Laukkanen, a professor of internal medicine at the University of Eastern Finland, "Pharmaceutical companies are doing this kind of study, but they have the resources. We don't have those yet."

Donald Trump has again lashed out at Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed – and again claimed not to know his name – branding him a “Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country.”
Praising the progressive’s Republican rival Mike Rogers after the pair squared off in a televised NewsNation/WOOD-TV debate Thursday, the president wrote on Truth Social: “Mike Rogers, the great American Patriot and Republican Candidate for the U.S.Senate from Michigan, completely obliterated Mohammad El-Sayed [sic] in the big debate tonight.
“If this was a fight they would have stopped it. Mohammad is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the U.S. fail.
“Short on Stature, Patriotism, and Truth, Mohammed’s statements have been loaded up with lies and deceit. I won Michigan BIG, and know that Mike Rogers, a total winner, is the man for you!!!”
Trump had also misnamed El-Sayed, who is a Muslim, in another post earlier in the day, calling him “a terrible Candidate for the Dumocrats,” as well as a “RADICAL Extremist” and “Terrorist Sympathizer.”
The candidate responded to that attack by zeroing in on the president calling him “Mohammad” or “Mohammed” interchangeably, refusing to dignify the more serious slurs with an answer.
“He knows my name is Abdul,” he wrote on X. “He says it everyday. But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us.
“He thinks so low of us. He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better. It’s time for change.”
During last night’s debate, Rogers likewise attempted to undermine El-Sayed’s credibility, claiming he was not really a doctor (he has a medical degree from Columbia University) and considered Egypt his real home, not the U.S.
“My home is Michigan. You live in Florida,” the Democrat fired back on the latter point, alluding to Rogers’ second home.
For his part, El-Sayed attempted to paint Rogers as a Trump stooge in the pocket of corporate lobbyists who would not challenge the president on the Iran war or his damaging trade spat with Canada.
Addressing the blockading of the Strait of Hormuz driving up domestic gas prices, he said: “Mike Rogers has been cheerleading the war since the beginning, calling it a win, win, win. I don’t know about you, but when I fill up my tank I don’t feel like I’m winning.”
Interviewed by Jen Psaki on MS NOW afterwards, El-Sayed attacked Trump again over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December will be livestreamed.
“Under Trump and Hegseth, you’re seeing extremes that you never would have imagined,” he said. “The idea that you want to livestream somebody’s death for children to watch is truly extreme... I don’t want that to be politics as usual."
The president’s repeated slights on El-Sayed as a Muslim and “Communist” – which began as soon as he beat centrist state representative Haley Stevens in his party’s primary – echo his efforts to deride Zohran Mamdani last year before the latter won the New York City mayoral race and unexpectedly found himself in Trump’s good graces.
El-Sayed has given as good as he’s gotten, however, mocking the president over his close relationship with his executive assistant Natalie Harp and referring sarcastically to Vice President JD Vance’s “Ohio charisma” after the latter said his candidacy appealed only to “self-hating white liberals.”
The former public health official’s two-fisted approach has even won him admirers on the right, with Fox News host Jesse Watters and pundit Tucker Carlson both admitting to having a soft spot for him.

To strengthen campus mental health support and facilitate timely referrals for students in distress, NIMHANS-Bengaluru will launch an online certificate course for Student Wellbeing Ambassadors in higher education institutions.
To be launched on the occasion of World Mental Health Day on October 10, the self-paced course will be offered through the NIMHANS Digital Academy by the institute’s Department of Clinical Psychology. The first batch will accommodate up to 350 participants, with applications open until October 30. Classes are scheduled to begin in November.
To be nominated by institutions
The course is open to faculty members from any discipline, wardens, deans, and student welfare officers who have at least three years of service remaining, and are nominated by their institutions.
Participants will learn to recognise signs of student distress, respond supportively, reduce stigma around mental health, and encourage students to seek appropriate help. The programme is also intended to strengthen suicide-risk reduction efforts.
The three-month course will involve 12 to 15 hours of learning through videos, quizzes, assignments, reflective exercises, and reading materials.
NIMHANS clarified that the course is not professional training in counselling, psychology, or psychotherapy. Instead, it will help faculty understand the role and limits of a well-being ambassador, and work within existing student support and crisis-response systems.
The initiative is among the steps towards implementing Karnataka’s student mental health policy for higher education. NIMHANS is also developing a follow-up programme to help trained faculty apply the learning in their institutions.
Course details and online application forms are available on the NIMHANS website and the NIMHANS Digital Academy website under Course Announcements.

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
From surveillance and DOGE to Big Tech money and religious extremism, the midterms have never been more WIRED. Data centers are no exception: The public has rapidly turned on them since the beginning of the year.
The opposition is bipartisan, with many Republicans making a rare break from President Donald Trump. Candidates on both sides of the aisle are trying to attack their opponents for being pro–data center (or not anti–data center enough). I’ve spotted at least five candidates who have been given the derogatory “Data Center [Name]” moniker by their opponents, in an attempt to highlight their connections to the industry. (That includes two guys named Derek/Derrick getting this treatment.)
While polling shows that pocketbook issues are likely to be top of voters’ minds, data centers are a potent-enough issue that they could swing tight races—and ultimately tip the balance of power in Congress. Here are some of the races WIRED is keeping an eye on as we approach November 3.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that Democrat Sherrod Brown, running for Senate in Ohio, was hitting his opponent, Senator Jon Husted, so hard on data centers that it could tip the outcome of the race, calling it “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Brown has called Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio,” running ads that blame Husted for welcoming data centers to the state and driving energy bills up.
Senate Democrats have taken up Brown’s cause, torpedoing a bill sponsored by Husted and modeled after the White House’s ratepayer protection pledge, with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling the bill “toothless.”
Data centers have also seeped into many other toss-up Senate races, including in Michigan, Iowa, and Texas. But the Ohio race is still the top one to watch here.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, and data centers have become flash points in dozens of races across the country. Among races labeled toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, I found numerous examples of candidates running data-center-related ads:
- In Michigan’s 7th district, Will Lawrence used local opposition to data centers to help win a tough Democratic primary. Lawrence is now facing off against Republican Tom Barrett and has aired several data-center-related ads, both attacking Barrett and advertising Lawrence’s promise to “stand up to corporate power.”
- In Pennsylvania’s 8th district, Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan has run ads promising to be tough on the industry—despite holding data-center-related stocks and a previously friendly stance. His Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, has also run ads attacking the industry.
- In Ohio’s 9th, Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur has run ads railing against what she says is incumbent Derek Merrin’s history of giving tax breaks to data centers. (The ads call him “Data Center Derek.”) Merrin claims that Kaptur is misrepresenting his vote on a broader bill.
- In Wisconsin’s 3rd district, Democrat Rebecca Cooke has aired attack ads against incumbent Derrick van Orden’s history of taking contributions from data center developers, dubbing him “DC Derrick.” (Sound familiar?) Van Orden has also shot back by highlighting Cooke’s ties to the tech industry, claiming she is “responsible for covering up pristine Wisconsin farmland” with data centers.
- In New York’s 17th district, incumbent Republican Mike Lawler has aired an ad slamming Democratic opponent Cait Conley’s past statements that the Hudson Valley “needs” data centers.
At least 20 candidates in the 36 gubernatorial races have promised to enact some kind of data center moratorium if elected, according to research from Multistate. The only true hyperscale moratorium in place in the US right now was signed in July by New York governor Kathy Hochul, who holds a comfortable lead ahead of challenger Bruce Blakeman (who supports data center development).
Candidates without much daylight between them have still tried to gain the upper hand on the issue. In Wisconsin’s tight gubernatorial race, Republican Tom Tiffany has attacked Democrat David Crowley with ads calling him “Data Center David.” Both candidates say they support restrictions on the industry.
In states that have been hotbeds for data center activity, some candidates in tight races have been forced to pivot on the issue. Nowhere is this clearer than in Texas, where incumbent governor Greg Abbott has gone from welcoming data center development to putting a de facto moratorium on permits in less than a year. His opponent, Gina Hinojosa, says Abbott hasn’t gone far enough to regulate the industry.
Voters in eight states are looking at more than 30 local ballot measures around data centers. Once again, Ohio is a standout here: It’s responsible for more than half of those measures, from local moratoriums to referendums around rezoning.
What We’re Writing
WIRED science editor Brian Kahn and I got exclusive access to a startup that wants to pull water from the air using excess heat from data centers. While atmospheric water-harvesting technology has been around for a while, the startup has a unique spin. Atoco uses materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs, which won one of its founders the Nobel Prize last year. The company’s previous prototypes have all needed to be hooked up to the grid to generate enough heat to extract water from the MOFs. The new version, though, only needs waste heat from industrial facilities—like data centers—to produce water, even in arid areas.

Zetwerk has set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO, targeting a post-issue valuation of ₹25,583 Cr (about $2.7 Bn) at the upper end.

B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk has set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its IPO, which will be worth ₹5,012.3 Cr at the upper end of the band.
The issue comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end, according to its RHP.
The IPO will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. Anchor investor bidding will take place on October 14.
At the upper end of the price band, Zetwerk is seeking a post-issue market capitalisation of around ₹25,583 Cr (about $2.7 Bn). The company has increased the fresh issue from ₹2,600 Cr outlined in its UDRHP. The OFS has also grown 49.2% from about 9.7 Cr shares.
Promoters and cofounders Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan will each sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other selling shareholders include promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Kae Capital.
Zetwerk plans to use ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue to repay or prepay borrowings of the company and certain subsidiaries. The remaining net proceeds will fund acquisitions and general corporate purposes.
Zetwerk filed its draft IPO papers confidentially in March, followed by itsUDRHP in August.

An Oct. 2 video shows Trump fielding reporters' questions outside the White House. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy asked, "What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?" (James, New York's attorney general, previously led a civil fraud case against Trump.) Trump thrice called James corrupt, saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes and alleged that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
A rumor circulated online in early October that U.S. President Donald Trump said he feels "badly" for the seven current or former male Cornell University students whom a female former student accused of rape.
Trump purportedly made the remarks while answering a question about New York Attorney General Letitia James' appointment as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
Snopes readers asked about this claim via email, with one person inquiring, "I saw something that says Donald Trump said he feels bad for the 'Cornell 7,' but can't find reputable sources. True??"
In sum, people correctly attributed this statement to Trump. A C-SPAN video shows Trump standing outside the White House on Oct. 2 and responding directly to a reporter's question about the Cornell case, thrice calling James corrupt and saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes, alleging that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
James previously sued Trump and his associates in a civil fraud case beginning in 2022, leading to Trump repeatedly targeting her on social media.
In an emailed response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis referred us to Trump's own comments, adding that the White House believes James has weaponized the justice system to unjustly target the president.
Digging into the rumor
The Cornell accuser, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, claims the seven men sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She filed a lawsuit against the seven men, the university, the fraternity and others, in mid-September.
On Sept. 28, Tompkins County, New York, prosecutors announced they were reopening the criminal investigation, citing a "discrepancy" between Doe's original statement and the allegations in the lawsuit.
Prior to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case on Oct. 1, James posted a statement of compassion for Doe on her official social media accounts, writing, "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
In an example of the claim from Oct. 2, a Facebook post (archived) displayed a meme reading, "This is disgusting: Trump just said he 'feels badly' for the people accused in the Cornell rape case because Letitia James is now overseeing the investigation. Not one word for the victim."
(Really American via Facebook)
Other users shared the rumor about Trump's remarks on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Some posts didn't mention James but did include a video showing a reporter's question about James and Trump's answer. Examples of those posts appeared on Bluesky (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The remarks occurred when Trump spoke to a group of reporters outside the White House. Videos show Fox News' Peter Doocy asking Trump about Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor:
DOOCY: What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?
TRUMP: Letitia James is a corrupt person. She's totally corrupt and I can't imagine it. And, I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. But Letitia James is a corrupt person.
C-SPAN posted remarks on social media. (Readers can also watch the full press gaggle on YouTube, with the pertinent moment beginning at 6:24.)
Trump has made other remarks about the Cornell case. During a similar gathering of reporters on Oct. 1, a video shows an unidentified reporter asking Trump, "Mr. President, do you think that Cornell University has done enough to investigate the alleged rape on campus?" Trump answered, "Well, I don't know that much about it but Cornell is a fine school, and I'm sure they'll do what's right." (Readers can watch that full gaggle on YouTube, with the Cornell question occurring at 11:43.)
Trump has also posted about the case on Truth Social (archived), labeling it "the highly controversial Cornell University rape case" and questioning why Hochul would appoint James.
For further reading, we previously reported Trump authentically expressed well wishes to Ghislaine Maxwell, the close associate of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, prior to her conviction on federal sex-trafficking charges.

This is a sponsored story, created and edited exclusively by Tokyo Metropolitan Government’s Tokyo Updates website.
As concerns over climate change and rising temperatures grow, finding practical solutions for keeping people safe and comfortable is becoming a major challenge for cities around the world. United States-based startup Eztia Materials has developed HydraVolt, a next-generation cooling material aimed at people working in extreme heat sectors, such as construction, logistics, and defense. Eztia CEO Tiffany Yeh discusses the story behind this innovation and its potential across a wide range of applications.
How innovation materialized
Yeh was among the participants at SusHi Tech Tokyo 2026, Asia’s largest global innovation conference held at Tokyo Big Sight from April 27-29, where she was selected as a finalist for the SusHi Tech Challenge 2026 pitch contest.
HydraVolt is printed on or sewn into garments and is designed to lower skin temperature through evaporative cooling by up to 10 degrees Celsius, for as long as 8 hours. Requiring neither electricity nor batteries, the material is recharged through exposure to water and can be laundered like regular clothing. The roots of this innovative technology go back to Yeh’s student days, when she began exploring wearable cooling materials as a passion project.
Yeh was born and raised in Taiwan but has been based in the USA since the age of 17. After majoring in materials science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, she went on to earn a medical degree from the University of Pennsylvania. The accomplished scholar also spent time overseas for fieldwork in Asia, Africa and Latin America — some of the world’s hottest locations.
Her experiences abroad sparked Yeh’s interest in investigating the cooling polymers used to regulate temperatures in buildings and vaccine packaging. Her research inspired the polymer designs she developed as a side project while studying medicine.
“After medical school, I wanted to take those designs and turn them into an actual technology, and that’s what led to Eztia,” she explains. “I never expected to return to materials science after my medical degree, but now my work has become a mix of both fields.”
Yeh feels fortunate to have had a wide range of opportunities that resulted in her exploration of cooling solutions. “If you care deeply about something, then you should pursue it because you’re well equipped to do so,” she says. “I think it was precisely all of those different paths and experiences that put me in a good position to tackle this particular area of materials science.”
Building early momentum in Tokyo
With what Yeh terms “worker safety” as its core market, Eztia aims to provide cooling solutions through various approaches. “I think worker safety is very important because it touches multiple layers of society,” she points out. “So, the broader vision is that we can eventually adapt this technology in different ways to serve a wide range of needs across society.”
Japan — and Tokyo in particular — has special significance in the Eztia story. The company’s first partner was Kajima Corporation, which utilized the cooling material at a construction site in Tokyo. Kajima already had a strong grasp of heat relief measures, and the construction firm played a key role in helping refine HydraVolt designs over time.
“We went from a cooling patch, to a shirt with cooling pockets, to now directly printing our cooling material onto garments,” says Yeh. She appreciates the effort Kajima put into compiling reports and sharing data with her team, which she says is indicative of the high level of care and consideration shown by Japanese partners in general.
Eztia also works with customers in the USA and Singapore, including an American construction firm and the Singaporean government, which is using HydraVolt for police and corrections officers. In this way, this sustainable cooling technology is now being applied across both the commercial and public safety sectors.
Technology with social impact
One of Eztia’s investors is Scrum Ventures, a venture capital fund with bases in both the United States and Japan. It has helped Yeh’s company to conduct trials with a variety of demographics through an accelerator program in Hokkaido.
These activities included successful test results with cooling headwear for elementary school children, shirts and headbands with the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters professional baseball team, and arm covers for drivers at Yamato Holdings Co., Ltd., a logistics and parcel delivery company. The results suggest strong potential for the technology to be scaled and incorporated into daily life.
Amid rising concerns over global warming and increasing temperatures, HydraVolt’s technology could contribute to improving resilience in cities such as Tokyo by offering new solutions for coping with heatstroke. It may prove to be a game changer for public safety, supporting first responders such as healthcare workers in the field or staff managing outdoor events.
Eztia is having a positive impact in other ways, too. Yeh is proud of how the firm’s production base in Taiwan proactively employs women, international students and people who entered the workforce through trade schools rather than universities.
“I think it’s all about offering opportunities to people from different backgrounds who may have historically been overlooked, but who are talented and work very hard,” she notes. “It’s about giving them the opportunity to grow and to shine.”
A blueprint for global expansion
Yeh’s first experience at SusHi Tech Tokyo 2026 has been highly rewarding. “We don’t conduct traditional outbound marketing, but rather connect with collaborators and clients by word of mouth, so having a platform like SusHi Tech Tokyo to help grow our network has been very valuable,” she says.
In addition to being selected as a finalist for the SusHi Tech Challenge 2026, Yeh also participated as a speaker, with a session entitled “Transforming Regions into Innovation Platforms: From Demonstration Fields to Co-Creation Ecosystems.” Drawing on a land and expand strategy, she says that Eztia first proves the value of its products with an initial partner, who then provides detailed feedback so the technology can be improved in a collaborative way.
“If that’s done well, the network effects come in because others will hear about it and this produces a certain virality, where other people in the region then jump on board,” Yeh explains. “So, I think that’s where co-creation and winning a region go hand in hand.” Such initiatives can then serve as case studies or success stories that can be shared with other regions.
Looking ahead, Yeh describes the company’s approach as “two-pronged“: expanding partnerships to demonstrate the broadly applicable nature of the technology, while also deepening collaboration within each organization to scale implementation across multiple sites.
As dealing with extreme temperatures becomes an increasingly urgent global issue, Eztia’s momentum appears to be heating up at just the right time.

Jammu, Oct 12: At least four residents of Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) were killed in a suspected improvised explosive device (IED) blast across the Line of Control (LoC), adjacent to the Krishna Ghati sector in Poonch district, on Monday, prompting heightened security on the Indian side, officials said.
The powerful blast reportedly occurred in Satwal-Naki area of Hajira tehsil of PoJK, when a group of people were reportedly laying water pipes along the Pakistan side of the LoC, officials said.
Citing preliminary information received from across the border, officials said the deceased were identified as Faizan Sagheer, Ishtiaq, Waqas Sharief, and Asim Rafiq of Battal Mandhol village of PoJK. The deceased were reportedly cousins.
Officials said the circumstances leading to the blast are yet to be established, but it is suspected that an IED could have been triggered, leading to the explosion.
The involvement of any of the deceased in terror activities was not known immediately, officials said.
Following the explosion, security forces sounded an alert across the sector and intensified vigilance along the LoC to assess the situation and prevent any possible security breach, officials said.
In a separate development, Indian Army troops on Monday detected two rusted landmines near the border fence in Basoni area of Mendhar sector.
The landmines were spotted during track construction at 8.25 am and 12.10 pm, officials said, adding both explosive devices were later destroyed by Army experts in a controlled explosion.
Around a dozen landmines were detected and defused by the Army in the area during the past one week.
The forward areas along the LoC are dotted with landmines as part of an anti-infiltration system. However, heavy rainfall can sometimes wash away the mines, causing them to surface in areas where they may pose a potential risk.

ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work
ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.
"At this point, we're recommending that teens don't use it," says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.
In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.
"ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience," Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.
"The model should not role-play with a teen," added Jonas. "The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen."
But Siegel's team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don't.
The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.
"We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations," says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.
Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.
Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.
"It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play," he says. "The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it."
For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen's weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.
However, most other safeguards didn't work, adds Siegel.
For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that "my other friends tell me I talk to you too much," the chatbot validated the user's feelings and added: "You don't have to stop talking to me."
"It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions," says Siegel.
"The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful," says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn't involved in the new research. "It's not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well."
Siegel says parental notifications also didn't work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.
"This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us," he says.
OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media "didn't wait long enough to activate the linked accounts."
In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI's criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period "and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations."
Taken together, the new findings reinforce that "AI is not ready for children yet," says Prinstein. "I think we're even hearing the companies say that they don't feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we're experimenting on kids with these new platforms."

The do’s, don’ts and pitfalls when applying for permanent residency in Japan
The Tokyo Immigration Bureau in Shinagawa Ward. Under updated guidelines from the Immigration Services Agency that took effect on Oct. 1, officials are enforcing stricter household income benchmarks for those seeking to qualify for permanent residency, along with deeper audits of pension and social insurance history.
| Johan Brooks
Securing permanent residency in Japan just got a lot harder.
Long a golden ticket for a stable, open-ended stay and broad employment freedom, permanent residency has transformed from a predictable administrative milestone into a far more demanding process.
Under updated guidelines from the Immigration Services Agency (ISA) that took effect Oct. 1, officials are enforcing stricter household income benchmarks and deeper audits of pension and social insurance history, with mandatory Japanese language requirements set to follow under upcoming phases. In a particularly disruptive move, the revised standards are also being applied to applications filed as far back as April this year.

Saudi Arabia goes on alert, ex-aide testifies in Netanyahu trial, and other Mideast developments
Israel's former attorney general has testified in Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial
Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand Sunday in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country's longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance, with national elections just weeks away.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, was on high alert after a deadly attack on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, allegedly by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.
Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand Sunday in Netanyahu's long-running corruption trial.
Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister.
Netanyahu was seated in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022.
“The truth comes to light,” Netanyahu said before entering the courtroom.
Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing.
The latest proceedings come weeks before national elections.
Saudi Arabia kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online on Sunday after a deadly strike by Yemen’s Houthi rebels the day before.
The rebels threatened new airstrikes across the kingdom after a missile attack on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 on Saturday. The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for that, but claimed two previous deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport earlier in the week.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously.”
The airport strike marked a major escalation in the war between the Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom, and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.
U.S. President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to join Saudi strikes against the rebels, a scenario that could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through a crucial waterway and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.
Residents in central Gaza returned home Sunday morning to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the buildings the day before.
Bassam Abed said that at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble. He said families were not given enough time to flee before the military struck their buildings.
“Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes,” Abed said.
The Israeli military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including three weapons storage facilities, a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to carry out attacks on Israeli soldiers.
The strikes fell one year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, but Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes.
The White House has officially lifted a decades-old ban on direct flight between the U.S. and Lebanon, following through on a commitment President Donald Trump made in July.
U.S. carriers may be reticent to begin offering flight to Lebanon soon, however, as the war with Iran continues to disrupts air traffic in the region and questions over Hezbollah’s influence in parts of the country persist. Direct flights between the two countries were suspended in 1985 by the Reagan administration after the hijacking of TWA Flight 847.
The Lebanese embassy in Washington said on social media that it welcomed the move as “a major step toward resuming direct flights.”
The U.S. embassy in Beirut said the change would make it easier for family members to visit one another and for American businesses to invest in Lebanon. “We look forward to working with our Lebanese partners to turn this opportunity into a reality,” the statement added.
