A vote on a partnership between the National Rugby League (NRL) and Super League is close; it is understood the NRL would want to increase Super League to 15 teams and add London Broncos into the competition for 2027
Monday 12 October 2026 16:44, UK
Leeds Rhinos, St Helens, Hull KR and Hull FC have released statements in favour of the NRL's investment in Super League after Leigh Leopards owner Derek Beaumont came out against the deal on social media.
Talks have been ongoing for months regarding the Australian competition's potential future involvement in Super League to bring alignment between the top two rugby league competitions in the world.
As a requirement of the deal, it is understood the NRL would want London Broncos added to the top flight as the 15th team from the 2027 season onwards which has been a potential sticking point for some clubs, with Leigh Leopards owner Derek Beaumont taking to social media to say he is against the deal because of that particular point.
Beaumont said it is "just not right to put London in Super League".
The Leigh owner's particular grievance is that London finished 16th in the gradings, outside of the automatic Super League spots.
Not only that, if they were to be added to Super League, he would want a similar process to take place to the one that saw Toulouse Olympique and York Knights elevated in 2026. Their applications went through an independent panel.
However, other clubs see the partnership as a "landmark" and "defining" moment for the sport.
A deadline for the deal to go through is reportedly at the end of this week at which clubs will vote on whether they want the partnership to take place.
Beaumont said on Sunday that he would vote against the deal. Since then, Leeds, St Helens and both Hull clubs have released statements to confirm they are in favour of the partnership, the two Hull teams releasing a symbolic joint statement in a show of solidarity between the city rivals.
Leeds owner Paul Caddick said "Leeds Rhinos and the Caddick Group give their wholehearted support to a working arrangement between the Super League and NRL and I believe this will be a gamechanger for the sport in this country".
St Helens then followed to say they "reaffirm their long-standing support for a strategic partnership as part of an exciting plan to globalise the sport".
The joint statement between Hull KR and Hull FC then followed, in which they "confirmed their united support for a proposed strategic partnership between Super League and Australia's National Rugby League, in what could represent a defining moment for the future of rugby league in the northern hemisphere".

For close to two years, Bhavish Aggarwal has been stuck between a rock and a hard place. All to keep Ola Electric and his other ventures going without giving up control of the company he built. Between November 2024 and March 2025, Aggarwal pledged Ola Electric shares to raise debt for Krutrim Data Centre, the AI infrastructure and services company that he founded in 2023. Then in December 2025, he sold part of his stake in Ola Electric to repay the ₹260 Cr loan that covered the pledge and release the encumbered shares, selling 3.93% of his holding in the company. At the time, Ola Electric said repaying the loan meant the company should operate with zero pledge overhang. But ten months later, another pledge is here. On 30 September, Aggarwal pledged 20 Cr Ola Electric shares, or 4.32% of the company, against non-convertible debentures (NCDs) issued by Krutrim Data Centre. CTL Trusteeship holds the pledge on behalf of the debenture holders. Neither the filings nor Ola have disclosed how much Krutrim Data Centre is raising through these debentures. What is clear is that this is a bigger pledge than before — 20 Cr shares (4.32%) against 17.3 Cr shares (3.93%) that secured a ₹260 Cr loan in the previous instance. Ola Electric said that the pledge is solely meant to fund his subscription to the company's upcoming ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, and that no shares are being sold, and that Aggarwal will invest on the same terms as every other shareholder Shriram Subramanian, founder of advisory firm InGovern Research, said that the EV firm scores poorly on what investors call the "say-do" ratio: how often a company does what it says. The situation around the pledges highlights this. He added that investors will read a founder pledging, clearing and pledging again as a sign of stress for the promoter or the promoter's group entities, "and that may not be a good sign." Especially after Ola raised ₹780 Cr through a qualified institutional placement (QIP) in June 2026. Four months later, it is asking shareholders for more. Ola Electric’s Cash Problem One thing we need to point out: Ola Electric’s rights issue is coming on the heels of the improved operating metrics. Market share rose from 5.1% in Q4 FY26 to 8.4% in Q1 FY27, but short of the 15–20% it targeted for 2026. But in the same quarter, rival Ather delivered 83,173 scooters, more than twice Ola's 39,192, while posting a lower loss. Ola's dealership rollout is still under way, and its gigafactory has not yet reached its 6 GWh target. Both are drags on its bottom line. In Q1 FY27, Ola Electric reported revenue of ₹455 Cr, down 45% from a year earlier and below its own guidance of ₹500–550 Cr. Its net loss narrowed to ₹336 Cr, the lowest in seven quarters, but free cash flow was still negative at about ₹351 Cr. At that rate, the ₹780 Cr raised in June covers roughly two quarters of cash burn. The rights issue, approved by the board on 28 September, would add up to ₹1,000 Cr. According to the draft letter of offer, about ₹350 Cr will go towards repaying or prepaying borrowings and ₹400 Cr towards organic growth. Of the money earmarked so far, nearly half goes to paying down debt. These are partly paid shares, which means investors pay in installments. The issue price, entitlement ratio and payment schedule are yet to be announced. The Idea Behind Pledging Instead Of Selling A rights issue is offered only to existing shareholders, in proportion to what they already own. Aggarwal still holds roughly 26.2% of Ola Electric shareholding. If he sits out this rights issue and does not buy in, his stake and therefore his control will shrink. According to the legal experts we spoke to, Agarwal also cannot simply borrow debt from Ola Electric. Section 67(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 bars a public company from giving financial assistance, directly or indirectly, through a loan, guarantee or security, for anyone to buy or subscribe to its own shares. Selling shares to invest in the rights issue would be counterproductive to Aggarwal’s goal of maintaining his stake in the company, so pledging shares is the only option on the table The money comes through Krutrim Data Centre, which, as a company, can issue debentures in a way an individual cannot. Aggarwal has used this route before, with the same company and the same kind of pledge. What has changed since is his priority. In December, he faced a similar choice and went the other way. With the stock near a record low at that time and his pledged shares closer to a margin call, he sold part of his stake to repay the loan and release the pledged shares. A margin call on pledged shares would have meant that Aggarwal would have had to deposit funds or securities to cover for the dropping market value of the pledged collateral. Aggarwal avoided this eventuality by selling a portion of his stake in December 2025, but now he is looking at pledging shares to protect his stake. For now at least, it would seem that retaining his control on Ola Electric matters more than any overhang from the pledge. The Krutrim Link The current shares pledged by Agarwal aim to secure debt on behalf of Krutrim Data Centre. That also puts a private company's balance sheet directly behind a listed company's shares. If, for instance, Krutrim Data Centre struggles to repay these NCDs, the pledged Ola Electric shares are exposed, and could be sold by the lender group, even if Ola Electric has recovered financially. InGovern Research’s Subramanian said that if Krutrim's debt goes bad and the lender enforces the pledge, it could sell the shares, which would weigh on the stock. He called this an extreme scenario, but said the risk alone is an overhang: public investors will keep watching whether Krutrim is able to pay back the debt. But the lender has to give reasonable notice, sell, and return any surplus, and Aggarwal can redeem the shares until then. It is also not clear how the money raised by Krutrim reaches Agarwal, whether as a loan, an advance or in some other form, or whether all of it is meant for the rights issue. That route of funds transfer from Krutrim to Agarwal also matters, according to VPS Law Associates’s VP Singh. He says that under Section 185 of the Companies Act, a straight loan from Krutrim to Agarwal is not applicable, however it could be a likely scenario of Krutrim repaying some loan it already owes to Agarwal or Krutrim directly subscribing to Ola Electric rights issue through entitlements Aggarwal renounces in its favour. For Ola Electric itself, this would not be a related-party question. “A transaction only between Krutrim and Aggarwal does not automatically become an Ola Electric related-party transaction. That will kick in when Ola Electric or its subsidiaries deal with a related party,” Singh added. In the scenario that the lenders decided to enforce the pledge, Ola Electric’s board would have no say. "The shares are the promoter's property and freely transferable; the company's obligation is only confined to disclosure," Singh said. Can Falling Stock Trigger A Crisis? A pledge is a loan secured by shares, and the value of that security moves with the stock price. That is exactly what makes it a double-edged arrangement. At around ₹37 a share, the 20 Cr pledged shares by Agarwal are worth roughly ₹740 Cr. Brokerages like Citi have set a target price of ₹26 for the next 12 months, indicating that investors should sell. Lenders in a pledge arrangement typically respond to a price fall by asking the borrower to pledge more shares. If the promoter cannot provide them, lenders can sell the pledged shares in the market. That is likely to result in a runaway effect where the price is pushed down further, triggering the call for more shares or more funds to cover the pledge. Subramanian elaborated, but he stressed that this is an extreme scenario. “If Ola's stock keeps falling, the value of the pledged shares drops against the margin the lender requires. So more and more shares would have to be pledged. Either the promoter pledges more shares to hold the margin, or investors sell their shares to recover some money, which adds to the downward spiral,” Ola Electric's investors have already seen a version of this. When Aggarwal sold shares in December to clear his earlier pledge, the stock fell 11% in two days and came close to its record low. Ola Electric's stock has fallen about 30% over the past year and trades at less than half its IPO price of ₹76. While legally, there is no law that bars Agarwal from pledging the shares in a listed firm to secure debt for his private company, the cost he and Ola Electric pay is of credibility. The share entitlements to key shareholders and the schedule of funds payments will all be keenly watched out for. After that, the question is purely operational in nature. Ola needs to bring its quarterly cash burn down before the money from the QIP and the rights issue runs out. If Ola Electric needs to raise money again, Agarwal will face the same choice between selling and borrowing, and the cycle will begin anew. Microsoft's president says AI is less regulated than a carton of milk
Brad Smith said the lack of US action gives the UK a unique opening to lead in terms of regulating AI.
Milk can't hack companies and governments like AI definitely can, but it's still subject to more regulation, Microsoft president Brad Smith told ITV on Friday. "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI," Smith said in the interview. "Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."
Major US AI giants like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google's DeepMind have spoken in favor of an AI development slowdown. However, US President Donald Trump has said that, if anything, the US AI industry needs to accelerate to stay ahead of China.
Rather than government, Trump would prefer that AI companies regulate themselves. At his so-called Super Intelligence summit, AI bosses including Google Sundar Pichai, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Elon Musk and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang signed a pact with several key tenets. Those include implementing self-regulation, safeguards to keep pioneer models from going rogue and using "independent auditors" to assess models.
Critics were unimpressed, though, with one telling the BBC that it allows firms to "define what counts as safety" and another saying that "the accord should be ignored for the distraction it is."
Microsoft's Smith thinks the lack of US action gives the UK a unique opening to lead in terms of regulating AI. "In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels — that's a strength," he said. "I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country. [W]hen you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk, I would say: the moment has arrived."

Propagate Content, the production and talent powerhouse founded by Ben Silverman and Howard T. Owens, and The Natural Studios have launched “Adventure Garage With Bear Grylls,” an eight-episode adventure series featuring survivalist Bear Grylls and “Top Gear’s” Rutledge Wood.
In the new series, Grylls and Wood transform ordinary vehicles into extreme adventure machines, then push them to their limits in wild and unpredictable missions across some of the world’s most rugged terrain.
The series is produced by The Natural Studios (a Banijay joint venture), Banijay’s Workerbee, Sovereign’s Capital and Tablehouse.
Popular on Variety
Ben Simms serves as showrunner and executive producer, with Liz Schulze as executive producer. Executive producers include Grylls, Delbert Shoopman and Ben Simon.
Propagate is bringing the series to market. The company’s track record of unscripted hits includes Food Network’s “Chopped” franchise and Netflix’s Emmy-nominated “Untold” franchise.
The show reunites Propagate with Grylls following the success of “Running Wild With Bear Grylls,” the long-running adventure series where Grylls took celebrities on supervised wilderness expeditions. The series has run for multiple seasons across NBC, National Geographic and Fox.
Grylls is represented by UTA.

Salman Khan is set to return to the coffee couch. The actor will be the very first guest of Koffee With Karan Season 9, the ninth and final season of Karan Johar's long-running celebrity chat show. JioHotstar unveiled a teaser-promo on Monday, 12 October, confirming the news ahead of the premiere.
Salman Khan to feature as the first guest at Koffee With Karan 9 premiere; watch promo
The promo shows Salman in his signature candid style, announcing his return to the show himself. His appearance sets the tone for a season that is being billed as a farewell run.
This will not be Salman's first time on the show. He has previously delivered some of its most talked-about and viral moments. He opened Season 4, and he was part of the milestone 100th episode in Season 5, which he shared with his brothers Arbaaz Khan and Sohail Khan.
View this post on Instagram
The announcement follows Karan Johar's confirmation, on Instagram a few days ago, that the show is drawing its final curtain. The filmmaker-host said that the ninth edition will mark the definitive conclusion of the franchise.
Since its debut in 2004, Koffee With Karan has run for eight seasons and 161 episodes over a 22-year span. In that time, it became a significant part of pop-culture commentary and celebrity discourse in Indian entertainment. The show hosted many of the biggest names in Indian cinema, offering a mix of unfiltered debates, playful rivalries, romance confirmations and personal revelations that often made national headlines.
With the series set to end, the farewell season aims to go out on a high note, and the makers have chosen one of the show's most recognisable guests to start it. Koffee With Karan Season 9 will premiere exclusively on JioHotstar on October 14, 2026, with Salman in the hot seat.

Missing Australian hiker found dead weeks after embarking on solo trekking trip in Peru
Jordan Yap from Melbourne was preparing for a 120km hike through remote Huayhuash mountain range when he last contacted friends and relatives on 14 September

An Australian man who disappeared while trekking alone in Peru’s Andes has been found dead, his family and friends have confirmed, weeks after he was last heard from.
Jordan Yap, 30, was preparing for a 120km hike through the remote Huayhuash mountain range when he last contacted friends and relatives on 14 September.
The trek, in the Peruvian Andes about 400km northeast of Lima, was expected to take 10 days.
His disappearance prompted a search involving local rescue teams, police, and people who helped circulate appeals for information.
In a social media statement posted on Saturday, his friends and family announced his death, writing: “With a heavy heart, we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.
“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.”
“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.
“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”
Yap, who was from Melbourne, was last seen near the start of the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, a demanding high-altitude route through a remote section of the Andes.
His father, Vinh Dao, previously told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that Yap was an experienced trekker but his trip to Peru was his first solo one.
Concern mounted when he did not return as expected, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz, and missed a flight booked from Lima to Cusco.
He had also lost a satellite beacon he had been carrying in the days before setting out, adding to concerns about his safety in an area where the terrain and altitude can make trekking particularly challenging.
“Time is of the essence because ultimately, as much as we were saying he’s been missing since the 23rd, he’s had no contact with anyone since the 14th,” Yap’s longtime friend, Kevin Nguyen had earlier said.
“It’s a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it’s very uncharacteristic no one’s seen him since day one or day two,” he told the Australian Associated Press.
Australia’s department of foreign affairs and trade confirmed it was assisting the family of an Australian who had died in Peru.
“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” a spokesperson said.
Earlier, Yap’s family had raised $90,500 from an online appeal to cover the cost of the private search operation. “If any funds end up not being used for this purpose, they will be returned,” they said.

Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other INDIA bloc leaders marched towards Supreme Court in Delhi to protest against the CEC. (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: A Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA bloc march to the Supreme Court against alleged electoral irregularities encountered police barricades in central Delhi on Monday before the opposition leaders eventually reached the court and filed a joint petition against the Election Commission of India (EC).The march, dubbed "March for Democracy", brought together opposition leaders, MPs, party workers and activists, with Rahul Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav among those who joined the procession.The march was initially halted at Bhagwan Dass Road, where police had erected barricades to prevent the procession from proceeding towards the Supreme Court. As the crowd swelled and the standoff continued, several leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Akhilesh Yadav and Tejashwi Yadav, climbed atop a vehicle as supporters raised slogans against the government and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.As per Supreme Court website, their legal team had filed the petition against the EC as the leaders failed to reach on time.Subsequently they reached the Supreme Court premises and filed the petition in a show of strenght.
Visuals released by the news agency showed Rahul Gandhi, Kharge and other INDIA bloc leaders filing the plea.The march came after the Chief Justice of India refused to meet the opposition leaders who had sought an appointment to submit a memorandum over alleged electoral irregularities. CJI Surya Kant had said the matter was already before the court and advised the leaders to pursue the judicial route by filing a petition.ALSO READ: 'Ready to contest on ballot paper': Himanta lobs dare at Cong but with a big rider
11 leaders named in the petition
The petition names Rahul Gandhi as the lead petitioner, along with 10 other opposition leaders from INDIA bloc parties. The petitioners are:
Rahul Gandhi, Congress
Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress
Saugata Roy, Mamata-TMC
Akhilesh Yadav, Samajwadi Party
Tejashwi Prasad Yadav, Rashtriya Janata Dal
Sanjay Raut, Shiv Sena (UBT)
MA Baby, CPM
D Raja, CPI
Mahua Majhi, Jharkhand Mukti Morcha
Supriya Sule, NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar)
ET Mohammed Basheer, Indian Union Muslim League leader
The Election Commission of India has been named as a respondent. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the other two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, have also been named as respondents, according to the Supreme Court website.
What does the petition seek
The petition filed by Rahul Gandhi and 10 other opposition leaders in the Supreme Court has challenged the manner in which the Election Commission has taken decisions relating to the SIR of electoral rolls, news agency ANI reported.It seeks disclosure of the EC’s complete files, agendas, minutes, notings and objections concerning the disputed decisions, including the June 24, 2025 decision to commence the SIR, as well as ECINET and ERONET access logs.It also seeks a judicial examination of whether these decisions were taken in accordance with Article 324 of the Constitution, the 2023 law governing the Election Commission and the Supreme Court’s ruling in TN Seshan vs Union of India.The petition seeks several safeguards against voter deletions during the SIR, including a direction that no elector be removed from the electoral roll without prior notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
It also seeks the booth-wise publication of deleted electors, along with the reasons for their deletion and demographic details.The petition further calls for an independent committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge to audit deletions and modifications in electoral-roll databases, including ECINET and ERONET. It also seeks an interim suspension of the ongoing SIR until the court adjudicates the matter.Additionally, the plea asks the court to direct the Election Commission to ensure that “every decision of the Election Commission relating to the Special Intensive Revision is taken and duly minuted” in accordance with the 2023 Act.

French defense contractor Thales will establish a maintenance and operational support base in Japan in what is seen as the first such move by a foreign firm in the country, a report said Monday.
Thales Chairman and CEO Patrice Caine told the Nikkei business daily that the base “will mark a milestone toward Thales’s long-term engagement in Japan.”
It is believed to be the first time a foreign defense company has established a dedicated base in Japan for the maintenance and operation of Japanese defense equipment, the Nikkei said.
It added that Thales may also expand its Japan-based business to civilian use in the future.
The report comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi boosts defense spending in the face of China’s rapid military expansion and an unpredictable North Korea, moving away from the traditional pacifist stance that limited the use of force to self-defense.
Thales already supplies equipment to the Self-Defense Forces, the Nikkei said.
Caine cited technologies such as radar and sonar as possible areas to share with Japan, saying that he hoped to “provide support in areas where Thales has an advantage in terms of performance.”
Thales will transfer its technology to partner Japan Steel Works and production of the 2R2M heavy mortar system will begin in Japan from next year, the Nikkei said.

Conventional wisdom is that cars are bad investments. Drive one off the lot, and it starts losing value the minute its wheels touch the road. That makes what’s happening with the 2026 Toyota Rav4 downright weird.
Some used vehicles are listing for $3,000 to $6,000 above brand-new dealership prices, according to new data from the online automotive marketplace CarGurus. The months-old cars are aging like fine wine.
The crossover SUV—one of the top-selling in the US—went all-hybrid last year, after Toyota announced it would drop the gas-powered model from its lineup. That’s likely why we’re catching a glimpse of an economic Upside Down. Kevin Roberts, director of economic and market intelligence at CarGurus, says the situation reminds him of the pandemic-era chip shortage, when a supply crunch for new cars also drove up used prices, and buyers flipped them months later for a profit.
“Hybrid demand is so strong, the Rav4 is still in that 2021 world,” he says. Toyota can’t make new models fast enough.
The leaves are changing, and America’s hot hybrid summer has become a toasty hybrid autumn, for new cars and for old ones. Toyota reported this month that its hybrid sales are up 29 percent in the third quarter of 2026; Kia said its sales more than doubled. Nearly one in six new US cars sold is a hybrid, according to Cox Automotive data.
“The American market has a reputation for gas guzzlers, but we're starting to shake that reputation because of how much we like hybrids,” Roberts says.
The major driver is gas prices. They’ve skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war and the ensuing conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, a global center of oil and gas production and shipping. Nationally, a gallon costs an average of $4.40, up 40 percent from this time last year, according to AAA; Californians pay an average of $6.36. Car buyers are a simple bunch, Roberts says—when prices start rising, they immediately look for more fuel-efficient cars. Soon, drivers actually start buying them.
For now, struggles in the US electric vehicle market are hybrids’ gain. New EV sales are down by almost half from last year, after the Trump administration cut a federal tax credit that made the often-expensive powertrains more affordable. Unlike electrics, hybrids don’t necessarily force drivers out of their familiar gas station routines. (Even plug-in hybrids sometimes need a gas top-up, though smart owners depend mostly on electricity.) Finally, more hybrids are available now than before. A buyer interested in nearly every major sort of passenger vehicle—three-row SUVs, pickups, minivans, or luxury cars—can find one with the powertrain
Interest has spread to the used market, where hybrid prices are up almost 5 percent over last year, according to the automotive data website iSeeCars.com. At $34,500, the average price of used hybrids is higher than used EVs or gas-powered cars. Used buyers seem to be especially keen on long-term fuel savings.
Hybrid tech has been around for decades, but it still may be just the beginning of its reign in the US. “Certainly from a philosophical, functional, and cost perspective, they make the most sense,” says Karl Brauer, iSeeCars’ executive analyst. Several hybrid models already outsell their gas counterparts, including the Toyota Highlander and the Ford Maverick. Soon, he predicts, most US cars will come with a hybrid drivetrain.
US automakers seem to see the hybrid writing on the wall. At the beginning of the decade, General Motors said that 40 percent of its 2025 lineup would be electric. That didn’t happen, and the subsequent pivot left it well behind its Asian counterparts in the new hybrid race. Now, GM has changed its tune. Hybrids “are part of the plan,” an executive told CNBC this week. “We’re not tone-deaf to our customers. We know what they want, and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can.”

Smart just unveiled a new ultra-compact EV at the Paris Motor Show
The Smart #2 is absolutely teensy and gets around 180 miles per charge.
Smart just unveiled its #2 ultra-compact EV at the Paris Motor Show, four years after the company introduced the Smart #1. The Smart #2 looks to be a return to (miniature) form for the company, after a string of SUV releases. This thing is teensy and similar to the iconic Smart Fortwo ultra-compact.
The Smart #2 fits two people and has been designed to make "navigating tight city streets and parking in narrow spaces effortless." They will be available in a variety of two-tone color options, which recall the original Fortwo.
There's a rear-mounted 60kW electric motor that provides 130Nm of torque to the back wheels. These rear tires are actually larger than the front wheels, which should enhance stability.
The floor-mounted battery can get up to 180 miles (290km) per charge, which is a decent enough metric for an ultra-compact. The car also supports fast-charging, which can go from 10 to 80 percent in 20 minutes at the outlet. Smart promises "sportier handling and greater comfort," due to a five-link rear suspension system.
The Smart #2 may look like an old-school Fortwo, but it's packed with modern features. It comes equipped with driver assistance systems, a 10.1-inch central screen and an 8.8-inch driver display. These EVs can connect wirelessly to devices via 4G, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
There will be several trims available to choose from here. The Pure is the entry-level model, and includes everything I mentioned above. The Pure+ adds 11kW AC charging and a heated driver seat. The Premium adds even more perks, like a glass roof, heated leather seats and a seven-speaker Sennheiser sound system. There are also more color options here. Finally, the Couture Edition includes a white exterior, a gold-painted roof and tires with gold detailing. This one will be limited to 999 units.
We don't have exact pricing or availability just yet, but Smart says the starting price will be under $26,500 (£20,000.) Preorders will open in the Spring and deliveries should happen at some point during the summer.
However, this car likely won't be coming across the pond. Smart hasn't sold anything in America since 2019 and this country seems to dislike small and budget-friendly EVs.

This story is based on an interview with Vincia Gordon, 56, an operational manager for two call centers, living in Baltimore County, Maryland. It has been edited for length and clarity.
My mom, Hyacinth Lynch, 92, lived in the US Virgin Islands, but constantly visited my family and me in Maryland, staying for months at a time.
She lived by herself after my father died in 2020 at the age of 94. Longevity runs in our family.
However, she started to show signs of decline in the summer of 2023. A physical exam confirmed she had high blood pressure and other issues, such as a hernia.
In September, one of our friends from the islands called to ask if there was something wrong with Mom. She had called her twice one morning, asking her the same thing.
It was the first sign of her dementia. Other friends were concerned, too. I told them to keep their eyes on her and report to me anything that was askew.
I didn't like the idea of a care home
She flew over for the holidays — and never left. Her mobility had gotten much worse, as well as the hernia. She had surgery in the Spring of 2024.
The dementia progressed. Her long-term memory stayed intact — she could rattle on about looking after my daughters when they were young — but her short-term memory was a problem.
I talked to her medical team, who put her on the drug donepezil. It helped slow things down and remove some of the brain fog.
There was no question in my mind that she should stay at home with me. I didn't like the idea of a care home, because I compared them to overcrowded classrooms.
You'd question your children's education if the teacher had 30 kids on any given day. How could Mom get the attention she needed without a specially designated aide?
I contacted the senior living advisory, A Place for Mom, for help finding providers and other services. They put me in touch with some private carers, who usually visit between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m.
They charge $44 an hour, and they mostly spend the time doing cognitive exercises. Mom has always been a word search queen and loves doing puzzles.
We also have visits from other professionals, including a social worker and an occupational therapist. Meanwhile, I keep on top of things such as keeping her clean, monitoring her blood pressure, and administering her medication.
I couldn't manage without FMLA
I'm very accountable and write everything down in a copybook in case I need to consult a provider.
People ask me how on earth I manage to run two call centers — one in the US and the other in the Philippines — while caring for my mother. My days are knee-deep in meetings and calls with staff.
The answer is FMLA. I receive 480 hours a year, and my salary is not affected. I usually take it in increments of two or three hours, but it can extend into days if necessary. I also use my allotted PTO.
It's always a balancing act, and the juggling is hard. Still, I wouldn't have it any other way. Mom is absolutely here to stay.

SHANGHAI/BEIJING – China’s deal with the European Union to curb exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc is a fresh hit to Chinese EV makers that have ramped up hybrid shipments exempt from EU tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, as sales growth slows at home.
China’s exports of hybrids to the EU’s 27 member states tripled to $7.5 billion in the first half of this year from $2.5 billion a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. The figure was nearly nine times the $845 million exported in all of 2021.
Since the EU imposed additional tariffs on Chinese-made EVs in 2024, Chinese automakers have increasingly turned to plug-in hybrids, which are exempt from the extra duties. Weak charging infrastructure in parts of Europe has also supported demand for plug-in hybrids, which are marketed for their long range and strong fuel economy.

Egypt’s Fayoum mummy portraits to travel abroad for first time after restoration
Egypt has unveiled a restored version of the "Tondo of the Two Brothers," a prized 2nd-century painting from the Fayoum portraits
CAIRO -- Egypt unveiled Sunday a restored version of the “Tondo of the Two Brothers,” a prized 2nd-century painting from the famed Fayoum portraits.
Specialists from Rome worked alongside conservators from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir — where the collection is usually kept — for three weeks to restore the artwork, officials said at a press conference.
Fayoum mummy portraits were painted primarily on thin wooden panels and placed over the faces of the deceased within mummy wrappings, combining Egyptian funerary traditions with artistic influences from the wider Greco-Roman world.
Egypt will lend a major part of the collection to a temporary exhibition in Rome, marking the first time it will travel abroad.
“The restoration of the Tondo of the Two Brothers is an important example of what can be achieved through international cooperation in the preservation and study of cultural heritage,” said Sherif Fathy, Egypt’s minister of tourism and antiquities. “Egypt and Italy share deep historical and cultural ties, and this project brings together Egyptian and Italian expertise to preserve an exceptional work of art for future generations.”
Experts describe the painting as unusual because of its circular shape and its depiction of two people instead of one, and rank it among the most vivid surviving portraits from Roman-era Egypt. It was painted using a technique in which pigments are mixed with molten wax, and restorers were able to recover the features of the brother on the right.
Aly Abdel Halim, director general of the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, said the conservation required careful intervention because both the wooden support, damaged by termites, and the painted surface were fragile.
The portraits will be featured in an exhibition in Rome from November to May 2027.
Tomaso Radaelli, chairman of MondoMostre, the exhibition’s organizer, said it will bring together more than 110 objects, including painted panels, funerary shrouds, masks, marble portraits, plaster casts and ancient jewelry.

Indian businesses paying for overseas software, cloud storage and consulting services may face tighter goods and services tax (GST) compliance requirements as the government considers expanding e-invoicing to imported services and purchases from unregistered suppliers covered under the reverse charge mechanism.
The proposal, recommended by the 57th GST Council, applies to businesses with an annual turnover of ₹5 crore or more. If implemented, it could require companies to modify how they document, validate and report transactions on which they pay GST under the reverse charge mechanism.
Under the existing framework, Indian businesses purchasing services from overseas suppliers are generally required to account for applicable GST under reverse charge. Since foreign suppliers do not issue Indian GST invoices, the Indian recipient issues a self-invoice where required under GST rules.
Quick answers to key questions
The proposal recommended by the 57th GST Council would apply to businesses with annual turnover of ₹5 crore or more. It could cover imported services and purchases from unregistered suppliers subject to reverse charge.
Indian businesses generally account for applicable GST under the reverse charge mechanism. Because overseas suppliers do not issue Indian GST invoices, the Indian recipient issues a self-invoice where required under GST rules.
The proposal could bring transactions involving imported services into a more standardised e-invoicing framework. The detailed requirements, including how these invoices would be integrated into the Invoice Management System, have not yet been clarified.
The proposed mechanism aims to reduce mismatches between tax liabilities declared in returns and input tax credit claimed. It could strengthen reconciliation between GSTR-3B and credit available in GSTR-2B.
The proposed changes could take effect from the April 2027 return period. The revised mechanism is to be published for time-bound consultation, and final requirements will depend on the detailed framework and approval.
The proposed expansion could bring these transactions into a more standardised e-invoicing framework, although the precise implementation requirements are yet to be clarified.
Alongside the e-invoicing proposal, the council has recommended a mechanism to correct tax liabilities and input tax credit (ITC) reported in GST returns. The changes could take effect from the April 2027 return period.
The revised mechanism will be placed in the public domain for time-bound consultation. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has been authorised to approve modifications based on stakeholder feedback.
According to the council, the proposed changes aim to reduce discrepancies between tax liabilities declared by businesses and the ITC they claim. This could help limit demand notices and system-generated intimations arising from mismatches in GST returns.
The proposals come as GST compliance increasingly relies on the Invoice Management System (IMS), which allows buyers to accept, reject or keep supplier invoices pending for review.
The proposed changes could strengthen the reconciliation of credit reported in GSTR-3B with the credit available in GSTR-2B. Businesses may therefore need to improve invoice validation, supplier verification and the accuracy of their accounting data.
Most companies may not need to replace their existing accounting systems, but modifications could be necessary to accommodate the additional compliance requirements, according to experts.
Businesses that depend heavily on manual reconciliation could face greater operational challenges as invoice matching and return reporting become more closely integrated.
The transition could also create reconciliation issues involving credit notes, delayed supplier adjustments and ITC reversals. Companies may need closer coordination among procurement, accounts payable and tax teams to ensure that invoices and credit claims are recorded correctly.
For imported services, a standardised self-invoicing process could improve the connection between GST payments, return reporting and ITC claims.
However, the manner in which invoices relating to imported services will be integrated into IMS remains to be clarified.
Experts said the GST Council’s recommendations indicate a gradual shift towards an IMS-driven compliance framework. The proposed measures are intended to improve reporting accuracy and reduce mismatches, while businesses may need to strengthen internal controls and review their existing GST compliance processes.
The final operational requirements will depend on the detailed framework issued after stakeholder consultation and approval of the proposed changes.

Economic frustration helps fuel Alberta separatism — and these 4 charts suggest why
Years of economic pressure drive calls for independence, but leaving Canada has financial risks
Alberta has long been seen as a province with an economic advantage — the wealthiest in Canada in terms of GDP per capita, rich in natural resources and no provincial sales tax.
But not all Albertans are feeling that prosperity.
Albertans frustrated with Ottawa point to a "lost decade" marred by unstable oil prices, cancelled pipeline projects and unemployment.
Morad Rizkalla, a retired petroleum engineer who spent nearly 40 years working in Alberta's energy sector, says cancelled pipelines have cost Alberta and Canada economic opportunities.
"We're like 20 years behind here," he said.
Years of economic frustration have helped fuel the province's separation debate, which is culminating in a vote this month to decide if Alberta should pursue independence.
"Over the past 10 years, the fact that Alberta has underperformed economically has probably given a bit more momentum ... to the movement and a bit more new support," said Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist with Alberta-based Servus Credit Union.
When oil prices crashed in 2014, investment in oil and natural gas projects plunged and the province fell into a recession in 2015 and 2016.
While the economy eventually recovered, the energy industry changed. Oil companies became more efficient and construction of major projects that once drove investment and job creation became harder to justify.
St-Arnaud says Albertans are still feeling the impact.
"We've seen the purchasing power of Albertans being lower. So it's 10 per cent lower now than it was in 2014," he said.
"That decline was sudden in 2015-2016, but then it has been stagnating since. So for the average Albertan, they're looking at their own situation and [thinking], well, I'm not getting ahead."
Alberta's unemployment rate has tracked above the national average since 2016, according to Statistics Canada, while average weekly earnings have struggled to keep pace with inflation over the same time.
Despite a decade of economic headwinds, there is plenty of optimism in Alberta's energy sector in 2026 as oil prices have reached $100 US per barrel again. A series of major projects are also in the works including the Pacific Link pipeline and LNG Canada Phase 2, in addition to record oilsands production.
The federal government has signalled support for Alberta's oil development by ending Canada's consumer carbon tax and the oilpatch emissions cap, but voters like Rizkalla haven't forgotten setbacks of the previous Liberal government.
"If something like the Northern Gateway and Energy East were built, they would have been just coming on now. Here we are in another oil boom and there would have been a huge impact on Canada — not just on Alberta, but on Canada and its GDP, unemployment all across the country."
Rizkalla says he plans to vote for the option on the Oct. 19 ballot that would direct Alberta to begin the process to hold a binding referendum on separation.
Rizkalla wants his vote to send a message to Ottawa to negotiate on issues such as equalization, Alberta's political representation in Parliament and access to markets.
But Rizkalla says he hasn't looked closely at the practicalities of separation — or the potential cost of forming a new nation, which some experts say could cost tens of billions.
What would separation actually change?
Some of the financial pressures facing Alberta would remain, regardless of its constitutional status.
Oil prices are determined by the rise and fall of global markets. Even with a return to skyhigh oil prices, companies have become more selective about investing billions of dollars into new projects.
In recent years, reinvestment in Alberta's oilsands has been a fraction of what it was before 2014.
Alberta would also still need to get its oil and natural gas to customers outside its borders.
"There's little doubt that Alberta has the economic ability to be on its own, in my opinion. But if you add in the uncertainty around Alberta being landlocked, that's a significant issue," said Martin Pelletier, senior portfolio manager at Calgary-based Trivest Wealth.
An independent Alberta would also have to determine pensions, currency, banking, taxation and trade.
Prominent voices for separation maintain Alberta would be better off economically on its own and say any outstanding issues could be resolved through negotiations with its neighbours.
"Our view is we can become independent, we can operate as an independent country and we can be successful financially," said Dennis Kalma, co-lead of independence organization Alberta Transition Council.
More like Brexit than Quebec?
Canada has been through separation debates before.
St-Arnaud lived in Montreal during the 1995 Quebec referendum and later in London during Britain's Brexit vote.
"In the case of Alberta, similar to Brexit, a lot of the reason for holding a referendum is more political than kind of social and cultural, as it was in Quebec. In Quebec, it was clear — let's create a French-speaking nation," he said.
Former British prime minister David Cameron, who called the 2016 Brexit referendum and campaigned against leaving the European Union, wouldn't necessarily draw the same comparison.
"Brexit was about whether we wanted to stay in a trade association with an element of political union. Canada is not a trade association with an element of political union. Canada is an amazing country with an incredible history," said Cameron while speaking at an energy conference in Calgary last month.
Still, Brexit showed how complicated a breakup can be. "Leave" voters have since expressed regrets about rising food prices, border issues and political polarization.
"It's going to look like a divorce," said St-Arnaud. "It's going to be a long argument, a lot of lawyers involved and it's going to take a long time."
Former British Prime Minister David Cameron drew on his own referendum experience during a visit to Calgary on Sept. 28, saying there is never a guarantee what the results are going to be. (Josh McLean/CBC)
Independence supporters have pushed back on Brexit comparisons.
Lawyer Keith Wilson, who is also an advocate for separation with the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide, says the situation is "fundamentally different."
"Brexit was about the U.K. moving away from its largest market, being Europe," he said in June. "Alberta independence is about Alberta moving closer to its largest market and the largest market in the world, the United States."
What could separation cost?
There have been varying estimates on the cost of Alberta separating.
Late last month, the Alberta Transition Council (ATC) released a budget and costing plan estimating one-time transition expenses of $5 billion, while predicting an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of between $22.2 to $32.1 billion each year.
- Alberta separation group releases report touting affordable transition to independence
- Establishing independent Alberta could cost up to $170B over 5 years: report
A University of Calgary School of Public Policy report commissioned by the Alberta government predicts the cost of establishing a new country could range between $50 billion to $170 billion over a five-year period. The report found total provincial debt could skyrocket to between $324.1 billion to $442.3 billion.
Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta and a member of the report's advisory panel, says there's a lot of uncertainty.
"At the end of the day, it all affects our pockets," said Legge, who represents 130 business leaders in the province.
"I think that's a very financially challenging and risky gamble for all Albertans because nothing would be in our control."
But for now, he says the debate doesn't appear to be impacting business decisions.
"None of them have put anything on pause. None of them have said we're going to wait until we see what happens on Oct. 19."
Legge says that could change if Alberta moves toward independence.

Everton up for sale again - so what next as owners TFG look for a way out?
- Published
When Everton's owners The Friedkin Group released a 170-word statement on Friday morning announcing they were effectively putting the club up for sale, it was as low-key and underwhelming as their tenure on Merseyside.
TFG, also owners of AS Roma in Italy's Serie A, paid more than £400m for a 99.5% share of Everton in December 2024, releasing the club from the financial crisis and toxicity that characterised the final days of Farhad Moshiri's chaotic regime.
It was meant to be the start of a bold new era for the club as they waited to move out of Goodison Park into a magnificent new stadium at Bramley Moore Dock.
Instead, TFG will now test the market, with football finance expert Kieran Maguire telling BBC Sport he expected them to seek a price between £750m and £800m for a complete sale, taking on current debts of around £468m.
In contrast to the high hopes and confidence that accompanied their arrival, TFG have effectively been absentee owners focusing their efforts on Roma - a stance illustrated by the fact chairman Dan Friedkin has never attended an Everton game or, even more startlingly, never spoken to manager David Moyes since he arrived back at the club in January 2025.
Moyes made that revelation in the aftermath of a botched summer transfer window that transformed the relationship between Everton's fans and TFG from cold acceptance to outright toxicity.
- Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Everton told to pay Burnley £35m over PSR breach 
  - Published10 June
Armstrong fiasco beginning of the end
The catalyst was TFG's attempt to sell teenager Harrison Armstrong, one of the finest products of Everton's Academy in recent years, to Nottingham Forest in a £40m deal.
The move was agreed by TFG until news leaked out, prompting loud threats of "a riot" from Everton fans during the game at Bournemouth later that day.
Such was the reaction, TFG went into damage limitation mode to block the deal for the 19-year-old midfielder, but it was little more than a face-saving PR exercise after a catastrophic decision that instantly alienated the fanbase.
Everton then sold Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m and striker Beto - hardly elite but a recognised striker - to Fiorentina, before a move for Monaco forward Folarin Balogun collapsed with no time to seek alternatives.
It left Moyes a striker light and with only 18 senior outfield players. From that moment the credits were rolling for TFG, leading to the announcement they are looking to sell their stake in the club.
Why have TFG decided now is the time to sell?
Maguire said: "I think there are various factors at play. I suspect they were shocked by having to pay Burnley more than £35m for a breach of financial rules."
In 2024 Everton were found to have broken Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) over a three-year period. Burnley argued the breach had impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League in the 2021-22 season and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
TFG injected £38m into the club to cover the cost, while Everton have subsequently appealed.
"I think that perhaps they thought English football was going to become as litigious as trying to operate in the United States," added Maguire. "This will not have appealed to them.
"It is also a good time to sell because it is such a buoyant market. The Americans will be interested. There are only 20 Premier League clubs you can buy. There are lots of potential buyers out there. There is that scarcity factor.
"I'd say TFG will look for £750m to £800m to sell. It can take 5 billion dollars or even more to buy a sporting franchise in the United States.
"I think they can see this as something they can flip - in other words, buy low and sell high."
What TFG have brought to Everton is a measure of financial stability following Moshiri's era of crisis, which Maguire believes will make them an attractive proposition to potential suitors.
"Everton have history and heritage," he said. They are Premier League perennials. They look like they will stay there and they have a passionate fanbase who fill a superb 50,000-plus stadium.
"You are not having to spend money on an upgrade of that stadium. I have a lot of respect for the finance people at the club. Unlike some of the chaos of Moshiri and what he left behind, you can lift up the carpet now at Everton and nothing unpleasant will come out.
"To paraphrase a former Prime Minister, you have got an 'over ready' football club coming on to the market. If you are an owner who wants to accelerate things at a football club, you have a starting point for that.
"And my start point for potential buyers would be the States."
There is no doubt, however, that Houston-based TFG's relationship with those back at base on Merseyside hinted at the dysfunctional.
The lack of a close relationship with manager Moyes was again emphasised when he admitted he only heard about Everton's potential sale at the same time as the wider public - only adding to the sense of disconnect between TFG and the club, compared to how they work at Roma.
Speaking at his press conference before Sunday's match away at Hull, Moyes said: "I'm disappointed that Evertonians have to go through another period of 'who are our owners?'
"I truly believed with new ownership we were in it completely. My ambition coming back was trying to get Everton back to the levels they have been in the past, and that is challenging for Europe more often.
"It has been a difficult summer for us. I only found out this morning. Maybe, I am a little bit surprised, but maybe I shouldn't be that surprised."
On TFG's approach, Maguire added: "They have not really engaged with the club or Liverpool as a city. Dan Friedkin has never been to an Everton game, which shows the difference.
"With Roma, they have got a club in the Champions League - with all that entails financially - and one with a far greater chance of being there on a regular basis which, and we are only stating a fact, is not the case with Everton."
How will TFG's tenure be remembered?
"With a mixture of disappointment and indifference," added Maguire. "I think they now have the right people at Everton, while I think under the Moshiri regime there were some there for decoration rather than substance."
TFG will hope to do a quick deal.
"Because so much due diligence has been done by the Friedkins themselves, all of the gremlins will have been highlighted and dealt with," said Maguire.
"It is now down to satisfying the Premier League's owners and directors' scenario. Are you a wrong 'un? Do you have the money? Can you prove where the money has come from - not just to buy the club but to run it?"
And Moyes is happy to give a reference as he added: "I'm looking forward to getting the right people in to take the club further forward.
"It's a great club. If anyone wants to speak to me then I will be the first person to let them know that it is certainly worth buying."

The trailer for Netflix’s high school-set horror series The Body, has arrived just in time for spooky season. The show premieres November 11 on Netflix.
This raunchy teen psychodrama from creator Quinn Shephard (Not Okay, Under the Bridge) takes the intense pressures, rivalries, and intimacy of high school female friendships and treats them with almost biblical, high-stakes importance – all set in the fun backdrop of the early 2000s.
“Can a person really contact the devil?” a student asks in the opening of the clip, answered by an instructor that “Lucifer wouldn’t be a true foe if he couldn’t be summoned, would he?”
It looks like another student gets a bloody nose as the red liquid drips onto her desk in class and a curious classmate asks how one would know if Lucifer was present.
Watch on Deadline
“There would be signs,” the ominous answer reveals.
The Body centers around a dance team, who audition three new girls for their squad in tryouts, telling them to roar like their mascot, the Lions. Sofia Wylie’s Grace stands in the middle of the trio, the girl to her right cheering normally and the girl to her left, Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) roaring animalistically. Lisbeth gets invited to some sort of costume party, where a dance-team initiation goes very wrong.
As a result, the whole town starts asking the same question: “What happened to Grace?”
The girls scramble to cover up what happened at their shindig, agreeing to not tell anyone they had it and also omit that drugs were present.
Tension builds across the school as Sara Boustany’s Elise is carried out of what looks like mass, winking at students in the pews as she hangs limply.
The clip ends with Shirley Chen’s Maddie googling “Is my friend possessed by the devil?”
The Body consists of eight episodes, starring Kristina Bogic, Sara Boustany, Sofia Wylie, Geena Meszaros, Shirley Chen and The Traitors winner Gabby Windey. Still more cast include Nnamdi Asomugha, Jackson Kelly, Orlando Norman, Emily Roman, Kyra and Phallon Pierce, Bella Neuspiel and Sarah Abbot. Amy Israel, Peter Chernin and Johs Stern executive produce for North Road alongside Riley Keough, Gina Gammell and Sacha Ben Harroche for Felix Culpa.

The No Man’s Sky universe is about to get a little bit smaller — but in a good way. Hello Games announced that its long-running sci-fi exploration game will be coming to iOS, with versions for both the iPhone and iPad available starting on October 28th.
No Man’s Sky is coming to the iPhone and iPad
A decade later, and the No Man’s Sky updates just keep coming.
According to Hello’s Sean Murray, the mobile version of the game is essentially the full No Man’s Sky experience. “I guess I should say this is not No Man’s Sky Lite,” he wrote in a blog post. It includes all of the game’s many, many updates that have come out since launch — like the gigantic Voyagers expansion from last year — and the only major features missing will be multiplayer and the planetary settlements. Murray likens the iOS version to when the game initially launched on the original Switch. “On Switch we have listened to players and built from there, including with a much expanded version on Switch 2,” he says. “Based on feedback and player numbers we will support iOS in a similar way.”
The game will be playable on the iPhone 11 and 3rd generation iPad Air and above, and the studio says that the download comes in at a surprisingly scant 5GB. It also has newly-designed touch controls, as well as support for controllers, screen casting, and mouse-and-keyboard on the iPad. Murray also notes that “Perhaps most importantly we’ve put tons of work into battery life and thermodynamics, and we’re super proud that No Man’s Sky can be enjoyed for really long comfortable play sessions.” It’ll be “free to try” at launch, though it’s not clear how much the full version will cost.
It’s now been a decade since No Man’s Sky first launched, and the game has changed dramatically since its debut. iOS will be joining a huge list of supported platforms, including Mac, PC, and essentially every modern console, and there’s also a VR version available. Just as significant, Hello has continued to keep the game vibrant with a constant stream of free expansions, including the recent Cosmos update in September, which fleshed out the vast expanse of space with more things to explore.

Tesla’s most advanced driver-assistance feature is named Full Self-Driving (Supervised), but it can’t actually drive itself. While the feature can handle tasks like accelerating, braking, steering, and parking, the automaker requires drivers to stay alert and intervene at all times. Now, the company has officially renamed it to Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe as it works to convince regulators to allow its use on public roads.
Tesla offered to change the name, according to a statement by the German Transport Ministry. The statement says that German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger found the “FSD” name “somewhat misleading.” After discussions with Tesla last month, Bilger said he would now advocate for European regulators to approve the feature “as quickly as possible.” The EU will likely vote on its approval by the end of the year.
On Friday, Tesla began using the Tesla Assisted Driving language on its European sales website. The automaker didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tesla has resisted changing the feature’s name for years, even defending it in court. Last year, California’s Department of Motor Vehicles concluded that Tesla’s use of the terms “Full Self-Driving” and “Autopilot” (an older and less advanced driver-assistance feature) was misleading and violated state law. After the agency threatened to suspend Tesla’s manufacturing and dealer licenses in the state, the automaker stopped using the term “Autopilot.” It has also continued to append “(Supervised)” to the official name of its Full Self-Driving tech.
Tesla drivers say FSD has improved tremendously since its introduction in 2020, and fans online say they’ve been able to take entire trips without intervening in their Tesla’s driving. But FSD has faced plenty of scrutiny. In March, the US federal government opened a probe into the system after nine incidents in which FSD allegedly failed to respond because of reduced visibility and didn’t warn its drivers to take over. Tesla recalled an older version of the software in 2023, after the US government found that it didn’t follow some traffic laws.
Tesla and CEO Elon Musk have pushed for other global markets to approve its driver assistance technology for years. That would likely create a lucrative, software-based funding stream for the world’s most valuable automaker. (Currently, Tesla charges $99 per month for a Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription in the US.) Australia and New Zealand approved it last year. The Netherlands became the first European government to give Tesla provisional permission to launch FSD this past spring. A version of the feature became available to Chinese customers in May.
This week, Reuters reported that Tesla presented misleading safety data to European regulators as it lobbied for FSD approval. Safety researchers have accused the automaker of also using misleading statistics to promote its tech in the US.

A video showing a few men unloading garbage on the road is being shared with the claim that Municipal Corporation vehicles are littering the roads leading to Jantar Mantar before the student protests (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing Delhi Municipal Corporation vehicles littering the roads leading to Jantar Mantar before the student protests.
Fact: These visuals show sanitation workers in Panipat, Haryana, protesting by dumping garbage on the road at Samvidhan Chowk on GT Road in August 2026. The protest was part of their agitation over various pending demands, involving sanitation, sewer, and fire department workers. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post featuring the same visuals, dated 17 August 2026, shared by the handle @Journalistkulwantsingh. The caption stated that the video showed a sanitation workers’ strike in Panipat. This makes it clear that this video predates the Delhi protest.
Further, a relevant keyword search led us to multiple media reports featuring the same video (here, here). According to these reports, sanitation workers in Panipat, Haryana, protested by dumping garbage on the road at Samvidhan Chowk on GT Road. The protest was part of their agitation over various pending demands, involving sanitation, sewer, and fire department workers.
Based on these reports, we geolocated the protest site to Samvidhan Chowk on GT Road in Panipat, Haryana. A comparison of the viral video with the geolocated location is shown below.
To sum up, this video shows sanitation workers’ protest in Panipat; It’s not related to the Delhi protest.

The final electoral rolls of all 117 Assembly constituencies were published on Monday (October 12, 2026) following the completion of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in Punjab, and the names of around 13.60 lakh people went unrecorded as a result of permanent relocation, absence, death or duplicate entries.
Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Anindita Mitra said that as on June 9, 2026, Punjab had 2,14,61,043 registered electors, comprising 1,11,76,866 males, 1,02,83,478 females and 699 third gender electors. The SIR began on June 25. The electorate increased from 1,93,94,435 in the draft roll to 2,01,00,727 in the final roll.
“During the house-to-house enumeration phase (June 25 – August 3), Booth Level Officers [BLOs] distributed enumeration forms to registered electors and collected the same. The draft electoral roll was published on August 13, 2026 with a total of 1,93,94,435 electors. Copies of the draft electoral roll were handed over to representatives of political parties Statewide for their active participation during the claims and objections period,” the CEO said.
Ms. Mitra said the notice phase and disposal of claims and objections was held between August 13 – October 8, 2026. “And 86,038 of the 35,49,036 electors who were issued notice were marked ineligible after extensive verification and through speaking orders.
The electorate increased from 1,93,94,435 in the draft roll to 2,01,00,727 in the final roll, representing a net increase of 3.64%. The final roll comprises 1,03,76,026 male, 97,24,195 female, and 506 third gender electors,” she said in a statement.
“The final electoral roll of the special summary revision relating to service voters, with reference to October 1, 2026 as the qualifying date, has also been published,” she added.

The death of actor Nana Patekar, 75, has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, a condition in which a blood clot forms in an artery supplying the heart. What causes these clots, who is at risk, and how is the condition diagnosed and treated?
The story so far:
According to published accounts of the autopsy report, actor Nana Patekar died after a blood clot blocked the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a large part of the heart muscle. A blockage in this artery can severely restrict blood flow to the heart and cause a heart attack. The reported finding has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, the formation of a blood clot within a coronary artery.
What is coronary thrombosis?
Coronary thrombosis occurs when a blood clot forms in one of the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. These arteries carry oxygen and nutrients that the heart needs to function. When a clot partly or completely blocks an artery, less blood reaches the heart muscle. If the blood supply is cut off for too long, the heart muscle can become damaged, leading to a heart attack. The severity depends on how much of the artery is blocked and how quickly blood flow is restored.
This form of thrombosis is often associated with atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up in the artery walls. These deposits, called plaques, can remain unnoticed for years.
When a plaque ruptures or its surface is eroded, platelets gather at the site and a clot may form. The clot can then obstruct blood flow, sometimes suddenly. Damage to the inner surface of an artery can trigger the process of clot formation. Additionally, at rupture, the material beneath the plaque’s surface comes into contact with blood, prompting platelets to gather and the clotting process to begin. A clot may grow quickly and block the artery.
What are the warning signs?
A clot that significantly restricts blood flow through a coronary artery may cause chest discomfort, pressure or tightness. Pain may spread to the arms, shoulders, back, neck or jaw. Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue may also occur.
The symptoms depend on the artery affected and the extent of the blockage. Some people may have less typical symptoms or no obvious warning signs before the blockage becomes serious. Symptoms alone cannot confirm coronary thrombosis; medical assessment and investigations are needed.
Suspected coronary artery blockage accompanied by chest pain or breathlessness requires emergency medical attention.
Who is at risk?
People living with coronary artery disease are at greater risk of coronary thrombosis because fatty deposits can build up in their arteries and trigger clot formation if a deposit ruptures. Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet can increase the risk of developing this artery disease.
In some cases, a clot may form in an artery affected by other conditions, including inflammation or injury to the blood vessel.
Older age and a family history of heart disease at a younger age are also risk factors. However it can occur even in people who have not been diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The underlying plaque build-up may have gone undetected until it triggers the formation of a clot.
How is this condition diagnosed?
Doctors assess symptoms and medical history and use tests to determine whether a coronary artery is blocked and whether the heart muscle has been damaged. An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart’s electrical activity, while blood tests measuring cardiac troponin can help identify damage to the heart muscle.
Coronary angiography uses a contrast dye and X-rays to show the coronary arteries and identify the location and extent of a blockage. This can help doctors decide how best to restore blood flow. Other tests may be used depending on the patient’s condition.
How is it treated?
Treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent the clot from growing or new clots from forming. The approach depends on the location and severity of the blockage and the patient’s condition.
Angioplasty may be used to reopen the affected artery. A thin tube is guided to the blockage, where a small balloon is inflated to widen the artery. A stent, a small mesh tube, is often placed to help keep it open.
Doctors may also use antiplatelet medicines, which reduce the tendency of platelets to clump together, and anticoagulants, which interfere with the blood-clotting process. In selected cases, clot-dissolving medicines may be used. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be considered when the pattern of blockage makes it a more suitable option.
Preventing further clots involves managing the underlying risk factors and following the prescribed treatment plan. This may include controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, stopping tobacco use, maintaining physical activity appropriate to the person’s condition and taking prescribed medicines.

Delhi Police detained journalists for a second consecutive day on Sunday, October 11, while they covered the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Left-wing student outfits demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Journalists from mainstream outlets and independent houses were among those held, and several said they were detained even after showing press credentials. The detentions came on the same day the Supreme Court said lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be hindered in their duties “in any manner whatsoever.”
Three journalists from Indian Express Hindi, Shashwat, Siya and Vijay, were among those detained. The organisation said on X that the three told police they were journalists doing their job but were forcibly put into a bus. It said Shashwat sent a video he recorded on his phone as the bus passed through Connaught Place, and that Siya’s phone was seized by police. The three were later released at Chhatrasal Stadium, the organisation said.

They were taken to Chhatrasal Stadium and have since been released.

Among those detained was independent journalist Shyam Meera Singh. The incident was particularly disturbing because before being detained, Singh had been heckled by a violent mob. In an interview with Jansatta, Singh narrated what he identified as a pattern.
According to him, in A Block of Connaught Place, people linked to the BJP and RSS were moving around and gathering in an organised manner. Singh alleged that they targeted protesters, particularly those who were alone, including journalists and activists. Once they identified someone critical of the government or perceived as anti-establishment, they would ask the police to detain the person. According to Singh, the police acted on these demands, detaining the targeted individuals rather than the people in the mob.
Singh said he was reporting on Sunday morning when a group of people linked to the BJP and RSS gathered around him and began raising slogans against him. Fearing an assault, he approached the police and pleaded for protection. He also sought help from armed forces personnel present at the spot, but said they did not come to his aid.
Singh then approached a Delhi Police constable and told him, “Please protect me.” Instead, when members of the crowd began shouting, “Detain him, detain him, detain him,” the constable moved to detain Singh as he was leaving the spot with two or three others. Singh alleged that the constable grabbed and manhandled him, acting at the crowd’s behest.
As the constable took him towards a bus, Singh began raising slogans of “Inquilab Zindabad”, “Bhagat Singh Zindabad” and “Amit Shah Murdabad”. When the policeman questioned him, asking, “Why are you abusing?”, Singh retorted, “When did I abuse anyone? You aren’t stopping the people who are abusing, and you’re saying this to me.”
Singh alleged that the constable had already hit him three times with a baton. “However much you want to beat me, go ahead,” he told the policeman, adding, “I am a journalist, but because of your mindset, you have become a sycophant of the Sangh or the BJP, that’s why you’re targeting me.” Despite the constable’s anger, Singh said, he continued raising slogans of “Inquilab Zindabad”. Following this, he was detained and out in a police van.
