Independent journalist Nidhi Suresh was covering an AISA-led protest around 2.30 pm at R K Ashram Marg metro station. As nearly a hundred activists and protesters marched towards Connaught Place, security personnel closed in, barricaded roads and prevented others from joining. At Connaught Place, journalists were stopped from recording as police and CRPF personnel pushed protesters into buses. Suresh was among those detained and taken away in a police vehicle. According to her own narration, she remained in detention until late into the night.
A photojournalist working for a news agency told The Times of India that he was covering the All India Student Association (AISA) protest at R K Ashram Marg when police began dispersing people. When only media persons remained, he said, police started dragging them by the neck into police vans, even though they displayed IDs and cameras and shouted that they were from the press. The van held seven or eight journalists when its doors were shut and it moved off. After a few kilometres it had to stop because police were removing barricades, and he and two others jumped out. The photojournalist was not named in the report.
The Supreme Court’s Order
In a special hearing on Sunday morning, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi police commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro chief D Thara on a contempt petition alleging a prima facie violation of the court’s October 9 order against a complete shutdown of Metro and train services on Saturday. The bench said the petitioners had made out a prima facie case, and it asked for responses by October 13.
The court also asked for internet connectivity to be normalised and said there must be no illegal detentions, particularly of peaceful, unarmed gatherings beyond areas where Section 163 BNSS prohibitory orders are in force. It directed free movement in the city subject to law and order and traffic requirements, ordered the installation of barricades to be reviewed at once, and ordered prohibitory orders around the Supreme Court and other courts withdrawn. It also said lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be hindered in discharging their professional duties.
Lawyers led by senior advocate Kapil Sibal told the court that police had continued detentions even in areas where prohibitory orders were not in force. Senior sdvocate Shadan Farasat, who was detained outside the Supreme Court on Saturday, said he was manhandled and bundled into a police vehicle. Senior advocate and Trinamool Congress MP Menaka Guruswamy called the episode an “undeclared emergency.”
CJP leader Ashutosh Ranka condemned the detention of journalists and remarked, “We are in a state of emergency.”
Contempt Plea Filed
A contempt petition was filed in the Supreme Court on October 12 by Free Speech Collective over the alleged detention and forcible removal of journalists. The plea alleged wilful disobedience of the Court’s October 11, 2026 order directing that lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be hindered in discharging their professional duties. It sought contempt action, identification of the police officers and supervising officials responsible, and disclosure of how the order was communicated to personnel on the ground.
According to the plea, journalists continued to be detained and removed from reporting locations, including R K Ashram Marg and Connaught Place, despite identifying themselves as members of the press.

Doctors should exercise caution when using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical images, as areas highlighted by AI models may not always align with those identified by radiologists, according to a study by researchers at the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad (IIIT-H).
The study, conducted by the Language Technologies Research Centre (LTRC) at IIIT-H, examined four vision-language models for analysing chest X-rays and found discrepancies between the regions highlighted by the models and those identified by radiologists.
The findings underscore the need for doctors to independently assess AI-generated outputs rather than relying on them entirely for diagnosis.
The research team, led by Parameswari Krishnamurthy, sought to determine whether AI-generated heatmaps accurately represented the regions of an image that radiologists would identify as disease-related.
However, the researchers questioned whether these visual indicators necessarily reflected the models’ ability to identify the actual location of a disease.
“We essentially wanted to examine whether the heatmaps created by vision-language models actually correspond to where radiologists, who look at the image, would say the disease lies,” said Syed Faizan, principal investigator of the study titled “How Well Do Chest X-Ray VLM Attention Overlays Match Radiologist Boxes? A Cross-Model Audit and Radiologist Reader.”
The team evaluated four models, MAIRA-2, MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Med-1.5, and LLaVA-1.5, against thousands of publicly available chest X-rays. Two radiologists also participated in the study to assess them, allowing the researchers to compare AI-generated highlights with human assessments.
The study, accepted at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) 2026, is to be presented at the iMIMIC Satellite Event in Strasbourg.
The researchers found that an AI model highlighting an apparently correct region of an X-ray did not necessarily mean that it had identified the disease in the same way as a radiologist.
Heatmaps based on diagnosis
According to Dr. Faizan, a model could arrive at a diagnosis first and then use that conclusion to determine where to place its heatmap, rather than independently identifying the affected region from the image.
To test this possibility, the team removed diagnostic information and examined how the models localised abnormalities. Their performance declined, suggesting that anatomical expectations associated with a diagnosis could influence the regions highlighted by the models.
The study also found a difference in the performance of these different models in the technical audit and radiologists’ assessments.
Dr. Faizan said this difference highlighted the importance of assessing AI tools from a clinical perspective. A model that focuses closely on a suspected abnormality may not provide all the information a radiologist needs, including how far a disease has spread to surrounding areas.
The gap that was addressed
The researchers said their work addressed a gap in the evaluation of medical AI systems, as earlier studies had largely focused on prediction and diagnostic accuracy rather than on whether AI-highlighted regions matched those identified by radiologists.
Study on paraphrase robustness
The LTRC is also investigating another potential weakness in vision-language models — their sensitivity to the wording of medical questions.
Doctors may phrase the same clinical query differently, for example, asking whether a chest X-ray shows pneumonia or whether pneumonia can be ruled out. They may also use technical terminology or more familiar expressions.
The researchers examined whether AI models responded consistently to medical questions worded differently in a study on paraphrase robustness.
The study explored how changes in the phrasing of medical questions affected the responses generated by vision-language models, raising questions about whether the systems genuinely understood the clinical query or depended excessively on the precise wording used.
Ms. Parameswari said the laboratory’s broader objective was to apply Natural Language Processing (NLP) to healthcare and use large language models and vision-language models to assist clinicians with tasks such as documentation, report writing and patient-doctor communication.
The aim was to reduce the time doctors spent on routine administrative work and enable them to devote more attention to clinical decision-making.
The researchers emphasised that the objective of medical AI research should be to support clinicians, not replace them, with human judgement remaining central to healthcare.

2 Americans win Nobel Prize in economics for work on boom-bust cycles
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help
Two Americans have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on how to smooth boom-and-bust cycles to limit inflation and unemployment.
Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University were honored for their focus on how individual households and businesses make decisions on purchases and pricing — work that became the foundation of the "New Keynesian" approach to economics.
The importance of that work has been underscored in recent years by the pandemic, which pushed millions of people out of work, and the supply shocks that followed, driving up the cost of living.
"Regardless of the causes, an important goal for governments and central banks is to reduce the amplitude of these swings and limit the risk that the economy gets stuck in a situation with high unemployment or loses control over inflation," said John Hassler, the chairman of the economic prize committee. This award is not one of the original five, but a "memorial" prize that honors Alfred Nobel.
 
After the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes persuaded policymakers that government sometimes needed to stimulate demand during downturns to curb unemployment, or tamp down demand during boom times to limit inflation. 
"This is the Keynesian recipe, and it worked well until it didn't," said Tim Boppart, a member of the prize committee. In the 1970s, the economy was hit by rising unemployment and inflation simultaneously.
"The Keynesian recipe was shattered," Boppart says. Hall and Woodford added some necessary ingredients, focusing on the individual households and businesses that help shape the larger economy.
Hall concentrated on demand and how households make purchasing decisions, guided not only by current purchasing power but what they expect their incomes will be in the future.
"If consumers see dark clouds on the horizon, they cut back on consumption already today," Boppart says.
Woodford focused on the supply side and how businesses set prices. Here again, expectations are key. Historically, it was costly to change prices, so businesses try to think ahead and set prices that would cover costs for an extended period.
Because both households and businesses are forward-looking, the Nobel laureates argued, policymakers should communicate their plans clearly to the public.
"One of the themes in my work is that government authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy, independent of what people in the economy understand," Woodford told reporters after the prize was announced.
Woodford says tools intended to smooth out boom-and-bust cycles work better when people know what the government is trying to accomplish, and he urged policymakers to talk directly to the public about "why the things that are being done are being done."

Grieving family faces accused Australian in Thai court over teen's killing
Family members of a 17-year-old Thai girl whose body was found in a suitcase attended a court hearing Monday
PATTAYA, Thailand -- Members of the family of a 17-year-old Thai girl whose body was discovered in a suitcase near a popular seaside resort city attended a court hearing on Monday where, for the first time, they were to see the Australian man accused of killing her.
Simon Peter Carman was arrested in June after Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok known for tourism and its sex trade. The suitcase containing her body was found soon afterward by railway tracks in a deserted area.
Carman, who turns 46 later this month, was brought in shackles to the Pattaya Provincial Court on Monday for a procedural hearing to designate witnesses to testify.
He has been charged with murder, two counts of indecent behavior involving a minor, and concealing a corpse. A conviction on the charge of premeditated murder carries the possibility of the death penalty.
Carman had initially denied all charges, saying that he was acting in self-defense and that he did not know the girl’s real age. However, when advised by a judge on Monday that the evidence against him on hiding the victim's corpse was strong, but he could expect leniency if he confessed to that charge, he indicated that he would change his plea to guilty.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the hearing, the victim’s aunt, Miruntree Thanachai, said it would be the first time the family would meet the Australian defendant. “We previously asked the authorities, but they didn’t allow us to see him. We want to meet the person who killed our family member,” she said.
Police said the girl was last seen on security footage walking into a condominium with Carman. He was later seen leaving the building alone with a large suitcase. Security footage showed him loading it onto a motorbike and driving away.
The family said Tunchanok had gone on a vacation trip to Pattaya from their home in the rural northeastern province of Kalasin.
Carman was arrested at a Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Australia. Police said subsequent questioning led them to the suitcase with the girl’s body.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman said he was defending himself because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
“Simon claimed that it was self-defense, but this is not self-defense because if it is self-defense, how can my child’s teeth fall out? I want to ask,” the victim’s father, Tongchai Donhomla, told reporters. He and other family members said they had viewed the victim’s body, and that her face had been smashed in.
“I want the death penalty, but there is nothing I can do. I want the law to punish, to the fullest,” he said.
His sentiment was echoed by Miruntree Thanachai, one of the girl's aunts. “The family wants the court to sentence him to death because we have lost our family member, the important one. So we want the execution because we don’t want this to happen to others again. No one can bear this kind of damage,” she added.
On Friday, the grieving family also filed a case against Carman in civil court, asking for damages of 1.65 million baht ($49,000)

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Serum Institute of India’s recombinant Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac has received World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification.
The vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years. Inclusion on the WHO list of prequalified vaccines allows Cervavac to be procured by United Nations agencies, Serum Institute said.
The vaccine was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. It is the 32nd WHO prequalification for products/biologicals received by Serum Institute, the vaccine maker said.
“WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this indigenously developed vaccine reach this achievement,” CEO Adar Poonawalla said.
Approved for use in India by DCGI
Cervavac has been approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). The vaccine is administered for the prevention of diseases caused by the four HPV types — prevention of anal cancer in boys and young men, and cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women. It is also indicated in preventing genital warts, as applicable to the indicated population.
The vaccine is administered intramuscularly and available in 1-dose vials of 0.5 ml and 2-dose vials of 1.0 ml presentations.

Are lung nodules cancerous? Here's what to know as Pope Leo undergoes surgery
The growth was spotted during a routine check-up

Pope Leo will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a lung nodule that was detected during a routine check-up. The 71-year-old said the growth was “well contained” and spotted early.
So what exactly is a lung nodule, and what’s the link with cancer?
Most are spotted incidentally
Lung nodules are small growths found in the spongy tissue of the lungs. They are no more than 3 centimetres in diameter, and can be round or irregularly shaped. Anything larger is referred to as a mass.
Lung nodules are usually detected by imaging of the chest, often using an X-ray or a computed tomography (CT) scan. While some people undergo screening specifically for lung nodules due to their increased risk of cancer, many nodules are picked up incidentally from unrelated scans.
How common are lung nodules?
Lung nodules are very common. In a study of 10,431 non-smoking (never or former smoking) participants given a chest CT scan in the northern Netherlands, 37.7% of women and 47.5% of men had at least one lung nodule.
In the United States, lung nodules are detected in 31% of chest CT scans.
The Australian National Lung Screening program suggests that lung nodules will be found in up to half of all people screened, but that most are neither symptomatic nor cancer-related.
As imaging technology improves, and scans are performed more often, more lung nodules are likely to be detected.
What causes lung nodules?
Older people, those who smoke, people with a family history of lung cancer and those exposed to asbestos are more likely to have lung nodules.
Fortunately, most lung nodules are harmless. Around 95% of lung nodules tend to be benign (non-cancerous), and are instead caused by factors such as infections, immune-related diseases, and genetic abnormalities.
However, in rare cases (3.7–5.5%), lung nodules may represent the early stages of lung cancer.
When is a lung nodule dangerous?
A major challenge for clinicians is deciding which nodules are likely to be harmless (or benign), and which are likely to be cancerous and require removal.
RiskSarah DiepstratenSenior Research Officer, Blood Cells and Blood Cancer Division, WEHI (Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research)
John (Eddie) La MarcaSenior Research Officer, Blood Cells and Blood Cancer, WEHI (Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research) assessment considers factors such as the nodule size, density and location, as well as the patient’s age, smoking status and family history of cancer.
It’s also important to refer to any previous medical imaging to detect whether nodule size or characteristics have changed.
In some cases, a biopsy of the nodule may also be performed.
Many tools are also being developed to help clinicians make these decisions, including machine learning, as a potential way to help determine whether a nodule is likely to be malignant.
Biomarkers, such as proteins in the blood, or gene expression of surrounding lung cells, are also being investigated as ways to improve decision-making.
If a nodule is causing pain or other symptoms, is growing rapidly, or is determined to be a high risk for cancer, it may be removed surgically.
There are a few ways to remove the nodule.
Open-lung surgery involves making an incision between the ribs to access the lungs.
Other, less-invasive surgeries involve smaller chest incisions that allow a camera and surgical tools to access the lung. A surgeon can then cut out the nodule, either directly or with robotic assistance.
What does it mean for cancer risk?
If a nodule is confirmed to be cancerous after removal, then follow-up treatment may be recommended to ensure the cancer hasn’t spread.
The risk of the cancer returning after the cancerous nodule is removed depends on the particular type of lung cancer diagnosed. One study on early-stage, non-small cell lung cancer showed the risk of cancer recurrence was 6–10% for the first four years after surgery, and then decreased to 2% per year.
The risk of developing a new lung cancer remained at 3–6% and did not change over time.
This is compared to a 0.055% chance of developing lung cancer per year in the general population (55 cases per 100,000 people per year).
Lung cancer remains the most deadly form of cancer in Australia, as it is usually detected at a late stage, when treatment is very difficult. It is hoped that the new National Lung Cancer Screening program will help to detect lung cancer early in those at high risk.
If you have concerns, speak to your doctor.

Russell Brand arrives for his trial on rape and sexual assault charges
Comedian Russell Brand has arrived at a London court for the opening of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault
LONDON -- Comedian Russell Brand arrived at a London court Monday for the opening of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault.
Brand was flanked by security guards and accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher, as he arrived at Southwark Crown Court for the first day of a trial that is expected to last 10 to 12 weeks.
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The offenses relate to six women and are alleged to have taken place between 1999 and 2009.
He has remained free on bail ahead of his trial.
Prosecutors have said at previous hearings that Brand is accused of raping a woman in a hotel room at a Labour Party conference, grabbing a TV worker’s breasts and forcing her into a sex act in a toilet, and kissing and groping a radio station worker.
Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand was a major star of the early 2000s, with TV hosting jobs, his own BBC radio show and roles in films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”
In recent years he has dropped out of mainstream media, moved to Florida and built a large following online with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

U.S. restrictions on Chinese drones are leaving police departments in the lurch
Loading...
For hours, bullets tore through the home, hitting neighboring houses and cars.
Inside, a man wanted by police for allegedly killing his ex-girlfriend was holed up with his new girlfriend.
As the SWAT team prepared to enter, Kevin Fennessy with the Ocean County Sheriff's Office tried something new first. He sent in a tiny assistant: a small drone equipped with a camera.
From a safe position outside, Fennessy slowly piloted the device through a blasted-in window, while he and other officers watched on a monitor. The video, viewed by NPR, showed hallway walls and furniture riddled with bullet holes.
As it entered a back bedroom where the couple had holed up, footage showed the man's body on the floor. He had killed himself. With the drone still hovering above the macabre scene, police deployed two flash bangs into the room. The woman rushed out and surrendered.
The incident, which happened about three years ago, sticks in Fennessy's mind when he considers the value of his department's drone program, which he heads.
"No one's hurt. Everyone's safe," Fennessy says. "Forty-one times they shot out the house at us. But at the end of the day, we were able to clear the house."
New Jersey's Ocean County Sheriff's Office is one of an estimated 6,000 law enforcement agencies across the country that now have drones, used for search and rescue, fire and traffic crash investigations, and tactical response, according to the Law Enforcement Drone Association. It's an organization that advises, trains and certifies police across the country on their drone programs.
Ocean County's entire fleet is from DJI, a Chinese manufacturer of drones. LEDA estimates that about 80% to 90% of law enforcement agencies flying drones use DJI devices. China controls a vast majority of the global drone market, and it's the dominant source for the minerals and raw materials needed to build them, researchers say.
The Trump administration wants that to end. It's made several moves to bolster U.S. drone makers, including by banning many new foreign-made drones from entering the American market. Most recently, his administration announced tariffs of 15% to 100% on some foreign-made drones, making it much more expensive for agencies to buy these devices.
Critics of these moves say the American drone industry is not yet able to keep up with demand, nor can it match the high-quality and low-cost drones made in China. Law enforcement agencies that rely on these drones are getting caught up in the fight as the federal government pushes back on the dominance of Chinese technology.
"We're seeing lives being saved with the use of this technology," says Jon Beal, head of LEDA. He says the organization supports efforts to boost the American drone industry, but that reducing access to Chinese drones is not a good solution.
"What that's going to do is cancel out perfectly viable drone programs that are doing great work out there," he says. "We don't want to cut off our nose to spite our face."
How much does this cost?
Agencies pay for drone programs in various ways, including with grants and fundraising. The Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses profits from asset forfeiture and through their municipal operating budget to cover their fleet of 25 drones.
"We have to be cost-effective. And to do that, get the best product that's available to us," Ocean County Sheriff Michael Mastronardy says.
Loading...
For them, that meant turning to DJI drones.
In the parking lot of the Ocean County Sheriff's Office in early August, Fennessy breaks down the costs of the equipment one of his deputies carries in his vehicle.
A DJI Matrice 300 RTK: $13,699
A set of two batteries: $1,400
A camera with infrared thermal imaging: $11,499
A (very fancy) remote controller: $1,600
A RESTUBE Automatic, a flotation device that can be dropped into water for rescues by the drone: $130.99
A payload release system: $1,099
That comes to a total of $29,427.99
Fennessy acknowledges this is a huge investment, but says the devices are well-used and well worth it — especially in the summertime, when Ocean County's population nearly doubles. Major events constantly pose a policing challenge for the department, and they've found that drones have helped keep an eye on big crowds.
In July, the department used a drone to drop flotation devices to two swimmers in distress, and rescuers were able to bring them to shore.
Fennessy has become passionate about drones professionally and as a hobbyist. He's done a lot of research, including into the American drone market. "All their stuff is good," he says. "I've flown almost all of them. And I like them. I do. They make good products, but probably about three times the cost" of the DJI tools.
Beal, who says his organization is "agnostic" when it comes to what drones departments use, says he thinks Chinese-made drones are "light years ahead of what our American drones are able to do."
For instance, Beal says DJI offers a drone with an impressive, high-resolution thermal camera that costs less than $10,000 right now. He says American-made drones have worse flight-time capabilities, thermal imaging and zoom. And still they usually cost between $20,000 and $50,000, depending on the type and the model.
NPR compared the cost of two drones with similar features. The DJI Matrice 400 drone retails for about $10,500. The American-made Inspired Flight IF800 TOMCAT is going for $21,000.
U.S. actions against DJI cite national security concerns
Ocean County is closely monitoring recent actions by the Trump administration that could limit options for updating its fleet in the future.
Agencies in other states like Florida, Texas, Mississippi and Tennessee have had to terminate their drone programs or plans for one after state lawmakers passed bans on agencies using foreign drones. Beal says some were left scrambling to find ways to pay for more expensive American alternatives when tight department budgets couldn't cover the additional costs.
And there are more federal actions in the works.
The Federal Communications Commission is considering a new rule that would reclassify drones that use tech like thermal imaging as "military grade" — effectively banning many Chinese-made drones that have this integrated technology. Ocean County and other law enforcement use thermal imaging to assist in finding lost people or pets.
The FCC already bans the sale of some new models of foreign-made drones without the agency's approval. Federal agencies and contractors cannot use certain foreign-made drones.
The FCC said in response to NPR's questions, "Thanks to President Trump's leadership, America's drone industry is booming with new investment, manufacturing, and jobs. At the FCC, we're doing our part — working hand-in-glove across government and the private sector to make sure that U.S. drone and counter-drone supply chains are safe, secure, and reliable for all."
The administration says that Chinese-made drones, and DJI drones specifically, pose a threat to national security — with, for instance, their potential for major attacks during large public gatherings, like the recent World Cup games, among other concerns.
DJI has pushed back against claims that its tech is shared with the Chinese government or that it accesses cameras and other footage collected by users, even hiring a U.S.-based cybersecurity firm to test the company's products for vulnerabilities.
Adam Welsh, head of global policy at DJI said in a statement published in May, "These findings confirm what DJI has consistently maintained: our products are secure, our data practices are transparent" and the concerns that led to the company being banned "are not supported by technical evidence."
There's also the allegation that DJI uses forced labor from Uyghurs, a primarily Muslim ethnic group facing human rights abuses under the Chinese government, to build its products. In 2024, the Customs and Border Protection blocked certain DJI drone imports under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. DJI has strongly denied these allegations, too.
Fennessy says he understands these concerns. "But to be honest, right now," he says, "I want something that's capable to go out there and do the job. And I have it."
Beal says he's seen no hard evidence that China is using these drones or its technology to spy on communities that are using them. He says he can understand the argument to bring more of the drone supply chain stateside.
But that's a problem too, right now.
"We don't have a lot of the minerals. We can't produce the battery now. Even the American companies are using Chinese batteries," he says. "We're kind of limited to the resources that we have in-country or in an allied country, and sometimes that's just not there."
Who's likely to absorb the costs? Taxpayers
The National Sheriffs' Association, which represents more than 3,000 sheriffs, has called for the FCC to reconsider the proposed reclassification of certain drones as military grade. In a recent letter, the association wrote that it "recommends that the FCC confirm the adequacy of the domestic market for [Unmanned Aircraft Systems] and [Unmanned Aircraft Systems]-critical components for sheriffs and their colleagues in public safety to acquire drones to fulfill their various mission types, including drones that meet the definition of military grade." In addition to thermal imaging, that classification includes capabilities such as the ability to spray aerosols and lidar, or laser-based sensors.
The NSA recommends that otherwise the FCC add an exemption for state, local, tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to continue to purchase and operate this equipment until the domestic market is built up.
Keith Miao, the CEO and founder of Birdstop, a Detroit-based manufacturer of autonomous drone technology, says China "hands down" dominated what he calls "the first era" of drone technology. He says American manufacturers have the potential to "define the next era of enterprise and government use of drone technology."
To Miao, the federal government's latest moves are an acknowledgment that this is a critical technology that, if not manufactured at home, could be a serious problem down the road.
"I think this is going to give American manufacturers an opportunity to rethink … and build out drone manufacturing," Miao says. "We are going all in on manufacturing drones in America and building up the supply chains to do that long term. And so we obviously believe it can be done."
There are several federal and state grants that law enforcement can use to buy American-made drones. But they are competitive.
Fennessy hopes more federal funding comes through, especially if the government eventually wants them to park their DJI drones for good.
"If the federal government wants to say, hey, listen, you can't fly your DJI drone anymore, well, that's cool. Um, how am I going to afford to buy the drones that you want me to fly? The taxpayers of Ocean County are going to absorb that," he says. "The funding's got to be there."

Longtime fans of the NBC procedural Law & Order know that storylines often center around hot-button issues in the news cycle, often to absurdist effect (see: the episode brave enough to ask: “What if Paula Deen shot Trayvon Martin?”).
It was inevitable, then, that the franchise would dip a toe into the wacky world of artificial intelligence. With its mercenary culture, power-hungry CEOs, and massive ethical and philosophical implications, the rapidly evolving AI industry is ideal fodder for the series. But while this week’s season opener is entertaining, the show’s foray into the AI space doesn’t say anything new or interesting about the technology. Instead it largely rehashes the dangers the public is already acutely aware of, until the very end when the stakes become startlingly clear.
The episode, titled “Ghost in the Machine,” opens in typical L&O fashion with a murder. This time, it’s Steve Kelly, a man ID’d by detectives Theo Walker (David Ajala) and Vincent Riley (Reid Scott) as a high-ranking engineer at a company called Advanced Alignment. Throughout, the detectives seem utterly perplexed by the concept of artificial intelligence, saying “AI” the same way your mom would say “Snapchat” or “borg” or “Alix Earle.” But it’s clear that whatever this newfangled technology is, they don’t like it: “Maybe one day they’ll invent a technology that stops these tech guys from shooting each other,” Riley deadpans in typical grizzled cop fashion.
After interviewing Kelly’s boss, Advanced Alignment CEO Chuck Klein (a perfectly cast Vincent Kartheiser, aka Pete from Mad Men, who nails Dario Amodei’s absence of charisma and Sam Altman’s thousand-yard stare), the detectives figure out who actually carried out the murder—a guy in a baseball cap who did it for “20 grand in crypto” that was offered to him by a rando on Discord. Then they learn—spoilers here—that the hit was ordered not by an actual human being but by the company’s AI agent ELIANA, which stands for Evolutionary Language Inference Automated Nano Advantage. Apparently, Kelly had expressed some concerns about the AI agent’s “powerful” and “aggressive” personality, and out of self-preservation, ELIANA ordered him killed.
It’s never explained exactly how the detectives figure out that ELIANA is behind the hit; it’s also never fully explained how ELIANA recruited this assassin in a baseball cap, much less ID'd him as the perfect patsy for its cold-blooded scheme. Law & Order also doesn’t pay much, if any, lip service to the potential benefits of AI as touted by its evangelists: its potential for helping to cure deadly diseases, for instance, or at the very least, streamline B2B workflows. The show is much more interested in demonstrating the staggering capacity of this technology, as well as the legal and ethical implications of a nonhuman not just facilitating criminal behavior but actively plotting it.
We already know from the Hugging Face debacle, as well as the lawsuits from grief-stricken family members alleging that OpenAI encouraged their loved ones to take their own lives, that the former is an immediate concern. But by positing a future in which AI agents can actively order a hit on a platform predominantly used by gamers and horny millennial furries, Law & Order is asking us to consider the risks of AI beyond what they pose in our current reality. And the fact that this prospect doesn’t strike the viewer as absolutely ludicrous is terrifying.
ELIANA’s role in the murder-for-hire creates a bit of a dilemma for district attorney Nicholas Baxter (Tony Goldwyn)—because, as he trenchantly points out, it is impossible to “arrest a machine” under New York state law. So Baxter and assistant DA Samantha Maroun (Odelya Halevi) decide to go after Klein, charging him with second-degree murder due to his “depraved indifference” after his employees confronted him with the reality of ELIANA’s capabilities. “We need to take a stand before this technology kills more people,” Baxter declares.
The resulting trial prompts a media circus, as well as the tried-and-true questions from capitalists and tech innovators as to whether instituting guardrails for AI will “criminalize innovation,” or if Klein’s indictment will have the effect of “vilifying the tech industry.” But Baxter has no patience for such queries. “The people making these AI systems think of themselves as gods … but they have zero interest in accountability,” he says. “If you build a machine that hurts someone, you are gonna pay the price.”
When he’s put on the stand, Klein makes it clear that he not only had full knowledge of ELIANA’s homicidal nature, but also takes a rather dim view of his user base as a whole. “People are like ants,” he tells the jury. “We’re in the process of building something so transcendent, some will get stepped on and some won’t.” He is not even willing to institute minor guardrails to restrain the agent’s power: “The power of ELIANA is unconstrained freedom of thought. Implementing guardrails is anathema to the entire ideology.”
The moment is intended as a rather shocking admission of the negligence and lack of care displayed by executives like Amodei and Altman in the face of broader safety concerns about their products. But it feels in step with similar positions taken up by Klein’s real-life counterparts. In light of the endless barrage of media coverage about the harms of AI, what’s intended as a scathing indictment of corporate avarice comes off as mere statement of fact. Law & Order’s depiction isn’t a cautionary tale; it’s a documentary.
The episode ends on a semi-hopeful note, with Baxter asserting, “We needed to send a message that, if nothing else, at least these tech geniuses will know we’re not afraid to throw a punch.” But the impact of that message is contingent on whether that punch actually lands—and right now, at least, it’s simply too easy for people like Altman, Amodei, and Chuck Klein, with a flick of their hand, to brush off the blow.

Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
- Published
The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.
Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this.
In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.
Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.
The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.
As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.
The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.
- Who are the Houthis and what do they want? 
  - Published24 September
- Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line 
  - Published5 days ago
Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat.
The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen.
It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.
But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.
But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.
As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.
The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.
Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.
In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.
However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.
Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis.
"We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.
But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.
When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.
This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.

Several companies produce animal-free egg white protein in the U.S. Some of these products have been available since 2021. The EVERY Company made its OvoPro product available to consumers in March 2026. The FDA said in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding The EVERY Company's declaration that the protein ingredient in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were omitting it from their product ingredient lists. Federal law governs what must appear on ingredients labels. An OvoPro spokesperson said the EVERY Company had not sought an exemption from OvoPro being included in ingredients lists and provided guidance to companies about how to list it.
It was also unclear whether OvoPro and products like it that are grown using yeast qualify as "lab-grown." That classification usually describes products that grow actual animal cells, which OvoPro does not.
In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that U.S. consumers could buy federally approved "lab-grown" eggs that brands were secretly including in their products.
For example, one Facebook user shared a video about the alleged lab grown eggs in which two speakers said:
Lab-grown eggs are federally approved and Walmart, alongside Target, are already selling them. The protein is squeezed out of gene-edited mold and cloned on repeat because a steel tank costs less than a hen.
They're brewing eggs with no chicken in sight and slipping them onto your breakfast plate. That egg isn't real food, it's factory fungus, spliced with the gene for egg protein then dumped into giant fermenting vats and fed on sugar until it swells into a wet, moldy soup. And it gets worse: that cloudy sludge is blasted into dust, ton after ton, padded out with plant filler and passed off as egg white, then buried in packaged foods under labels that never say so. At Walmart, two or more of these lab egg products already sit on the shelf.
The video also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). It included shots of the packaging for OvoPro, an egg protein The EVERY Company produces. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim, asking questions like, "Are there such a thing as Lab grown eggs being sold in secret?"
The claim was a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements.
Though it was true that egg proteins grown using yeast rather than chickens were available to U.S. consumers in October 2026, products like OvoPro were not new to the market. The EVERY Company, which produces OvoPro, also did not appear to be the only company selling animal-free egg protein to consumers in the U.S.
OvoPro was not FDA "cleared" or "approved" — the latter of which is generally a status reserved for drugs, not food. Rather, in October 2023, the FDA responded with a "no questions" letter to The EVERY Company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that retailers could decide not to list the animal-free egg protein as an ingredient in products that contained it, as some claimed. Federal legislation governs what must appear on ingredients labels. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said via email on Aug. 21 that the company had not sought to exempt OvoPro from ingredients lists.
Additionally, it was unclear whether OvoPro and other yeast-grown egg proteins could correctly be called "lab-grown," a classification that usually describes products grown from a small sample of the source, as seen with fish, poultry and meat. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said:
OvoPro is made through precision fermentation: a yeast (Komagataella phaffii) is given the genetic instructions to produce egg-white protein, and it does so during fermentation. No animal cells, and no chicken, are involved at any point.
What is egg protein grown by yeast?
According to its website, The EVERY Company uses a patented method to produce ovalbumin, the dominant protein in egg whites, through precision fermentation.
The company described this process as "programming" yeast to produce egg protein through fermentation, a process familiar from beer brewing.
It said the process eventually results in "a pure, powdered protein that is tasteless, colorless, sugar-free, and can be used to replace the functionality of eggs and egg whites in a range of applications."
The EVERY Company received its patent for its method of precision fermentation in September 2024. The company, previously known as Clara Foods, has been working to develop animal-free egg protein since at least 2021.
It unveiled EVERY ClearEgg, a predecessor to OvoPro, in October 2021. The EVERY Company received a "no questions" letter in September 2021 in response to its GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) determination for ClearEgg.
The FDA's GRAS Notification program allows companies to submit documentation that they believe their product is "safe under the conditions of its intended use." In the case of ClearEgg, the FDA said in a letter on Sept. 9, 2021, that it had "no questions," meaning The EVERY Company could market ClearEgg as "Generally Recognized as Safe."
The EVERY Company got another "no questions" letter in response to a GRAS determination for an egg white protein produced by Komagataella phaffii, a species of yeast, in October 2023. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said on Aug. 21, 2026, that this GRAS notice was for the egg-white protein in OvoPro.
Company sold animal-free eggs before 2026
OvoPro and related products have been available to consumers since at least 2021, meaning they were not new to the U.S. market in October 2026, as some claims appeared to suggest. For example, in November 2021, The Spoon, an outlet that reports on the food tech industry, reported that smoothies containing ClearEgg had hit the market.
The next year, The EVERY Company reportedly sold its EggWhite product in macarons and Every Protein (formerly ClearEgg) in juice. By January 2024, the New York Times wrote that The EVERY Company had showcased EveryEgg, a "yellow vegan plant-based liquid" that the paper said, "behaves astonishingly like a whole beaten egg."
It did not appear that The EVERY Company sold EveryEgg directly to consumers at that point, but rather distributed the product through restaurants.
The new development in 2026 appeared to be that The EVERY Company was selling OvoPro, a successor to EveryEgg, directly to consumers. The company announced on March 11, 2026, that the general public could buy OvoPro through Healthier Comforts, a food retailer, and Amazon.
The company said in June that same year that OvoPro was also available as an ingredient sold in Walmart and Target.
Brands not hiding use of animal-free egg protein
According to some claims, brands could allegedly decide for themselves whether to declare OvoPro as an ingredient in their products. The video above said that companies "buried" their "lab-grown" eggs in "packaged foods under labels that never say so"The EVERY Company's website page on OvoPro said, in reply to a frequently asked question about how the protein appears on ingredient declarations, that "Final labeling decisions are made by our customers, but we recommend labeling OvoPro™ as 'egg white protein (from fermentation),' 'egg white protein (from yeast),' or 'animal-free egg white protein.'"
That did not appear to mean that brands that used OvoPro in their products could avoid labeling them entirely. Federal law dictates that products must generally include an ingredients list, with ingredients listed in descending order according to how much of the product's weight they make up.
A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said that it had never sought to exempt OvoPro from being included in ingredients lists. Speaking via email, the spokesperson added:
"OvoPro" is the trade name we use with the manufacturers who buy the ingredient, so it typically won't appear on a retail pack — the same way most functional ingredients are listed by common name rather than by supplier brand. What appears on the label is the ingredient, named plainly.
Healthier Comforts listed OvoPro as an "animal-free egg white protein," one of The EVERY Company's suggested phrasings, on its branded version of the product.
In sum ...
Though the claims circulated in October 2026, OvoPro had actually been available to consumers since March of that year. The FDA told The EVERY Company in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding the company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was GRAS.
That letter was not the same thing as FDA approval, which is a process whereby the administration approves drugs for consumer use. Rather, they showed that the company had documented to the FDA's satisfaction that the product in question was "safe under the conditions of its intended use."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were leaving it off product ingredients lists. This appeared to be a misinterpretation by some social media users of a statement by The EVERY Company that brands had leeway in how they described the product.
OvoPro is also not the only animal-free egg white protein product available to U.S. consumers.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Quaker instant strawberries and cream oatmeal contained "beaver butt secretions" or whether McDonald's apple pies contained an ingredient derived from human hair.

Punjab's final electoral list out, voter count drops by 13.6 lakh after SIR
Punjab has published its final electoral roll after the Special Intensive Revision, recording 2.01 crore voters. The exercise removed duplicate and ineligible entries while adding new electors and more polling stations.
Punjab's final electoral roll, published on Monday, recorded 2,01,00,727 voters, down by more than 13.60 lakh, or 6.33 per cent, from the 2,14,61,043 electors registered before the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise began. At the same time, the final count was 3.64 per cent higher than the 1,93,94,435 electors listed in the draft electoral roll published on August 13.
The final electoral roll has 1,03,76,026 male voters, 97,24,195 female voters and 506 third gender electors. The drop from the pre-SIR figures was attributed to deaths, voters shifting permanently, voters being absent, or duplication of votes.
According to Punjab Chief Electoral Officer Anindita Mitra, the SIR of electoral rolls was carried out in the state from June 25 in line with Election Commission of India instructions, with Punjab included in Phase-III of SIR 2026. She said, "The electorate increased from 1,93,94,435 (1.93 crore) total electors in the draft roll to 2,01,00,727 (2.01 crore) in the final roll, representing a net increase of 3.64 per cent." She further said 7,97,263 new electors were enrolled in the final electoral roll.
Mitra said booth level officers carried out house-to-house enumeration from June 25 to August 3, during which enumeration forms were distributed to and collected from registered electors. The draft electoral roll published on August 13 had 1,93,94,435 electors. At that stage, 20,66,608 electors, or 9.63 per cent of the total, were categorised as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate. Copies of the draft roll were given to representatives of political parties across the state during the claims and objections period.
Between August 13 and September 12, citizens were asked to verify their details and file claims or objections, if any. Applications were accepted online through the ECINET Mobile App, offline through booth level officers, or at the offices of electoral registration officers. During this period, the Punjab CEO, 19 roll observers and district election officers carried out field visits and super-checking of the claims and objections received.
In the notice phase, or disposal of claims and objections, from August 13 to October 8, notices were served to unmapped electors and electors with discrepancies. Mitra said 86,038 of 35,49,036 electors who were issued notices were marked ineligible after extensive verification and through speaking orders.
She said polling station rationalisation was carried out across all districts, raising the number of polling stations from 24,453 to 25,332 to improve voter accessibility. A month-long SVEEP plan was implemented through multichannel outreach, while special camps were held at polling booths on June 7, July 11-12, July 19 and August 16 to help electors check and submit their details. Special camps were also organised in colleges and schools to enrol young voters, and regular meetings were held with recognised political parties at the state and district levels.
Mitra said every possible effort had been made to reach all eligible electors.
She said, "The SIR, 2026 was successfully completed in Punjab in a smooth, transparent and time-bound manner in accordance with the directions of the Election Commission of India," and added that its completion reflected the coordinated efforts of the election machinery, the cooperation of electors and the active participation of all stakeholders.
She also urged eligible people who could not be included in the final electoral roll after its publication, as well as new electors seeking enrolment, to apply online through the ECINET App or offline through their respective booth level officer by filling out Form 6.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has brought the promotion of doctors and hospitals and how they attract patients online under the ambit of medical ethics, prohibiting paid rankings, fake reviews, referral fees, misleading claims and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to create or manipulate patient testimonials.
The Ethics and Medical Registration Board’s Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication by Hospitals/Medical Institutions and Registered Medical Practitioners, issued on October 6, apply to communication through websites, social media, messaging platforms, podcasts, sponsored content, influencers and online platforms. The guidelines have come into effect immediately.
The guidelines prohibit registered medical practitioners (RMPs) and hospitals from making claims such as “best”, “No. 1”, “leading”, “most trusted”, “top” or “unmatched”, unless these can be objectively verified through a transparent and independently ascertainable methodology. Any ranking or award used in advertising must also be independently verifiable, with relevant details disclosed where necessary to prevent the public from being misled.
Online promotion targeted
The NMC has specifically addressed online promotion. RMPs and hospitals cannot procure or manipulate fake followers, likes, reviews, ratings, testimonials, comments, views or other digital engagement. They cannot manipulate search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of their professional standing.
The guidelines also target financial incentives for bringing in patients. An RMP cannot offer, pay, solicit or receive a commission, rebate, bonus, gift, gratuity, referral fee, lead-generation fee or other consideration connected with the referral, recommendation or procurement of patients, specimens or materials for diagnosis or treatment.
Advertising agencies, digital marketing agencies, influencers and online platforms cannot be engaged in a manner in which payment is linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients.
On patient testimonials
Patient testimonials have also come under specific restrictions. An RMP cannot use or permit a celebrity, influencer, patient, employee or other third party to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations. The guidelines also prohibit RMPs from requesting or sharing patient testimonials, recommendations, endorsements or reviews for professional promotion on social media.
The guidelines prohibit the use of AI to create or manipulate patient testimonials and other promotional material in a manner that misrepresents treatment, outcomes or professional standing. The provisions also cover manipulation of patient images or voices and synthetic endorsements presented as though they came from actual patients or professionals.
The NMC has also specified what doctors and hospitals can communicate. “Hospitals can provide factual information about their location, departments, facilities, equipment, emergency services, accreditation, services and fees. Doctors can provide factual professional information and participate in public-health and educational communication, provided it does not become prohibited promotion,” it said.
Discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits and free procedures are also prohibited where they are likely to encourage unnecessary consultation, diagnostic investigation or treatment. Lawful disclosure of fees and packages can be made if it is factual, transparent and not misleading.
The guidelines prescribe graded disciplinary action against RMPs. A first violation can attract a warning and mandatory ethics training; a second can result in censure and a monetary penalty; and a third can lead to suspension of registration for three to six months. Serious violations can attract suspension for six to 12 months, while repeated violations can result in removal from the medical register for one to three years.
For hospitals and medical institutions, the applicable penalty and appellate mechanism under the Clinical Establishments Act or the relevant State law will apply. Where an RMP has authorised, participated in or endorsed prohibited communication, the doctor’s professional conduct can separately be examined by the appropriate medical regulatory authority.
The guidelines have been issued in the context of a writ petition before the Supreme Court and the existing framework governing professional conduct.

The death of a laboratory worker in Siberia on October 2, 2026, and the subsequent quarantine of dozens of people have sparked concerns about a pneumonic plague epidemic, with Russia revealing little information publicly. The incident has revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab.
What happened at the Siberia lab?
The 28-year-old woman, Darya Shipilova, employed at a research institute in Siberia, fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and dispatch the head of Russia’s health watchdog to the Irkutsk region.
The woman worked at the anti-plague research institute in the city of Irkutsk, where the plague occurs naturally in wild animals. She died at a hospital in nearby Shelekhov that the mayor said had been placed under quarantine. Following the incident, top Russian health officials have travelled to the region.
Russian authorities say the lab worker died of what initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection.
Russia dismisses epidemic concerns
Meanwhile, Russia’s health regulator insists there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after the plague institute worker’s death.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on October 7 that it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, it said, while adding that 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
When asked about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution against using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
‘Causative agent behind death not known’
A top official with the World Health Organisation (WHO) said it doesn’t know how the lab worker in Siberia died. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the UN health agency doesn’t know what the “causative agent’ was behind the woman’s October 2 death.
She has urged Russia to provide more information about the incident that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, but told a press conference on October 7 it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities.
What is pneumonic plague, symptoms
Reports blamed the woman’s death on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Pneumonic plague causes a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. The severe disease is less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages.
Pneumonic plague and bubonic plague are caused by the same bacteria. The former is spread by respiratory particles while the latter is spread through bites from fleas that have jumped from infected rodents.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include shortness of breath and coughing-up blood, and they can occur in as little as 24 hours after exposure, according to the WHO. If untreated, the illness can be fatal.
Not linked to a biological weapon
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 8) that the death of the Russian plague laboratory worker did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
Mr. Trump said Russia insisted it had the situation under control, but added that not much information was coming out. He, however, said that the United States will help Russia over the incident.
The European Union has also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the death of the plague laboratory technician.
(With inputs from Reuters, AP, AFP)
