Elon Musk is a very familiar figure to Ars readers, given his massive influence (for better and worse) on the technology sector over the last 20 years. Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney’s latest biographical documentary—simply titled Musk—covers a lot of well-known ground and challenges the carefully crafted public image of Musk as a visionary tech titan.
Gibney’s documentary presents Musk as more of a Gilded Age confidence man, rejiggered for the 21st century: an investor cosplaying as an inventor whose real genius is pumping stocks and dazzling investors and the public alike with visions of a high-tech utopian future. The film is bound to push all the right outrage buttons, whether one is a Musk fan or a detractor—which makes it very much a product of the peculiar social media-driven era in which we live.
Gibney has been making documentaries since the 1980s, covering such varied subjects as Jimi Hendrix, Hunter S. Thompson and gonzo journalism, WikiLeaks, Scientology, Steve Jobs, Elizabeth Holmes (the subject of another forthcoming documentary, You Can See Everything, featuring comedian Nathan Fielder), Boris Becker, The Sopranos creator David Chase, alleged Russian interference in the US 2016 presidential election, the opioid epidemic, and cyclist Lance Armstrong. He snagged his first Oscar nomination for 2005’s Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, and won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature two years later for Taxi to the Dark Side.
Tackling the subject of Elon Musk seems like a natural progression from those earlier works. Gibney has never been one to shy away from controversy, but even before Musk’s release, the film drew the ire of its subject and threats of a defamation lawsuit. There were even (as yet unfounded) rumors that Universal Pictures was getting cold feet about theatrically releasing the film in international markets.
There’s certainly no shortage of material for Gibney to work with and the film covers the most well-known aspects of Musk’s life: Tesla and the fatalities linked to its driver-assistance systems, SpaceX, Starlink, his purchase of Twitter, his shift from warning about the risks of AI to fully embracing it with Grok, his embrace of Trump, the creation of DOGE, his alleged drug use, and his 14 (possibly more) children. Those interviewed include ex-wife Justine Musk, Kara Swisher, Martin Eberhard, Geoffrey Hinton, former MAGA influencer Ashley St. Clair (who bore a child by Musk), Cory Doctorow, Adam Becker, and Sam Harris. David Byrne co-wrote and performed an original song for the soundtrack, “Let Me Sell You a Dream,” incorporating more of Musk’s words.

Americans have more trust in science than most of the rest of the world, according to a new survey of people in 140 countries, a finding that may seem difficult to explain in a country deeply divided by issues such as the benefits and harms of vaccines.
According to the newest edition of the Wellcome Global Monitor, 52 percent of Americans report having “a lot” of trust in science. Across the globe, that number is a mere 26 percent.
Americans, in aggregate, are also more eager to get vaccines compared to peer nations; 45 percent of Americans say they would want to get vaccines recommended by a nurse or doctor “right away.” In Germany only 28 percent say the same.
And while the share of people globally who agree that science benefits most people in their society has dropped from 42 percent in 2018 to 37 percent in 2025, the share of Americans who agree with that statement has actually increased from 48 percent to 57 percent.
But the aggregate statistics don’t tell the whole story. STAT’s analysis of the Wellcome data demonstrates that while America may, in general, appreciate and trust science, it is also far more divided than peer nations.
Take the religious divide: According to STAT’s analysis there was, on average, a 5 percentage point gap between the percentage of religious and non-religious people in high-income nations who said science benefits most people in their country. In the United States that gap was 24 percentage points.
A similar divide — 19 percentage points — separates urban and rural Americans on the question of science’s benefits. The divide across other high-income nations is just three points. Education level divides Americans as well — just 47 percent of Americans without four-year degrees reported believing that science benefits most people, compared to 71 percent of college grads.
Wellcome, a British foundation focused on scientific research, funded the survey in 2018, 2020 and 2025. The most recent version was administered as part of the Gallup World Poll through a combination of in-person, telephone and online surveys of more than 140,000 adults. The global findings were weighted “to ensure that global estimates accurately reflect the relative populations of countries in the survey.”
The survey does not offer an explanation for why the United States appears to be outpacing its peers on trust. But at least some of Americans’ seeming polarization may be explained by Americans’ tendency toward extremes.
Americans are “more extreme responders to public opinion surveys,” said Matthew Motta, an associate professor at Boston University School of Public Health who is an expert on public opinion research.
For example, a smaller proportion of Germans than Americans said they would “not get vaccines at all.” Only 8 percent of Germans were completely anti-vaccine, compared to 13 percent of Americans. Instead, the vast majority of Germans said they would “prefer to think about it for some time.”
The survey also showed that Americans who historically have been less trusting are not necessarily souring on science and its benefits. STAT’s analysis finds that the proportion of Americans who identify as religious and who believe science benefits most people increased by four percentage points, from 46 percent in 2018 to 50 percent in 2025. Self-reported religious Americans are also more likely to report an eagerness to be vaccinated when compared to peer countries.
A similar pattern plays out with Americans without four-year degrees. The percentage of non-college grads who say science benefits most people increased by three percentage points over that seven-year period, and they too are more likely than residents of peer nations with similar education to want vaccines right away.
So what is causing America’s growing divide over trust in science? The poll shows it is growing enthusiasm for science among highly educated, secular Americans. Both reported substantial increases in their appreciation of the benefits of science: 13 percentage points for college grads, and 15 percentage points for secular Americans over seven years, the Wellcome survey found.
In short, America is divided not because certain groups are souring on science, but because others are becoming more appreciative of its benefits.
That might seem like good news. But the divide nonetheless underscores that the benefits of science are not reaching a large swath of Americans in ways they can see and feel.
“People are feeling left behind, they are not understanding how this benefits me,” said Brian Castrucci, president and CEO of the de Beaumont Foundation, which focuses on strengthening public health.
Some divisions facing Americans will be difficult to combat in a country as large and diverse as the United States. City dwellers with cancer who can access care at a top-rated university medical center will inevitably see science’s impact on their lives more than people in a rural area who might have to travel a great distance for even the most basic hospital care.
Wellcome found that trust in science is closely associated with confidence in a nation’s health care systems, which presents a problem for the United States as well. Just 40 percent of Americans reported a lot of confidence in U.S. hospitals and health clinics, the same proportion as in Portugal and Uruguay.
Anti-science sentiment coming from America’s top political officials is likely playing a role too, several experts said. Diverging views on science among America’s political parties became apparent during the Tea Party movement of the 2010s and was amplified during Trump’s presidency, said Yotam Ophir, an associate professor of communication at the University at Buffalo.
But experts STAT spoke to underscored that this new data doesn’t just indicate the need for the sorts of systemic changes that can take decades to fulfill. Scientists need to hone their ability to discuss the benefits of science in people’s everyday lives, and to stop expecting the public to blindly trust them, several experts told STAT.
“What we need to do is be better communicators, not better debaters. We are not going to be able to lecture people into trusting us,” Castrucci said.
Mark Henderson, Wellcome’s executive director of corporate affairs and engagement, said scientists who wish to take steps based on the report’s findings should “meet people where they are.”
“Approach people on a level with understanding and engagement and respect, and you’re going to get a better outcome,” Henderson added. “It’s not rocket science, but it often surprises me how hard people in the scientific community find it to do that.”

18 Quirky Gifts That Lego Lovers Will Adore
Featured in this article
Lego isn't going anywhere. Those beloved little bricks won't biodegrade, are machined to incredibly tight tolerances, and—unless your dog chews one up—retain what Lego refers to as their “clutch power” for decades. Their relevance in terms of cultural pastiche isn’t fading on me either. They're as irresistible to me today as they were as a kid.
If you and your loved ones are also obsessed with Lego sets, we have some great gift ideas. For more recommendations, don't forget to check out our other gift guides.
Updated October 2026: I added the Lego Ideas Peanuts: Snoopy's Doghouse, a Lego Batman game, Star Wars Advent Calendar 2026, Star Trek light kit, and Lego Architecture Paris: City of Love.
- Their Favorite Themed Set Lego Speed Champions One of the reasons that Lego sets are so popular is the company's innumerable licensing deals. No matter what you're into, Lego has signed a deal to make a Lego set about it. (And then, in an ouroboros of advertising, the company will then make a movie about the Lego set about the franchise.) Anyway, this is a long and roundabout way of saying that my son and I are obsessed with the Lego Formula 1 sets. I even got to watch the Lego cars hit the track at a Formula 1 race. Ever since then, we've been watching the races and Netflix's Drive to Survive. It's the perfect collaboration because Lego bricks and Formula 1 engineers are on the same page when it comes to precise engineering and tight tolerances. Also, once you're done building, the cars work as toys as well as sets. —Adrienne So
- Smart Bricks Lego Star Wars Smart Play Throne Room Duel and A-Wing If you’re curious about Lego’s new Smart Play system, the Star Wars Throne Room Duel and A-Wing set is a great way to dip your toe in the water. This fun build enables you to reenact the climax of Return of the Jedi, with Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker duking it out as Emperor Palpatine looks on and a space battle rages outside. Smart Bricks add lightsaber noises, lasers, explosions, heavy breathing, and even a rendition of “The Imperial March.” They also light up, but you’ll have to remember to charge them.
- A Lego Centerpiece Lego Botanicals Bouquet of Pink Roses My daughter and my husband love the Lego Botanicals collection. These gorgeous tree and flower sets work well as holiday centerpieces once you're finished building—you can leave them right out on the table, instead of hiding them away in your Lego basement once you're done. My 11-year-old built this lovely rose bouquet, which has articulated heads so you can arrange them in the case. For the winter holidays, we also recommend the Lego poinsettia set ($50), which was our centerpiece last year. —Adrienne So
- A Lego Videogame Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight A superbly loving parody that throws the best of Batman’s movie outings into the blender with a pinch of slapstick comedy and plenty of charm. Gotham is packed with collectibles, puzzles to solve, and an endless supply of thugs to bash. Melee combat is fun, as you counter and dodge to build combos, and there’s plenty of gadgetry to try out. This is the most fun I’ve had with a Lego game in years, and it’s perfect for split-screen couch co-op. If you’re not a Batman fan, there are tons of other great Lego games, based on other worlds, like Star Wars, Ninjago, and Marvel.
- A Fan-Created Set Lego Ideas Peanuts: Snoopy's Doghouse Who doesn’t love Snoopy? This set is an easy build and includes Snoopy, his doghouse, and Woodstock. There’s also a typewriter (fans will recognize the line, “It was a dark and stormy night”) and a campfire, with alternative legs if you want Snoopy to stand, hunch over to type, or lie back on the top of his doghouse. The Ideas range from Lego is based on fan creations that have been shared and voted on to become real sets. This one is lovely, but it’s definitely a display set, not something you’d actively play with.
- A Lego Stocking Stuffer Lego Note Brick If you have a coworker who likes Lego and would like to gift him or her something tiny and thoughtful, I suggest this little notepad. It's very cute, with 224 pieces of paper, and one side looks like a brick. The notes themselves are about 5 inches long, which is big enough for a pretty substantial note! Chronicle Books has a whole line of Lego books, puzzles, and stationery for your Lego-obsessed friend. You could also throw in a pack of these brick erasers ($36) to make a little care package. —Adrienne So
- Lego Playing Cards Lego Brick Playing Cards If you also have an 8- or a 10-year-old, let me recommend a simple life hack—instead of caving to their demands to let them look at your phone while you're out, just always carry a deck of cards in your bag. It's crazy how many times my kids have settled down and waited patiently in a doctor's office or restaurant, as long as they can start a game of Crazy Eights or Go Fish (I do not recommend Speed). These Lego playing cards are beautiful and brightly colored, feel sturdy, and have held up to several rounds of shuffling around a table. The box comes in a pack of two, so your kids can split it. —Adrienne So
- An Advent Calendar Lego Star Wars Advent Calendar 2026 With the holidays approaching, this is a great alternative to regular advent calendars. You get a Star Wars–related minifigure or build behind each door, including irresistibly cute Mando and Grogu figures in Christmas jumpers, critters like a Bantha and Dewback, and tiny ships like an X-wing and the Razor Crest.
- Ornaments for Your Tree Lego Snowman Ornaments I wish we were a family that kept treasured family heirlooms all wrapped up in tissue paper, ready to be marveled over at the next year's tree decorating. Unfortunately, every year finds us with some Christmas tree–related disaster or the other. Our new puppy has chewed the stuffed animals that an uncle has sent us; my son has sent a baseball crashing into the ceramic horse head that I got as a kid. We always need new ornaments, so why not new Lego ones? These are very cute, and my son assembled them in a matter of minutes. —Adrienne So
- A Big Lego Book Page Street Kids The Big Book of Amazing Lego Creations With Bricks You Already Have Have all your sets now become disassembled, and do you need some inspiration while looking at the giant wheelbarrow of Lego bricks on your front porch? This is my kids' favorite book for ideas on what to build. It has been a struggle to not “lose” it from the library. All of the builds are fairly easy, and so far I haven't seen any that require specialized pieces. However, you will probably need more than just 12 red bricks or 14 yellow ones to make many of the builds, so you should make sure your Lego loved one has a substantial collection already. If you want other sources of inspiration, we also like The Art of the Brick ($40), and I would be remiss if I did not include our own Brian Barrett's book, The Art of the Minifigure ($35). —Adrienne So
- A Family Activity Lego Christmas Tree Puzzle If you're having relatives over for the holidays, I suggest having a little puzzle like this to whip out while everyone's waiting for you to put the final touches on dinner. It's not one big puzzle, which can feel overwhelming and makes it hard to get off the dinner table—it's four separate little puzzles. Your kids, or parents, or fun uncle ("funcle") can work on each small puzzle separately and attach them together later. Each of the backs is patterned differently, so you can tell the different puzzles apart when you're putting them away or back together again. —Adrienne So
- A Lego Head Mug Lego Large Ceramic Mug As Lego-branded toys rolled into my house, I do have the caveat that my kids were very confused. ("Why are all these Lego gifts coming in but none of them are Legos?") However, my son was immediately thrilled and delighted with this mug and demands that I wash it every morning for him to drink out of. There are several faces to choose from if your children don't want to match. It's ceramic and can hold about 17 ounces of liquid—so, pretty big for a 7-year-old but nothing their little hands can't handle. It's dishwasher-safe. We've also received these off-brand Lego mugs ($13) as gifts, but again, the clutch power of off-brand Lego bricks is unsatisfactory and the bricks don't stick on very well. —Adrienne So
- A Lighting Kit Light My Bricks Lego Star Trek Enterprise Light Kit You can bring some of your favorite Lego sets to life with third-party light kits. There are various options, but the best brand might be Light My Bricks. This particular light kit is for the Lego Icons Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D set, and it’s pretty pricey. That said, the kit is very well-made, with slim components that slot into place neatly; thin, flat cables; and no exposed solder or circuitry. The kits are also globally certified as safe, and the finished effect is awesome. Light My Bricks also makes light kits for a ton of other sets.
- The Best Lego Notebook Lego IQ Stationery Locking Notepad Do you have an artsy little Lego lover? My daughter has been obsessed with this notebook and carries it around everywhere she goes. It's about 6 inches square, so small enough to fit in a backpack or tote bag, with a decent 176 lined sheets. It has a wonderful conceit—the Lego gel pen matches the color of the binding and clicks right into it, so it both locks the notebook shut and ensures you never lose your pen. That's unless you're 10 and leave your pen on the kitchen table, where your puppy finds it and eats it (see next). —Adrienne So

She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
- Published
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.
India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.
That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.
Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.
Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.
Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.
Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.
The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.
In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.
Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.
Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.
Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.
Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.
Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.
Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.
"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.
"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.
"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."
Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.
In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.
The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.
Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.
Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.
Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.
The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.
She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.
An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.
Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.
That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.
The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.
Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.
Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.
India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.
With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi is showcasing how ground robots are reshaping offensive warfare.
In the opening stages of this complex operation, Ukrainian forces used uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, as distractions. The robots drew Russian attention and exposed surveillance systems and firing positions while assault troops slipped through and seized key territory.
Robots have also conducted airborne assaults, delivered explosives, attacked enemy command centers, and supported infantry operations amid this major counteroffensive in eastern Ukraine.
NC13, a strike UGV unit within the Third Assault Brigade of the Third Army Corps, has played a leading role in Vivaldi. Mykola Zinkevych, the unit's commander, told Business Insider that his forces have used robots across a wide range of missions to inflict defeats on the Russians.
Over the course of the operation, the robots evolved from diversions that enabled Ukrainian advances into armed strike platforms targeting Russian command posts, drone operators, and large troop concentrations in the rear.
Zinkevych, who goes by the call sign "Makar" and spoke through a translator, said these efforts disrupted Russian command and control and logistics, making it harder to bring in more soldiers and limiting Moscow's ability to conduct operations.
Robots also carried out what the commander described as full-scale robotic assault operations, independently and in support of Ukrainian infantrymen.
Most notably, NC13 used heavy bomber drones to carry armed robots over the front lines and drop them in enemy territory, surprising Russian troops and creating additional pressure, Zinkevych said. He added that it also affected their morale.
Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, revealed the use of this tactic in late September and said that his forces had become the "first in the world" to operationally air-drop robots from drones in combat.
Beyond explosive-laden robots, NC13 also deployed robots armed with grenade launchers, Zinkevych said, adding that the unit was the first to do so in combat. He said the Russians apparently mistook the UGVs for an infantry assault, which led to confusion and disorientation.
These innovative tactics come amid broader efforts by Kyiv's forces to integrate ground robots into combat operations. Ukrainian officials have said they want machines to replace humans in dangerous front-line missions, particularly in logistics and casualty evacuation roles.
Vivaldi, which Ukraine launched over the summer to halt Russian advances in the northern part of the Donetsk region, has already seen Kyiv retake control of dozens of square miles of territory, according to analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a US think tank.
Zinkevych attributed Vivaldi's success in part to strike robots, but he also credited Biletskyi's planning and coordination. Conventional weaponry, specifically artillery, has played a key role, too, according to Western analysts and the Ukrainian military.
The Third Army Corps said last week that Ukrainian artillery fire has prevented Moscow from bringing up reserve forces, equipment, and ammunition to regain positions it had lost. Drones assessed damage and eliminated remaining targets.
Artillery was responsible for a larger share of casualties in the war's early stages, but drones are now the biggest killer. ISW analysts wrote in an October 9 battlefield assessment that artillery remains relevant even in a drone-dominated fight.

The Trump administration plans a public killing
Pete Hegseth’s “barbaric” plan for a livestreamed execution, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is planning a public killing.
What’s happening? On Thursday, the Pentagon announced that it would execute Nidal Hasan, a former Army major sentenced to death for a 2009 mass shooting on a military base, publicly and on livestream.
The execution, if it happens, would be unprecedented: The last widely reported public execution in the US was 90 years ago, in Kentucky, but to stream a death live would be something else entirely. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promoted the announcement with something approaching glee, telling a reporter that “we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.”
What’s the context? According to the Pentagon, Hasan will be executed via firing squad on December 3 — the first such execution by the military in more than 80 years.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 by a military jury following a court-martial for the 2009 shooting, when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at Fort Hood in Texas. The execution is set to be carried out at the same Army post.
Will the Pentagon go through with this? It’s unclear, for multiple reasons. The Pentagon’s announcement that Hasan’s death will be livestreamed has generated a great deal of bipartisan pushback, as well as condemnation by religious groups, though that is unlikely to stop the execution itself.
The head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops decried the decision to livestream the execution as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death,” and retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) called it the decision “beyond disgusting.”
“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis wrote in a post on X.
On Friday, Vice President JD Vance also said that he was unsure if the livestream would take place.
Hasan’s legal team could also delay the execution substantially — potentially for multiple years — by challenging his detention in federal court, though he has exhausted the military appeals process.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

3 killed as ‘drunk’ man rams his Mini Cooper into scooter in Keralam
The accused, identified as Suhail Sajeev, has been charged with culpable homicide.
A 19-year-old allegedly driving under the influence of alcohol rammed his Mini Cooper into a scooter near Cochin International Airport in Keralam in the early hours of Sunday, killing three people, police said.
The accused, identified as Suhail Sajeev, has been charged with culpable homicide, and police are investigating social media videos that purportedly show him driving at speeds exceeding 200 kmph on a highway.
The deceased were identified as Devika (21), a resident of Wayanad, Gopika (22), from Palakkad, and Ijaz (21), a resident of Dakshina Kannada in Karnataka. All three worked at a handicrafts shop and were travelling on the scooter when the accident occurred.
Eyewitnesses apprehended Sajeev and handed him over to the police.
“Prima facie, the accused was drunk at the time. We have collected his blood and urine samples for confirmation. We will also check if he had consumed any narcotic substances. He has been charged with culpable homicide,” said KS Sudarshan, Superintendent of Police, Ernakulam Rural.
The accident took place around 1.45 am on Sunday on the road leading to Cochin International Airport near Nedumbassery. The Mini Cooper, reportedly speeding, rammed into the scooter from behind, throwing the three riders onto the road with great force. They were rushed to nearby hospitals but succumbed to their injuries.
Priyad, a fellow employee of the deceased who was present at the time of the accident, told reporters that the Mini Cooper was being driven beyond permissible limits.
“All of us had stepped out at night to grab a cup of tea. The accident occurred while we were returning. While Devika, Gopika and Ijas were on a scooter ahead of us, I and a friend, were on a two-wheeler behind. Suddenly, I saw this Mini Cooper drive past me at great speed. I had to move sideways to avoid being hit. Soon, I heard a big sound ahead of us. It was a turn and I saw my friends splayed out on the road. The Mini Cooper had rammed into it,” Priyad told reporters.
Videos circulating on Instagram purportedly show Sajeev driving the Mini Cooper at speeds exceeding 200 kmph on a highway. Police are examining his social media accounts to determine whether he has a history of rash and negligent driving.
“Prima facie, it looks like he has a history of rash driving. We are verifying Instagram videos as well as footage from CCTV cameras at the spot. Forensic examination of the vehicle is also being done to look for traces of drugs,” Sudarshan said.
Police said the accused would undergo a medical examination before being produced before a magistrate on Sunday.

NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman pitched India’s investment opportunities to global institutional investors and financial institutions during a four-day visit to Singapore, highlighting infrastructure, semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), renewable energy and financial services as key areas for greater capital flows, the finance ministry said in a statement on Monday. The visit, from 8 to 11 October, included meetings with Singapore’s political leadership, financial authorities and major global investors, including BlackRock, JPMorgan Chase, Temasek, GIC, Carlyle and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA). Sitharaman encouraged investors to explore opportunities through the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and the Gujarat International Finance Tec-City International Financial Services Centre (GIFT IFSC). The government also highlighted select infrastructure projects for potential investment. Discussions focused on mobilizing long-term institutional capital for India’s infrastructure and development priorities and strengthening bilateral investment and financial cooperation, the ministry said. At a business roundtable with global investment firms, participants discussed India’s economic resilience amid global uncertainties, financial market developments and the implications of rapid advances in AI. Investors expressed confidence in India’s growth prospects and called for predictable, fiscally prudent and growth-oriented policies, alongside continued infrastructure investment. Separate meetings with senior executives of financial institutions and global corporations, including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Standard Chartered Bank, DBS Bank, Wellington Management, TPG, Intel and British International Investment, covered opportunities across several sectors. Discussions spanned consumer markets, start-ups, financial technology, healthcare, manufacturing, micro, small and medium enterprises, and trade finance. Other areas included data centres, semiconductors, renewable energy, electric mobility and aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul services. Meetings with Singapore’s financial authorities explored cooperation in emerging financial technologies, including asset tokenisation, digital money, central bank digital currencies and interoperable payment and settlement systems. The Monetary Authority of Singapore shared its approach to developing the digital asset ecosystem, including asset tokenization. Both sides discussed potential efficiency gains, regulatory challenges and the need for trusted settlement arrangements, the finance ministry said. The two countries also reviewed progress on the outcomes of the fourth India-Singapore Ministerial Roundtable and discussed ways to deepen their comprehensive strategic partnership. Talks covered capital markets, payments connectivity, digitalization, semiconductors, AI and cybersecurity, as well as stronger India-ASEAN economic cooperation ahead of Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship in 2027. Sitharaman also met Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Deputy Prime Minister and Trade and Industry Minister Gan Kim Yong, and Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan. India’s exports to Singapore fell 8.57% to $11.86 billion in FY26 from $12.98 billion in FY25, even as the two countries seek to deepen economic and investment ties. Singapore remains a key trade and investment partner for India. It was India’s largest trading partner within ASEAN in FY25, with bilateral trade of $34.26 billion, and a major source of foreign direct investment. The two countries have a Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA), in force since 2005, and are working to deepen trade and investment ties. Jota comeback helps Celtic lift gloom in strong response
- Published
After weeks of acrimony at Celtic, the full-time scenes at Fir Park on Sunday provided welcome cheer for a disgruntled fanbase.
Off the back of three straight defeats before the international break - two of them inflicted by rivals Rangers - Martin O'Neill's side returned to winning ways as they deservedly beat struggling Motherwell 2-0 and returned to the Scottish Premiership summit.
Camilo Duran fired the visitors in front early on and midfielder Benjamin Nygren made sure of victory in the second half.
On top of the performance and result, influential winger Jota made his long-awaited return from injury after almost 18 months on the sidelines and it was the Portuguese who led the post-match celebrations.
Jota had been introduced as a 74th-minute substitute and almost provided an assist with his first touches in a lively cameo.
"I was waiting on this for a long time," he told Sky Sports. "Just happy to be back. I've been working hard, the guys have been helping me as well. It was just the normal nerves, but after I stepped on the pitch everything goes well."
The 27-year-old was asked about the mental toll of his long spell out of action.
"Imagine if someone takes away your child and I've got my child back today - that's how I've been feeling the last year," he said.
"I found my child again today and I just want to keep it as long as I can.
"I'm feeling very good and I'm ready to play more and more and help the team. I know what I can do."
'O'Neill has his mojo back'
The party atmosphere at full-time was in stark contrast to the general gloom that has surrounded the club lately.
On top of the disappointing run of results before the international break, Celtic's largest shareholder, Dermot Desmond, was the target of a protest during the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament in St Andrews.
O'Neill questioned whether he had the energy to continue as manager after Rangers won at Parkhead last month, before committing to stay on.
"I could only imagine the pressure on Martin O'Neill - I know what it's like in Glasgow if you are beaten by Rangers twice," former Scotland defender Willie Miller said.
"But it seems like he's got his mojo back and is back to his old form and that's what results do.
"All round, when you look at his team, it must give him a lot of satisfaction."
O'Neill himself added: "Of course, there was a lot of noise and a lot of it we brought on ourselves as well too. So, nice to win.
"We have to take the criticism at the time. We lost three matches in a week - two to our big rivals. But we fought back today and let's see what Thursday brings.
What Thursday brings is undoubtedly a sterner test for O'Neill and Celtic with Portuguese giants Benfica lying in wait in the Europa League.
Celtic then host Hearts - who Benfica beat 7-2 on aggregate in European qualifiers earlier this term - before facing Celta Vigo in another stiff Europa League test.
They missed a heap of chances against Motherwell, with opposition goalkeeper Alex Paulsen making 12 saves, but O'Neill was not concerned by his side's profligacy.
"We had a lot of chances and we could have [scored more]," he said.
"The first goal's really important, a great goal by Camilo and it settled us down which was good.
"A lot of things have flashed across the box, a number of chances in both halves, but delighted to win.
"Just really pleased. Pleased with the performance, pleased with the energy that we showed and delighted to win.
"It's psychologically a big boost to play as well as we did and go back to the top of the table."

Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung
Pope Leo XIV has announced he will undergo surgery to remove a nodular lesion on his lung
VATICAN CITY -- Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a nodular lesion on his lung that was recently discovered during medical checks.
The 71-year-old pope said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or well-localized. The Vatican later said Leo would undergo surgery in the first days of the week, with an expected recovery time of a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is considered physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said during a recent medical check, “doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it."
“The surgery is already scheduled for the coming days. Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers,” he said.
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs.
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, to Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days.” In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.

New rule, no change - has cricket missed a trick again with bad light?
- Published
It is one of cricket's oldest and most frustrating problems: bad light.
A fascinating passage of play halted when things get too gloomy.
The issue has reared its head again this week in the fascinating first Test between South Africa and Australia in Durban, wiping out more than 60 overs across the first three days.
The fact a solution was added to cricket's rules just last week, an option so far unused around the world, only adds to the frustration.
- Australia veterans shine against South Africa 
  - Published11 hours ago
Bad light in mid-afternoon - what's gone on in Durban?
Play is already starting early, at 09:30 local time in Durban, given this is the first October Test at Kingsmead, a setting where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this time of year on South Africa's eastern coast.
Still, on day one, play was halted at 15:23 local time after clouds built. Only 65.2 of the scheduled 90 overs had been bowled and the players were unable to return.
Day two was slightly better with play continuing until 16:25, but that finish was still 35 minutes earlier than it could have been. Day three's end came at 16:31.
On each occasion, the first two sessions have been played in hot, sunny conditions, only for clouds to build in the afternoon - a familiar weather pattern in Durban.
"Very quickly in the morning, as temperatures have risen inland as the sun heats the ground, a sea breeze has formed with winds coming from the sea into Durban," said BBC weather presenter Chris Fawkes.
"This has increased humidity levels through the morning and brought some cloud in. As temperatures have started to fall again towards the evening, this has increased the relative humidity with the air getting increasingly saturated.
"That has caused the cloud to get thicker and lower."
What about the change in playing conditions?
Following a trial earlier in the year, the International Cricket Council amended its playing conditions to allow the pink ball to be used in Tests.
It was supposed to help in these exact scenarios.
Crucially, it does not allow a red ball to be switched for pink when the light becomes poor - something previously suggested by former England captain Michael Vaughan.
Instead, if problems with the light are expected, it allows teams to agree before a Test starts to use the pink ball throughout.
No such discussions were held between the Proteas and Australia before the Durban Test, however.
'There is a stigma around the pink ball'
The pink ball has been a fixture of day-night Tests because it is easier to see than the darker red in night-time conditions.
Former South Africa bowler Shaun Pollock was part of the ICC committee which recommended the change and he believes there is a "stigma" around the pink ball in the game.
"They say it moves too much," Pollock said.
"If Australia were 124-6 [as they were on day one] and we were using the pink ball, everyone would have said it was the pink ball's fault.
"If Australia were 124-6 and got to 390 [as they did in their first innings] everyone in South Africa would have said it was the pink ball's fault, that it got soft.
"The pink ball would have meant we played 45 more overs of Test cricket and that is why I am keen to introduce it, and not just for day-night games."
Why might teams not want to use the pink ball?
One narrative exists that the pink ball moves more under floodlights, though that is not backed up by ball tracking data.
Instead, various batters have spoken about the pink ball being more difficult to see. Batting averages are lowest in the evening of day-night matches.
Australia have also played in 15 of Test cricket's day-nighters - 10 more than anyone else.
Unsurprisingly, the four leading wicket-takers in day-night matches are all Australians. Left-armer Mitchell Starc's haul of 89 wickets in 15 Tests has positioned him as the undisputed pink-ball king.
You would not blame teams if they would rather face Australia with the red ball.
Former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander said he prefers the idea of switching balls during the match if conditions require it, but that would raise questions over the Test's integrity.
Is the potential injustice of one team having to face a pink ball outweighed by the need to get more action of the field?

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.
The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

“Have you ever clicked your mouse HERE? You will.” That was the text accompanying the first banner ad on the internet, launched by telecommunications company AT&T on HotWired.com in 1994. The ad reportedly clocked a 44% click-through rate in its first four months, a figure that would be extraordinary by the standards of almost any digital marketing channel today. Over three decades, online advertising has evolved from banner ads to search, social media, programmatic buying, influencer marketing and performance marketing. Then, with the emergence of search engine optimisation (SEO) practices, brands started optimising websites, building backlinks, targeting keywords and creating content to improve their visibility. Over time, SEO grew into a $90 Bn industry. But the search box is now changing again. Today, a growing number of consumers are turning to AI assistants instead of typing keywords into Google and opening a dozen links. Whether they are looking for accounting software, a nearby restaurant or the best smartphone under ₹50,000, they can simply ask an AI assistant for recommendations. Their interaction with AI is no longer limited to a query or a list of results. Users/consumers ask follow-up questions, compare options, refine their requirements, and direct AI to recommend what they should buy. This is where answer engine optimisation (AEO) and generative engine optimisation (GEO) have emerged as a new trend. But there is no single platform to optimise for, no standard ranking system and no clear way to measure success. Much like what the SEO function was in its early days, marketers are still figuring out what works. Agencies are experimenting with how brands appear in answers generated by ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI-powered search products. They are tracking brand mentions, citations and recommendations, while trying to understand why one company gets surfaced over another. But as brands scramble to show up in AI-generated answers, a bigger question is emerging: How can they ensure they are not just recommended by AI, but show up at the right moment? The Missing Link In AI Marketing Currently, for brands, the challenge is not how to appear in AI answers but figure out whether that visibility brings more visitors, customers or sales. Google historically gave marketers detailed visibility through tools such as Search Console and keyword-level paid search data. This model is considerably harder to replicate when consumers interact with AI through multi-step conversations. AI platforms currently offer limited visibility into the prompts driving discovery. A user may start with a broad question, ask several follow-ups, compare products, and only then arrive at a purchase decision. For marketers, identifying which interaction influenced that journey is harder than attributing a click to a specific search query. Organic visibility is also inconsistent across platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity. For queries around the “best” or “top” products and services, AI models may rely heavily on third-party publishers, reviews and user-generated content rather than brand websites. As a result, brands need to build a consistent information ecosystem across websites, ads, influencers and third-party platforms. “So, eventually, for optimising, it becomes a lot more important to produce content in the broader ecosystem. We often ask brands to be consistent with their communication,” said Rishabh Mahendru, senior vice president of client success and growth at AdLift. Marketers are also grappling with how much control they have over their brands' visibility in AI-driven discovery. AI platforms can answer users' questions without sending them to an external website. These zero-click answers may be convenient for consumers, but they can reduce traffic to publisher and brand websites. Even when AI search leads to a sale, tracing that purchase back to a specific interaction can be difficult. A consumer may discover a brand through an AI assistant, research it elsewhere and make a purchase days later. Traditional last-click attribution models may fail to capture the role AI played in that journey. There is also less certainty around where and how brands appear. AI platforms determine which ads match a user's intent, while changes in how models cite sources can make organic visibility unpredictable. Brands also risk appearing alongside misinformation, hate speech or polarising content in AI-generated responses. To address these, OpenAI is exploring geo-based ad experiments and brand-suitability pilots to give advertisers more insight into where their ads appear and how they perform. Overall, with its ChatGPT Ads in India, OpenAI is bringing sponsored messages into conversations on the AI chatbot in one of its largest markets. Ads have been rolled out to users on Free and Go tiers, while Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Education users get an ad-free experience. More than 50 brands were planned to go live during the initial rollout, with WPP and Omnicom as OpenAI's first agency partners in India. Businesses can access ChatGPT's self-serve Ads Manager, with daily budgets starting at ₹725. The Next Frontier Of Brand Visibility With no standard way to measure AI search visibility or predict which brands will surface in AI-generated answers, startups are building tools to help businesses navigate the new landscape. Antler-incubated RankinLLM, for instance, is building a GEO and AI search visibility platform. “We operate across three layers: an observability layer to track LLM activity, an intelligence layer to extract meaningful signals from noisy data, and an optimisation layer to fix identified gaps. Optimiser agents create a closed loop, while KPIs such as brand mentions, share of voice, citations and sentiment measure the impact,” said cofounder and CEO Kartik Sharma. Bengaluru-based TruCommerce has taken a different approach. It initially built a tool to track how often brands appeared in AI-generated answers. But it found that much of the traffic coming from AI platforms was being wrongly counted as direct website visits. This led the startup to shift its focus to helping brands sell directly through AI platforms. TruCommerce now connects brands' product catalogues and inventory with AI assistants. This helps businesses track visitors coming from AI, make product information easier for AI tools to understand, and enable customers to buy products without leaving the conversation. Meanwhile, Lightspeed-backed Gushwork helps small and medium-sized businesses attract potential customers through traditional search engines and AI tools. Its AI agents create content designed to appear in search results, while its platform tracks the enquiries this content generates. Other startups, including Nexad, Parsnip and AdCreative AI, are also building tools to help brands advertise and improve their visibility across AI platforms. For marketers, however, this shift is still in its early stages. Traditional SEO took decades to develop its tools, metrics and best practices. AI is at the same crossroads.

Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
- Published
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".
Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.
For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.
Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.
The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.
In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.
The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.
Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.
The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.
Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune
He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October.
Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.
Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.
A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.
To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.
Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.
When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.
Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.
Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.
An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.
MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.
A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".
MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.
This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.
Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.
So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.
Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.
Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."
In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.
MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.
It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.
Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.
MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.
Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.
Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents."
Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal."
Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate".
Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
MeritServus closed following the Cyprus Confidential leak.
