I’ve Been Tracking My Weight for Years. These Are the Best Smart Scales
Featured in this article
After years of sleepiness, the smart scale world has finally woken up—driven almost certainly by the GLP-1 craze, as millions of consumers find themselves wondering if those weekly jabs are actually working.
What was previously a category occupied by dated gear has abruptly exploded, and for good reason. Today’s smart scales don’t just report on your weight; they do things like measure your heart rate and break down muscle composition, and some can even give you an eye on your heart health, courtesy of technology like integrated ECG systems. Through mobile apps, they can track all of this information over time.
The big shift in the category in the past year has been a flood of new full-body scanners hitting the market from all corners. Essentially bathroom scales with handlebar-based scanners, these don’t just use bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) to measure conductivity (and, thus, body fat percentage) through your feet. They can now scan through your hands, too, giving you a much more holistic (and ostensibly accurate) look at your body metrics than a floor scale will provide. I’ve personally seen body fat percentage numbers swing up to 6 percent between the two types of scales. (Spoiler: The full-body scanner data is always higher.)
Do you really need all that information? I’ve long suggested that it’s really the trend line that matters most, not the absolute numbers, and as long as your metrics are headed in the right direction, it doesn’t matter quite as much whether things are off by a small percentage. Consistent weigh-ins are the most important part of the process, along with tracking that information over time to determine whether your diet and workout regimen (or medication routine) is getting you the results you need.
Mind you, scale prices are headed up, and new full-body scanners can now top $600 for top-tier tech. That’s part of the reason why I still recommend a standard scale for most users, as these devices are considerably less expensive, and the results they offer are likely to be good enough for all but serious athletes.
Either way, this roundup has an option for every type of user.
Updated October 2026: I've added Withings’ BodyScan 2 and new honorable mentions from Runstar, Tanita, and Withings. I've also added scales to avoid and ensured up-to-date prices throughout.
How Do Smart Scales Work?
Smart scales come in two basic flavors: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. The former connects directly to your phone to sync its readings. The latter uses your home’s wireless network to sync readings straight to the cloud, which your phone’s app can then access. Wi-Fi scales are generally more expensive but more versatile. While older scales often featured erratic wireless connections, newer models have many of their kinks worked out—and firmware updates have improved connectivity.
Virtually all smart scales use the same type of system to gauge your additional vitals: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which involves sending a minuscule electric current up one leg and measuring what happens when it comes down the other side. Some mathematical magic converts all of this into any number of derived measurements about things like your body’s percentage of fat, water, and bone; body-mass index (BMI); and, sometimes, arcana like your basal metabolic rate (BMR), which is a measure of your body’s energy consumption at rest. All the scales I tested can sync data with Apple Health and Google's Health Connect, either directly or by passing data via the app.
When Is the Best Time to Weigh Yourself?
Most experts say that the best time to weigh in is first thing in the morning, before you’ve eaten and after you’ve used the restroom. The main reason for this is consistency: Weighing yourself at the same time every day is the best way to ensure that consecutive weigh-ins are taken under conditions that are as controlled as possible. Since eating and drinking will cause your weight to fluctuate considerably, weighing yourself on an empty stomach means you’re getting an apples-to-apples comparison each morning.
As a small bonus, your weight is usually at its lowest right after you wake up, so you potentially stand to give yourself a gentle confidence boost by stepping on the scale then instead of after dinner.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Other Smart Scales
Renpho MorphoScan for $170: The Renpho MorphoScan full-body scanner looks surprisingly similar to the Runstar FG2015, including a near-identical display attached to the handlebars. Well, spoiler alert: They are basically the same scale. They even use the same app to collect data (you can use both scales simultaneously with the app).
Runstar Smart Body Fat Scale (FG2015) for $140: My former pick for best full-body scanner, this admittedly garish offering tracks 20 metrics and supports 24 users, effectively breaking down information, limb-by-limb, in its Starfit mobile app. USB-C rechargeability is a nice plus, but the price tag—just $140 if you buy it directly from Runstar—is probably its best feature.
Tanita RD-953 InnerScan Pro for $230: One of the few new feet-only smart scales to hit the market this decade, Tanita’s RD-953 is defined by its Cylonesque looks—and its relative simplicity. The costly Bluetooth-only scale scans quickly, though the placement of its display in the center of the scale, right between your feet, can be awkward for those with even a small breadbasket between their head and the floor. I also didn’t love the very high and hopefully overstated body fat reading the scale gave me, but my harshest criticism is directed at the Healthy Edge app (a different app than is used by Tanita’s other scale), which is about as engaging and motivational as a shopping list on a Post-It Note.
Withings BodyFit for $230: The middle child in the Withings family sits comfortably between the no-holds-barred BodyScan 2 and the feet-only Body Comp Smart Scale, offering a pleasant alternative for users who want full-body analysis but don’t need (or want to pay for) the fitness extremism of Withings’s top-tier model. It’s a sleek and demure unit with a small but informative color screen, quick Wi-Fi connectivity, and fast performance—and, of course, it works seamlessly with Withings’s excellent app.
Arboleaf Body Fat Scale CS20W for $50: This affordable Bluetooth scale isn’t the most eye-catching I’ve tested in light of its big silver electrodes and an oversized display that comes across as a bit garish. While weight is easy to make out, the six additional statistics showcased are difficult to read, all displayed simultaneously. I like the Arboleaf app better than the scale, where five additional metrics are available, each featuring a helpful explanation when tapped. It’s a solid deal at this price, but the upsell to get an “intelligent interpretation report” for an extra $40 per year is probably safe to skip.
Hume Health Body Pod for $229: Hume Health’s Body Pod, another full-body scanner with handles, is heavily advertised—at least to the apps on my phone—and touted (by Hume) as the Next Big Thing in the world of body management. While the app is indeed glossy and inviting, I was shocked to discover how flimsy the hardware felt, that it lacked Wi-Fi, and that some features are locked behind a $100-a-year Hume Plus subscription plan. It works fine enough, but you can get results that are just as good with a cheaper device.
Garmin Index S2 for $200: Five years after its release, the Index S2 is still Garmin’s current model, a surprise for a company otherwise obsessed with fitness. It’s still noteworthy for its lovely color display, which walks you through its six body metrics (for up to 16 users) with each weigh-in. The display also provides your weight trend over time in graphical form and can even display the weather. The scale connects directly to Wi-Fi and Garmin’s cloud-based storage system, so—unlike with Bluetooth-only scales—you don’t need a phone nearby to track your progress. A phone running the Garmin Connect app (Android, iOS) is handy, so you can keep track of everything over time. Unfortunately, as health apps go, Connect is a bit of a bear, so expect a learning curve—especially if you want to make changes to the way the scale works. You can turn its various LCD-screen widgets on or off in the app, but finding everything can be difficult due to the daunting scope of the Garmin ecosystem. The color screen is nice at first, but it ultimately adds little to the package.
Omron BCM-500 for $85: With its large LCD panel, quartet of onboard buttons, and oversize silver electrodes, the Omron BCM-500 is an eye-catching masterwork of brutalist design. If your bathroom is decked out in concrete and wrought iron, this scale will fit right in. The Bluetooth unit syncs with Omron’s HeartAdvisor app (Android, iOS), but it provides all six of its body metrics directly on the scale, cycling through them with each weigh-in (for up to four users). It can be difficult to read the label for each of the data points, in part because the LCD isn’t backlit, but the app is somewhat easier to follow, offering front-page graphs of weight, skeletal muscle, and body fat. On the other hand, the presentation is rather clinical, and the app is surprisingly slow to sync. For a scale without a Wi-Fi connection, it’s also rather expensive.
Smart Scales to Avoid
Renpho MorphoScan Lite for $95: This new entry-level offering in the MorphoScan line is specifically designed for new GLP-1 users. It's a simpler device, ditching the handheld display and, critically, Wi-Fi connectivity. It’s also one of the flimsiest scales I’ve tested—too lightweight for you to extend the handlebars without inadvertently dragging the scale across the floor. If this were a mega-bargain in line with foot-only scale pricing, I’d be sold, but the meager savings compared to other MorphoScan scales don’t justify considering it.
Tanita RD-545 InnerScan Pro for $480: This monstrous, industrial scale looks more like it belongs in the mailroom than the bathroom, and its level of complexity only provides more supportive evidence. The Bluetooth-only scale is confusing to set up and difficult to use correctly, and I was only able to get successful measurements by first opening the mobile app and ensuring the scale was connected before carefully stepping onto it. Then, I had to wait for a prompt to pick up the handles (while balanced on the device). Testing feels like it takes forever, and that’s even if you get it right the first time. For $480, the scale is a questionable value at best, despite its 40 measurements offered. No Wi-Fi at this price, really?

Ahead of the INDIA alliance’s planned march to the Supreme Court on Monday, Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant responded to a letter from the Leader of the Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, advising him to invoke the Court’s judicial powers under Article 32 rather than submit a memorandum. The opposition’s planned "Chalo Dilli – March for Democracy" comes at a time when there are growing concerns over alleged vote theft, irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, and the conduct of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Quick answers to key questions The CJI declined the meeting but did not publicly disclose the specific reason, citing the confidentiality of his letter. The reports also said similar matters were sub judice in the Supreme Court. He advised Gandhi to invoke the Supreme Court’s judicial powers under Article 32 and file a petition rather than submit a memorandum. They sought to raise allegations of ‘vote theft’ and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and to present their demands to the CJI. The reported demands included ending alleged vote theft, halting the SIR exercise and seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. The leaders also sought a return to paper ballots. The alliance planned a march to the Supreme Court and said it would file a petition against alleged vote theft and irregularities in the SIR exercise. According to Bar and Bench, which shared a copy of the letter on social media, CJI Surya Kant told Congress MP Rahul Gandhi and party president Mallikarjun Kharge that a "meeting to discuss pending cases would violate the principle of separation of powers and be incompatible with judicial ethics and propriety," and noted that the apex court does not have any "administrative powers to deal with the issues raised in their letter." Responding to the letter written by Gandhi and Kharge, CJI Surya Kant noted that the issues raised were similar to those listed for a hearing before the court on 13 October. He also advised the opposition leaders to invoke the Court’s judicial powers under Article 32 instead of submitting a memorandum. Further, the leaders were informed that they could file petitions physically on Monday between 10:30 am and 4:30 pm or through e-filing at any time. The Wisconsin gubernatorial race was one of the most closely watched Democratic primaries in the country this year, pitting a democratic socialist, state Rep. Francesca Hong, against Milwaukee Democrat David Crowley, who received the endorsement of the state’s sitting Democratic governor, Tony Evers.
Why Francesca Hong is still on the campaign trail
After a loss in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial primary, Hong is focused on ensuring a Democratic trifecta in the state.
Hong lost the race, setting up Crowley to face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in the general election this fall. But she’s already back on the campaign trail, this time trying to help Democrats win a trifecta in the state: the governor’s race and both legislative chambers.
Unifying the state’s voters to achieve that won’t be easy, though. Hong spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about her own loss, Evers’s role in it, and whether or not the voters who felt so passionate about her own campaign would find enough to love in Crowley’s campaign — in particular on the increasingly important issue of data centers.
Astead and Hong also talked about what Wisconsin means for the Democrats nationally, and what lessons the party should take from her race, including her loss.
“I said this, and I will continue to say it — the person who is most electable is the person who ended up getting the most votes, and that was Crowley this time around,” Hong said. “But I think there’s a disservice when you have the most powerful Democrat in the state choosing to ignore a lot of voters and people who were inspired and energized and coming out to participate in politics for the first time through our campaign. I think it was shortsighted to use electability almost as a fear tactic.”
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Hong, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Part of the reason we wanted to come here was because we saw you were getting back on the campaign trail, and specifically around that idea of energizing Wisconsin toward a trifecta.
Now, just tell me the difference in terms of the importance of Democrats winning it all — not only the governor’s mansion, but both houses of the state legislature — versus just the governor’s mansion. How does that change the possibilities of what the party could do?
For the last 16 years, a Republican majority in the state legislature has meant that passing the types of policies that we know can drastically improve the lives of everyday folks here in Wisconsin stalled. And we have a historic opportunity to flip the assembly and the state Senate and hold the governor’s mansion and the entire executive branch to a Democratic majority, meaning the opportunity to pass the policies that the majority of our state supports — things like increasing minimum wage, things like legalizing marijuana, codifying abortion.
We also need to repeal Act 10 [which dramatically restricted collective bargaining rights for public-sector employees]. Wisconsin is where workers’ rights, things like unemployment insurance, Social Security were born, and we moved backwards with the Republican majority. That’s all on the table with the Democratic trifecta.
It also, though, raises the political standard of what Democrats would have to do to achieve that, and some of it goes through these more rural communities.
Why do we think the party has fallen behind in more rural communities, and what could be done to reverse that?
I think it’s important to look at what’s happened in the rural communities when we’ve seen manufacturing jobs leave the state, when we’ve seen fewer and fewer supports for our small farmers.
And so much of this — what connects it — is actually the growth of massive wealth and corporate control and corporate greed, and more people feeling the impacts of that. There’s an opportunity right now to say, ‘Hey, Republicans have been in the legislature, they’ve been in power, and things have not improved for you or your community … Now’s the opportunity to make sure that we’re actually able to see our shared Wisconsin values of working hard and taking care of our kids be reflected back in Madison through laws.’
So much of your campaign was focused on data centers, stopping data centers. Should I think of that as a rural issue?
I think the issue around data centers is an everyone issue. It’s a democracy issue. It’s people wanting to feel like there are folks who care about what happens to communities, and that they have control and an actual say in what happens in their communities.
To that point, is it a mistake for David Crowley, the Democratic nominee, to have not gone as far as you did and say, “We won’t be building more data centers for a period of time”?
He’s fighting for communities and community control when it comes to data centers.
But it’s not a moratorium.
But it’s not a moratorium. It isn’t, but he’s also committed to 100 percent renewable energy, clean energy to power data centers.
And achieving that is going to be incredibly difficult, and it is going to be the developers having to pay their own way, and these are things that he’s committed to that we know can slow down the growth and development of data centers.
Have you had time to reflect on your primary loss? If you had to diagnose, why do you think you lost?
I’m still doing a lot of reflection. But I think that I want to continue to look forward. And what I’ve learned from our election is that it’s so important to continue to stay grounded in becoming accessible to people. I think that as an organizer and an elected official, it’s my responsibility to continue to go to the people and remain very in touch with what’s going on on the ground.
I have a couple more questions about the nature of the loss. Evers’s endorsement changed that race, so much so that your opponent David Crowley was able even to win in some smaller communities, like places where you were pitching yourself as the voice of more rural communities.
Does that disprove any of this thesis around, say, data centers? If that was the top priority for Wisconsin voters, wouldn’t you be the nominee?
I think it wasn’t all rural communities. It wasn’t all suburban communities. We saw certain demographics but also ZIP codes where we outperformed David significantly.
And I think that where the governor’s endorsement played a bigger role was areas where he was also more popular.
Did it surprise you when Evers endorsed Crowley?
I was disappointed.
Why?
I was disappointed because I was getting a lot of feedback from folks who hadn’t committed to any candidate yet that this felt like the governor was putting his thumb on the scale.
I wanted to ask about electability, because it seemed as if Evers’s endorsement was about a fear that maybe you couldn’t win in November.
So much of the primary concern was around the DSA label, even campaigning with folks like Hasan Piker. In retrospect, was any of that a mistake?
We knew going in that we would have to encourage new voters to come out, folks who typically do not come out for primaries, quote-unquote low-propensity voters. And we knew that we would have to campaign in places where folks weren’t expecting to see a gubernatorial candidate. And those included Twitch streams.
Those also included going to dive bars and bowling alleys and making sure that we were accessible and shaping our policies based on what the people were telling us they wanted to see happen and also what they wanted to see out of their governor. I think electability… I said this, and I will continue to say it — the person who is most electable is the person who ended up getting the most votes, and that was Crowley this time around.
But I think there’s a disservice when you have the most powerful Democrat in the state choosing to ignore a lot of voters and people who were inspired and energized and coming out to participate in politics for the first time through our campaign.
I think it was shortsighted to use electability almost as a fear tactic, when Democrats need to be inspiring and project a vision where everyone can see themselves in it as everyday working-class folks.
When you’ve got a party that has struggled with elitism to then cave to an establishment narrative … being more afraid of labels when I’m hearing from people on the ground that they’re interested in solutions and solving problems, maybe somebody who knows the hustle of the service industry and running restaurants and has worked across the aisle to pass bipartisan legislation. There are ways that we can maneuver around labels and what the loudest narrative might be.
I wish our governor hadn’t fed into that.
To be fair, to your point, the establishment label doesn’t fully fit even someone like Crowley, who comes from a working-class background. But am I hearing that you think Evers’s move made your life in the general election more difficult?
Is it harder to re-inspire if young people who are invested in the Hong campaign think that the establishment squashed them out?
We still had over 300,000 votes. We lost by fewer than 4,000 votes. I had more votes than Evers did during his primary. That’s not squashing our voices.
We’re still here, and it’s so important that people find avenues to continue to exercise their voice and their new organizing power. And I’m definitely going to continue to work to make sure that we get results and that we win the trifecta, and that’s the most important thing we should be focusing on right now.
I hear why a trifecta matters in the state context, particularly the state policy.
If I’m someone, though, who’s not in Wisconsin, who’s just worried about Donald Trump running amok in Washington, why should I care if Democrats win the governor’s mansion and the state legislature? Does that matter for folks outside of the state?
Because we will start to see that when you feel government actually working and you see change happening in your lives, these are then voters who are going to continue to come out and vote for Democrats.
We’re a pivotal state when it comes to the federal elections as well. We’re actually in a swing district right now.
We have an opportunity, through Wisconsin, to actually start improving the brand for Democrats. And if we do that here, this trickles out to the rest of the country.
The premise being that delivering creates a connection for Democrats that is helpful in the presidential election, and it’s helpful in all these other ways too.
Yeah. We’re not going to be fighting every single midterm and presidential for our lives based on what’s happening in just one state.
But I think if we can start showing durable power for Democrats in a state like ours because of the policies that we’re prioritizing, and you have more folks coming out to vote for Democrats, that’s good for the health of democracy.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO says he's prepared to fight Canada in court over Stelco layoffs

The CEO of the American company that owns Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco says he's prepared to fight the Canadian government in court to preserve Stelco's plan to lay off hundreds of workers.
Speaking Sunday on CBC's Rosemary Barton Live, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government's characterization that the company is violating binding employment commitments under the Investment Canada Act.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said last week that Cleveland-Cliffs' 2024 purchase of Stelco included "undertakings to continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced" through 2029.
"There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years," Goncalves said on Sunday. "If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted."
Goncalves reiterated Stelco's position that the layoffs are a temporary measure until Canada and the U.S. reach a trade agreement, and that the jobs will be restored.
He also said he's open to selling the company and voiced support for U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, despite Stelco citing tariffs as a key reason for its economic struggles.
Ultimatum from Canadian government
Joly issued an ultimatum to the company last week: share a plan to save the up to 500 jobs that could be impacted at the Hamilton plant or face potential legal action.
Prime Minister Mark Carney also said last week that Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the Ohio-based company to the "fullest extent of the law."
Stelco Inc. said in a letter responding to Joly that the company will proceed with the layoffs and the government's characterization of the move as a breach of undertakings is "false."

The company emphasized "Stelco's situation is a result of factors beyond its control," citing the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs.
But Goncalves said Sunday he supports steel tariffs against Canada.
"I am in favour of tariffs against all the countries in the entire world that dump steel into the United States," he said, adding that the Section 232 tariffs have brought "the American steel industry back."
A drone photograph shows the Stelco Hamilton Works steel mill, owned by Cleveland-Cliffs, in Hamilton last month. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)
"I'm in favour of Section 232. There's no doubt about it."
Asked whether he would consider selling the company, Goncalves said, "For a good offer, yes," but added that he still believes the company can "continue to be a good citizen in Canada."
He told CBC News in a previous interview that he "would not have acquired the Stelco if I knew that Canada and the United States would become what they became — enemies in trade."

Quick Answer
Turn rough screen recordings into polished demos with tools that auto-zoom on clicks, follow and smooth the cursor, add clean framing, and highlight key actions. Options include Screen Studio, FocuSee, Screen Awesome, and ScreenCursor.
When you record a two-minute walkthrough of your app, for instance, a setting buried five menus deep, or a spreadsheet trick you are proud of, there is something that can leave you frustrated. You press play, and the cursor is dancing all around without highlighting what you actually wanted to show. Either the text is too small to read on a phone or the whole thing looks like security-camera footage of your desktop. The old-school way is to use a video editor, add zooms by hand, pan the camera to follow your cursor, and nudge keyframes for an hour. Thankfully, there is a newer batch of screen recorders that automatically do that part for you.
In this guide, we have covered four of them. They not only differ in price, platform, and functionality, but each one also has one detail that surprised me.
|  | Screen Studio | FocuSee | Screen Awesome | ScreenCursor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Works on | Mac only | Windows and Mac | Chrome (also Edge, Brave and similar) | Chrome (Mac, Windows, Linux) | 
| Price | $9/mo billed yearly, or $29/mo | Free trial, paid plans | Free | $49 one-time (early pricing) | 
| Best for | Maximum polish on a Mac | All-in-one AI extras | Privacy and zero cost | Pay-once simplicity | 
Table of Contents
Why do raw screen recordings look so rough?
When you use any standard screen recorder, like the one built into your OS, it captures pixels and nothing else. It has no idea what mattered. It doesn’t know if you clicked a tiny button that you want the viewers to look at. The result? You get a full-screen recording of everything, including your cursor wandering here and there. Viewers watch these videos on laptops and phones, and since the important part is not zoomed in or clearly shown, they will miss it. A better screen recording would be one where:
- Zoom is on the action so people can actually read what you click.
- A camera that follows your cursor instead of leaving viewers guessing.
- A cursor that glides rather than jitters.
- A clean frame, such as a gradient background and rounded corners.
With all of the above, your screen recording not only looks professional but also provides clear instructions for viewers.
Screen recorders with auto cursor follow and zoom
Here are some of the best screen recorders that you can use for automatic cursor follow and zoom.
Screen Studio: The one the others get compared to
If you are on Mac, then Screen Studio is one of the best options for screen recording with automatic cursor follow and zoom. When you’re recording using Screen Studio, it looks at what you did, like where you clicked, and zooms in on the moments that matter. Every zoom is balanced and animated automatically; you don’t have to worry about handling them. The best part is that you can choose between two styles: Classic zoom is the one you usually see in polished product videos. Then there is Loupe zoom, which is a magnifier-style alternative. If you want to zoom somewhere the app did not automatically add one, you can drop it onto the timeline and point it where you like. Notably, the cursor gets the same treatment. Shaky movement is smoothed out into a steady glide, and clicks get a soft ripple. Fast movements pick up motion blur so they look filmed rather than captured. You also have the option to change the cursor’s size and style later. Some of the notable features of Screen Studio are:
- Edit by transcript: Delete a sentence from the transcript, and it disappears from the video. Filler words and long pauses can be cleared in one pass.
- One recording, many shapes: Record once, then switch the aspect ratio between wide (16:9), square (1:1), and vertical (9:16). Zooms can be re-aimed, layouts rearranged, and captions moved to stay readable. You can also choose the “Reel mode” that shows where Instagram’s or TikTok’s interface would cover your video, so you’re in the grey area where your inputs get hidden.
- Hide the private stuff: If the recording shows an API key or email address, you can mask it after the recording is complete, and the mask blends into the interface around it.
- iPhone and iPad framing: Plug your iPhone or iPad into a USB cable, pick the device, and record. Screen Studio wraps the footage in a matching device frame.
FocuSee: The Windows-friendly all-rounder
FocuSee comes from the house of iMobie and is a screen recording tool that works on both Windows and Mac. This already makes it the practical choice for many people working on either OS. FocuSee’s auto zoom follows your clicks and even your typing. This tool adds a spotlight to highlight areas worth noticing, making it much easier for anyone following your instructions. You can also choose a “3D Motion” mode that adds tilt and perspective that follows your cursor, for a more cinematic look. The cursor can fade out when you are not actively using it or don’t need it and reappears when you do. Similar to other screen recording tools, you can swap the cursor style and click animations. There are a bunch of features that deserve to be highlighted.
- A built-in teleprompter: You can show your script on screen while recording with the option to adjust the font size, speed, and position. If you tend to forget the script midway, this alone might sell you.
- An annotation suite: You can add text, shapes, arrows, callouts, spotlights, and blur effects. Moreover, you can stack several layers to walk viewers through a tricky step, or blur out something sensitive.
- An AI avatar: This one is for those who are camera-shy or do not want their face in the video. FocuSee can create a digital presenter, or in simple words, an AI avatar. It is a niche feature, but a handy one for company tutorials.
- Smart cleanup: You can remove filler words and silence with just one click, and also enhance voice and reduce noise with just a button.
- Background fixes for your webcam: It can blur or replace a messy room behind you after recording without needing a green screen.
- Add Subtitles: FocuSee supports speech recognition in over 50 languages, with accuracy above 98%. You can add your own subtitles and make it easier for the follower to go through the steps.
Screen Awesome: Free, and it can’t upload your recordings
Screen Awesome is a different kind of tool. It’s actually a free Chrome extension built by a developer named Nitinbhai Viras. On one hand, most apps say “we respect your privacy” and simply ask you to take their word; Screen Awesome does things a bit differently. Screen Awesome points you at Chrome’s own permission screen and requests no access to any website. It is not allowed to contact any server. That means it cannot upload your recordings, even if it wanted to. The best part is that you can verify this yourself in about 30 seconds. Head over to chrome://extensions, find Screen Awesome, click Details, and look at the Site access line. According to the developer, it reads none. On the extension’s settings page, there is a button that jumps you straight there. On top of this security, you get this tool for absolutely free. Here are some features that set Screen Awesome apart:
- Auto-zoom to clicks: While recording a browser tab, Screen Awesome notes where you click. A virtual camera follows each click and pans between them. You have the option to preview it, turn it off, or export the file. This works for tab recording.
- Serious annotation tools: Arrows, pen, highlighter, shapes, text, speech bubbles, step counters, emoji stamps, and a blur that destroys the pixels rather than just smudging them. You can edit all of these marks.
- Product-shot framing: You can place a recording on a backdrop with rounded corners, a soft shadow, and an optional browser window around it, and also change its aspect ratio to 16:9, etc.
- Formats: You can export your recording in MP4, WebM, or an animated GIF.
- Webcam and voice: Screen Awesome lets you mix in your microphone and the tab’s audio, and even add a movable webcam bubble while recording if you want to show your face.
ScreenCursor: Pay once, and record in Chrome
ScreenCursor is another screen recording tool that works as a Chrome extension. However, its approach is the opposite of Screen Awesome’s. Notably, it does one thing and tries to do it well, which is turning clicks into camera moves with as little fuss as possible. When you hit the record button, ScreenCursor waits three seconds before it starts. That gap is deliberate, and it exists because Chrome shows its own “sharing your screen” bar while recording, and unfortunately it cannot be switched off. With this delay, you get the time to collapse the bar before the screen recording starts. Every click, drag, and keystroke gets zoomed in. Each zoom happens a beat before the action; this way, viewers are already looking at the right spot, then the camera holds steady and follows your cursor. ScreenCursor gives you the option to manually retime a zoom, push its depth in or out, switch the motion between snappy and gentle, or delete the zoom you don’t want. Here are some of the highlights of ScreenCursor:
- Zoom focus point: Right-click any zoom, drag a box over the part you want people to see, and the zoom shows exactly that. You can use this on recordings of desktop apps, since ScreenCursor can record your whole screen.
- Customization: You also get wallpapers, gradients, or use your own image as a backdrop. There is a browser frame that carries the real page title. Editing is also possible, as you can split the clip, delete boring stretches, and speed up slow ones.
- Price and limits: It costs $49 once, which is labeled “early pricing,” with $79 shown as the regular price. After one-time payment, you will continue to receive updates and can work on up to three of your own computers.

PRAGUE -- A political group led by Prime Minister Andrej Babiš faced a strong challenge from the opposition in the Czech Republic’s first round of voting to fill one-third of the seats in Parliament’s upper house, the Senate, according to the final results released on Sunday.

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal
- Published
According to the man who helped catch them, it was blind luck.
Sandpapergate, the scandal that engulfed Australia eight years ago, was blatant cheating played out in real time on live television to a global audience.
As the Aussies prepare for their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering controversy in Cape Town, the director of the TV coverage that day admits serendipity took down Steve Smith and co.
"The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke," Alvin Naicker, in charge of SuperSport's live broadcast from Newlands, tells BBC Sport.
Not just one fluke, but a series of them.
That the "leadership group" of the Australian team hatched their plan during the lunch break on that Saturday afternoon in March 2018; that an alert camera operator lingered on Cameron Bancroft when others would have turned their attention elsewhere; that the big-screen controller showed in the ground what was also being broadcast to millions around the world.
In understanding how Bancroft was rumbled, a little knowledge of how live cricket is shown on TV is helpful.
"Coverage of rugby and football is very coordinated. It's camera one and two, then when the ball is dead you tell the story with close-up shots," explains Naicker, a highly respected and popular figure in the TV industry with more than 30 years' experience.
"Because cricket has so much dead time, there is a lot more storytelling. There are between 80 and 100 people coming together and putting the story together in a matter of seconds, coordinated by the director."
Captain Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Bancroft later explained they cooked up the ball-tampering plot during lunch on the third day of the third Test.
Reverse-swing had been a key factor in the first two Tests of a bad-tempered series: Warner clashed with Quinton de Kock in the first Test in Durban, then Smith was involved in an altercation with Kagiso Rabada in the second.
Australia were exposed before the afternoon session was done, thanks to Naicker and his team. At the time, SuperSport were not on the lookout for cheating, despite the shenanigans of the first two Tests.
"No one mentioned anything to me," says Naicker. "The first Test in Durban spiralled out of control in terms of behaviour, then in Port Elizabeth for the second Test, there were still some fireworks going on. We still didn't understand."
Reports written live by ESPNCricinfo suggest the ball began reversing in the first hour after lunch, 35 overs into the South Africa second innings. In the 43rd over, Bancroft was caught in the act.
"The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft and he was shining the ball," says Naicker. "First it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm.
"When he threw the ball on, he put his hand in his pocket. The cameraman - and these are big, big lens cameras - he zoomed into his pocket. The slow-mo operator looked at it, spooled it back and forth, then zoomed in and could see the yellow spot."

- Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed 
  - Published19 hours ago
Bancroft's work on the ball was not shown live, but as a replay later in the over. Inside Newlands, the operator of the big screen – working independently from Naicker – showed the same footage.
"They take a feed from broadcast but they also have to insert their own graphics and commercialisation," says Naicker.
"Between deliveries they tend to stay with live play, then at the end of the over they go to their commercials or whatever in the stadium. It was quite fortunate that when we showed it, it was in between deliveries, not at the end of the over."
Bancroft would later admit he "panicked" when he saw himself on the big screen. Comically, he hid the sandpaper inside his trousers. SuperSport caught that, too.
"When Bancroft looked up at the screen and saw it, he removed it and put it in his jocks," says Naicker. "The cameraman recorded it. It still wasn't live, we played a replay."
Bancroft, with Smith by his side, was challenged by on-field umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong.
The opener turned out his pockets, revealing only a black bag for his sunglasses. The ball was not changed and Australia were not given a run penalty. Play continued, yet SuperSport were on to what had happened.
"Australia coach Darren Lehmann was on the walkie-talkie to 12th man Peter Handscomb, who went on to the field, then the umpires get involved," says Naicker.
"An entire team of cameramen played their part. There was one following the ball, one on Handscomb, one on Lehmann, one on Warner. They all told a story that I happened to put together with this great team of replay operators."
As for Naicker, there was no hesitation in airing what his team had captured, even with the realisation of the magnitude of what was unfolding.
"A lot of people who watch cricket on SuperSport will know we are quite brave in terms of being quite creative and editorially sound," he says.
"It was a natural instinct. It wasn't something I previewed with 10 other people to say 'What do you think, should we show it?' I just went for it."
The footage was pored over by Naicker's team of commentators, while his phone was "WhatsApping off the hook" with messages from around the world, asking him to show it again and again. Replays drew the attention of the third umpire, Englishman Ian Gould.
"He's got comms with me while I'm directing," says Naicker. "There was a moment when he asked me 'I think that's enough now, do you mind not showing it?'
"My response to him was 'I'm quite comfortable in what I'm doing in my job and I think you should do yours'."
When the day's play finally ended, Naicker and his team went to a bar and heard Bancroft and Smith confess in their news conference. Both men and Warner were sent home from the tour and handed lengthy bans. When he returned to Australia, Smith broke down in a tearful address to the press in Sydney.
"It became disheartening for us," says Naicker. "It started becoming emotional to see how they were feeling.
"The most difficult thing for me was to see Steve Smith shedding tears. That was not nice and never the intention. You have to have some emotion for those guys."
1 of 3
There was still a fourth and final Test to complete. Feelings were raw, and SuperSport's access to interviews from Australia was heavily restricted.
Naicker and his team faced allegations of bias, that they were somehow part of an orchestrated plot to take down the Australians. Now, with the Aussies back in town, Naicker maintains he would have pounced on the same "fluke" had it been South Africa caught cheating.
He also highlights the power of television. Bancroft and Australia were exposed mere moments after their act of cheating. TV viewers knew before the on-field match officials.
Naicker points to a conversation he had with Stuart Broad, who also faced tampering accusations for treading on the ball on a tour of South Africa in 2010 and is now building a post-playing career as a pundit.
"When you played the Broad footage in ultra-motion, it looked worse than it was," says Naicker. "He said he never realised how much control and power the TV crew has until he worked in the commentary box.
"I said that's what you have to remind your team-mates. You can't hide any more in international cricket. There are too many cameras and technology around."

When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It's not 15 years from now; it's in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that's not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It's not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn't I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We're not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”

On 10 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised a major protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which protesters claim led to arbitrary voter deletions. In response to the demonstrations, authorities imposed a security crackdown, shutting down dozens of metro stations, cancelling trains, and enforcing prohibitory orders across the capital. Police have detained thousands of individuals, including political figures like Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Mamata Banerjee, as well as CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who were later released.
Against this backdrop, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows protesters at Jantar Mantar demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar, demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video was uploaded on 20 July 2026 and shows an earlier protest demanding Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. It is unrelated to the October 10 CJP protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same video (archive), uploaded to the Facebook page of Samar Moto Vlog on 20 July 2026. According to the post, the video shows a protest at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, demanding the resignation of then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
This indicates that the video is unrelated to the CJP protest held at Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026. Delhi Police also stated that the video was an old one from July 2026 and urged users to refrain from spreading misinformation. We have previously debunked several old and unrelated visuals falsely linked to the October 10 protest.
To sum it up, a video from July 2026 is being falsely shared as footage of the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar.

Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
- Published
US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.
Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.
This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.

Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.
Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.
Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

The Rejinagar and Nandigram by-elections in West Bengal concluded on October 9, Friday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) clinching victory in both seats. BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar won in Rejinagar and Hasirani Rath won the Nandigram seat.
Polling in both the assemblies were, however, marred by allegations of electoral malpractices, with the Congress demanding repolling.
Amid these allegations, digital censorship emerged as another flashpoint, with social media content documenting alleged electoral malpractice and vote rigging being restricted in India. The restrictions also added to concerns over the growing suppression of online criticism of the ruling party. For the past couple of months, Alt News has reported extensively on this social media censorship frenzy in India.
On October 7, the Facebook page of the Murshidabad district wing of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress (@DCCMurshidabad) was restricted under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. The page remains unavailable at the tome of this article being written.
ALSO READ: Bengal bypolls: Facebook restricts local news pages covering Opposition campaign in Rejinagar
On the same day, prominent local news outlet NBTV Bangla’s (@nbtvbngla) Facebook page was also restricted in India for seven days following the same notification. With over five lakh followers, the outlet reported critically on issues of the government or law enforcement in the context of the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls.
Alt News learnt that the two videos uploaded by the Facebook page of NBTV which were restricted in India directly addressed allegations of voting malpractices in the Rejinagar by-election.

Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
- Published
A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early.
Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher.
A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know.
On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief.
"I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC.
The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations.
But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.
That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.
Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".
"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.
For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication.
"I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said.
Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15.
"I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said.
She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her.
She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened".

Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful.
"It's like nothing ever happened," she said.
Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation.
Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings".
He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases.
Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java.
He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest.
Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student.
The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response.
